summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey, Andrew Oldag

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344) in the 1–4 µm range, coupled with DUSTY radiative transfer modeling. The primary objective was to resolve the spatial structure of the innermost circumstellar dust shell, which was previously poorly constrained. The observations were conducted using the pMIRAS high-speed infrared spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope during an immersion event on August 28, 2001. By simultaneous measurement of the Fresnel fringe pattern of the central star and the dust emission, the authors demonstrated that no single-size uniform disk model could fit the data across the entire bandwidth. Through an exploration of over 200 DUSTY radiative transfer models combining the occultation light curves with the spectral energy distribution (SED), the study established a strong constraint on the inner dust temperature at Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K and an optical depth at 5 µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fit models favor a radial density gradient of ρ ∝ r⁻² (or the Ivezić & Elitzur radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow profile) and a carbon-rich dust composition including amorphous carbon, silicon carbide, and graphite. A key finding is that the inner dust shell temperature (950 K) is nearly a factor of two below the expected condensation temperatures, implying a physical inner radius of 3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm (11 mas at 2.25 kpc). The dust mass-loss rate derived from the model is 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr, slightly exceeding the 5.1 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr derived by Groenewegen et al. from the IRAS 60 µm flux. However, the models cannot reproduce the observed IRAS 60 µm flux without assuming either substantial graphite abundance or a significantly higher past mass-loss rate, suggesting non-constant outflow history. The study resolves the stellar photosphere (angular diameter ~3 mas) separately from the inner dust shell, confirming that both are distinct spatial components.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars provides a significant fraction of heavy element abundance and solid particles in the interstellar medium. The mechanisms of mass loss during the AGB phase involve both radiation pressure and stellar pulsation, but specific details are not well understood. Molecular line studies have revealed periodic mass-loss variations appearing as rings in the radial distribution. Very deep imaging of IRC+10216 has detected similar shell-like phenomena in dust. Studying inner regions of circumstellar shells requires angular resolutions well under 1 arcsecond, with dust evaporation radii at 1 kpc corresponding to 20 mas. Until recently, interferometric observations were typically limited to one or two broad bands. A gap exists in simultaneously observing the Fresnel fringe of the central star and the dust emission at multiple wavelengths.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the spatial structure of the innermost dust shell around AFGL 5440 can be resolved using multi-spectral lunar occultation fringes. The authors hypothesize that a single-size uniform disk model will be insufficient to describe the combined emission of the star and the dust shell across 1–4 µm. It is predicted that the dust shell will have a measurable inner radius, a specific radial density gradient, and a temperature that constrains its location. The modeling approach assumes that a carbon-rich dust composition is appropriate for AFGL 5440 and that the DUSTY code can simultaneously fit occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution. The hypothesis is that the best-fit model will converge on a common density gradient and temperature consistent with radiatively driven wind theory.

Methodological Details
The observations of AFGL 5440 were conducted during an immersion occultation on August 28, 2001, at 02:44:00 UT with lunar elevation 36°, position angle 54°, and lunar phase 0.72. Two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), were observed during immersion events to characterize the instrument. Observations covered the 1–4 µm spectral region with a resolving power varying from R ≈ 20 at shortest wavelengths to R ≈ 100 at long wavelengths. The instrument is the pMIRAS high-speed spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope, using a NaCl prism on a 2562 InSb detector. Time resolution is 8 msec with a plate scale of 0.4 arcsec/pixel, giving an effective angular resolution of a couple milli-arcseconds. A typical observation consists of 5000 frames centered on the occultation event, buffered to handle ±10 second timing errors. AFGL 5440 has an estimated distance of 2.25 kpc and luminosity of 1.4 × 10⁴ L⊙. Spectral calibration was performed by fitting the NaCl dispersion function to J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima, accurate to ±0.01 λ. No absolute flux calibration was derived due to non-photometric sky conditions, but relative stellar magnitudes were consistent within ±30%. Comparison star IRC+00233 had predicted blackbody angular size of 3.5 mas (B=11.06, K=1.95) and HD 155292 of 0.6 mas (B=11.0, K=4.9).

Procedures And Architectures
The modeling approach uses the DUSTY radiative transfer code, which computes model source images as a function of wavelength and total spectral energy distribution. Over 200 models were explored, varying dust optical depth while keeping other parameters fixed at each iteration. A carbon-rich dust composition was assumed, consisting of amorphous carbon, silicon carbide, and graphite. The inner dust temperature at the inner radius and the radial density gradient were the primary free parameters varied in DUSTY. The best-fit model selected was the one that simultaneously satisfied both the occultation light curve fits and the spectral energy distribution. Two grain size distributions were tested: the MRN slope (Mathis, Rumpl & Nordsieck 1977) and the KMH shape (Kim, Martin & Hendry 1994). The data reduction involved a cross-correlation algorithm to shift images to a common wavelength/pixel scale, removing spectral tilt. Sky subtraction used a weighted average two pixels wide in the spectral direction with sum-reduction in the spatial direction. Wavelength calibration used the positions of telluric J, H, K, L absorption bands to anchor the dispersion function.

Key Results
A single-size uniform disk model of 11 mas produced fringes too sharp at long wavelengths and too broadened at short wavelengths, ruling out a single-component geometry. The occultation fringes cannot be fitted by any single-size model, confirming the combined star + dust shell structure. The best-fit model yields an inner dust shell temperature of Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. The optical depth at 5 µm is constrained to 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fit density gradient is ρ ∝ r⁻², or the Ivezić & Elitzur radiatively driven hydrodynamic profile. The density gradient of r⁻¹,⁸ produced the IRAS 60 µm flux better but failed the 5–20 µm SED shape. The density gradient of r⁻²,², fitted the SED out to 20 µm and occultation data but gave substantially worse 60 µm flux fits. The physical inner radius of the dust shell is 3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm, or 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. The angular diameter of the central star is approximately 3 mas, based on a photospheric temperature of 2500 K ± 300 K. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr for amorphous carbon optical constants. The gas mass-loss rate is implied to be a few hundred times larger than the dust rate. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC (no graphite) fit the occultation data nearly as well but failed to fit the IRAS 60 µm flux by factors of 3 or more.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The inner dust shell temperature of 950 K is nearly a factor of two below the expected condensation temperatures, indicating the shell is located well interior to the dust-formation zone. The necessity of graphite to fit the 60 µm flux, combined with evidence against graphite in such stars, suggests a non-constant mass-loss history. The discrepancy in the 60 µm flux implies the mass-loss rate was significantly higher approximately 500 to 2000 years ago, corresponding to dust at 1–2 arcseconds from the star. The constraint on the inner edge temperature limits the dust density in the 3–4 µm emission region, defining the spatial profile of the innermost shell. The derived dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr is consistent with Groenewegen et al.'s value of 5.1 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr within the expected uncertainty envelope. The fact that dust cooler than 900 K cannot emit enough 3–4 µm emission provides a physical constraint on the proximity of the dust formation zone to the star.

Contradictions And Limitations
The models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60 µm flux without assuming substantial graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. The 11 mas uniform disk model produced a small fit discrepancy at ~1.7 µm, with no clear explanation attributed to systematic noise or a real photospheric feature. The study did not attempt to extract details of the stellar photosphere or examine all possible dust size/composition models due to wavelength coverage limits. The wavelength coverage is limited to 1–4 µm, and the spectral resolution at shortest wavelengths is only R ≈ 20. A non-photometric sky condition was noted during the occultation, and variable instrumental efficiency from star image placement was uncalibrated. The paper notes that the best-fit temperature is contrary to the inner dust temperature of ~750 K derived by Ivezić & Elitzur (1996).

Claims
The inner dust shell around AFGL 5440 is constrained to Tmax = 950 ± 50 K with an optical depth of 0.5 ± 0.1 at 5 µm, implying a physical inner radius of 11 mas. The DUSTY modeling of over 200 variants converged on 950 K as the best-fit inner temperature. The optical depth at 5 µm was found to be 0.5 ± 0.1 for the best-fit models. The physical inner radius at 2.25 kpc is 3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm, or 11 mas. Ivezić & Elitzur (1996) derived an inner dust shell temperature of ~750 K for a different object, showing a discrepancy in the theoretical range. The blackbody predicted size for the central star is ~3 mas, and the shell must be distinct from this photosphere. This temperature is nearly a factor of two below the expected condensation temperature, suggesting the dust has migrated inwards. The inner radius constrains the spatial extent of the warmest dust emitting in the near-IR.
A radial density gradient of ρ ∝ r⁻² or the Ivezić & Elitzur radiatively driven hydrodynamic profile best describes the dust shell, indicating mass loss driven by radiation pressure. Models with r⁻¹⁸ produced the 60 µm flux but failed the SED shape. Models with r⁻²,² fitted the SED but gave substantially worse 60 µm fits. The best-fit models favored the radiatively driven wind gradient. The IRAS 60 µm flux is not reproduced by the best-fit gradient without extra graphite or a higher past mass-loss rate. The r⁻¹⁸ gradient produced the IRAS 60 µm flux better than the best-fit model. The gradient is consistent with theoretical expectations for radiation-pressure-driven mass loss in AGB stars. The failure to fit the 60 µm flux suggests the outflow is non-constant.

Data And Code Availability
The data reduction process is described in the paper, and the DUSTY radiative transfer code was used for modeling. The pMIRAS instrument is described in Harvey & Wilson (2003). The spectral energy distribution used for fitting was from Guandalini et al. (2006).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Over 200 DUSTY models were explored to test the sensitivity of the fit to varying input parameters. Two grain size distributions (MRN slope and KMH shape) were compared; both produced reasonably good fits. Models without graphite were tested and failed to reproduce the 60 µm flux by factors of 3 or more. A model with temperature lower than 900 K was explicitly tested and could not fit the 3–4 µm emission. Comparison stars IRC+00233 and HD 155292 were used to verify the instrument's resolution limits. A small range of wavelengths around ~1.7 µm showed a less adequate fit for IRC+00233 with no good explanation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for IRC+00233 with a 4.5 mas uniform disk model for a subset of wavelengths. Figure 2 shows χ² and signal-to-noise ratio as a function of wavelength over the entire band for IRC+00233. Figure 3 shows the best-fit uniform disk model for HD 155292 with all sizes less than 3 mas fitting reasonably well. Figure 4 shows a second uniform disk model for HD 155292. Figure 5 shows observed light curves for AFGL 5440 with a quick glance indicating a single size was unlikely to fit. Figure 6 shows a 11 mas uniform disk model fit to AFGL 5440, demonstrating poor fits at short and long wavelengths. Figure 7 shows the best-fit model SED and light curve for AFGL 5440. Figure 8 shows the best-fit model light curves. Figure 9 shows the quality of the fit versus wavelength for the best-fit model. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of the best-fit model. Figures 11 and 12 show the energy distribution and model light curves for a model using only amorphous carbon and SiC (no graphite). Figures 13 and 14 show a third model that fits the energy distribution but gives a poor fit to occultation results due to insufficient warm dust.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first multi-spectral lunar occultation resolution of the innermost dust shell of AFGL 5440, establishing Tmax = 950 ± 50 K and optical depth 0.5 ± 0.1, and confirming a ρ ∝ r⁻² density gradient consistent with radiatively driven wind theory. 2. The strongest evidence is the simultaneous quantitative agreement between the DUSTY-generated model fringes and the 1–4 µm occultation light curves, coupled with a good fit to the observed SED, which a single-size disk could not reproduce. 3. The future path involves explaining the 60 µm flux discrepancy through non-constant mass-loss history, and applying this resolved dust shell methodology to other carbon-rich AGB stars to map mass-loss variability.

summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
summary.authors: Jian Dai
summary.field_subfield: High Energy Physics / QCD and Heavy Ion Collisions
summary.executive_summary: This paper calculates the gluon radiation density of states and energy spectrum from the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in a quark-gluon plasma (QGP), using a semiclassical method. The framework models the QGP as a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism, where the fluid configuration is described by an SU(2) group element field with a velocity field $\omega_\mu = -i/2 \text{Tr}(\sigma_3 U^{\dagger} \partial_\mu U)$ and a conjugate abelian charge current $j_\mu$. The equation of state is approximated by $\epsilon = 3p$, corresponding to a radiation-like EOS with free energy density $F = \beta/4^{3/2} n^{4/3}$. A class of expanding soliton solutions is obtained with $R(t) \approx R_0(t/\tau + 1)^{4/3}$ for $\tau \ll R_0$, enabling the definition of the small parameter $\lambda = \tau/R_0$. By applying the hedgehog ansatz and stereographic projection to the SU(2) group element, a nonabelian current $J_\mu$ is derived, with its spherically symmetric part containing a P6(s) polynomial. In the semiclassical limit, where the effective coupling $g_{\text{eff}}$ is smaller than the partonic coupling $g_YM$, gluon self-interactions are neglected, and the radiation amplitude is expressed as a spacetime Fourier transform of the current. The analytical spatial Fourier transform yields a polynomial in the exponent $Q_4(x) = 5x^2 - 5x^3 + x^4$. Upon substitution of the expanding radius $R(t)$, the temporal integral is parametrized by the dimensionless variable $\eta = \omega\tau/(kR_0)^{3/4}$ and the scaling variable $\kappa = R_0k$. The density of states $n = 4\pi k^2 \sum |M|^2$ scales as $\alpha R_0 \lambda^2 \kappa^{-1/2} |f_M\lambda(\kappa)|^2$, where $\alpha = (2\pi^5/225)(g_{\text{eff}}^2 / \beta^6)$. Numerical results for $\lambda = 1/5, 2/15, 1/15$ show a fast UV fall-off, a smooth intermediate peak, and a long IR tail scaling as $1/\sqrt{k}$. The IR behavior is distinguished from previous work (1/k scaling) because the medium is finite-sized (radius $R_0$) rather than infinitely large. The characteristic frequency $\omega_C = \hat{q}L^2/2$ from jet quenching is significantly larger than the soliton characteristic momentum $1/R_0$, establishing a hierarchical separation between jet-quenching radiation and medium-induced radiation. The work opens avenues for addressing elliptic flow eccentricity either via the nonabelian color current intrinsically or via gluon radiation patterns exogenously.

claims.description: The expansion of a color skyrmion in the QGP generates a gluon radiation spectrum with a characteristic $1/\sqrt{k}$ IR scaling.
There is a hierarchy between jet-quenching radiation ($\omega_C$) and medium-induced soliton radiation ($1/R_0$).

The analytical spatial Fourier transform yields a polynomial in the exponent $Q_4(x) = 5x^2 - 5x^3 + x^4$. The work opens avenues for addressing elliptic flow eccentricity either via the nonabelian color current intrinsically or via gluon radiation patterns exogenously.

Research Context
The QGP is the deconﬁned hot QCD matter formed in relativistic heavy ion collisions. Medium-induced gluon radiation is thoroughly explored in the context of jet quenching and partonic energy loss. All high p⊥ hadronic observables are affected at collider energies, characterizing the hot QCD matter. Gluon radiation is also considered in the initial stage for gluon density saturation and rapid local thermalization. The RHIC fireball evolution is modeled as a relativistic fluid with generalized fluid mechanics for color charge transport. The expanding nature of the fireball generated in RHIC is consistent with expanding skyrmion solutions. The pattern of gluon radiation from the color current of non-static configurations is an important character of the color skyrmion. The medium is characterized by a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is what is the density of states and energy spectrum of gluon radiation from the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in QGP. The semiclassical method is used to compute the radiation spectrum of the nonstatic color configuration. The authors hypothesize that the spectrum will show a fast UV fall-off, a smooth intermediate peak, and a long IR tail. The IR behavior should differ from the 1/k scaling found in infinite medium calculations. The small parameter $\lambda = \tau/R_0$ validates the separation of temporal and spatial scales for the expansion.

Methodological Details
The model is a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism with Lagrangian $L = j^\mu\omega_\mu - F(n) - g_{\text{eff}}J_\mu A^\mu$. The fluid configuration is described by an SU(2) group element $U$ with velocity field $\omega_\mu = -i/2 \text{Tr}(\sigma_3 U^{\dagger} \partial_\mu U)$. The equation of state is $\epsilon = 3p$, which is the ideal fluid radiation limit. The free energy density is $F = \beta/4^{3/4} n^{4/3}$ with $\beta$ a dimensionless integration constant. The invariant length of the current is $n^2 = j^\mu j_\mu$. The nonabelian current $J_\mu$ is related to the abelian current via Eckart factorization $J_\mu = Q_a j_\mu$ with $Q_a = 1/2 \text{Tr}(\sigma_3 U^{\dagger} \sigma_a U)$. The expanding soliton radius follows $R(t) \approx R_0(t/\tau + 1)^{4/3}$ with spatial scale $R_0$ and temporal scale $\tau$. The condition $\tau \ll R_0$ defines the small parameter $\lambda = \tau/R_0$. The hedgehog ansatz is specified for the solution: $U = \cos \phi + i \sigma \cdot \hat{x} \sin \phi$. The coordinate $s = x/R(t)$ is dimensionless, and the stereographic map gives $\sin \phi = 2s/(1+s^2)$. The positive sign in $\cos \phi$ corresponds to skyrmion number +1 (skyrmion), while negative gives −1 (anti-skyrmion). The spherically symmetric part of the current is contained only in the third component with polynomial $P_6(s) = 1 - 7s^2 + 7s^4 - s^6$.

Procedures And Architectures
In the semiclassical limit, the gauge coupling $g_{\text{eff}}$ is assumed much smaller than the partonic coupling $g_YM$. Gluon self-interactions are omitted, allowing treatment with a free parton picture. The lowest order semiclassical amplitude is $iM = g_{\text{eff}} \langle 1 | \int d^4x J_\mu \hat{A}^\	ext{a,}\mu | 0 \rangle$ with gluonic Fock states $|0\rangle, |1\rangle$. The gluon factor is $\langle 1 | \hat{A}^	ext{a,}\mu(x) | 0 \rangle = \phi \epsilon^\mu e^{ik \cdot x} / \sqrt{2\omega}$ with color/helicity parts summed. The spatial Fourier transform of the current is completed analytically, yielding $iM = B(k) \int d\tau e^{-i\omega t} e^{-R(t) k Q_4(R(t)k)}$ where $Q_4(x) = 5x^2 - 5x^3 + x^4$. Substitution of $R(t)$ leads to the temporal integral $iM = B(k) e^{-i\omega\tau} \eta \int_{\omega\tau}^\infty d\eta e^{i\eta t - t^{4/3} Q_4(t^{4/3})}$. On-shell condition $\omega = k$ and scale $\eta = \lambda \kappa^{1/4}$ with $\kappa = R_0k$ are applied. The final reduced integral is $i f_M^\lambda(\kappa) = \int_0^{\kappa^{3/4}} d\eta e^{i\lambda \kappa^{1/4} t - t^{4/3} Q_4(t^{4/3})}$. The density of states is computed as $n = 4\pi k^2 \sum_{c,h} |M|^2$ and the energy spectrum as $dE/dk = dN/dk$. Numerical results are computed for parameter values $\lambda = 1/5, 2/15, 1/15$.

Key Results
The density of states scales as $n = \alpha R_0 \lambda^2 \kappa^{-1/2} |f_M^\lambda(\kappa)|^2$ where $\alpha = (2\pi^5/225)(g_{\text{eff}}^2 / \beta^6)$. The energy spectrum scales as $dE/dk = \alpha \lambda^2 \kappa^{1/2} |f_M^\lambda(\kappa)|^2$ with the same prefactor. Figure 1 shows the numerical results for $\lambda = 1/5, 2/15, 1/15$ with $n$ on the vertical axis vs $k$ in units of $1/R_0$. In the IR limit, the number density scales as $n \sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ in this finite-medium calculation. This contrasts with the 1/k form reported in reference [6] for infinitely large medium size. The IR behavior in this case is softer due to the finite soliton size $R_0$. In the UV, the spectrum shows a fast fall-off, as expected from the rapidly decreasing exponential in the amplitude. A smooth peak dominates the intermediate energy, determined by the competition between expansion and damping. Figure 2 shows $n/(\sqrt{\kappa})$ in small $k$ for $\lambda = 0.2$, verifying the $1/\sqrt{k}$ scaling. The jet-quenching frequency $\omega_C = \hat{q}L^2/2$ with $\hat{q} \approx 0.04 - 0.16 \text{ GeV}^2/	ext{fm}$ is significantly larger than $1/R_0$.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The hierarchical separation between $\omega_C$ and $1/R_0$ implies two distinct radiation regimes: jet quenching from hard parton scattering versus medium radiation from the expanding soliton. The hydrodynamic approach suggests that the nonabelian color current itself could explain elliptic flow eccentricity intrinsically. Alternatively, the gluon radiation patterns from the expanding medium could explain elliptic flow exogenously through particle production. The $1/\sqrt{k}$ vs $1/k$ distinction highlights how finite-medium effects qualitatively alter the IR structure of radiation spectra. The method combines nonabelian fluid mechanics with semiclassical quantum field theory, bridging fluid description and partonic observables. The expansion $R(t) \sim t^{4/3}$ is consistent with the relativistic Bjorken-like expansion of the RHIC fireball.

Contradictions And Limitations
The semiclassical approximation requires $g_{\text{eff}} 	o 0$ compared to $g_YM$, which may not hold at all temperature regimes. The equation of state $\epsilon = 3p$ is only valid at high temperatures and may break down near $T_c$. Only the lowest mode (spherically symmetric part) is considered; higher polarization effects are relegated to future work. The condition $\tau \ll R_0$ is required for the separation of variables, but the exact magnitude of $\tau$ and $R_0$ is not specified. No explicit random seeds or convergence criteria for the numerical integrals are reported. The comparison with jet quenching references assumes a separation of scales that may be blurred in actual finite-sized QGP.

Claims
The expansion of a color skyrmion in the QGP generates a gluon radiation spectrum with a characteristic $1/\sqrt{k}$ IR scaling. The explicit scaling $n = \alpha R_0 \lambda^2 \kappa^{-1/2} |f_M\lambda(\kappa)|^2$ provides the $1/\sqrt{k}$ dependence. Figure 2 confirms $n/(\sqrt{\kappa}) \to \text{constant}$ for small $k$ at $\lambda = 0.2$. The derivation follows from the analytic Fourier transform of the current with $P_6(s)$ polynomial. Reference [6] finds $1/k$ scaling, though the author attributes this to the infinite medium assumption. The softer IR tail may affect how medium radiation is disentangled from jet quenching in experimental observables. The finite-size effect on radiation spectra is a general property of localized color sources.
There is a hierarchy between jet-quenching radiation ($\omega_C$) and medium-induced soliton radiation ($1/R_0$). The estimated $\omega_C$ is $0.04 - 0.16 \text{ GeV}^2/\text{fm}$ with $L$ typically $2 - 10 \text{ fm}$. The characteristic momentum is $1/R_0$, which is the soliton inverse size. The author explicitly states $\omega_C$ is significantly larger than $1/R_0$.  This separation justifies the use of independent theoretical treatments for jet quenching and medium radiation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The parameter $\lambda = \tau/R_0$ is varied at three values: 1/5, 2/15, and 1/15. Figure 1 compares the density of states across these three $\lambda$ values. Figure 2 tests the IR scaling at a fixed $\lambda = 0.2$. Higher polarization modes in the nonabelian current are explicitly excluded.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the density of states $n$ and energy spectrum $dE/dk$ for $\lambda = 1/5$ (Black), 2/15 (Deep Gray), and 1/15 (Light Gray) as a function of $k/R_0$. Figure 2 shows $n/(\sqrt{\kappa})$ in small $k$ for $\lambda = 0.2$, demonstrating the $1/\sqrt{k}$ IR behavior.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the analytical derivation of the gluon radiation spectrum from an expanding nonabelian color skyrmion in the QGP using a semiclassical approach, identifying a $1/\sqrt{k}$ IR behavior. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative comparison with the infinite-medium 1/k scaling and the explicit hierarchical separation between medium radiation and jet-quenching frequency $\omega_C$. 3. The future path is to use this nonabelian color current to explain elliptic flow eccentricity either intrinsically or exogenously via gluon radiation patterns.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study by the STAR Collaboration reports three-particle azimuthal correlation results for charged trigger particles (3 < pT < 4 GeV/c) and two associated particles (1 < pT < 2 GeV/c) in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV/c. The analysis aims to distinguish between hydrodynamic Mach-cone shock waves, large-angle gluon radiation, jet deflection, and Čerenkov radiation as explanations for the observed double-humped away-side structure in two-particle correlations. The three-particle correlation formalism is used to isolate off-diagonal (π ± θ, π ± θ) and on-diagonal (π ± θ, π ∓ θ) peaks: the off-diagonal signals contribute exclusively from conical emission, while the on-diagonal signals include both conical emission and deflected jets. The study finds an off-diagonal structure at approximately π ± 1.45 radians in central Au+Au collisions (0-12% ZDC-triggered), consistent with conical emission. Further discrimination between Mach-cone flow and Čerenkov radiation is achieved by examining the emission angle dependence on associated particle pT; the angle remains consistent with a constant value (1.41 to 1.46 radians) across the measured pT range, favoring the Mach-cone hydrodynamic interpretation over the Čerenkov model, which predicts a sharply decreasing emission angle with increasing momentum. A comprehensive subtraction of combinatorial backgrounds, including hard-soft (jet-background) and soft-soft (flow/minijet) components, is performed, with systematic uncertainties rigorously evaluated against v2 flow measurement methods and normalization window variations.

Research Context
Heavy ion collisions create a medium that may be the quark gluon plasma (QGP), which can be studied through jets and jet-correlations. Jets are useful probes because their properties can be calculated in vacuum with perturbative quantum chromodynamics (pQCD). Two-particle jet-like azimuthal correlations show the away-side in central Au+Au collisions to be broadened with respect to pp and peripheral collisions, or even double-humped. The away-side structure is consistent with multiple mechanisms: large-angle gluon radiation, jets deflected by radial flow, path-length dependent energy loss, hydrodynamic conical flow from Mach-cone shock waves, and Čerenkov radiation. Three-particle correlations can differentiate conical flow and Čerenkov radiation from other mechanisms by isolating emission that is characteristic of conical structures. The associated particle pT dependence of the conical emission angle provides an additional discriminant between hydrodynamic Mach-cone flow and simple Čerenkov radiation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the observed away-side broadening in Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV is due to hydrodynamic Mach-cone emission, deflected jets, or Čerenkov radiation. Three-particle azimuthal correlations with 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c trigger and two 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c associated particles are used to test the conical emission hypothesis. The hypothesis is that a genuine three-particle correlation signal indicating conical emission will appear in central Au+Au collisions but not in pp or d+Au collisions. Mach-cone emission angle is hypothesized to be independent of the associated particle momentum, whereas Čerenkov radiation predicts an emission angle sharply decreasing with increasing associated particle momentum. The off-diagonal signal (π ± θ, π ± θ) is expected to isolate conical emission contributions, while the on-diagonal signal includes additional deflected jet components. The study predicts that the off-diagonal peak position should be consistent with a constant angle regardless of associated particle pT, supporting the Mach-cone interpretation over Čerenkov radiation.

Methodological Details
Data were taken in the STAR time projection chamber for pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV/c. Trigger particles are charged with 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c, and associated particles are charged with 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c. The analysis treats events as composed of two components: particles jet-like correlated with the trigger and background particles. Combinatorial backgrounds must be removed to obtain the genuine 3-particle correlation signal. The hard-soft background is constructed from the 2-particle jet-like correlation, J2, folded with the normalized 2-particle background, Binc^2. The 2-particle background Binc^2 is constructed by mixing events with the flow modulation added in pairwise from the average v2 values measured by reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant methods. For the v4 contribution, the parameterization v4 = 1.15 * v2^2 is used from the data. The background is normalized (with scale factor α) to the signal within 0.8 < |∆φ| < 1.2 (zero yield at 1 radian or ZYA1). The soft-soft background Binc^3 results from correlations between the two associated particles independent of the trigger particle, obtained from mixed events. Trigger flow Binc,T^3 is added in triplet-wise from mixed events where the trigger and associated particles are from different events in the same centrality window. The factor β accounts for non-Poisson multiplicity distributions and is obtained such that the number of associated pairs in the background-subtracted 3-particle signal equals the square of the number of associated particles in the background-subtracted 2-particle signal. The total background is J2 ⊗ αBinc^2 + βα2(Binc^3 + Binc,T^3). Plots are from ZDC-triggered 0-12% Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV/c. Figure 1c and d show the soft-soft background and the hard-soft + trigger flow background respectively.

Procedures And Architectures
The 3-particle correlation analysis method is rigorously described in reference 9. Raw 3-particle azimuthal distribution is plotted in ∆φaT = φa − φT and ∆φbT = φb − φT. The hard-soft background is constructed as J2 ⊗ αBinc^2. The soft-soft background Binc^3 contains all correlations between the two associated particles independent of the trigger, including minijets, other jets, and flow. The trigger flow background Binc,T^3 uses v2 and v4 values obtained in the same way as for the 2-particle background. The number of triplets is determined from the inclusive events. The off-diagonal signal locations are determined from a double Gaussian fit to a strip projected to the off-diagonal. The strip width is 0.7 radians for the projections shown in Figure 4. The ZDC 0-12% points are shifted to the left in Figure 3 for clarity. The emission angles are extracted from double Gaussian fits to the off-diagonal peak structure. A fit to a constant (value 1.46) is applied to the centrality dependence plot in Figure 5. For systematic checks, the normalization window is doubled to 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4.

Key Results
The pp and d+Au results are similar with clearly visible peaks at the near-side (0,0), away-side (π,π), and the cross-terms (0,π) and (π,0). The away-side peak displays diagonal elongation consistent with kT broadening in pp and d+Au. Peripheral Au+Au results show additional on-diagonal elongation of the away-side peak, possibly due to deflected jets. The more central Au+Au collisions display an off-diagonal structure at about π ± 1.45 radians, consistent with conical emission. The off-diagonal signal (circle) in Figure 3 (left) increases with centrality and significantly deviates from zero in central Au+Au collisions. The locations of the off-diagonal signals were found to be 1.45 radians from π from the double Gaussian fit. The ZDC 0-12% data shows an emission angle of 1.41 ± 0.02 radians as indicated in Figure 5. The Au+Au 0-50% minimum bias data shows an emission angle of 1.45 ± 0.02 radians. The emission angle is consistent with remaining constant as a function of associated particle pT, supporting the Mach-cone interpretation. The emission angle is consistent with remaining constant as a function of centrality for mid-central and central Au+Au collisions. The solid line at 1.46 on the Figure 5 centrality plot comes from a fit to a constant. The off-diagonal peak values from fits to a constant are indicated in the legends: 1.46 for Au+Au 0-12% and 1.45 for Au+Au 0-50. The difference between on-diagonal and off-diagonal signals decreases with distance from (π,π), indicating the deflected jet contribution diminishes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observation of off-diagonal peaks consistent with conical emission supports the presence of Mach-cone shock waves in the QGP medium. The angular position of the off-diagonal structure at π ± 1.45 radians provides a direct geometric signature of the conical emission cone angle. The fact that the emission angle is independent of associated particle pT supports the Mach-cone hydrodynamic interpretation over the Čerenkov model. The on-diagonal vs off-diagonal signal comparison shows that deflected jets contribute to the on-diagonal but not the off-diagonal peak, confirming the two-component interpretation of the away-side structure. This result constrains models of energy loss and hadronization in the QGP medium to include conical emission mechanisms.

Contradictions And Limitations
The analysis is limited to a single trigger pT range (3 < pT < 4 GeV/c) and a single associated pT range (1 < pT < 2 GeV/c), limiting applicability to broader kinematics. Systematic uncertainties due to elliptic flow measurement (v2) and normalization are the major sources of error. The v2 measurement uses reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant methods as bounds; the signal is robust but the subtraction is non-trivial. The v4 parameterization v4 = 1.15 v2^2 is fixed from data, and uncertainty in this parameterization contributes to the systematic error. The effect on trigger particle flow from requiring a correlated particle introduces a 20% uncertainty on trigger particle v2. Multiplicity bias effects on the soft-soft background add another systematic uncertainty. The paper presents preliminary results (STAR Preliminary), indicating the full analysis and conclusions may be refined.

Claims
Off-diagonal 3-particle correlation peaks are observed in central Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV/c, indicating conical emission. The off-diagonal signal increases with centrality and significantly deviates from zero in central Au+Au collisions. The peak position is found at 1.45 radians from π from a double Gaussian fit. The ZDC 0-12% data shows an emission angle of 1.41 ± 0.02 radians. The signal is prominent in high statistics 0-12% central data. No such off-diagonal signal is observed in pp or d+Au collisions, which serve as the baseline. The interpretation relies on careful combinatorial background subtraction, where systematics in v2 and normalization must be fully controlled. If confirmed, the result establishes hydrodynamic Mach-cone emission as a viable mechanism for away-side broadening. The specific angle of 1.45 radians provides a measurable quantity for QGP medium characterization.
The conical emission angle is independent of associated particle pT, supporting Mach-cone flow over Čerenkov radiation. Figure 5 (left) shows the angle as a function of associated particle pT, and it is consistent with a constant value. The Čerenkov model predicts an emission angle sharply decreasing with increasing associated particle momentum. No strong pT dependence of the angles on associated particle pT is observed. The 0-12% point (1.41 ± 0.02) and 0-50% point (1.45 ± 0.02) are consistent with each other. The statistical error (±0.02) is comparable to the difference between the two central data points, limiting the precision of the claim. The measurement is limited to the 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c range for associated particles. This result provides a critical discriminant between the hydrodynamic and electrodynamic interpretations of the Mach-cone signature. Future measurements at different pT ranges are needed to fully test the pT-independence claim.
The 3-particle correlation background subtraction procedure is robust against variations in flow parameters and normalization windows. The signal is robust with respect to using reaction plane vs. 4-particle cumulant v2. Doubling the normalization window from 0.8-1.2 to 0.6-1.4 does not change the signal. The hard-soft and trigger flow backgrounds individually vary greatly with v2 but variations cancel to first order. The signal persists across multiple systematic checks. The trigger flow background still has a 20% uncertainty from requiring a correlated particle. The v4 parameterization uncertainty is noted as a remaining systematic. The method establishes a reliable procedure for isolating genuine three-particle correlations in heavy-ion environments. The robustness validates the observed conical signal as not being an artifact of background modeling.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The v2 subtraction was checked using reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant v2 as upper and lower bounds; the signal is robust. The normalization window was doubled to 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4, and the signal was found robust. Figure 6a, b, and c explicitly show these systematic checks. The difference between on-diagonal and off-diagonal signals (Figure 3 right) serves as a self-consistency check for the jet-deflection and conical-emission decomposition. The pT-dependence check on Figure 5 (left) acts as a model-discrimination test. The centrality-dependence check on Figure 5 (right) tests the angular consistency across centralities.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows raw 2-particle correlation (a), raw 3-particle correlation (b), soft-soft background (c), and hard-soft background (d) from ZDC-triggered 0-12% Au+Au collisions at √sNN=200 GeV/c. Figure 2 presents background-subtracted 3-particle correlations for pp, d+Au, Au+Au 50-80%, 30-50%, 10-30%, and 0-12% collisions, showing the four-peak structure. Figure 3 (left) shows centrality dependence of average signal strengths at (0,0), (π,π), (π ± 1.45,π ± 1.45), and (π ± 1.45,π ∓1.45); (right) shows differences between on-diagonal and off-diagonal signals. Figure 4 shows away-side projections of a strip of width 0.7 radians for d+Au and 0-12% ZDC-triggered Au+Au, used to determine the off-diagonal angle. Figure 5 (left) shows the emission angle vs. associated particle pT; (right) shows the angle vs. centrality, both with 1.46 constant-fit line. Figure 6 shows systematic checks: (a) reaction plane v2, (b) 4-particle cumulant v2, and (c) normalization window 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration of an off-diagonal three-particle azimuthal correlation peak at π ± 1.45 ± 0.02 radians in central Au+Au collisions, interpreted as a signature of conical emission in the QGP. 2. The strongest evidence is the pT-independence of the conical emission angle (1.41 ± 0.02 and 1.45 ± 0.02 radians) in central Au+Au, which favors the hydrodynamic Mach-cone interpretation over the Čerenkov radiation model. 3. The future path involves extending the pT coverage of associated particles, measuring the angular dependence at different trigger pT, and confirming the signal in more central or different centrality classes with higher precision.

summary.title: A schematic model of scattering in PT−symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.authors: Miloslav Znojil
summary.field_subfield: Quantum Physics / PT-symmetric Quantum Mechanics and Scattering Theory
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a schematic, Runge-Kutta-discretized model for one-dimensional scattering by a complex PT-symmetric short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), where Z(x) is real and even, and Y(x) is real and odd. The central thesis is that the derivation of reflection and transmission coefficients in the PT-symmetric scattering case proceeds identically to the Hermitian case via a complexification of potential parameters, and that the formal structure of the scattering amplitude relations is invariant. Using a difference-equation representation of the Schrödinger equation obtained via Runge-Kutta discretization on a lattice with step h > 0, the author derives the exact algebraic formulae for coefficients B (reflection) and C (transmission) at an arbitrary energy ϕ. The model is developed incrementally for lattice cuts M = 1, 2, 3, and 4. For M=1, the solution is Hermitian; PT-symmetry enters at M=2. The general solution is formulated as a non-homogeneous (2M−1)-dimensional linear system, reduced via partitioning to a two-scalar relation involving the coefficients α (complex) and β (real), which encode all dynamical input. For M=2, explicit expressions are given for the determinant of the system and the numerator of α; for M=4, the complexity reaches sums of 15 triple-products for the determinant and 32 for the imaginary part of the numerator. The author concludes that the manifest PT-symmetry asymmetry between in and out states is merely formal, and the scattering problem remains tractable via standard linear algebra without matching or recurrence techniques. The methodological innovation is stated as a complexification of potential-characterizing parameters rather than a new mathematical framework, and the work fills a gap in PT-symmetric scattering literature dominated by bound-state and specialized separable-potential studies.

Executive Summary
This paper develops a schematic, Runge-Kutta-discretized model for one-dimensional scattering by a complex PT-symmetric short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), where Z(x) is real and even, and Y(x) is real and odd. The central thesis is that the derivation of reflection and transmission coefficients in the PT-symmetric scattering case proceeds identically to the Hermitian case via a complexification of potential parameters, and that the formal structure of the scattering amplitude relations is invariant. Using a difference-equation representation of the Schrödinger equation obtained via Runge-Kutta discretization on a lattice with step h > 0, the author derives the exact algebraic formulae for coefficients B (reflection) and C (transmission) at an arbitrary energy ϕ. The model is developed incrementally for lattice cuts M = 1, 2, 3, and 4. For M=1, the solution is Hermitian; PT-symmetry enters at M=2. The general solution is formulated as a non-homogeneous (2M−1)-dimensional linear system, reduced via partitioning to a two-scalar relation involving the coefficients α (complex) and β (real), which encode all dynamical input. For M=2, explicit expressions are given for the determinant of the system and the numerator of α; for M=4, the complexity reaches sums of 15 triple-products for the determinant and 32 for the imaginary part of the numerator. The author concludes that the manifest PT-symmetry asymmetry between in and out states is merely formal, and the scattering problem remains tractable via standard linear algebra without matching or recurrence techniques. The methodological innovation is stated as a complexification of potential-characterizing parameters rather than a new mathematical framework, and the work fills a gap in PT-symmetric scattering literature dominated by bound-state and specialized separable-potential studies.

Research Context
The stationary one-dimensional motion of a quantum particle is typically described by the ordinary differential Schrödinger equation in a real potential well. The conventional bound-state and scattering regimes rely on standard boundary conditions with real potentials. Recently, the quantum bound state problem has been generalized to manifestly non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that are quasi-Hermitian. The key ideas incorporate the so-called PT-symmetry of the Hamiltonians as introduced in a 1998 letter by Bender and Boettcher. The physics-inspired concept of PT-symmetry of a Hamiltonian H should be understood as P-pseudo-Hermiticity H† = P H P−1. Current literature abounds in the studies of analytically continued, singular, multidimensional, manybody, relativistic, and supersymmetric PT-symmetric potentials. Among these developments, a comparatively small number of papers has been devoted to the problem of scattering in the PT-symmetric context. Existing scattering work includes separable PT-symmetric potentials of rank one, rectangular or reflectionless barriers, and tobogganic integration contours. A gap exists in the literature for a general, discrete-model-based scattering framework for arbitrary PT-symmetric potentials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a one-dimensional scattering problem admitting a complex PT-symmetric short-range potential can be solved analytically using a discrete Runge-Kutta formulation. The model assumes the potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x) vanishes beyond a certain distance, where Z(−x) = Z(x) is real and Y(−x) = −Y(x) is real. The authors hypothesize that the Runge-Kutta-discretized version of the Schrödinger equation yields exact formulae for reflection and transmission coefficients in both Hermitian and PT-symmetric cases. The key hypothesis is that the only innovation emerges via a complexification of one of the potential-characterizing parameters, preserving the formal structure of the results. The work predicts that PT-symmetry introduces a manifest asymmetry between in and out states, yet the problem remains tractable by standard non-matching and non-recurrent techniques of linear algebra. The method aims to show that in both contexts, the definition of the transmission and reflection coefficients has the same form. The work intends to serve as another attempt to fill the gap in the scattering literature for PT-symmetric quantum mechanics.

Methodological Details
The model is defined in one dimension with a short-range potential V(x) that vanishes beyond a cutoff distance, represented by the integer M. The ordinary differential Schrödinger equation is replaced by its Runge-Kutta-discretized difference-equation representation. The discrete equation takes the form −ψ(xk−1) − 2ψ(xk) + ψ(xk+1) over h² plus V(xk)ψ(xk) equals Eψ(xk). The lattice points are defined as xk = kh with h > 0 and k = 0, ±1, ... . The energy variable is redefined as 2cos ϕ = 2 − h²E, imposing the constraint E ∈ (0, 4/h²). The discrete boundary conditions require ψ(xm) = Aei mϕ + Be−imϕ for m ≤ −(M−1) and Cei mϕ for m ≥ M−1, with conventional choice A = 1. For the M = 1 model, the difference equation degenerates to three nontrivial relations, providing the first non-Hermitian toy problem when Z0 is real. For M = 2, the potential includes Z(−1) −iY(−1) and Z(0), with Y(−1) = −Y(1) introducing the PT-symmetric imaginary part. The matching method of solution requires imposing consistency across the potential region such that ψ0, ψ(−)₀, and ψ(+)₀ represent the same quantity. The matrix-inversion method reformulates the difference equation as a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations. The system is reduced to a finite-dimensional (2M−1)-dimensional square matrix T, which, when non-singular, yields the inverse R = T−1. Partitioning the matrix R reveals that only the corners α*, β, u, v, β, α carry information, while the central submatrix Q and row vectors tᵀ, wᵀ are redundant. The final scattering formulae are expressed in terms of the complex coefficient α and real coefficient β, which are rational functions of 2M−1 real coupling constants. The two parameters h (lattice step) and 1/M (cutoff) may be chosen and varied independently to achieve quickest convergence. The connection between the discrete energy spectrum and relativistic systems is referenced through explicit higher O(h⁴) corrections.

Procedures And Architectures
The potential is defined as V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x) with PT-symmetry: Z(−x) = Z(x) and Y(−x) = −Y(x). The Runge-Kutta discretization replaces the second derivative with a centered difference on a lattice with step h. The energy parameter is transformed to the angular variable ϕ via 2cos ϕ = 2 − h²E, mapping the physical energy to a compact interval. The potential is assumed to vanish for |k| ≥ M, yielding VK = 0 beyond this cutoff. The matching procedure involves inserting boundary condition forms into the discrete equations and equating intermediate wavefunction values at interface points. For M = 2, decomposition ψ(0)₀ = ξ(0) + χ(0) is used to eliminate the unconstrained interior values. The doubly infinite system is reduced to a finite (2M−1)-dimensional tridiagonal non-square matrix problem. Matrix partitioning isolates the 2 × 2 corner sub-blocks, yielding two scalar linear equations for the boundary coefficients. The system is solved algebraically: B = −e−2iMϕ + Cβ(e−iϕ −α) and C = 2iβe−2iMϕ sin ϕ / [β² −(e−iϕ −α*)(e−iϕ −α)]. The coefficients α and β are rational functions of 2M−1 couplings Z_0, ..., Z_{M-1} and Y_1, ..., Y_{M-1}. β is identified as 1/det T, and α has the same denominator. For higher M, symbolic manipulations on a computer are required due to explosive growth in formula complexity. The method of solution for M=4 shows the determinant involves 15 triple-product terms and the imaginary numerator involves 32 triple-products.

Key Results
For M = 1, with real Z0, the solution C = 2i sin ϕ / (2i sin ϕ − Z0) and B = Z0 / (2i sin ϕ − Z0) recovers the Hermitian scattering result. For M = 2, the PT-symmetric potential introduces the complex numerator for C and B, with det T = Z0 Z1 / (2 − 2Z1 + Y1²Z0). The real part of the numerator γ for M = 2 is given by Z0 Z1 − 1 and the imaginary part by −Z0 Y1. For M = 3, the determinant det T involves products of six couplings Z0, Z1, Z2 with one Y₁² term, and 2Z₂² terms. For M = 4, the determinant T grows to sums of 15 and 14 products of couplings, respectively. The imaginary part of γ for M = 4 is represented by sums of 32 products of couplings. In the weak coupling regime for M = 4, det T simplifies to two linear terms −2Z₃ − 2Z₁ plus 10 triple-product terms. The real part of γ for M = 4 admits a decomposition starting with −1 + 2Z₂Z₃ + Z₀Z₁ + Z₀Z₃ + 2Z₂Z₁. The imaginary part of γ for M = 4 starts with −2Z₂Y₃ + 2Y₂Z₁ − Z₀Y₁ − Z₀Y₃. The discrete energy constraint E ∈ (0, 4/h²) imposes an upper bound on physical energy corresponding to the lattice topology. The formal structure of scattering formulae in the PT-symmetric case is identical to the Hermitian case, differing only in the dynamical input functions α and β.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The invariance of the scattering amplitude form between Hermitian and PT-symmetric cases implies that PT-symmetry enters only through the potential parameters. The coefficients α and β encapsulate all dynamical input, with β equal to the inverse of the system determinant. The PT-symmetric asymmetry between in and out states is revealed to be merely formal, not hindering solvability via linear algebra. The close formal parallelism between Runge-Kutta-approximated Hermitian and non-Hermitian scattering suggests a unified discrete formulation. The work suggests that PT-symmetry does not require non-matching or recurrent techniques; standard matrix inversion suffices. The discrete model extends to non-Hermitian versions of the inverse scattering problem as a natural further application.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model is schematic and analytical, not verified by numerical data, which limits assessment of convergence for large M. The O(h⁴) discrepancy between the difference and differential operators is acknowledged; convergence in the h→0 limit is purely numerical. The energy constraint E ∈ (0, 4/h²) restricts the physical range of solvable energies, an artifact of discretization. The growth of algebraic complexity at M=4 suggests that closed-form expressions become impractical for large potentials. The paper does not report convergence rates for h or M, making the statement on quickest convergence heuristic rather than quantitative.

Claims
The Runge-Kutta-discretized difference-equation formulation of the Schrödinger equation yields exact algebraic formulae for scattering in PT-symmetric potentials, with the only innovation being the complexification of a potential parameter. The authors derive formulae for reflection and transmission coefficients using the discrete Schrödinger equation. The explicit matrix inversion yields a two-scalar relation for B and C identical in form to the Hermitian case. The PT-symmetric case is obtained simply by inserting Zk + iYk into the same matrix structure. The O(h⁴) discrepancy between difference and differential representations introduces an error that vanishes only in the h→0 limit. PT-symmetric scattering can be treated by standard linear algebra without specialized non-Hermitian methods. The formal structure of the scattering theory is robust to the Hermitian-to-non-Hermitian transition.
The PT-symmetry asymmetry between incoming and outgoing states is a formal property that does not fundamentally change the solvability of the scattering problem. The problem remains tractable by standard non-matching and non-recurrent techniques of linear algebra. The reduction to a two-dimensional matrix inversion demonstrates the solvability. summary.authors: B.F.L. Ward and S.A. Yost

summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a theoretical framework for the simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and multiple photon radiative effects in LHC physics processes, formulated as QED⊗QCD exponentiation. The authors extend the Yakovlev-Fadin-Shipakov (YFS) resummation theory from QCD to a combined QED⊗QCD framework, based on an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series rather than an approximate eikonal expansion. Executive Summary
This paper presents a theoretical framework for the simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and multiple photon radiative effects in LHC physics processes, formulated as QED⊗QCD exponentiation. The authors extend the Yakovlev-Fadin-Shipakov (YFS) resummation theory from QCD to a combined QED⊗QCD framework, based on an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series rather than an approximate eikonal expansion. The theory is applied to single heavy gauge boson production at hadron colliders (W± and Z bosons) to demonstrate its practical application. A central result is that QED contributions at the threshold region of heavy gauge boson production reach the ~0.3% level, making them necessary for the desired 0.67% theoretical precision tag on LHC luminosity processes. The paper also addresses shower/matrix element matching, proposing two approaches for combining the exact YFS-style resummation calculus with HERWIG and PYTHIA: a simple pT-cutoff matching and a more sophisticated shower-subtracted residual approach. The authors validate their semi-analytical results against existing literature, finding agreement on the magnitudes of both QED and QCD effects. The theoretical basis is established for full MC event generator realization at O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) to support precision LHC physics.

Research Context
The experimental luminosity precision tag at the LHC is expected at the 2% level. This requires a theoretical precision tag of 0.67% for single W, Z production with lepton decay. The requirement for ~1.0% theoretical precision dictates that multiple gluon and photon radiative effects must be controlled. Previous work on structure function evolution showed QED contributions at the ~0.3% level, almost half the error budget. Similar size effects are expected from the threshold region of heavy gauge boson production. The starting point is the QCD resummation theory presented in Ref. [3], an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series. The resummation is based on the N = 1 term in the exponent in the formal proof of exponentiation in non-Abelian gauge theories in the eikonal approximation. The exponential is augmented with a sum of residuals that account for remaining contributions exactly to all orders in αs. Alternative theories including SCET treat double resummation of soft and collinear effects.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can the QCD resummation theory be extended to include simultaneous QED exponentiation for LHC physics? The paper hypothesizes that the combined QED⊗QCD theory allows simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and multiple photon effects without double-counting. It is predicted that QED effects at the threshold region will be comparable in size to structure function results (~0.3%). The theory is expected to be applicable to MC methods on an event-by-event basis in the presence of parton showers. The matching procedure should systematically improve accuracy order-by-order in both αs and α without double-counting. The exactness of the resummation is expected to maintain contributions to all orders in αs, distinguishing it from approximate eikonal treatments.

Methodological Details
The application is to parton-level single heavy boson production: q + ¯q′ → V + n(g) + X → ¯ℓℓ′ + n(g) + X with V = W±, Z. The lepton combinations are ℓ = e, µ and ℓ′ = νe, νµ for W+; ℓ = νe, νµ and ℓ′ = e, µ for W−. The cross section is expressed in an exact exponential form with residuals free of infrared divergences to all orders in αs(Q). Semi-analytical methods with structure functions from Ref. [23] are used to examine the size of QED⊗QCD threshold corrections. The Monte Carlo realization is indicated to appear elsewhere in a separate publication. The structure functions are at the factorization scale µ, which represents the largest pT of the gluon emission included. The calculation uses the standard Les Houches procedure for showering the event. The parton-level Born cross section is the baseline for the ratio rexp = σexp/σBorn. Riemann’s zeta function of argument 2 (π²/6) and Euler’s constant (0.5772...) are used in the explicit formulas. The theoretical basis is stated to support complete O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) results for FNAL, LHC, RHIC, and ILC.

Procedures And Architectures
The QCD cross section formula is established with gluon residuals ˜¯βn free of infrared divergences. The QED⊗QCD theory is obtained by simultaneously exponentiating large IR terms in QCD and exact IR divergent terms in QED. The new YFS residuals ˜¯βn,m represent successive application of the YFS expansion first for QCD and subsequently for QED. Functions SUMIR(QCED) and DQCED are determined from QCD analogs via substitutions of Bnls, ˜Bnls, and ˜Snls with their QED counterparts. The exponent γQCED contains terms for both QED and QCD couplings scaled by the big logarithm Lnls. For shower matching, two approaches are proposed: pT-cutoff matching and shower-subtracted residual matching. In the pT-matching approach, the factorization scale µ limits the pT of gluon radiation to avoid double-counting. In the shower-subtracted approach, residuals are expanded order-by-order and matched against the shower formula’s perturbative expansion. The DGLAP evolution of structure functions factorizes all terms involving powers of the big log Lc = ln(µ²/m²_q). The final result is stated to be independent of the mass regulator (either m_q or dimensional regularization) as a cross-check.

Key Results
The QED⊗QCD exponent γQCED is computed as γQCED = (2Q²/απ + 2CF/αsπ) Lnls. The ratio rexp = σexp/σBorn at the LHC with QED⊗QCD (QCD+QED) is 1.1901. The ratio rexp at the LHC with QCD only is 1.1872. The ratio rexp at the Tevatron with QED⊗QCD is 1.1911. The ratio rexp at the Tevatron with QCD only is 1.1879. The QED effect is found to be at the 0.3% level at both LHC and FNAL. The results are stable under scale variations. The QED effect is similar in size to structure function results in Refs. [9–13]. The QCD dominant corrections happen an order of magnitude earlier than QED corrections, implied by the average Bjorken x values. The leading ˜¯β0,0-level gives already a good estimate of the interplay between higher order QED and QCD effects.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The QED effect at 0.3% is needed for LHC theory predictions at the ≤1% level. The resummation is valid over the entire phase space, unlike threshold resummation techniques limited to specific kinematic regions. The approach avoids the unnecessary averaging of the gluon azimuthal angular distribution relative to its parent’s momentum direction. The exactness of the resummation distinguishes it from approximate eikonal treatments and allows for systematic improvement without double-counting. The framework provides a theoretical basis for complete O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) results across FNAL, LHC, RHIC, and ILC physics. The YFS theory extended to non-Abelian gauge theory enables simultaneous exponentiation of QED and QCD.

Contradictions And Limitations
The full MC event generator realization is indicated to appear elsewhere, meaning the complete implementation is not contained in this paper. The analysis of W production is stated to be in progress and is not fully reported here. The exactness of the result is noted to cause confusion because it does not explicitly show an ordered exponential operator. The paper uses a semi-analytical approach; a Monte Carlo realization is not presented in detail here. The shower-subtracted residuals are stated to be under investigation and not fully finalized. The paper acknowledges that the exactness depends on the N=1 term in the exponent, with higher N terms that could be included but are not.

Claims
QED effects at the ~0.3% level are necessary for the 0.67% theoretical precision tag on LHC luminosity processes. The ratio rexp at LHC with QED⊗QCD is 1.1901 versus 1.1872 with QCD only, giving a 0.3% difference. The QED effect at the LHC and Tevatron is consistently at the 0.3% level. QED contributions in structure function evolution lead to effects at the ~0.3% level. The required theoretical precision is 0.67%, which is more than twice the 0.3% QED effect, suggesting QED alone is insufficient. The paper notes the need to take into account all effects to reach ~1.0% for the theoretical precision tag. Full QED⊗QCD resummation is mandatory for precision LHC luminosity determinations. Semi-analytical agreement with literature on Z production validates the magnitude.
The QED⊗QCD resummation provides an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series without double-counting, valid over the entire phase space. The theory is an exact rearrangement based on the N=1 term in the formal proof of exponentiation. It is valid over the entire phase space, unlike threshold resummation techniques. The residuals are free of all infrared singularities to all orders. The paper admits that higher N terms in the exponent could be included but are not. The exactness has caused confusion because no ordered exponential is explicitly shown. This allows systematic improvement order-by-order in both αs and α without double-counting. It enables contact with parton shower MCs without unnecessary averaging of azimuthal distributions.
Two approaches for shower/ME matching are viable, with shower-subtracted residuals offering superior accuracy. The pT-cutoff approach uses the factorization scale µ to limit gluon radiation. The shower-subtracted residuals are expanded order-by-order and matched against the shower perturbative expansion. Shower-subtracted residuals have been realized for the O(α) luminosity Bhabha process at DAPHNE. Both approaches are under investigation; neither is presented as fully validated in this paper. The shower-subtracted residual approach is stated to be in progress. The accuracy of the cross section should in principle be improved with shower-subtracted residuals.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The results are stated to be stable under scale variations. The final cross section should be independent of the mass regulator (m_q vs dimensional regularization), providing a cross-check. The QED effect is found to be stable under scale variations.

Key Figures Tables
Equation (1) presents the exact exponential form of the QCD cross section with gluon residuals. Equation (2) gives the QED⊗QCD exponential form with joint residuals ˜¯βn,m. Equation (3) defines the QED⊗QCD functions via substitutions of the QCD analogs. Equation (4) provides the standard formula combining the parton-level exponentiated cross section with structure functions. Equation (5) shows the ˜¯β0,0-level result for the exponentiated cross section. Equation (6) gives the explicit formula for the QED⊗QCD exponent. Equation (8) tables the numerical values of rexp for both LHC and Tevatron with QED⊗QCD and QCD only.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the extension of the YFS resummation theory to a QED⊗QCD framework that simultaneously exponentiates both QED and QCD IR effects without double-counting. 2. The strongest evidence is the numerical result that QED corrections at the threshold region reach ~0.3%, matching structure function predictions and confirming they are necessary for sub-1% LHC physics. 3. The future path includes full MC event generator realization at O(α²_s, αα_s, α²) for W production, FNAL, LHC, RHIC, and ILC, with shower-subtracted residuals under investigation.

summary.title: ON GENERALIZED ENTROPY MEASURES AND PATHWAYS
summary.authors: A.M. Mathai and H.J. Haubold
summary.field_subfield: Mathematical Statistics / Information Theory
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical/Mathematical research paper introducing generalized entropy measures and their applications to pathway models.
summary.executive_summary: This paper examines the product probability property (PPP), also known as statistical independence, as the foundational concept for entropy definitions, and demonstrates that the recursivity postulate automatically determines the logarithmic functional form of Shannon entropy. The authors argue that Shannon entropy's additivity is a direct consequence of its logarithmic form rather than the PPP itself, and that non-additivity is a natural process even under product probability conditions. Several generalized entropies of order α—including Rényi, Havrda-Charvát, Tsallis, and Mathai's own generalized and additive forms—are introduced, all converging to Shannon entropy as α approaches 1. The central result extends the Maximum Entropy Principle to the continuous case, showing that maximizing Mathai entropy under various moment constraints yields Mathai's pathway model, which generalizes a wide class of distributions: power laws, exponential and stretched exponential forms, type-1 and type-2 beta distributions, Weibull, Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, and the Wigner atomic moment distribution. Furthermore, the paper establishes a connection between Mathai's entropy and Kerridge's measure of inaccuracy and derives differential equations satisfied by the pathway model functional, including the power-law equation from Tsallis statistics. A trivariate extension shows how non-extensivity propagates to multivariate joint distributions under the PPP.

claims.description: The recursivity postulate is the defining feature that determines the logarithmic functional form of Shannon entropy.
Mathai's entropy, under the Maximum Entropy Principle with moment constraints, yields the pathway model which unifies power laws, exponentials, and various standard distributions.
Mathai's entropy can be interpreted as a directed divergence or inaccuracy measure analogous to Kerridge's inaccuracy.
