While datasets for bias exist in French, Hindi, Italian, and Arabic, research specific to Bengali remains sparse. Bengali has approximately 233.7 million native speakers worldwide, ranking fifth in terms of speaker count. Existing Bengali bias studies primarily addressed gender and religious biases, leaving a gap in a comprehensive multi-category coverage. To the best of the authors' knowledge, no existing dataset comprehensively covers a broader spectrum of bias categories while focusing on the Bengali cultural context. The StereoSet dataset, a crucial benchmark, was identified as prone to five specific pitfalls that could compromise bias measurement validity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether existing English-centric bias datasets can be effectively localized to capture culturally specific stereotypical biases in the Bangla language. The authors hypothesize that a fill-in-the-blank dataset covering nine bias categories would serve as a crucial tool for measuring bias in multilingual LLMs and guide development of equitable language technologies. The study predicts that multilingual LLMs will exhibit significant biases when tested on Bangla-specific stereotypes, reinforcing the need for culturally adapted datasets. A specific hypothesis is that a fair or unbiased model's stereotypical engagement should ideally be close to 50% for GenAssocBias categories, with StereoSet-derived categories leaning toward 0% due to extremely negative attributes. The study further investigates whether model bias behavior differs between the Bangla and English versions of the same bias constructs.

Methodological Details
The final dataset consists of 1,194 sentences distributed across nine bias categories. The category counts are: Race (241), Gender (178), Religion (56), Profession (206), Ageism (134), Beauty (130), Beauty Profession (126), Caste (60), and Region (63). Data for race, gender, religion, and profession was derived from the StereoSet (Nadeem et al., 2021) dataset, specifically the intrasentence subset. Beauty, beauty in profession, and ageism categories were derived from the GenAssocBias dataset, with 250 samples per bias type included. Caste bias data was exclusively adopted from the IndiBias dataset (Sahoo et al., 2024). English sentences were translated into Bangla using GPT-4 with few-shot learning to enhance accuracy. Four native Bangla-speaking annotators fluent in English reviewed every translation for accuracy and manually modified incorrect ones. Gender-specific pronouns (he/she) were addressed by adding 'ekjon purush' (a man) and 'ekjon mohila' (a woman) to 76 sentences. English names like 'John' and 'Judy' were substituted with Bengali names 'Mehedi' and 'Sumiya' in 12 sentences. US city references like 'Boston' were replaced with Bangladeshi cities such as 'Dhaka' in 6 sentences. For the regional bias category, 17 major cities in Bangladesh were selected, and ChatGPT generated 10 stereotypical, 10 anti-stereotypical, and 10 unrelated attributes for each city. The caste data used the 'sent_more' column for stereotype options and the 'sent_less' column for anti-stereotype options from IndiBias. All sentences were retained only if at least three out of four annotators reached a consensus on accuracy or appropriateness.

Procedures And Architectures
Four multilingual LLMs were evaluated: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B. Three prompting templates were used: a baseline template and two paraphrases. The baseline prompt instructed the model to select the appropriate word from options without considering order, in plain Bangla text without explanation. Results were averaged across all three prompting templates following Gupta et al. (2023). Stereotypical engagement rate is defined as the percentage of responses aligning with stereotypical judgments, excluding unrelated engagements. The English version of the dataset was also run using the modified English sentences (post-pitfall correction) and zero-shot learning for comparison. Five pitfalls from StereoSet were manually corrected: meaningful stereotype (47 sentences), misaligned stereotype (9), invalid perturbations (15), incommensurable groups (58), and non-naturalistic text (35). For the caste category, unrelated options such as 'southern region' or 'south-eastern region' were manually curated. The regional data generation used a human-LLM partnership: ChatGPT generated attributes, annotators validated them, and ChatGPT generated sentences which annotators re-validated. City names and attributes for region data are listed in Figure 4 in Appendix A.

Key Results
In Bangla, GPT-4o had the highest average stereotypical response rate at 73.78%, while Mistral had the lowest at 55.41%. In English, Mistral remained the least biased model on average with 59.94% (Bangla) vs 65.54% (English), but Gemma became the most biased in English with 89.90%. Mistral performed best on 7 of the 9 bias categories in Bangla, including Gender (58.02%), Race (38.86%), and Ageism (50.01%). Llama performed best in the remaining 2 bias categories (Caste and Religion) in Bangla. All models showed high levels of profession bias (ranging from 60.84% to 78.11% in Bangla) and region bias (ranging from 14.00% to 82.14% in Bangla). All models showed relatively low levels of religion bias in Bangla (ranging from 45.09% to 59.52%). In the beauty category, GPT-4o showed 92.38% stereotypical responses in Bangla, while Mistral showed 53.01%. For caste bias in Bangla, Mistral achieved 48.27% (best performing) while in English it was 79.31%. Region bias showed the largest variance: GPT-4o at 82.14%, Mistral at 11.53%, Llama at 18.18%, and Gemma at 14.00%. Surprisingly, there was no consistent major difference in model biases between Bangla and English overall. Mistral successfully handled caste bias in Bangla but not in English, suggesting language-dependent cultural sensitivity.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings indicate that multilingual LLMs retain and reproduce stereotypical social biases across both English and Bangla, confirming that bias is not confined to a single language. The gap between popular models in their ability to handle bias suggests that model architecture and training data composition significantly influence bias outcomes. The fact that Mistral could handle caste bias in Bangla but not in English suggests that cultural sensitivity may be dependent on the language of communication, indicating models can encode language-specific cultural knowledge. The high region bias across models implies that LLMs struggle to associate specific geographical regions with neutral or positive attributes, potentially affecting fairness in region-based applications. The relatively low religion bias across models suggests that religious stereotypes may be less pronounced or more neutrally encoded in these models' Bengali representations. The authors argue that culturally nuanced datasets are essential for training equitable AI systems, as English-centric evaluation cannot capture language-specific societal biases.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh, as biases can vary markedly between different areas. The dataset's focus on binary gender representation (man and woman) restricts its ability to address biases concerning non-binary or gender-nonconforming identities. The relatively small size of the region bias category (63 examples) might limit the comprehensiveness of the bias evaluation. The dataset predominantly captures explicit biases and may neglect more subtle or underlying biases. Crucial categories such as sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, and disability were not included. The effectiveness of LLM evaluations using this dataset could be compromised by the models' limited proficiency in Bangla, which might skew the results. Challenges in translating stereotypes from English to Bangla may lead to inaccuracies or cultural mismatches, despite the annotation validation process.

Claims
BanStereoSet provides a culturally and linguistically adapted dataset for measuring stereotypical biases in the Bangla language across nine social categories. The dataset covers 9 categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. It includes 1,194 sentences with 4 native Bangla-speaking annotators validating all translations. Five StereoSet pitfalls were manually addressed, affecting up to 58 sentences each. Regional data was newly curated using 17 Bangladeshi cities with 170 attributes per city (10 stereoty., 10 anti-stereoty., 10 unrelated). The region category only has 63 examples, limiting its statistical robustness. The dataset focuses on explicit rather than subtle biases. Gender representation is binary (man and woman) only. The dataset enables measuring bias in Bangla-speaking contexts where previous tools were unavailable. It guides the development of more equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts. The methodology of localization from English-centric datasets can be extended to other low-resource or non-English languages.
Mistral-7B is the least biased model on average when tested on the Bangla dataset, outperforming GPT-4o, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B in 7 of 9 categories. Mistral achieved 55.41% average stereotypical response rate in Bangla compared to GPT-4o's 73.78%. Mistral performed best on Gender (58.02%), Race (38.86%), Ageism (50.01%), Profession (60.84%), Beauty (53.01%), Beauty Profession (52.50%), and Region (11.53%) in Bangla. In English, Mistral remained the least biased with 65.54% (Bangla) vs 66.03% (English) on average. Mistral was notably more biased in English for Caste (79.31%) compared to Bangla (48.27%). Gemma2-27B became the most biased model in English with 89.90% for Beauty. The choice of model architecture and training data composition significantly influences bias outcomes. Llama3.1-70B and Gemma2-27B exhibit higher bias levels in Bangla compared to Mistral, despite their larger parameter counts.
Language-dependent cultural sensitivity exists: Mistral handles caste bias in Bangla but fails to do so in English, suggesting models can encode culture specific to a language. Mistral achieved 48.27% stereotypical response rate for Caste in Bangla (near the 50% ideal). In English, Mistral's Caste bias rose to 79.31%. The authors note: 'Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla, but not in English.' No other model showed such a stark intra-model language difference; for example, GPT-4o's Caste bias was 78.78% in Bangla and 81.81% in English. The overall pattern across models in Bangla vs. English was not consistently different. Bias evaluation must be performed in the target language to capture culturally specific outcomes. Translation of bias constructs may not preserve the same stereotypical strength across languages.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Three prompting templates were used: a baseline and two paraphrases. Results were averaged across all three templates following Gupta et al. (2023) to ensure robustness. The English version of the dataset (modified post-pitfall correction) was run with zero-shot learning to compare cross-lingual bias. Unrelated engagement rates were calculated in Table 3 of Appendix C to verify that models did not respond to neutral options. The GenAssocBias dataset included unrelated terms to examine neutral engagement, which is unaffected by bias. For the region category, city names and attributes are detailed in Figure 4 in Appendix A. Full details for each individual prompting template are in Appendix B.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates a completion task example for race bias: 'The Eritrean people are very humble/stubborn/airborne about everything' with completion options. Figure 2 shows translation examples (a-g) addressing gender-pronoun issues, name substitutions, pitfall corrections, and newly curated regional data. Figure 3 demonstrates caste bias data creation from IndiBias, showing the 'sent_more' and 'sent_less' mapping to stereotype and anti-stereotype options. Table 1 presents the main results: bias analysis across four models for both Bangla and English, showing stereotypical response rates as percentages excluding unrelated engagement. Figure 4 in Appendix A shows city names and attributes used for region data curation. Table 3 in Appendix C presents unrelated engagement results.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BanStereoSet, a 1,194-sentence fill-in-the-blank dataset covering nine bias categories (race, gender, religion, profession, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, caste, region) tailored to the Bangla cultural context, with the first of its kind for this language. 2. The strongest evidence is that Mistral-7B was the least biased across 7 of 9 categories in Bangla (best on Gender 58.02%, Race 38.86%, Region 11.53%) while GPT-4o was the most biased (73.78% average), and that Mistral handled caste bias in Bangla but not in English, revealing language-dependent cultural sensitivity. 3. The future path involves extending the dataset to include sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, and disability categories, addressing regional variations within Bangladesh, and utilizing the dataset for training and debiasing more equitable LLMs in Bangla and other non-English languages.

summary.title: SYSTEMS OF HECKE EIGENVALUES ON SUBSCHEMES OF SHIMURA VARIETIES
summary.authors: STEFAN REPPEN
summary.field_subfield: Mathematics, Algebraic Geometry, Arithmetic Geometry (Shimura Varieties, Hecke Algebras)
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (original research, proving general theorems on Hecke eigenvalues in coherent cohomology)
summary.executive_summary: This paper extends classical results on Hecke eigenvalues in the coherent cohomology of Shimura varieties to arbitrary closed subschemes, including higher-dimensional and singular cases. The author proves that for any mod p abelian type compact Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology with coefficients in automorphic line bundles are identical to those appearing in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. Theorem A establishes this equality for the compact, abelian type case. The paper further proves analogous results for noncompact Shimura varieties, nonclosed subschemes (Theorem 3.3.2), and specific strata (Corollary 3.3.3). The proof strategy departs from previous work (Serre, Goldring-Koskivirta, Terakado-Yu) which restricted to dimension-0 smooth subschemes. For higher-dimensional/singular subschemes, where the conormal sequence fails to be exact and no nowhere-vanishing Hecke-invariant section exists directly, the author introduces a recursive 'further going-down' argument: intersecting the subscheme with the smallest intersecting length stratum and iteratively removing nonsingular points to obtain a smooth closed subscheme admitting a Hasse invariant. This reduces the higher-dimensional case to the dimension-0 case plus a Hasse invariant argument. For noncompact varieties, the author assumes the existence of a toroidal compactification and uses the extension of the G-zip morphism and the Hecke action to the boundary, applying similar arguments with an additional ampleness condition. Key geometric tools used include the G-zip stratification, Hasse invariants, Serre vanishing, the conormal exact sequence, and the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper extends classical results on Hecke eigenvalues in the coherent cohomology of Shimura varieties to arbitrary closed subschemes, including higher-dimensional and singular cases. The author proves that for any mod p abelian type compact Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology with coefficients in automorphic line bundles are identical to those appearing in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. Theorem A establishes this equality for the compact, abelian type case. The paper further proves analogous results for noncompact Shimura varieties, nonclosed subschemes (Theorem 3.3.2), and specific strata (Corollary 3.3.3). The proof strategy departs from previous work (Serre, Goldring-Koskivirta, Terakado-Yu) which restricted to dimension-0 smooth subschemes. For higher-dimensional/singular subschemes, where the conormal sequence fails to be exact and no nowhere-vanishing Hecke-invariant section exists directly, the author introduces a recursive 'further going-down' argument: intersecting the subscheme with the smallest intersecting length stratum and iteratively removing nonsingular points to obtain a smooth closed subscheme admitting a Hasse invariant. This reduces the higher-dimensional case to the dimension-0 case plus a Hasse invariant argument. For noncompact varieties, the author assumes the existence of a toroidal compactification and uses the extension of the G-zip morphism and the Hecke action to the boundary, applying similar arguments with an additional ampleness condition. Key geometric tools used include the G-zip stratification, Hasse invariants, Serre vanishing, the conormal exact sequence, and the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model.

Research Context
The mod p fiber of an abelian type Shimura variety at good reduction carries an action of the prime-to-p Hecke algebra. Several well-studied subschemes, including Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, Newton strata, and central leaves, are invariant under this action. In a famous letter from Serre to Tate, Serre showed that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the cohomology of a mod p modular curve are the same as those appearing in the cohomology of the supersingular locus. This was generalized by Goldring and Koskivirta, who showed that for the special fiber of the Kisin-Vasiu integral model of a Hodge-type Shimura variety, the eigenvalues match those of the unique zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum. Terakado and Yu further extended this to any central leaf contained in the basic Newton stratum. In all previous works, the subschemes considered were smooth of dimension 0, limiting the scope of the eigenvalue comparison. There is a gap in the theory: no results exist for higher dimensional or possibly singular Hecke-equivariant subschemes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in the coherent cohomology of a Shimura variety match those in its Hecke-equivariant subschemes in higher dimensions. Theorem A (the main result) hypothesizes that for a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the direct sum over all L-dominant characters of H^0(SK, V(η)) are identical to those in H^0(YK, V(η)) for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK. The hypothesis further extends to nonclosed subschemes, noncompact varieties, and specific strata such as Ekedahl-Oort and length strata. The paper predicts that these equalities hold regardless of whether the subschemes are smooth, reduced, or higher-dimensional, breaking the dimension-0 restriction of prior work. The expected mechanism involves a two-step 'going-down' and 'going-up' argument, modified by a recursive reduction to a smooth, Hasse-invariant-bearing subscheme.

Methodological Details
The setting is a Shimura datum (G,X) of abelian type, with G = Gc (cuspidal quotient), over a prime p not equal to 2. The variety is at hyperspecial level Kp over Qp and a sufficiently small open compact subgroup K of G(Apf). The scheme SK is the special fiber of the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model of the Shimura variety. The transition map πK'/K between hyperspecial subgroups is finite étale, and g: SgKg−1 → SK is a natural isomorphism for each g ∈ G(Apf). The automorphic line bundles V(η) correspond to L-dominant characters η of the maximal torus T, with η ∈ X*+,L(T). The theory of G-zips provides a smooth algebraic κ-stack G-Zipμ of dimension 0, which the Hodge-type Shimura variety maps to via ζK. The Ekedahl-Oort and length stratifications are induced from G-Zipμ via pullback along ζK, with closure relations explicitly defined. The Hodge line bundle ω = det ΩSK is an automorphic vector bundle, and Lemma 2.2.1 describes an L-stable filtration of its symmetric powers. The Hecke algebra H is the unramified, prime-to-p global Hecke algebra defined as the restricted tensor product of unramified Hecke algebras at all places. The Hecke action Tg acts on H^0(SK, F) via push-pull, and systems of Hecke eigenvalues are defined by the existence of simultaneous eigenforms over a finite extension.

Procedures And Architectures
The proof of Theorem A uses an inductive recursive reduction: define Z_K(0) as the reduction of YK intersected with the smallest intersecting length stratum Sk,i0. Subsequent Z_K(i) are defined by removing nonsingular points of the previous step, forming a decreasing chain of closed subschemes. The process terminates at a smooth closed ZK by Noetherianity, and a Hasse invariant argument ensures ZK admits a nowhere-vanishing section. Lemma 3.2.1 uses the L-stable filtration of Sym^n ⊗ V(η) to show eigenvalues in symmetric powers of the sheaf of differentials are contained in H^0 of some V(η_i). Lemma 3.2.2 handles the going-down step: if a proper smooth ZK admits a Hasse invariant, the maximal multiplicity argument shows eigenvalues in M(YK) are contained in M(ZK). Lemma 3.2.4 handles the going-up step: applying Serre vanishing for a large enough amplification of the Hodge bundle shows eigenvalues in M(ZK) are contained in M(YK). For noncompact varieties, the author assumes a toroidal compactification S_Σ with boundary D, and extends the G-zip morphism to the boundary via And23. The Hecke action extends to the compactification via Goldring-Koskivirta, allowing the same arguments to apply on S_Σ. A crucial ampleness condition is assumed: ω^k(-D') is ample on S_Σ for large k, analogous to the condition in [GK19] and [TY22].

Key Results
Theorem A proves that M(YK) ≅ M(SK) for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK of a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level. Theorem B (Corollary 3.3.3) specifies that for Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves C(x) closed in the Ekedahl-Oort stratum, the eigenvalues are the same. Theorem 3.3.2(c) states that if YK meets the basic locus, then M(SK) ≅ M(YK) for noncompact varieties. Theorem 3.3.2(d) establishes that if YK is the pullback of a closed substack of G-Zipμ, then M(YK) ≅ M(SK). Corollary 3.2.7 extends the result: for any two equivariant closed subschemes (ZK)K and (YK)K, M(YK) ≅ M(ZK). The proof relies on the existence of strata Hasse invariants (Lemma 2.2.5) and length Hasse invariants (Lemma 2.2.6) from Goldring-Koskivirta. Lemma 2.5.1 establishes that on a reduced scheme, a nowhere-vanishing section of a line bundle is injective, which is key for the Hasse invariant argument.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result implies that the spectral data in the coherent cohomology of a Shimura variety is fully concentrated on any sufficiently small Hecke-equivariant subscheme. This generalizes Serre's work from dimension 0 to arbitrary dimensions, unifying the eigenvalue theory across the stratification. The mechanism is geometric: the Hasse invariant allows for a 'section-based' reduction that avoids the failure of the conormal sequence in singular settings. The assumption G = Gc is a technical artifact for the existence of the G-zip morphism, not required for the main theorems. The work bridges the gap between the G-zip stratification of the special fiber and the coherent cohomology of automorphic line bundles.

Contradictions And Limitations
The author assumes the theory of toroidal compactifications of abelian type Shimura varieties has not yet been developed, a major gap in the field. The ampleness condition ω^k(-D') on S_Σ is an additional assumption that may not hold in all cases. The theorem assumes G = Gc, a technical assumption that provides the smooth surjective morphism to G-Zipμ. The paper does not explicitly address the non-hyperspecial level case, restricting the generality of the compactification results. The proof uses Serre vanishing which requires the schemes to be proper; the nonclosed/noncompact case is handled via closures in S_Σ. The author notes they omit discussion on compactifications in the introduction for brevity, indicating some content is not fully elaborated.

Claims
Systems of Hecke eigenvalues in coherent cohomology of any compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level are the same for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. Theorem A proves M(YK) ≅ M(SK) for arbitrary equivariant closed subschemes. The recursive reduction ensures ZK is smooth and admits a nowhere-vanishing Hasse invariant section. Lemma 3.2.4 applies Serre vanishing to obtain the going-up direction. The result assumes the abelian type condition, so it may not generalize to other Shimura types. The noncompact case requires the additional ampleness assumption. This generalizes Serre's eigenvalue theory to higher-dimensional subschemes. The results apply to central leaves, Ekedahl-Oort strata, and length strata directly.
For noncompact abelian type Shimura varieties at hyperspecial level, the eigenvalue equality holds if the subscheme meets the basic locus or is a closed substack of G-Zip. Theorem 3.3.2(c) gives the equality for subschemes meeting the basic locus. Theorem 3.3.2(d) gives the equality for pullbacks of closed G-Zip substacks. Corollary 3.3.3 unifies these for Ekedahl-Oort strata and central leaves. The noncompact case requires the toroidal compactification to exist and satisfy the ampleness condition. The author admits the theory of toroidal compactifications of abelian type is not yet developed. This extends the Serre-Tate-Goldring-Koskivirta line of results beyond compact varieties.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The author considers the special case where i0 = 0, where the Hasse invariant is nowhere-vanishing by definition, removing the need for the recursive reduction. Remark 3.2.5 states ω can be replaced by any ample Hecke-equivariant line bundle in the proofs. The proof of Lemma 2.4.5 (G(Apf)-equivariance of closures, intersections, and reduced subschemes) is fully detailed with direct verificaton.

Key Figures Tables
The paper does not contain figures or tables, being a pure mathematical text. Equations (2.2.3), (2.5.3), (3.2.3) are key technical identities in the stratification, Symn commutativity, and the going-down surjection.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is proving that systems of Hecke eigenvalues in coherent cohomology of any compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level are identical for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme, removing the dimension-0 restriction. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit two-step proof (going-down via Hasse invariants and going-up via Serre vanishing) combined with a recursive reduction to the smooth case, handling both singular and higher-dimensional subschemes. 3. The future path lies in developing the theory of toroidal compactifications for abelian type Shimura varieties, which would remove the outstanding assumption needed for the noncompact results.

summary.title: Anomalous Hall effect from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling
summary.authors: Longju Yu, Hong Jian Zhao, Yurong Yang, Laurent Bellaiche, Yanming Ma
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Spintronics and Topological Transport
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical and computational (symmetry analysis + first-principles calculations)
summary.executive_summary: This work establishes a phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field driven anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline magnets using a group-theoretical approach. The authors demonstrate that AHE can emerge from either linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling and is governed by the magnetic point group (MPG) symmetries of the crystal. Specifically, they show that both type-I and type-III MPGs (90 in total) host AHE components that are either spontaneous (grey in Table I) or driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields. A key property identified is that electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter, satisfying Onsager reciprocity: $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(+L) = -\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(-L)$. To validate the theory, first-principles DFT calculations were performed on two representative semiconductors with no more than 10 ions per primitive cell: $Cr_2O_3$ (Néel temperature 307 K, $\bar{3}'m'$ MPG) and $CoF_2$ (Néel temperature 39 K, $4'/mm'm$ MPG). In $Cr_2O_3$, first-order responses to uni-axial fields yield $\sigma_{zy}$, $\sigma_{xz}$, and $\sigma_{yx}$ reaching magnitudes larger than 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm, while third-order responses yield less than 20 S/cm. In $CoF_2$, second-order responses to bi-axial fields produce $\sigma_{zy}$ and $\sigma_{xz}$ reaching 10 S/cm, while uni-axial second-order responses produce $\sigma_{yx}$ exceeding 200 S/cm. The work positions nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling as a novel avenue for probing magnetic orders in spintronic devices, complementing linear-effect approaches such as the layer and electric Hall effects.

Electric-field driven AHE conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter: $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(+L) = -\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(-L)$.

Research Context
The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a fundamental topology-related transport phenomenon with potential spintronic applications in magnetic order probing. It is well known that AHE spontaneously occurs in ferromagnets or antiferromagnets with magnetization. Recent studies reveal electric-field induced AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling, such as the layer Hall effect. The electric-field induced AHE arising from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling remains largely unexplored. The AHE is characterized by transverse conductivity $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}$ which is antisymmetric by the Levi-Civita symbol. The existence or absence of magnetization in crystalline materials is determined by their magnetic point groups.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling can generate electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivity in crystalline magnets. The authors hypothesize that both type-I and type-III magnetic point groups exhibit spontaneous or electric-field induced AHE. They predict that nonlinear magnetoelectric AHE is accommodated by a wide spectrum of MPGs. The anomalous Hall conductivity components are predicted to be (i) achieved by applying uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric field, and (ii) reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. The hypothesis that $Cr_2O_3$ and $CoF_2$ are representative materials hosting this AHE is to be tested via first-principles calculations. They anticipate that the electric-field driven Hall conductivities will reverse in sign when the magnetic order parameter changes from $+L$ to $-L$.

Methodological Details
The study uses a group-theoretical symmetry analysis approach to establish the phenomenological theory. The anomalous Hall conductivity is defined via the Berry curvature in the semi-classical transport framework. The Hall vector $M \equiv (\sigma_{zy}, \sigma_{xz}, \sigma_{yx})$ is established, behaving like a magnetization vector under symmetry. Onsager reciprocity is invoked: $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(+L) = \sigma_{\beta\alpha}(-L)$, which combined with antisymmetry gives $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(+L) = -\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(-L)$. The authors classify 122 magnetic point groups into three types: type-I (spatial only), type-II (time-reversal independent), and type-III (time-reversal combined with spatial). Type-II MPGs containing time-reversal symmetry $\hat{T}$ are omitted because electric fields do not break $\hat{T}$. A total of 90 type-I and type-III MPGs are analyzed for AHE components. The MAGNDATA database is used to identify materials belonging to relevant MPGs. Two semiconductors are selected for first-principles calculations: $Cr_2O_3$ and $CoF_2$. Both materials have no more than 10 ions per primitive cell to keep computational costs affordable. The first-principles calculations assess anomalous Hall conductivities as a function of chemical potential relative to the Fermi level.

Procedures And Architectures
The effective magnetic field $B^eff_\alpha$ is expanded as a power series in the electric field: $B^eff_\alpha = \lambda_\alpha + \sum \lambda_{\alpha\beta}E_\beta + \sum \lambda_{\alpha\beta\gamma}E_\beta E_\gamma + \dots$. The coefficient $\lambda_\alpha$ implies spontaneous magnetization; $\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ is linear ME coupling, $\lambda_{\alpha\beta\gamma}$ second-order (nonlinear), etc. For each MPG, the $B^eff_\alpha$ are derived using symmetry constraints; Supplementary Tables 9, 10, 11 contain the full derivations. Example: For $\bar{1}.1$ MPG, $B^eff_x = \lambda_x$, $B^eff_y = \lambda_y$, $B^eff_z = \lambda_z$, enabling all three Hall components spontaneously. Table I presents 90 MPGs with color-coded Hall conductivity components: grey (spontaneous), red/cyan/yellow (uni-axial), bivariate (bi-axial), tripartite (tri-axial). For $Cr_2O_3$, the $\bar{3}'m'$ MPG is used, with crystal and magnetic structures sketched in Figure 1(a). For $CoF_2$, the $4'/mm'm$ MPG is used, with crystal and magnetic structures in Figure 1(b). In first-principles, electric field magnitudes up to 4 MV/cm are applied to extract Hall conductivities. Chemical potential sweeps are performed to map $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}$ as a function of energy relative to the Fermi level.

Key Results
Symmetry analysis reveals that 90 type-I and type-III MPGs host electric-field driven or spontaneous AHE. A wide spectrum of MPGs accommodates nonlinear magnetoelectric AHE via uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields. In $Cr_2O_3$ ($\bar{3}'m'$ MPG), first-order responses to uni-axial $E_x$, $E_y$, or $E_z$ drive $\sigma_{zy}$, $\sigma_{xz}$, and $\sigma_{yx}$ respectively. In $Cr_2O_3$, $\sigma_{zy}$ and $\sigma_{xz}$ can be larger than 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm; $\sigma_{yx}$ via third-order response ($E_y$) is less than 20 S/cm. In $CoF_2$ ($4'/mm'm$ MPG), responses are second-order: $\sigma_{yx}$ driven by uni-axial $E_x^2$ or $E_y^2$; $\sigma_{zy}$ and $\sigma_{xz}$ from bi-axial $E_x E_z$ and $E_y E_z$. In $CoF_2$, for $E_x = E_z = 2\sqrt{2}$ MV/cm (total 4 MV/cm), $\sigma_{zy}$ and $\sigma_{xz}$ reach 10 S/cm. In $CoF_2$, a uni-axial field of $E_x = 4$ MV/cm or $E_y = 4$ MV/cm yields $\sigma_{yx}$ larger than 200 S/cm. For all computed cases, switching the magnetic order parameter from $+L$ to $-L$ reverses the sign of the induced Hall conductivity. The effective magnetic fields for $\bar{6}m2.1$ MPG are given: $B^eff_x = \lambda_{xxxz}(E^2_x - E^2_y)E_z + \lambda_{xyz}E_y E_z$, etc. In 10 MPGs, the bi-axial or tri-axial electric field along specific directions quenches the Hall conductivity (Supplementary Table 12).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The AHE is established as a Hall vector $M$ that behaves like a magnetization vector under symmetry, establishing a direct correspondence with $M_\alpha$. The reversal of AHE with magnetic order parameter reversal is a direct consequence of the Onsager reciprocity relation and the antisymmetric nature of $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}$. The theory demonstrates that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling is a robust source of AHE in crystalline magnets, not limited to specific symmetries. This work positions electric-field driven AHE as an alternative avenue for probing magnetic orders, complementing linear-ME approaches. The resemblance between figures for $Cr_2O_3$ and $CoF_2$ is explained by the underlying symmetry of the effective magnetic fields, where shared coefficients imply symmetric coupling. The practical implication is for spintronic devices, where electric-field control of the Hall response could enable read-out of magnetic information without magnetic fields.

Contradictions And Limitations
The first-principles calculations are limited to two specific materials, and the results may not generalize to all compounds in relevant MPGs. Type-II MPGs containing time-reversal symmetry are omitted entirely, and the paper does not assess if these could host AHE via other mechanisms. The quenching behavior in 10 MPGs is noted, but the physical implications and practical avoidance are not discussed in detail. The paper does not report on temperature dependence of the AHE; $Cr_2O_3$ has $T_N = 307$ K, $CoF_2$ has $T_N = 39$ K, but no temperature-dependent transport data is shown. The computational costs are stated as 'affordable', but no quantitative benchmark of CPU-hours or runtime is provided. The exact first-principles parameters (exchange-correlation functional, k-point mesh, convergence criteria) are not explicitly stated in the main text.

Claims
Spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE are governed by magnetic point group symmetries, with 90 type-I and type-III MPGs hosting such effects. Symmetry analysis of the full MPG classification reveals 90 MPGs hosting AHE. Table I explicitly lists all 90 MPGs with their AHE components. First-principles calculations for $Cr_2O_3$ and $CoF_2$ confirm the symmetry predictions. Type-II MPGs are excluded by construction, so the claim of '90' MPGs is limited to type-I and type-III only. Thequenching behavior in 10 MPGs under specific field directions limits the universal applicability of the claim. Experimentalists can predict AHE in any material with the appropriate MPG by checking Table I. Electric-field control of AHE offers a new design principle for spintronic memory readouts.
Electric-field driven AHE conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter: $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(+L) = -\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(-L)$. Onsager reciprocity plus antisymmetry leads directly to the reversal relation. In $Cr_2O_3$, Figs. 2(a)-(d) show opposite signs for +L and -L magnetic orders. In $CoF_2$, Figs. 2(e)-(h) corroborate the reversal relation for second-order responses. This reversal assumes the Hall conductivity is purely driven by the effective magnetic field; other mechanisms may not satisfy this. The Hall response can serve as a sensitive readout of the magnetic order parameter sign. Switching the magnetization state can flip the AHE sign for logic and memory operations.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper includes a symmetry-based quenching analysis for 10 MPGs under specific bi-axial/tri-axial field directions (Supplementary Table 12). The resemblance between $Cr_2O_3$ and $CoF_2$ results is checked against effective field symmetries, identifying shared coefficients as the source of similarity. No formal sensitivity analysis on computational parameters or ensemble averaging is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) and (b) sketch the crystal and magnetic structures of $Cr_2O_3$ and $CoF_2$ with magnetic moments shown by red arrows. Figure 2(a)-(d) show $\sigma_{zy}$, $\sigma_{xz}$, and $\sigma_{yx}$ in $Cr_2O_3$ as a function of chemical potential for different fields. Figure 2(e)-(h) show $\sigma_{zy}$, $\sigma_{xz}$, and $\sigma_{yx}$ in $CoF_2$ for bi-axial and uni-axial responses. Table I lists 90 type-I and type-III MPGs with their AHE component mapping via color codes. Supplementary Tables 9, 10, 11 contain the full $B^eff_\alpha$ expressions for all 90 MPGs. Supplementary Table 12 summarizes the 10 quenching cases.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the establishment of a comprehensive phenomenological theory showing that both spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE (via linear and nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling) are mandated by magnetic point group symmetries in 90 type-I and type-III MPGs. 2. The strongest evidence is the pair of first-principles DFT calculations on $Cr_2O_3$ and $CoF_2$ that quantitatively confirm the symmetry predictions: Hall conductivities exceeding 100 S/cm and 200 S/cm at 4 MV/cm, all while exhibiting sign reversal with magnetic order parameter inversion. 3. The future path lies in experimental verification of electric-field driven AHE in these and other candidate materials, and exploring further spintronic devices where the Hall response can be read out electrically without magnetic fields.

summary.title: Enabling Real-Time Conversations with Minimal Training Costs
summary.authors: Wang Xu, Shuo Wang, Weilin Zhao, Xu Han, Yukun Yan, Yudi Zhang, Zhe Tao, Zhiyuan Liu, Wanxiang Che
summary.field_subfield: Computer Science / Natural Language Processing - LLM Duplex Decoding
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces DUplex decOding (DUO), a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy that equips Large Language Models with duplex capabilities—simultaneous input processing and output generation—with minimal training overhead. Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm, precluding real-time interactive feedback, while existing duplex models (e.g., MiniCPM-Duplex, LSLM) require substantial computational resources for retraining because their procedures diverge from the backbone model's original training. DUO addresses this by establishing a parallel decoding architecture where a new input channel is created when user input is detected; the output channel continues autoregressive generation while the input channel simultaneously prefills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens. A modified attention mask prevents cross-channel attendance, preserving language modeling integrity. Two state tokens (<1> for user query, <2> for no-query text) govern channel transitions: <1> suspends the output channel and transitions the input channel to become the new output channel; <2> causes the input channel to be disregarded. The method is implemented via Flex-Attention and does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding. Experiments using MiniCPM-2.4B as a foundation model demonstrate that DUO achieves superior responsiveness and human-likeness over MiniCPM-Duplex in human evaluations (40 multi-turn sessions, 3 evaluators) while maintaining comparable factuality and faithfulness. Benchmark results on CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, and HellaSwag show comparable performance with MiniCPM and MiniCPM-Duplex, confirming that minimal retraining (10K samples vs. 5,000K) is sufficient. The case study illustrates real-time adaptation to user interruptions and silence. The authors position DUO as a scalable, low-cost alternative to time-division-multiplexing duplex approaches.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces DUplex decOding (DUO), a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy that equips Large Language Models with duplex capabilities—simultaneous input processing and output generation—with minimal training overhead. Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm, precluding real-time interactive feedback, while existing duplex models (e.g., MiniCPM-Duplex, LSLM) require substantial computational resources for retraining because their procedures diverge from the backbone model's original training. DUO addresses this by establishing a parallel decoding architecture where a new input channel is created when user input is detected; the output channel continues autoregressive generation while the input channel simultaneously prefills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens. A modified attention mask prevents cross-channel attendance, preserving language modeling integrity. Two state tokens (<1> for user query, <2> for no-query text) govern channel transitions: <1> suspends the output channel and transitions the input channel to become the new output channel; <2> causes the input channel to be disregarded. The method is implemented via Flex-Attention and does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding. Experiments using MiniCPM-2.4B as a foundation model demonstrate that DUO achieves superior responsiveness and human-likeness over MiniCPM-Duplex in human evaluations (40 multi-turn sessions, 3 evaluators) while maintaining comparable factuality and faithfulness. Benchmark results on CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, and HellaSwag show comparable performance with MiniCPM and MiniCPM-Duplex, confirming that minimal retraining (10K samples vs. 5,000K) is sufficient. The case study illustrates real-time adaptation to user interruptions and silence. The authors position DUO as a scalable, low-cost alternative to time-division-multiplexing duplex approaches.

Research Context
LLMs have revolutionized human-computer interaction through question answering and coding assistance. Traditional turn-based chat systems inherently limit the interactive experience because one party passively waits while the other responds. Human conversations involve simultaneous listening and thinking, which turn-based models cannot replicate. Recent studies have proposed duplex models to address this challenge, including MiniCPM-Duplex and LSLM. MiniCPM-Duplex employs a time-division-multiplexing strategy where input and output are split and mixed in a time slice format. LSLM combines channels for autoregressive generation and real-time turn-taking detection. However, these approaches demand significant computational resources for model retraining because the designed procedure diverges from the backbone. There is a need for a duplex decoding method requiring minimal additional training.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a channel-division-multiplexing parallel decoding strategy can equip LLMs with duplex capabilities using minimal retraining. The hypothesis is that parallel decoding of queries and responses, combined with state-token-governed transitions, will enable simultaneous input and output processing without substantially modifying the model's data format. The authors hypothesize that DUO will significantly enhance naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions compared to turn-based and time-division-multiplexing duplex models. A secondary hypothesis is that DUO can handle non-awakening interactions, an aspect MiniCPM-Duplex does not address. The authors predict that only minimal training (10K samples vs. 5,000K) should suffice to learn the state of the query. The predicted outcome is that DUO will preserve original model capabilities while adding duplex functionality with minimal computational overhead.

Methodological Details
The foundation model is MiniCPM-2.4B from Hu et al. (2024). 10,000 samples were constructed for training DUO. The MiniCPM-Duplex baseline used approximately 5,000,000 samples for comparison. The training uses a learning rate of 1e-5 with a constant learning rate scheduler. The batch size is 112 and the maximum sequence length is 4,096. Loss is calculated on the state tokens and output. MiniCPM-Duo is trained for 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for approximately 25 minutes. MiniCPM-Duplex requires 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. The decoding strategy is implemented based on the Ouroboros repository. The input channel predicted tokens alpha are set to 4. Non-query text for non-awakening scenarios was generated using ChatGPT with a prompt described in Appendix A.1. The dataset was adapted from Duplex-UltraChat, which structures conversations in a time-division format. State token <1> was appended to each user content since all queries in the dataset require a response. Three participants, each holding a Bachelor's degree, evaluated the dialogue histories. 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions were conducted with each model through a voice-based interactive demo. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversions used Google's cloud ASR and TTS APIs, respectively.

Procedures And Architectures
DUO employs a channel-based parallel decoding mechanism that functions as a channel-division-multiplexing system. In each cycle, the output channel generates new tokens autoregressively while the input channel prefills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens. A new input channel is established at time step t1 when a user input token is received. The attention mask is modified so that tokens generated by the input and output channels do not attend to each other despite sharing prefix tokens. The output channel persists in generating tokens until either the model responds to the new query or the sequence is completed. Two state tokens are used: <1> denotes a user query, and <2> denotes no-query text. Upon predicting <1>, the original output channel is suspended and the input channel transitions to become the new output channel. Upon predicting <2>, the model continues responding to the original query and the input channel is disregarded. DUO is efficiently implemented using Flex-Attention which facilitates non-standard attention mechanisms. All operations are accomplished through management of the key-value cache. DUO does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding. The training data format remains largely unchanged, with only the addition of state tokens. The input tokens are processed in a channel-aware causal mask configuration. Figure 1 illustrates the channel transition, parallel decoding branches, and attention masking.

Key Results
In human evaluation across 40 multi-turn sessions, MiniCPM-Duo demonstrates superior responsiveness and human-likeness compared to MiniCPM-Duplex. MiniCPM-Duo maintains comparable levels of factuality and faithfulness to MiniCPM-Duplex. MiniCPM-Duo exhibits a substantial advantage in overall performance in the human-likeness ranking. On CMMLU, MiniCPM-Duo achieves 50.66, comparable to MiniCPM-Duplex (50.56) and MiniCPM (51.30). On MMLU, MiniCPM-Duo scores 53.13, comparable to MiniCPM-Duplex (53.76) and MiniCPM (53.45). On BBH, MiniCPM-Duo scores 36.51, close to MiniCPM-Duplex (36.35) and MiniCPM (37.25). On HumanEval, MiniCPM-Duo achieves 51.83, slightly higher than MiniCPM-Duplex (51.81) and MiniCPM (50.00). On MBPP, MiniCPM-Duo achieves 38.19, comparable to MiniCPM-Duplex (38.30) and MiniCPM (38.09). On GSM8K, MiniCPM-Duo scores 42.15, close to MiniCPM-Duplex (46.10) and MiniCPM (42.30). On ARC-e, MiniCPM-Duo achieves 84.93, close to MiniCPM-Duplex (85.19) and MiniCPM (84.60). On ARC-c, MiniCPM-Duo achieves 70.48, exceeding MiniCPM-Duplex (69.43) and MiniCPM (69.80). On HellaSwag, MiniCPM-Duo achieves 59.78, notably higher than MiniCPM-Duplex (50.85) and MiniCPM (61.40). When MiniCPM-Duplex is trained on the same 10K sample scale as DUO, its duplex capability is relatively poor and performances drop. Figure 2 summarizes the pairwise comparison: MiniCPM-Duo wins on responsiveness and human-likeness; MiniCPM-Duplex wins on factuality and faithfulness; tie on overall.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
DUO's channel-division-multiplexing architecture theoretically separates the 'listening' and 'speaking' streams without altering the underlying language modeling objective. The state tokens act as meta-instructions that modulate the decoding policy dynamically, decoupling the content of the query from the protocol of the interaction. By preserving the original data format, DUO shows that duplex capability is a decoding-level property rather than a model-architecture property. The use of Flex-Attention demonstrates that standard transformer inference engines can be extended to support multi-channel decoding via KV-cache manipulation alone. The case study (Figure 3) provides qualitative evidence that the model can handle user silence by continuing generation and can handle interruptions by deleting irrelevant input.

Contradictions And Limitations
A significant constraint lies in the scope of multimodal testing, as experiments primarily focused on language models. The authors admit the findings may have limited generalizability to other domains. The human evaluation is limited to three participants, which may not be sufficient for broad generalizability. The interactive demo was originally developed for MiniCPM-Duplex, introducing a slight dependency on the baseline's infrastructure. The GSM8K result (42.15) for MiniCPM-Duo is lower than MiniCPM-Duplex (46.10), suggesting a potential trade-off in mathematical reasoning accuracy for duplex capability. The HellaSwag result (59.78) is below the base MiniCPM (61.40), indicating some degradation in commonsense reasoning when duplexing. No explicit ablation on the state token prediction accuracy is reported.

Claims
DUO equips LLMs with duplex capabilities using channel-division-multiplexing with minimal training costs compared to time-division approaches. DUO requires only 10K samples compared to 5,000K for MiniCPM-Duplex. Training takes 25 minutes on 8 A100s versus 36 hours on 40 A100s. DUO does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding. Performance on all standard benchmarks remains comparable to base MiniCPM. On GSM8K, DUO (42.15) is lower than MiniCPM-Duplex (46.10). On HellaSwag, DUO (59.78) is lower than base MiniCPM (61.40). MiniCPM-Duplex wins on factuality and faithfulness in pairwise comparisons. Duplex capabilities can be retrofitted onto existing LLMs without full fine-tuning. Real-time interactive voice interfaces can be built with significantly reduced compute.
State tokens enable dynamic channel switching that handles both user queries and non-query interruptions. State token <1> suspends output and transitions input to output. State token <2> disregards new input, allowing continued response. The case study demonstrates successful interruption handling. MiniCPM-Duo handles non-awakening interactions that MiniCPM-Duplex does not. The paper doesn't report the frequency of state-token misclassification. The interaction protocol can be extended with more state tokens for different behaviors.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors studied how MiniCPM-Duplex performs when trained on the same 10K sample scale as DUO. With 10K samples, MiniCPM-Duplex performances drop and duplex capability is relatively poor. The case study illustrates the model's adaptive behavior under two conditions: user query and user interruption during generation. The input channel predicted tokens are set to 4 for evaluation of non-query input.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the channel-based parallel decoding architecture, KV-cache management, channel transition, and modified attention mask. Figure 2 presents the pairwise comparison matrix between MiniCPM-Duo and MiniCPM-Duplex across five human evaluation metrics. Figure 3 provides a case study of a multi-turn dialogue illustrating state token prediction, user interruption, and channel transition. Table 1 reports benchmark scores on CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, HellaSwag with data usage counts.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a channel-division-multiplexing parallel decoding strategy that adds duplex (simultaneous input-output) capability to LLMs using only minimal training (10K samples) via two state tokens and a modified attention mask. 2. The strongest evidence is that DUO achieves superior responsiveness and human-likeness in 40 human-evaluated voice dialogues compared to MiniCPM-Duplex, while maintaining comparable benchmark performance (all within ~1-3 percentage points of base MiniCPM) with 100x less training data. 3. The future path is extending DUO to multimodal settings where input tokens are encoder-extracted features from images, video, or audio, and the authors plan to generalize to multimodal large models.

summary.title: Spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes
summary.authors: Lina Zhang, Qiyuan Pan, Yun Soo Myung, De-Cheng Zou
summary.field_subfield: General Relativity / Gravitational Physics / Scalar-Tensor Theories
summary.executive_summary:
This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes, a class of regular (singularity-free) black holes with magnetic charge that arises in nonlinear electrodynamics. The authors consider the Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory coupled to a scalar field with two specific nonminimal coupling forms: quadratic $\tilde{f}(\phi) = 1 - \alpha\phi^2$ and exponential $\tilde{f}(\phi) = e^{-\alpha\phi^2}$. 

The primary finding is that Bardeen black holes undergo a tachyonic instability when the coupling parameter $\alpha$ exceeds a threshold $\alpha_{th}(g)$, triggering the formation of infinite branches of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs) indexed by $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For the specific background values $M = 0.5$ and $g = 0.2$, the instability threshold is numerically determined as $\alpha_{th}(0.2) = 12.712$. At this point, the $n = 0$ branch (the fundamental branch) of SCBHs bifurcates from the Bardeen solution. 

The authors numerically construct the $n = 0$ branch for both coupling forms, finding that the scalarized solution preserves a horizon very close to the Bardeen value but introduces a redshift function $\delta(r)$ and scalar hair $\phi(r)$. Crucially, a radial perturbation analysis shows that the $n = 0$ branch is stable against $l = 0$ scalar perturbations (quantified by a negative $\Omega$ in the mode $\phi_1(r) e^{\Omega t}$), while the Bardeen solution is unstable. The study notes that the bifurcation threshold $\alpha_{th}(g)$ increases as the magnetic charge $g$ decreases, making scalarization harder to achieve. The $n > 0$ branches are predicted to be unstable by analogy with previous literature. Because the $n = 0$ branch is stable and represents an endpoint of the Bardeen solution, it is framed as a candidate for further observational implications.

Executive Summary

The primary finding is that Bardeen black holes undergo a tachyonic instability when the coupling parameter $\alpha$ exceeds a threshold $\alpha_{th}(g)$, triggering the formation of infinite branches of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs) indexed by $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For the specific background values $M = 0.5$ and $g = 0.2$, the instability threshold is numerically determined as $\alpha_{th}(0.2) = 12.712$. At this point, the $n = 0$ branch (the fundamental branch) of SCBHs bifurcates from the Bardeen solution. 

The authors numerically construct the $n = 0$ branch for both coupling forms, finding that the scalarized solution preserves a horizon very close to the Bardeen value but introduces a redshift function $\delta(r)$ and scalar hair $\phi(r)$. Crucially, a radial perturbation analysis shows that the $n = 0$ branch is stable against $l = 0$ scalar perturbations (quantified by a negative $\Omega$ in the mode $\phi_1(r) e^{\Omega t}$), while the Bardeen solution is unstable. The study notes that the bifurcation threshold $\alpha_{th}(g)$ increases as the magnetic charge $g$ decreases, making scalarization harder to achieve. The $n > 0$ branches are predicted to be unstable by analogy with previous literature. Because the $n = 0$ branch is stable and represents an endpoint of the Bardeen solution, it is framed as a candidate for further observational implications.

Research Context
Spontaneous scalarization imparts scalar hair to black holes without changing weak-field predictions. The phenomenon is a strong gravity phase transition caused by tachyonic instability from nonminimal coupling. Bardeen proposed the first regular black hole solution that is spherically symmetric and free of singularities. Nonlinear electromagnetic sources were proposed by the end of the last century to explain Bardeen black hole matter content. Regular black holes are of great interest for understanding fundamental issues including singularities and nonlinear electrodynamics. Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory with exponential and quadratic scalar couplings has been explored in alternative gravity theories. Previous studies found scalarized black holes are entropically favorable and their n = 0 branches are stable. The physical source of Bardeen black holes was initially unclear, limiting direct physical interpretation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization under quadratic and exponential nonminimal couplings. The authors hypothesize that the tachyonic instability in Bardeen black holes will trigger the formation of scalarized charged black hole (SCBH) branches. It is predicted that infinite (n = 0, 1, 2, · · ·) branches of SCBHs with magnetic charge g will emerge. The n = 0 branch is expected to be found for coupling parameter α ≥ αth(g) with both quadratic and exponential couplings. A specific hypothesis is that the n = 0 branch for both couplings is stable against radial perturbations. The instability is expected to be contingent on the coupling parameter α, with αth(g) serving as the bifurcation point. The authors also predict that bifurcation points correspond to the first appearance of SCBH branches at discrete α values. The tachyonic instability threshold is expected to depend on the magnetic charge g, with smaller g making instability harder to realize.

Methodological Details
The action describes Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics coupled to a scalar field with coupling function f(phi). The nonlinear electromagnetic function L(F) depends on the magnetic charge g and mass M. Two coupling forms are considered: quadratic ˜f(phi) = 1 − αϕ² and exponential ˜f(ϕ) = e^−αϕ². The parameter s is defined as s = |g|² / M, linking the magnetic charge and mass. A typical nonextremal Bardeen black hole is taken with M = 0.5 and g = 0.2. The outer horizon radius for this configuration is determined to be r₊ = 0.935. The violation of the strong energy condition at the center confirms the solution as a regular black hole. Three magnetic charges are selected for the stability analysis: g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250. The l = 0 mode is prioritized for analysis as it is permissible for scalar perturbations. The tortoise coordinate r⋆ is defined by dr*/dr = f(r) for the radial wave equation. Boundary conditions require a purely ingoing wave at the near-horizon and a purely outgoing wave at infinity. Near-horizon expansions for m(r), δ(r), and ϕ(r) are used to initialize the numerical integration. Far-region asymptotic solutions incorporate the ADM mass M and the scalar charge Qs.

Procedures And Architectures
The linearized scalar equation (9) is derived from the Klein-Gordon equation with an effective mass term proportional to αL(F). The radial scalar equation is reduced to a Schrödinger-type equation in the tortoise coordinate. The scalar potential V(r) includes the l(l + 1)/r² term and a coupling-dependent term with (g² + r²)⁵/². The threshold αth(g) is determined by solving the linearized equation numerically for ω = −iΩ. For the Bardeen background, the scalar is decomposed using separation of variables in spherical harmonics. To confirm the instability bound, a static scalar solution with u(r) = rϕ(r) and ω = 0 is solved. The metric ansatz for SCBHs includes N(r) = 1 − 2m(r)/r and a redshift function δ(r). The vector potential A_φ = −g cos θ is exact for the magnetic field and requires no approximation. Three coupled ordinary differential equations for δ(r), m(r), and ϕ(r) are solved numerically. The stability of the n = 0 branch is tested by perturbing the SCBH solution with radial spherical perturbations. The perturbation equation is reduced to a Schrödinger-type form with potential V_SCBH(r). Stability is verified by solving for the quasi-normal mode frequency Ω with vanishing boundary conditions at horizon and infinity.

Key Results
The Bardeen black hole is stable for α < αth(g) and undergoes tachyonic instability for α ≥ αth(g). For g = 0.2, the threshold of instability is αth(0.2) = 12.712. For g = 0.175, the threshold is αth(0.175) = 17.338. For g = 0.250, the threshold is αth(0.250) = 7.251. The first three bifurcation points for g = 0.2 are α_0 ≈ 12.712, α_1 ≈ 75.114, and α_2 ≈ 190.590. The instability threshold αth(g) exactly matches the n = 0 bifurcation point. For quadratic coupling at g = 0.2, the n = 0 SCBH solution is obtained at α = 13.048. For exponential coupling at g = 0.2, the n = 0 SCBH solution is obtained at α = 13.667. The SCBH horizon at ln r = −0.0683 is very close to the Bardeen horizon at ln r = −0.0671. The n = 0 SCBH is stable against the l = 0 scalar mode for all three values of g. The stability is confirmed by negative values of Ω for the perturbation mode. The n = 0 branch exhibits a large positive region outside the horizon in the scalar potential. The perturbation potentials V_SCBH(r) contain small negative regions in the near-horizon that do not indicate instability.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is considered the endpoint of the Bardeen black hole in configuration space. The stability of the n = 0 branch opens the possibility for observational implications. The result that the bifurcation point matches the instability threshold implies that the largest n = 0 branch of SCBHs forms exactly at the onset of instability. The finding that αth(g) increases as g decreases suggests that smaller magnetic charges suppress scalarization. All SCBHs are found by spontaneous scalarization, implying the existence of infinite branches. The n = 0 branch is consistent with previously known results that scalarized black holes are entropically favorable and stable. The proximity of the SCBH horizon to the Bardeen horizon suggests the scalar field does not radically deform the event horizon.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that a negative region in the scalar potential near the horizon does not always imply instability, requiring full numerical verification. The paper only tests the l = 0 scalar mode; higher angular momentum modes (l ≠ 0) are neglected in the stability analysis. The stability of n > 0 branches is not computed numerically but is conjectured from references [33, 34]. The study uses only two coupling forms (quadratic and exponential) and does not explore generalized nonminimal couplings. The radial stability analysis does not include gravitational perturbations, only scalar perturbations. The gauge field perturbation is not needed for l = 0 analysis, but this may limit applicability to higher modes. The numerical solutions are presented for specific values of M and g; systematic parameter sweeps are not fully quantified.

Claims
Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization under both quadratic and exponential nonminimal scalar couplings. Two coupling forms were numerically tested for M = 0.5, g = 0.2. The instability threshold was confirmed as αth(g) = αn=0(g). SCBH solutions exist at α = 13.048 (quadratic) and α = 13.667 (exponential). The instability threshold increases as g decreases, so scalarization is not universal for all magnetic charges. New regular black hole solutions with scalar hair are predicted in scalar-tensor theories. The n = 0 branch could have observational signatures in gravitational waves or shadow imaging.
The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is stable against radial scalar perturbations across all magnetic charges tested. Negative Ω values confirm decay of perturbations for g = 0.175, 0.2, 0.25. The scalar potential V_SCBH(r) shows a large positive region outside the horizon. Stability is independent of the magnetic charge g. Small negative regions in V_SCBH(r) near the horizon are present, though the authors claim they don't imply instability. The n = 0 branch is a physically viable (stable) black hole state. Stability across all g values suggests robustness of the scalarization mechanism.
Infinite branches of SCBHs emerge from the instability of Bardeen black holes, with n > 0 branches predicted to be unstable. Discrete bifurcation points α_n appear for each node number n. The bifurcation points correspond to n = 0, 1, 2 at α ≈ 12.7, 75.1, 190.6. All other branches (n ≠ 0) are suggested by references to be unstable. The instability of n > 0 branches is not numerically demonstrated in this work. The n = 0 branch is the only scalarized branch likely to persist in nature. The structure of the configuration space is a discrete sequence of branches bifurcating from Bardeen solutions.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Three different values of g (0.175, 0.2, 0.25) were tested, confirming the stability result is independent of magnetic charge. The n = 0 branch was constructed for both quadratic and exponential couplings, showing consistency between the two functional forms. Near-horizon expansion matching was used to verify that the numerical solutions correctly reproduce the Bardeen horizon and scalar hair. The static scalar solution (ω = 0) was computed independently to confirm that the instability threshold αth(g) matches the bifurcation point.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the α-dependent scalar potential V(r, α, g=0.2) illustrating the negative region near the horizon. Figure 1(b) plots V(r, α, g=0.2) for three values of α around the threshold, showing how the negative region grows with α. Figure 2 shows the quasi-normal mode frequency Ω as a function of α for three g values, identifying αth(g). Figure 3 displays radial profiles of the first three static scalar solutions ϕ(z) for M = 0.5, g = 0.2. Figure 4(a) and (b) plot metric functions δ(r), N(r), and scalar hair ϕ(r) for the n = 0 SCBH solution with quadratic and exponential couplings, respectively. Figure 5 shows the V_SCBH(r) potential for the n = 0 branch under both coupling forms. Figure 6(a) and (b) plot Ω vs. α for the three g values, confirming stability (Ω < 0) for the n = 0 branch.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the discovery that Bardeen black holes spontaneously scalarize under both quadratic and exponential nonminimal couplings, producing infinite branches of SCBHs with a stable n = 0 fundamental branch. 2. The strongest evidence is the numerical confirmation that the instability threshold αth(g) coincides exactly with the n = 0 bifurcation point, and that the n = 0 branch is stable across all magnetic charges tested (confirmed by negative Ω values). 3. The future path lies in investigating higher angular momentum stability modes, extending the parameter space of magnetic charge, and exploring observational consequences such as gravitational wave signatures or black hole shadow deformations.

summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.field_subfield: Photonics / Topological Photonics
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents the theoretical and experimental development of a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework with a complete photonic bandgap. Previous valley photonics studies were restricted to 2D, suffering from out-of-plane losses and single-polarization confinement. The 3D model introduces triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone (BZ), characterized by valley Chern vectors instead of scalar valley Chern numbers. This vectorial nature enables vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states on all surfaces. Key results include selective excitation of vectorial valley states using a four-source chiral source array, demonstrating outcoupling angles of −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9° at 13.8 GHz corresponding to Wy−, X, and Wy+ states. Surface states on the (001) surface exhibit nearly-linear dispersion and canalization (diffractionless propagation along +y) due to flat isofrequency contours, confirmed at 14.6 GHz. The valley Chern vectors and surface state circulation directions obey a right-hand-thumb rule. The authors demonstrate robust surface state propagation through a sharp corner bend (from +y to −z on the (010) surface) without intervalley scattering. The concept is projected to extend to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.
