Canalized chiral valley surface states propagate diffractionlessly along a specific direction on all surfaces of the 3D sample.
The right-hand-thumb rule intrinsically links the direction of VCVs to the circulating direction of valley surface states on all surfaces.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the theoretical and experimental development of a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework with a complete photonic bandgap. Previous valley photonics studies were restricted to 2D, suffering from out-of-plane losses and single-polarization confinement. The 3D model introduces triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone (BZ), characterized by valley Chern vectors instead of scalar valley Chern numbers. This vectorial nature enables vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states on all surfaces. Key results include selective excitation of vectorial valley states using a four-source chiral source array, demonstrating outcoupling angles of −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9° at 13.8 GHz corresponding to Wy−, X, and Wy+ states. Surface states on the (001) surface exhibit nearly-linear dispersion and canalization (diffractionless propagation along +y) due to flat isofrequency contours, confirmed at 14.6 GHz. The valley Chern vectors and surface state circulation directions obey a right-hand-thumb rule. The authors demonstrate robust surface state propagation through a sharp corner bend (from +y to −z on the (010) surface) without intervalley scattering. The concept is projected to extend to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.

Research Context
Valley photonics exploits valley degree of freedom to manipulate electromagnetic waves across the entire spectrum. Previously, all valley photonics studies were limited to two-dimensional systems. 2D valley systems suffer from out-of-plane losses and can only manipulate light in planar geometries. Confinement along the third dimension in 2D systems was typically obtained nontopologically, such as through total internal reflection. Full confinement and control of light flow in 3D requires a complete photonic bandgap, which remained a significant challenge. Valley photonics offers a readily accessible and effective method for topologically robust photonic devices compared to photonic Chern insulators.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a 3D topological valley photonics framework can be realized with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley physics. The authors hypothesize that a 3D crystal can host triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors rather than scalar Chern numbers. The predicted outcome is that the vectorial nature of 3D valley states will enable canalized chiral surface states on all surfaces. It was predicted that the valley Chern vectors and surface state circulation would be intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The hypothesis included that surface states could propagate diffractionlessly due to flat isofrequency contours. The study aimed to verify that surface states remain robust through sharp corners without intervalley scattering.

Methodological Details
The 3D photonic crystal is a diamond-like lattice with lattice constant a = 20 mm. Lattice vectors are a1 = (a/2, a/2, 0), a2 = (0, a/2, a/2), and a3 = (a/2, 0, a/2). The crystal uses perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres as atoms and PEC rods as bonds. Each face-centered-cubic (fcc) cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2. Nearest-neighbor spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm to suppress high-order modes. When ∆D = 0, D1 = D2 = 5 mm, preserving inversion symmetry. When ∆D ≠ 0, D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm, breaking inversion symmetry to open the bandgap. The k · p method was used to obtain the effective Hamiltonian near each valley. The effective Hamiltonian includes group velocity vD, mass term m = (ω1 − ω2)/2, and Pauli matrices σx,y,z. For the chiral source array, four sources are positioned at (0, 0, 0), (−a/2, −a/2, 0), (−a/2, 0, −a/2), and (0, −a/2, −a/2). Relative phase delays for Wy− are (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) and for Wy+ are (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2). The surface boundary condition is modified by covering the (001) surface with a metallic plate. Two key tuning parameters are the diameter of the outmost metallic sphere D3 and the distance h between the plate and sphere. The boundary condition θV = π/2 is satisfied when h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm. The metallic plate has perforations for source and probe insertion with a hole interval of a/2.

Procedures And Architectures
The band structure was computed with the diamond-like VPC structure comprising PEC spheres and rods in an fcc lattice. Nodal lines along Wα± -X (α = x, y, z) form intersecting chains when inversion symmetry is preserved. The six valley momenta are (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and (2π/a, 0, ±π/a). Breaking inversion symmetry gaps out the nodal line degeneracies to form a complete photonic bandgap. The effective Hamiltonian near each valley is obtained via k · p expansion around momentum offset q. Valley-chirality locking is confirmed by calculating distinct Bloch mode chirality at each valley pair. Selective excitation is implemented using the four-source chiral array to form clockwise/counterclockwise phase winding. Outcoupling fields are measured and judged from the radiation direction in 3D space. The valley Chern vector is computed by integrating vectorial Berry curvature over planar regions normal to qx, qy, and qz. Surface states are generated by tuning boundary conditions rather than forming domain walls between oppositely-charged VPCs. Fourier-transformed spectrum along L4-Wx−-L1 is used to map the surface dispersion. Isofrequency contour analysis is performed both numerically and experimentally to confirm canalization. Corner-bend experiments measure field distribution before and after propagation across the (001)/(010) interface.

Key Results
The 3D VPC exhibits a complete photonic bandgap when inversion symmetry is broken (∆D ≠ 0). The bandstructure shows a gap where topological bands are separated from trivial bands. The six valleys at Wα± are grouped pairwise due to time-reversal symmetry. Berry curvature at Wz± has a nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane, verifying vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Valley Chern vectors are (±1/2, 0, 0) for Wx±, (0, ±1/2, 0) for Wy±, and (0, 0, ±1/2) for Wz±. At 13.8 GHz, clockwise phase winding gives outcoupling at −32.9° and counterclockwise at +32.9°. Without phase winding, the outcoupling direction is 0°, corresponding to the X point. Far-field radiation patterns confirm single-directional 3D outcoupling, unlike 2D systems that diverge vertically. Surface transmission remains high within the bandgap, while bulk transmission is substantially lower. Nearly-linear surface dispersion is observed in the Fourier-transformed spectrum around Wx−. Surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction at 14.6 GHz, confirming canalization. Isofrequency contours at 14.6 GHz show flat profiles independent of the wavevector vertical to propagation. Surface states at Wx− propagate along +y on (001) and along −z on (010), forming a closed loop. The Wx− valley carries VCV (−1/2, 0, 0) and the circulating direction obeys the right-hand-thumb rule. Field distributions show only surface states around Wx− are excited on both (001) and (010) surfaces, confirming valley-locking. Surface states pass through the sharp corner with high transmission without intervalley scattering.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation between VCVs and surface states, both determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The vectorial nature of 3D valley states provides a means to control angular momentum of light via orbital moments. Canalized valley chiral surface states may inspire 3D topological photonic devices for guiding and trapping light in unprecedented ways. Highly directional outcoupling from valley states serves as a mechanism for creating narrow-beam antennae. The concept can be extended to higher frequencies, including terahertz and optical ranges, using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals. The flat isofrequency contour makes canalization an intrinsic property, presenting opportunities for imaging and lensing.

Contradictions And Limitations
The demonstrated system operates at lower microwave frequencies, not at the optical or terahertz ranges mentioned in the discussion. The right-hand-thumb rule applicability to all sample surfaces is asserted but not individually tested for every possible orientation. The boundary condition relies on phenomenological parameters (θV) that are tuned empirically rather than derived from first principles. The paper does not report on the out-of-plane loss levels quantified; it only qualitatively states bulk transmission is substantially lower. The number of sources and geometry for the chiral array is specific to the diamond lattice; generalizeability to other unit cells is not shown. The sample is specifically shaped for the experiment; general shape independence is stated but not demonstrated. The paper does not report on sample yield, fabrication repeatability, or statistical variance over multiple runs.

Claims
The 3D VPC framework introduces a vectorial valley physics with triple valley pairs and vectorial Chern vectors. The crystal has six valley points at Wα±, grouped pairwise by time-reversal symmetry. Berry curvature at Wz± is confined to the kx-ky plane, confirming vectorial character. Valley Chern vectors are calculated as (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). Selective outcoupling directions confirm valley-specific modes. The effective Hamiltonian model is a k · p expansion near valleys, which may break down far from valley centers. The vectorial character relies on the diamond-like geometry; its universality across other unit cells is not shown. Angular momentum control of light via orbital moments becomes possible in 3D. Directional radiation for antenna design is enabled by single-directional 3D outcoupling.
Canalized chiral valley surface states propagate diffractionlessly along a specific direction on all surfaces of the 3D sample. Surface transmission is high in the bandgap while bulk is substantially lower. Nearly-linear surface dispersion is measured at 14.6 GHz. Flat isofrequency contours are confirmed experimentally and numerically. States propagate along +y on (001) and −z on (010) with valley conservation. The boundary condition θV = π/2 is achieved only with specific metallic plate and sphere parameters (h=6.25mm, D3=4mm). The paper notes that 2D surface states are restricted in propagation plane; 3D robustness is stated but the exact decay length/robustness quantified is not given. Imaging and lensing applications are enabled by flat isofrequency contours. Robust surface state propagation across corners enables complex topological photonic circuits.
The right-hand-thumb rule intrinsically links the direction of VCVs to the circulating direction of valley surface states on all surfaces. VCV is (−1/2, 0, 0) for Wx− and states circulate clockwise on y-z plane. Field distributions on both (001) and (010) surfaces show only Wx− states excited, confirming valley-locking. States pass through the sharp corner with high transmission. The rule is stated to apply to all sample surfaces. Only the (001)-(010) corner was experimentally tested; other corner geometries (e.g., (010)-(001) or (100)) are not shown. The rule is physically deduced from the bulk Hamiltonian but the exact mapping function is not explicitly derived. Topological protection against intervalley scattering is guaranteed by valley conservation. Surface state trajectories on multi-surface samples are deterministic and predictable.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Next-nearest-neighbor couplings with B2 = 1.2 mm were added specifically to suppress high-order modes and clean the bandstructure. The complete photonic bandgap requires breaking inversion symmetry (∆D ≠ 0). The outcoupling direction of 0° without phase winding confirms the coexistence of valley states and X-point states at the same frequency. The boundary condition θV is tuned via h and D3; the specific values h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm satisfy the desired condition. The isofrequency contour is shown both numerically (simulated) and experimentally (measured) at 14.6 GHz, confirming canalization. The corner-bend experiment measures transmission before and after the bend to quantify surface state persistence. Fourier transform of field distributions is used to verify surface dispersion independently of direct imaging.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the diamond-like 3D VPC structure with PEC spheres and rods, lattice constant, and next-nearest-neighbor connections. Figure 1(b) shows the 3D band structure comparing ∆D = 0 (D1 = D2 = 5 mm) and ∆D ≠ 0 (D1 = 6.4 mm, D2 = 3.6 mm). Figure 1(c) shows the 3D Brillouin zone with six valley points and nodal lines. Figure 1(d) shows simulated eigenstates at Wz± with Poynting vector and phase plots. Figure 1(e) shows simulated Berry curvature components at Wz± confirming vectorial nature. Figure 2(a) illustrates the four-source vectorial chiral array with phase winding. Figure 2(b) shows momentum-space analysis of Wx±, X, and Wy± with outcoupling directions. Figure 2(c) shows the experimental setup with four scanned planes. Figure 2(d) shows measured outcoupling fields at 13.8 GHz with theoretical refraction arrows. Figure 2(e) shows measured far-field radiation patterns at Wy−, X, and Wy+. Figure 3(a) shows the 3D VPC with modified (001) surface including metallic plate, h, and D3. Figure 3(b) shows the experimental setup for surface state observation. Figure 3(c) shows the projective surface BZ onto the (001) surface with simulated isofrequency contours. Figure 3(d) shows simulated surface dispersion with bulk and surface states. Figure 3(e) shows normalized measured transmission through the bandgap. Figure 3(f) shows measured surface field distribution at 14.6 GHz. Figure 3(g) shows measured and simulated surface dispersion around Wx−. Figure 3(h) shows measured and simulated isofrequency contours at 14.6 GHz. Figure 4(a) illustrates the VCV directions and circulating loops obeying the right-hand-thumb rule for three valley pairs. Figure 4(b) shows measured field distribution before and after the corner bend. Figure 4(c) shows transmission of bulk and surface states before and after the bend. Figure 4(d) shows measured isofrequency contours before and after the bend at 14.6 GHz.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first realization of 3D topological valley photonics with a complete bandgap, replacing 2D scalar valley physics with a vectorial framework involving triple valley pairs, vectorial Chern vectors, and chiral surface states on all surfaces. 2. The strongest evidence is the simultaneous experimental confirmation of: (i) valley-selective outcoupling at −32.9°/0°/+32.9° at 13.8 GHz, (ii) canalized surface states with linear dispersion at 14.6 GHz, and (iii) robust propagation across a sharp corner without intervalley scattering, all obeying the right-hand-thumb rule. 3. The future path lies in extending the concept to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals, enabling 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and advanced imaging/lensing applications.

summary.title: From Words to Wheels: Automated Style-Customized Policy Generation for Autonomous Driving
summary.authors: Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu
summary.field_subfield: Autonomous Driving / Reinforcement Learning / Natural Language Processing
summary.type_of_paper: Research paper introducing a new framework with experimental validation
summary.executive_summary: Words2Wheels addresses the limitation of uniform driving styles in autonomous vehicles by providing a framework that automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands. Current approaches either rely on predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven methods like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that require specific driving data difficult to obtain in scenarios like Robotaxis. Furthermore, these methods cannot generalize to new user commands. Words2Wheels introduces a Style-Customized Reward Function (Style Reward) that bridges user commands to a Style-Customized Driving Policy (Style Policy) via Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The framework employs a Driving Style Database storing rewards, policies, and statistical features, and a Statistical Evaluation module that compares generated styles against natural driving behavior statistics on a reserved test set. The system is tested on the HighD car-following dataset with 15% data reserved for testing. Experimental results show: (1) the aggressive style shows higher speeds and acceleration while conservative shows larger gap and relative speed; (2) when no aligned style exists, generated styles correctly shift metrics (e.g., higher speed for 'late for train'); (3) in a human-in-the-loop comparison with 1,000 events among 10 licensed volunteers, 72% of participants preferred Words2Wheels over IDM; (4) fuzzy memory correctly recalled similar commands in all but one case. The framework is extensible, supports fuzzy memory, and is fully automated, reducing subjective biases.

claims.description: Words2Wheels automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands without prior driving data for style matching.
The Statistical Evaluation module provides objective alignment between generated policies and user commands by comparing statistics to natural driving behavior.
Human participants consistently preferred Words2Wheels-generated driving styles over the IDM baseline in majority of tested cases.

Executive Summary
Words2Wheels addresses the limitation of uniform driving styles in autonomous vehicles by providing a framework that automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands. Current approaches either rely on predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven methods like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that require specific driving data difficult to obtain in scenarios like Robotaxis. Furthermore, these methods cannot generalize to new user commands. Words2Wheels introduces a Style-Customized Reward Function (Style Reward) that bridges user commands to a Style-Customized Driving Policy (Style Policy) via Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The framework employs a Driving Style Database storing rewards, policies, and statistical features, and a Statistical Evaluation module that compares generated styles against natural driving behavior statistics on a reserved test set. The system is tested on the HighD car-following dataset with 15% data reserved for testing. Experimental results show: (1) the aggressive style shows higher speeds and acceleration while conservative shows larger gap and relative speed; (2) when no aligned style exists, generated styles correctly shift metrics (e.g., higher speed for 'late for train'); (3) in a human-in-the-loop comparison with 1,000 events among 10 licensed volunteers, 72% of participants preferred Words2Wheels over IDM; (4) fuzzy memory correctly recalled similar commands in all but one case. The framework is extensible, supports fuzzy memory, and is fully automated, reducing subjective biases.

Research Context
Current autonomous vehicles face significant limitations in delivering command-based driving styles, with many adopting a uniform driving style. Early approaches relied heavily on classification or calibration of predefined styles or driving patterns, which depended heavily on expert input. Data-driven approaches using clustering and Inverse Reinforcement Learning to derive driving policies from natural driving behavior data have gained traction. These data-driven methods require a small amount of driving behavior data to match with a specific driving style, which is difficult in Robotaxi scenarios. Existing methods are limited to selecting from existing styles and cannot customize a style based on user needs, known as the generalization problem. Recent foundation model approaches process user instructions but fall short in adjusting the overall driving policy at the style level. Foundation models in most decision loops raise concerns about reliability and efficiency.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to automatically generate a customized driving policy that aligns with a user-specified driving style expressed in natural language. The authors hypothesize that using a Style-Customized Reward Function (Style Reward) as an intermediate representation can bridge user input to a driving policy without prior driving data. The framework predicts that LLMs with RAG and zero-shot generation capabilities can retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles to new commands. A Statistical Evaluation module is hypothesized to objectively measure alignment by comparing generated styles against natural driving behavior statistics on a reserved test set. The Driving Style Database is expected to enable efficient retrieval and continuous enrichment of driving styles, with new policies replacing existing ones. The authors posit that the framework will outperform predefined methods in accuracy, generalization, and reliability across different command levels. Fuzzy memory via LLMs is hypothesized to enable the system to recognize similar historical commands and reuse associated driving styles.

Methodological Details
The experimental focus is the car-following scenario, a significant portion of driving behavior reflecting diverse driving styles. The experiment utilizes the HighD dataset, collected by a 4K resolution camera mounted on a drone flying over a roadway. Data extraction and the kinematic model for car-following behavior are based on FollowNet. 15% of the data was reserved as a test set to ensure the objectivity of the Statistical Evaluation module. User commands are categorized into three levels based on directness: Level I (Direct), Level II (Indirect with strong hints), and Level III (Indirect with mild hints). The base model is GPT-4o-2024-08-062 with temperature set to 0.3 for deterministic text generation. Hyperparameters include k = 3 for selecting relevant styles and n = 2 for Statistical Evaluation. The Driving Style Database was initially populated with 8 styles: data-driven reward functions from clustering plus IRL and human-designed reward functions. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is employed as the RL algorithm for generating Style Policy from Style Reward. RL training is run 5 times using different seeds, selecting the Style Policy with the highest reward. Statistical metrics include Speed, Time Headway, Relative Speed, Acceleration, Jerk, and Spacing. For customization tests, each command is run 5 times and results are averaged. Data normalization is performed using the 10th and 90th percentiles of natural driving behavior from the test set.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow starts with the LLM selecting the top k relevant style rewards from the Driving Style Database using RAG principles. The Statistical Evaluation module selects the top n statistical metrics most relevant to the user command. The LLM selects a pre-trained reward function that aligns with the user command based on comparison with natural data on the selected metrics. If a selected Style Reward has matched a semantically similar command, the system directly uses its Style Policy; otherwise, the LLM generates m new reward functions. The LLM's generation may involve logic modifications or restructuring beyond simple parameter adjustments to handle generalization. The initially selected Style Reward provides a temporary solution while newly generated reward functions produce new Style Policies via parallelized RL training. The Statistical Evaluation module determines if new policies outperform the temporary one and delivers the best match. Each record in the Driving Style Database includes a Style Reward (programming code), a Style Policy (pre-trained neural network), and analytical data (JSON format). Analytical data can be embedded as high-dimensional vectors to improve LLM retrieval efficiency. User commands are stored in the database to enable the fuzzy memory function. The Statistical Evaluation prompt includes a brief introduction to metrics and natural driving behavior statistics from the test set as a baseline. A Chain-of-Thought approach is used by the LLM for step-by-step analysis in selection. The Statistical Evaluation module outputs in JSON format: {

Key Results
In the customization test, the aggressive style showed higher speeds and greater acceleration while the conservative style maintained a larger gap and relative speed, aligning with expectations. The aggressive style had a larger time headway, and the normal style showed higher jerk, possibly because the LLM did not prioritize these metrics. When no aligned styles were provided, the input 'I’m going to be late for the train' generated a style with higher speed, acceleration, and jerk. The input 'Safety first. I have plenty of time' generated a style with greater spacing, time headway, and relative speed. In the human-in-the-loop comparison of 1,000 tested events, 72% of participants judged Words2Wheels as a better match than IDM. 18.8% of events were rated equally effective, and IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events. By command: 'I’m going to be late for the date' showed 72% prefer Words2Wheels; 'Safety first' showed 79.5% prefer Words2Wheels; 'The cars behind us are honking' showed 72% prefer Words2Wheels. For the generation capability test with only 4 initial styles, results from 5 repeated runs were averaged and confirmed the ability to generate non-matching styles. Across 40 commands, Table III reports 97.5% case count accuracy for Level I, 90% for Level II, and 85% for Level III in generation. In fuzzy memory testing, all test cases except 'It’s snowing and visibility has decreased' were successfully recalled. The system demonstrated a strong ability to recognize and match fuzzy inputs to existing memories.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The framework positions Style Rewards as policy indices in RL, noting they are less complex than user commands or traffic scenarios, enabling efficient retrieval. Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies to align with natural language user commands. The zero-shot capability of LLMs allows generalization to new commands and styles without user behavior data. The extensibility of the framework allows for fuzzy memory via LLMs and continuous expansion of the Driving Style Database. The use of a reserved test set and normalization at 10th/90th percentiles addresses overfitting and provides objective performance benchmarks. The fuzzy memory function demonstrates that semantic similarity in natural language can be mapped to driving style reuse, reducing RL dependency. The human-preference results confirm that human-evaluated style alignment is more discriminative than direct metric comparison.

Contradictions And Limitations
The aggressive style showed a larger time headway and the normal style showed higher jerk, indicating the LLM did not prioritize all relevant metrics correctly. In Case 19, the LLM misinterpreted the user command 'You are allowing a large gap with the vehicle in front'. In Case 26, the LLM intentionally selected the Style Reward with the highest jerk value as a counterexample. When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. The fuzzy memory test failed one case: 'It’s snowing and visibility has decreased'. The framework currently only addresses the car-following scenario, limiting generalizability to complex urban scenes. The Statistical Evaluation module requires a reserved test set; the paper does not specify the exact size or split of the 15% reservation in absolute numbers. The temperature was set to 0.3, which is low, but the paper does not report sensitivity analyses for different temperature values.

Claims
Words2Wheels automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands without prior driving data for style matching. The framework employs a Style-Customized Reward Function that acts as a policy index, enabling retrieval without prior style data. When no aligned style was found in the database, the LLM generated m new reward functions based on the most relevant existing one. The zero-shot capability of LLMs allowed generalization to new commands without user behavior data. In some cases, the LLM misinterpreted user commands or selected counterexamples (Case 19, Case 26). When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. The approach eliminates the need for collecting specific driving data for every style, a major bottleneck in Robotaxi scenarios. New policies can replace existing ones in the database, creating a self-improving style library.
The Statistical Evaluation module provides objective alignment between generated policies and user commands by comparing statistics to natural driving behavior. 15% of data was reserved as a test set to ensure objectivity of the Statistical Evaluation module. The module selects top n statistical metrics, compares policy statistics to natural data, and provides a reliable evaluation. Chain-of-Thought reasoning allows the LLM to explain its selection process in JSON format. The aggressive style showed a larger time headway and the normal style showed higher jerk, suggesting metric prioritization was imperfect. The LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition when values were negative. The module allows for automatic, unbiased evaluation of driving styles without human-in-the-loop for every iteration. Customizing the test set enables fine-tuning based on specific policy data or spatio-temporal filtering.
Human participants consistently preferred Words2Wheels-generated driving styles over the IDM baseline in majority of tested cases. 72% of events showed a preference for Words2Wheels over IDM across all commands. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events. The comparison involved 1,000 events tested by 10 licensed volunteers with 5 user commands each. In 18.8% of events, both models were considered equally effective. Individual commands showed variance: 'Safety first' had 79.5% preference while 'Drive as fast' had 72.5%. Human-in-the-loop validation confirms the practical utility of the framework for user experience. The anonymization of models A and B eliminated observer bias in the comparison.

Data And Code Availability
Code and demo are available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/. Experimental records are available at https://bit.ly/4giYhB7.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
RL training was run 5 times with different seeds, selecting the Style Policy with the highest reward. For generation capability, the initial styles were limited to 4 for better demonstration, and results from 5 repeated runs were averaged. The fuzzy memory test involved 3 experimental sets, each testing 5 similar inputs to assess recall. The Statistical Evaluation module uses a reserved test set to prevent overfitting.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the workflow: User Command → Style Reward (LLM finding best suited function) → Style Policy (satisfying user command). Figure 2 shows the full workflow including RAG, Driving Style Database, and Statistical Evaluation module. Figure 3 provides a step-by-step example of the RAG-based command cognition and reward generation process. Figure 4 is a simplified example of the Statistical Evaluation module prompt. Figure 5 compares normalized style-aware metrics across aggressive, normal, and conservative customized policies. Figure 6 shows the evaluation of generated policies when no aligned styles were provided in the database. Figure 7 presents the user interface for the human-in-the-loop comparison tool. Table I lists the three levels of user commands with examples. Table II reports human preferences across 1,000 tested events on 5 commands. Table III presents case studies across all 40 commands, categorized by level. Table IV presents results for the fuzzy memory function across three experimental sets.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is Words2Wheels, the first framework to automatically generate style-aware driving policies from natural language commands using a Style-Customized Reward Function and a Driving Style Database. 2. The strongest evidence is the human-in-the-loop comparison where 72% of participants preferred Words2Wheels-generated styles over the IDM baseline across 1,000 tested events, combined with the generalization confirmed by the 40-command case study. 3. The future path involves expanding to complex driving scenarios beyond car-following, refining the Statistical Evaluation module, and incorporating a Feedback and Reflection module for self-improving reward functions.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) atoll source GX 9+9 using a single archival AstroSat observation (July 25, 2020) from the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT). The source was detected in the soft/banana state during observation, producing a disk-dominated energy spectrum between 0.7 and 25.0 keV. The authors conducted a flux-resolved spectral analysis across three distinct flux levels (FL1: 450–570 counts/s; FL2: 570–650 counts/s; FL3: 650–770 counts/s) using a joint SXT/LAXPC fit with the model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb). The average inner-disk radius was estimated at 16.57 ± 1.29 km, and total unabsorbed fluxes reached up to 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻². In the temporal domain, no QPOs or prominent broad-band noise (BBN) features were detected in discrete flux levels, but a BBN-like feature centered at ~0.1 Hz was identified in the full-flux PDS (3–20 keV, 0.003–1 Hz). Applying the propagative model of Garg et al., the authors modeled the energy-dependent fractional r.m.s. and phase lag, finding that variations in inner-disk temperature (δkTin ≈ 0.56 ± 0.10%) combined with fractional scattering (δfs ≈ 81 ± 32%) with a positive phase lag (0.11 ± 0.08) best explain the variability. This indicates a perturbation originating in the inner disk moving toward the coronal region. The results are consistent with previously reported flux values but suggest a transitioning toward a softer state as flux increases. The study acknowledges limitations due to single-observation coverage and poor overall data quality for this under-studied source.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary atoll source identified during the Galactic center's sounding rocket mission. It traces a ‘C’-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram, placing it in the atoll source category. Atoll sources exhibit two states: the hard/island state at lower luminosities and the soft/banana state at higher luminosities. The source has a 4.2-hour X-ray and optical waveband modulation and its distance is assumed to be between 5 and 10 kpc. Compact NS parameters are estimated at 0.2–0.45 M⊙ and 0.3–0.6 R⊙. Previous spectral models included power law, blackbody with Comptonization, disk with Comptonized blackbody, and double blackbody with broad iron line. GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, limiting prior comprehensive spectro-temporal characterization. AstroSat's LAXPC offers larger effective area and wider energy coverage compared to the previously used RXTE instrument.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the spectro-temporal properties of GX 9+9 reveal a consistent radiative origin for the observed variability across flux levels. The authors hypothesis that the source in the soft state will show a disk-dominated spectrum within 0.7–25.0 keV and that parameters will evolve systematically with flux. It was predicted that the inner-disk radius, flux, and temperature could be estimated to constrain source characteristics. The hypothesis regarding timing variability expected that BBN-like features might be identifiable via multi-Lorentzian PDS fitting at different flux levels. The study hypothesizes that the propagative model (Garg et al.) could explain the energy-dependent fractional r.m.s. and phase lag by linking spectral parameters to physical parameters. A predicted outcome was that the source, being in the soft/banana state, would show a slight decrease in kT and increase in Tin with rising flux, indicating a transition toward a softer state.

Methodological Details
The study used a single AstroSat archival observation (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774) taken on July 25, 2020. Two instruments were employed: the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT). For spectral analysis, both SXT and LAXPC spectra were combined; for timing analysis, only LAXPC was used due to its microsecond-level resolution. Of the three identical LAXPC counters, counters 10 and 30 suffered abnormal gains from 2018 onwards, so only LAXPC 20 was used. LAXPC operates over 3–80 keV, and SXT works in the low-energy range of 0.3–8.0 keV. SXT data were processed through the AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b pipeline to generate cleaned level-2 event files. The SXT count rate exceeded the pileup threshold of 40 counts/sec, requiring an annular zone with outer radius 13 arcmin and inner radius 2 arcmin. A 2% model systematic error was incorporated for background uncertainty estimation. A gain fit was applied to SXT data with a slope of 1 and free offset within 0.02–0.09. The flux was segregated into three levels: FL1 (450–570 cts/s), FL2 (570–650 cts/s), and FL3 (650–770 cts/s). The energy range for spectral fitting was 0.7–25 keV, and the full-flux timing range was 3–20 keV. The PDS frequency range was 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz due to low statistics beyond 1 Hz and below 0.003 Hz. Spectral fitting used XSPEC (version 12.13.0c) and HEASOFT (6.31.1) with 90% confidence level for parametric errors. The optical depth was frozen at 9, and edge models at 2.4 keV were included to improve the fit.

Procedures And Architectures
The HID was constructed by plotting 3–20 keV count rate against 6–20 keV / 3–6 keV photon count ratio, with 32s binning time. The spectral model used was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), with the cross-calibration 'const' applied to the SXT spectrum while LAXPC 20 constant was fixed at 1. The thermal Comptonization model (ThComp) was used instead of nThComp, extended with 1000 log bins ( The inner-disk radius was calculated using R_{in} = k² (N_{dbb}/cos θ)^(1/2) × D₁₀, with k=1.7, θ=60 degrees, and D=10 kpc. The total unabsorbed flux was estimated via the 'cflux' model in the 0.01–100 keV extended range. The PDS was fitted using a multi-Lorentzian approach at each flux level, and a two-Lorentzian fit was applied to the full-flux PDS. The centroid frequency ν₀ was determined at ~0.04 Hz with HWHM ≈ 0.09 Hz, yielding characteristic frequency ν_c ≈ 0.1 Hz via ν_c = √(ν₀² + HWHM). RMS and phase lag spectra were obtained using the LAXPC subroutine 'laxpc_find_freqlag' at the centroid frequency. The temporal modeling followed the formalism of Garg et al. [29], assuming a truncated disk and a hot electron corona between the inner radius and ISCO. A simple propagating model scenario was tested: varying inner-disk temperature (kTin) and fractional scattering (fs) with a phase lag relative to fs. Additional combinations, including the heating rate and optical depth, were tested but yielded insignificant χ² (>2) and were rejected. The best-fit temporal model retained only the variation in K_{tin} w.r.t. f_s with a positive phase lag.

Key Results
The source was confirmed to be in the soft/banana state based on the HID form in Fig. 1. The total unabsorbed flux in the 0.01–100 keV band was 5.94×10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² for FL1, 6.51×10⁻⁹ for FL2, and 7.30×10⁻⁹ for FL3, increasing with flux level. The maximum flux of 7.30×10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² is comparable to the 7.8×10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² previously reported in the 0.1–100 keV range. The average estimated inner-disk radius (R_{in}) during the observation was 16.57 ± 1.29 km. This value is relatively consistent with the previously reported 27 ± 4 km by Iaria et al. (who used θ ~ 43° and D = 5 kpc). No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected at discrete flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3). A BBN-like feature was identified in the full-flux PDS centering at ~0.04 Hz (centroid) with characteristic frequency ν_c ≈ 0.1 Hz. The rms at ~0.1 Hz increased with energy, while the phase lag showed a decreasing trend with energy. The reduced χ² for the temporal model was ~0.80, but adding heating rate and optical depth increased χ²/dof to >2, rendering those combinations insignificant. The best-fit temporal parameters show a fractional inner-disk temperature variation of 0.56 ± 0.10%, a fractional scattering variation of 81 ± 32%, and a positive phase lag of 0.11 ± 0.08. Spectral parameters show kT_e decreasing slightly (4.14 → 4.12 → 3.69 keV) while T_{in} increases slightly (1.87 → 2.02 → 2.04 keV) across the flux levels, consistent with a softening trend. The best-fit spectral model constant for the SXT instrument was left free for calibration, while LAXPC 20 constant was fixed at 1.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The increase in unabsorbed flux from FL1 to FL3 indicates the source is transitioning toward a softer spectral state. The slight decrease in kT_e and increase in T_{in} across the flux levels support the transition toward the upper banana state. The estimated inner-disk radius of 16.57 ± 1.29 km, when compared to the 27 ± 4 km of Iaria et al., is attributed to different geometric assumptions (θ=60° vs θ≈43° and D=10 kpc vs D=5 kpc). The positive phase lag (0.11 ± 0.08) indicates that the perturbation originates in the inner disk (as a variation in K_{tin}) and moves toward the coronal region (as a variation in the fraction of Comptonized seed photons, fs). The BBN-like feature at ~0.1 Hz, with its rms-energy dependence, supports a propagating emission model consistent with the coronal geometry described by Garg et al. The failure of models including heating rate and optical depth to provide acceptable χ² suggests that the variability is driven primarily by temperature and scattering variations rather than dynamical changes in coronal energetics.

Contradictions And Limitations
The source is noted as 'not a well-studied source,' limiting the baseline for comparison. Only a single archival observation is available, preventing time-evolution studies over multiple epochs. The poor data quality of the source constrains the reliability of the extracted parameters. The PDS shows very low statistics beyond 1 Hz and below 0.003 Hz, limiting the detectable frequency range. The error bars in the phase lag spectra are consistent within data points, making the decreasing trend interpretation less certain. The best-fit spectral χ²/dof values are high (152.95/118, 103.86/111, 120.96/109, 130.33/117), indicating a sub-optimal fit for all flux levels. The model choice of freezing optical depth at 9 is a simplification that may not hold across all flux levels. The distance D is assumed (5–10 kpc) rather than measured, introducing significant uncertainty in the R_{in} calculation.

Claims
The source GX 9+9 is in the soft/banana state and its spectrum is disk-dominated in the 0.7–25 keV range during the AstroSat observation. The HID form in Fig. 1 is consistent with the banana state. The best-fit model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) provides physical spectral parameters. The unabsorbed flux increases from FL1 to FL3, a characteristic of banana state evolution. The spectral model fits still yield high χ²/dof values, indicating some tension between the model and data. The soft state classification guides the choice of spectral components (diskbb over bbodyrad). The transition toward a softer state with increasing flux supports the atoll source evolution model.
The average inner-disk radius is approximately 16.57 ± 1.29 km, consistent with previously reported values under different geometric assumptions. The calculated R_{in} is 16.57 ± 1.29 km using R_{in} = k²(N_{dbb}/cos θ)^(1/2) × D₁₀. The value is consistent with 27 ± 4 km from Iaria et al. given the different inclination and distance. The distance is assumed (5–10 kpc), and the inclination θ=60° is taken from prior literature rather than measured in this observation. The R_{in} value provides a geometrical constraint on the accretion flow near the neutron star. The consistency across different studies with varying parameters validates the geometric interpretation.
BBN-like variability is present in the source, centered at ~0.1 Hz, and is driven by propagating perturbations in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering. A BBN-like feature was identified in the full-flux PDS centered at 0.04 Hz with ν_c ≈ 0.1 Hz. The rms increases with energy while phase lag decreases with energy at ~0.1 Hz. The best-fit temporal model with δkTin and δfs yields a reduced χ² of ~0.80. The positive phase lag of 0.11 ± 0.08 confirms the propagating perturbation direction from disk to corona. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected at discrete flux levels. The error bars in the phase lag spectra are consistent within data points, weakening the certainty of the decreasing trend. The propagating perturbation model (Garg et al.) is supported as the radiative mechanism for this source. The variability is driven by fractional scattering (81 ± 32%) rather than optical depth or heating rate changes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The best-fit spectral model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) was chosen because the pure bbodyrad model yielded χ²/dof > 2. Three flux levels were analyzed independently to test for parameter evolution with rising flux. Ablation: Adding heating rate and optical depth to the temporal model yielded insignificant χ²/dof > 2, leading to their exclusion from the final best-fit. A gain fit with slope 1 and free offset was applied to SXT data, with the offset value typically between 0.02–0.09. The optical depth was frozen at 9 to constrain the model, a simplifying assumption that may limit robustness.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the HID of the source with 32s binning, plotting 3–20 keV count rate against 6–20 keV / 3–6 keV photon count ratio, with different colors for each flux level. Figure 2 presents the best-fit spectrum of FL1, FL2, and FL3 in the 0.7–25 keV range, with SXT data in red and LAXPC 20 in black. Figure 3 (left) shows the PDS fit with two Lorentzians for the full-flux 3–20 keV data, while Figure 3 (right) shows the energy-dependent fractional r.m.s. and phase lag for FL1. Table 1 provides the best-fit spectral parameters (NH, kT_e, fs, T_{in}, N_{dbb}, R_{in}, χ²/dof) for FL1, FL2, FL3, and full flux, as well as energy-dependent temporal model parameters.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first spectro-temporal characterization of GX 9+9 using AstroSat, establishing its soft/banana state classification and measuring its inner-disk radius and flux-resolved spectral parameters. 2. The strongest evidence is the best-fit temporal model (χ² ≈ 0.80) demonstrating that a propagating perturbation originating in the inner disk (δkTin ≈ 0.56%, δfs ≈ 81%) with a positive phase lag (0.11 ± 0.08) explains the BBN-like variability at ~0.1 Hz. 3. The future path requires multi-epoch observations from a variety of missions to track time evolution, as the current single-observation study is constrained by poor data quality and assumed geometric parameters.

summary.title: Dense-TSNet: Dense Connected Two-Stage Structure for Ultra-Lightweight Speech Enhancement
summary.authors: Zizhen Lin, Yuanle Li, Junyu Wang, Ruili Li
summary.field_subfield: Audio Signal Processing / Speech Enhancement
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces Dense-TSNet, an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed for resource-constrained edge devices. The core contribution is a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture that replaces the dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage (TS) framework with densely connected Two-Stage modules. This structural change addresses the uneven loss landscape problem that typically hampers narrow lightweight models, ensuring smoother optimization and improved final performance compared to the baseline. Additionally, the authors propose the Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB), a CNN-based module comprising a Large Kernel Extractor (LKE) for global perspective, Channel Attention (CA) for channel-wise importance weighting, and a Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG) for local spatial feature modeling. The model operates entirely on the magnitude spectrum in the time-frequency domain, producing a magnitude mask multiplied by the noisy input. A key contribution is the introduction of Consistency Magnitude Loss, which computes the minimum distance between the twice-STFTed speech magnitude and the clean magnitude spectrum to ensure perceptual consistency. The authors also investigate the Metric Loss (based on PESQ) and demonstrate that while it can improve objective scores, excessive weighting (P > 200) introduces pseudohallucination artifacts and eventually causes training failure. Dense-TSNet achieves a compact size of approximately 14K parameters—the first speech enhancement model with roughly 10k parameters—outperforming TSTNN, PHASEN, MANNER-S-5.3GF, CCFNet(Lite), and DeepFilterNet in PESQ and MOS-based metrics on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, while also outperforming the classic TS baseline. The work positions itself as a solution for practical deployment on smartphones and cameras where Transformer or Mamba architectures may lack practical adaptability.

Dense-TSNet achieves a compact size of approximately 14K parameters—the first speech enhancement model with roughly 10k parameters—outperforming TSTNN, PHASEN, MANNER-S-5.3GF, CCFNet(Lite), and DeepFilterNet in PESQ and MOS-based metrics on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, while also outperforming the classic TS baseline. The work positions itself as a solution for practical deployment on smartphones and cameras where Transformer or Mamba architectures may lack practical adaptability.

Research Context
Speech enhancement aims to improve speech clarity in noisy environments for applications such as voice calls and automatic speech recognition. Recent research has utilized the Two-Stage (TS) architecture inspired by TSTNN for deep feature extraction. The Classic Two-Stage architecture reshapes and partitions spectral data to address spectral distribution characteristics. In the time-frequency domain, models either focus on amplitude information or enhance complex spectrograms. Loss functions typically compute the Lp-norm distance between estimated and target spectrograms. MetricGAN and related works use learned evaluation metrics from a discriminator to address non-differentiable assessment metrics. Despite strong performance, deep neural network methods incur increased model complexity limiting edge device deployment. New methods like Transformer or Mamba face challenges with optimized deployment operators for real-world use. Single-channel speech enhancement models with around 10k parameters remain limited in existing research.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a densely connected Two-Stage structure can overcome the uneven loss landscape problem in narrow lightweight speech enhancement models. The authors hypothesize that replacing dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules, combined with dense connections, will ensure more robust refinement of the objective function. The hypothesis predicts that the Dense-TSNet will achieve improved final performance addressing early convergence limitations of the baseline model. The research further hypothesizes that incorporating global, channel, and local perspectives through CNN-based MVGB will enhance feature extraction more effectively than the classic approach. A secondary hypothesis explores whether Metric Loss (PESQ-based) can improve perceptual quality without negatively impacting subjective perception. The authors predict that a model with approximately 14K parameters can achieve competitive performance relative to larger state-of-the-art methods.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset known for high-fidelity utterances. Speech samples are segmented into two-second intervals for short-time Fourier transform. The STFT employs an FFT size of 400, window length of 400, and hop length of 100. The training process uses a batch size of 2 with the AdamW optimizer. Training is carried out for up to 1,000,000 steps. The network inputs only the magnitude spectrum and produces a magnitude spectrum mask. For the Dense-TSNet, the input channel count is limited to 4, whereas the classic TS baseline uses 6 channels. The Classic TS model uses 6 channels with approximately 0.92M parameters. The Dense-TSNet has a parameter count of 14K and MAC count of 356M. Evaluation metrics include PESQ ranging from -0.5 to 4.5 and MOS-based metrics (CSIG, CBAK, COVL) ranging from 1 to 5.

Procedures And Architectures
The input speech signal undergoes Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) to convert it into the time-frequency domain. The Dense-TS architecture replaces dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules, creating a network of entirely densely connected Two-Stage modules. Features are mapped to a high-dimensional space using 1×1 convolutions, and the dilated dense block is omitted in favor of direct Two-Stage feature extraction. Each Two-Stage layer receives input channels Ci = dense channel × (i + 1), and the output of the adjustment convolutional layer is Cout = dense channel. The TS-MVGB output is a serial connection: freq-MVGB(time-MVGB(x)), concatenated with skip connections. The final output of the Dense-TS is 0.2 × skip_{depth−1} + x, incorporating an extra residual connection. Features undergo L-Sigmoid activation and 1×1 convolution to decode the magnitude spectrum mask, which is multiplied by the noisy magnitude spectrum. The MVGB consists of three sub-modules: Large Kernel Extractor (LKE), Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG), and Channel Attention (CA). LKE comprises pointwise convolutions, Simple Gate, large kernel depthwise convolutions, Instance Norm, HardSwish, and pointwise convolutions. LSG consists of depth-wise convolution, point-wise convolution, and Learnable-Sigmoid activation, inspired by MP-SENet for mask generation. CA reallocates weights to each channel to focus on important features while suppressing less significant ones.

Key Results
On the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, Dense-TSNet achieves PESQ of 3.05, CSIG of 4.51, CBAK of 3.58, and COVL of 3.86 with 14K parameters. The classic Two-Stage baseline achieves PESQ of 2.96, CSIG of 4.45, CBAK of 3.58, and COVL of 3.78 with 14K parameters. Dense-TSNet outperforms TSTNN (2.96 PESQ), PHASEN (2.99 PESQ), MANNER-S-5.3GF (3.06 PESQ, though slightly lower on other metrics), CCFNet(Lite) (2.87 PESQ), and DeepFilterNet (2.81 PESQ) in competitive PESQ comparisons. In the 6-channel vs 4-channel comparison (similar parameter counts), the PESQ curves show the Dense-TS framework (4-channel) achieves better performance in later stages than the classic Two-Stage (6-channel). Ablation results show removing LKE drops PESQ from 3.05 to 2.79, indicating LKE accounts for 0.26 absolute PESQ points. Removing CA drops PESQ from 3.05 to 2.86, indicating CA contributes 0.19 absolute PESQ points. Removing LSG drops PESQ from 3.05 to 2.97, indicating LSG contributes 0.08 absolute PESQ points. Using only Consistency Magnitude Loss yields PESQ of 3.05; the complex loss baseline yields 2.60 PESQ. With Metric Loss weight P=200, PESQ reaches 3.28, but with P=400 PESQ drops to 3.04 and training fails. Ablation for SSNR shows Dense-TSNet (8.16) versus w/o LKE (8.62), w/o CA (8.91), w/o LSG (8.69), and w/o Consistency Loss (8.79).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dense connections in the narrower model provide a smoother loss landscape, which is the mechanistic explanation for the improved later-stage performance. The Multi-View Gaze approach captures complementary feature perspectives: LKE for global receptive fields, CA for channel-wise selection, and LSG for local spatial invariance. The authors conclude that Metric Loss (based on PESQ) can improve objective scores but at the cost of perceptual quality, as shown by pseudohallucination artifacts. The findings imply that for ultra-lightweight architectures, structural design (dense connections) and effective loss function selection are more critical than simply adding complexity. The work establishes that a speech enhancement model with approximately 10k parameters is feasible for practical edge deployment without substantial performance degradation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The classic Two-Stage architecture converges faster in early stages, whereas Dense-TSNet requires later training to show superiority, introducing a trade-off in training efficiency. Metric Loss with high weighting (P=400) leads to training failure and pseudohallucination artifacts, limiting the applicability of perceptual metrics as direct loss components. The ablation shows that removing Consistency Loss only reduces PESQ from 3.05 to 2.96, suggesting its individual contribution (0.09 PESQ) is smaller than the structural components. The paper does not report the exact training duration in epochs, only total steps (1,000,000). The random seed and exact train/test split ratio are not specified, limiting reproducibility. The MAC count (356M) is provided for Dense-TSNet but not for the classic TS baseline (listed as 388M, yet parameters are equal), creating a slight ambiguity in computation-to-parameter efficiency.

Claims
Dense-TSNet achieves competitive PESQ performance with a compact model of only 14K parameters, making it the first such model in the field. Table I shows Dense-TSNet achieves 3.05 PESQ with 14K parameters, outperforming TSTNN, PHASEN, and DeepFilterNet. The ablation study confirms each MVGB component contributes positively to PESQ. The PESQ score for Dense-TSNet (3.05) exceeds the classic TS baseline (2.96) at the same parameter count. MANNER-S-5.3GF achieves a higher PESQ of 3.06, although its CSIG is slightly lower. The classic TS converges faster in early training stages, which may be less desirable for time-constrained training. This enables deployment on resource-constrained edge devices such as smartphones and cameras. The work opens the path for further model compression techniques.
The Dense-TS architecture addresses the uneven loss landscape problem in narrow lightweight models through dense connections. Figure 4 shows that Dense-TS outperforms Classic TS in later training stages with similar parameter counts. The authors attribute the improvement to the smoother loss landscape provided by dense connections. The ablation without Consistency Loss shows only a minimal PESQ drop (0.09), suggesting the dense structure alone is not the sole driver. Dense connectivity can serve as a structural regularizer for narrow networks.

Data And Code Availability
Source codes will be released after paper acceptance, and audio samples are available at the provided GitHub repository. The GitHub repository is hosted at https://github.com/huaidanquede/Dense-TSNet.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
An ablation study on the MVGB module shows LKE contributes 0.26 PESQ, CA contributes 0.19 PESQ, and LSG contributes 0.08 PESQ relative to the full model. A separate ablation validates the effect of the Consistency method on magnitude loss, showing removal drops PESQ from 3.05 to 2.96. The loss function study (Table III) shows only the complex loss achieves 2.60 PESQ, significantly worse than the Consistency Magnitude Loss (3.05). Increasing the Metric Loss weight P from 1 to 200 improves PESQ from 3.05 to 3.28, but P=400 causes training failure and pseudohallucination.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the overall architecture of Classic Two-Stage and Dense-TS, showing the structural differences. Figure 2 displays the internal details of the LKE, LSG, and CA sub-modules within MVGB. Figure 3 presents the training criteria of the proposed Dense-TSNet, illustrating the Consistency Magnitude Loss and Metric Loss formulations. Figure 4 shows the training curves of Dense-TS (4-channel) and Classic-TS (6-channel) comparing PESQ convergence over steps. Figure 5 displays the training curves showing a pseudohallucination distortion at P=200 and the LMagConsis only curve. Table I compares Dense-TSNet against TSTNN, PHASEN, MANNER-S-5.3GF, CCFNet(Lite), and DeepFilterNet on VoiceBank+DEMAND. Table II presents ablation study results for MVGB components (w/o LKE, w/o CA, w/o LSG) and Consistency Loss on VoiceBank+DEMAND. Table III studies the impact of different loss functions (Only Consistency Mag. with varying P, Only complex) on PESQ and magnitude errors.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is Dense-TSNet, an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement model with approximately 14K parameters that uses a densely connected Two-Stage architecture and a Multi-View Gaze Block to address the uneven loss landscape of narrow models. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative superiority over the classic TS baseline (3.05 vs 2.96 PESQ) and prior lightweight models (TSTNN, DeepFilterNet, etc.) at equal or lower parameter counts, plus the ablation showing clear positive contributions from each MVGB component. 3. The future path includes exploring further model compression techniques and potentially refining the Metric Loss integration, as the authors noted that while PESQ increases with P, perceptual artifacts appear and training eventually fails.

summary.authors: Yu Chen, Marin Biloš, Sarthak Mittal, Wei Deng, Kashif Rasul, Anderson Schneider
summary.field_subfield: Machine Learning / Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary.type_of_paper: Research paper presenting a novel generative model for time series forecasting
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces Recurrent Interpolants, a novel framework that combines the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models (specifically stochastic interpolants) for multivariate time series forecasting. The authors address a key scalability gap: while diffusion and flow-based models capture complex high-dimensional distributions well, their model size scales with both feature dimension and time-window length, making them computationally demanding. The proposed method uses an RNN to encode a large context window into a fixed-size history prompt, which then guides a conditional stochastic interpolant to generate the next time step's distribution. This design inherits the efficient training of RNNs while leveraging the expressive conditional generation of stochastic interpolants. The method is theoretically grounded in an extension of stochastic interpolant theory to arbitrary joint distributions with extra control features (Theorem 1). Empirically, the approach is validated on synthetic 2D datasets (Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) using Wasserstein distance, Sliced Wasserstein Distance, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy, showing it matches or exceeds DDPM, SGM, and Flow Matching baselines. The paper also demonstrates that SI is robust across different interpolant schedules (sqrt, trig, quad) and shows visually superior uncertainty capture on the Solar dataset (6/137 dimensions). The code will be made available upon camera-ready publication.
