judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces Recurrent Interpolants, a novel framework that combines the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models (specifically stochastic interpolants) for multivariate time series forecasting. The authors address a key scalability gap: while diffusion and flow-based models capture complex high-dimensional distributions well, their model size scales with both feature dimension and time-window length, making them computationally demanding. The proposed method uses an RNN to encode a large context window into a fixed-size history prompt, which then guides a conditional stochastic interpolant to generate the next time step's distribution. This design inherits the efficient training of RNNs while leveraging the expressive conditional generation of stochastic interpolants. The method is theoretically grounded in an extension of stochastic interpolant theory to arbitrary joint distributions with extra control features (Theorem 1). Empirically, the approach is validated on synthetic 2D datasets (Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) using Wasserstein distance, Sliced Wasserstein Distance, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy, showing it matches or exceeds DDPM, SGM, and Flow Matching baselines. On four real-world multivariate forecasting datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki), the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on three out of four datasets using CRPS-sum, outperforming or matching DDPM, SGM, and FM-based models, and substantially beating the pure recurrent baseline Vec-LSTM. The paper also demonstrates that SI is robust across different interpolant schedules (sqrt, trig, quad) and shows visually superior uncertainty capture on the Solar dataset (6/137 dimensions). The code will be made available upon camera-ready publication.

Research Context
Recurrent neural networks and transformer models have become de facto tools for multivariate time series forecasting with applications in finance, biology, medicine, and geophysical applications. While these methods capture sequential dependencies, probabilistic output layers are confined to simple probability families because density parameterization must be differentiable. To capture sophisticated distributions and cross-feature dependencies, generative models using diffusion, flow-based methods, and neural SDEs have been proposed for time series imputation and forecasting. However, generative model predictors suffer from scalability issues because model size is related to both feature dimension and window size, unlike recurrent models where size is proportional only to the number of features. A more computationally friendly framework is needed for large-scale generative model-based time series prediction problems. If the generative procedure starts from an initial distribution proximate to the terminal data distribution, it can alleviate learning challenges and reduce inference complexity. Time series data is typically continuous and neighboring time points exhibit strong correlations, indicating the distribution of future time points is close to the current time point.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a framework blending recurrent neural network computational efficiency with diffusion-style stochastic interpolant modeling address the scalability-quality trade-off in probabilistic time series forecasting? The central hypothesis is that initiating prediction of future time point distributions from the current time point (rather than from pure noise) is more straightforward and yields better quality. The authors further hypothesize that longer temporal dependencies can be encoded by an RNN while the embedded history serves as guidance for conditional generation of future points. The framework is expected to benefit from efficient training inherited from the RNN while enjoying high-quality probabilistic modeling empowered by the diffusion model. A secondary question is whether stochastic interpolants outperform DDPM, Score-based generative models, and Flow Matching as the generative module for time series prediction. The authors predict that their SI-based model will achieve competitive or superior performance across real-world multivariate datasets compared to both pure generative and pure recurrent baselines.

Methodological Details
The study employs synthetic two-dimensional datasets including Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll for initial verification. These synthetic datasets were sourced from Chen et al. (2021) and Lipman et al. (2022), using their published code repositories. The real-world forecasting datasets consist of Solar, Exchange, Traffic (PEMS-SF), and Wiki datasets, commonly used in probabilistic forecasting tasks. Data preprocessing follows the steps established in Salinas et al. (2019). The generative models are trained to learn the conditional probability p(x_{t+1}|x_{t-P:t}) representing the multi-variate time series at time t+1 given context window of size P. In the training phase, the model learns the joint distribution p(x_{t+1}, x_t|x_{t-P:t-1}) where x_t ~ ρ_0 and x_{t+1} ~ ρ_1, with equal marginals. A recurrent neural network encodes the context xt−P:t−1 into a fixed history prompt h_t, which serves as the condition embedding. For the time series task, the generative model can not directly map the whole context to the target due to different vector sizes; thus an RNN is used as an intermediary. Importance sampling is leveraged to stabilize training, using a Beta distribution as the proposal distribution for the diffusion time integral. To ensure fair comparison, all models use the same neural network architectures for their field functions (noise prediction in DDPM, score in SGM, vector field in FM, velocity/score in SI). Hyperparameters including batch size, training epochs, and model parameters are held constant across all generative baselines. Multiple schedulers for the stochastic interpolant are tested: square root γ(s)=sqrt(2s(1-s)), quad γ(s)=s(1-s), and trig γ(s)=sin(πs)^2. Evaluation metrics include CRPS-sum, NRMSE via sample median, and point-metrics normalized deviance (ND), all using smaller values for better performance.

Procedures And Architectures
The model follows a time-Grad architecture where an RNN produces a hidden representation and the SI module performs conditional generation. The SI module implements a stochastic mapping x_s = α(s)x_0 + β(s)x_1 + γ(s)z, where s ∈ [0,1], z ∼ N(0,I), and α, β, γ are interpolant schedules. Boundary conditions are α(0)=1, α(1)=0, β(0)=0, β(1)=1, and γ(0)=γ(1)=0, so the ends are fixed at x_0 and x_1. The velocity function b(s,x) and score function s(s,x) are modeled by deep neural networks. Training minimizes the MSE losses for velocity L_b and score L_s over s sampled from Beta(0.1, 0.1). The velocity loss L_b penalizes the difference between the learned velocity and the analytic expectation: |∥b̂(s,x_s)||^2 - (ẑα x_0 + ẑβ x_1 + ẑγ z)^T b̂. The score loss L_s penalizes the score function using the auxiliary variable z: |∥ŝ(s,x_s)||^2 + γ^-1 z^T ŝ. During inference, the RNN generates h_t, then the forward SDE dx_s = [b(s,x,h) + ϵ(s)s(s,x,h)]ds + sqrt(2ϵ)dw is solved from s=0 to s=1. For multi-step prediction, the prediction is run recursively: the output of step t+1 becomes the context for step t+2. The SDE solver is discretized, with the forward SDE starting at the context vector xt as the sample at s=0 and producing xt+1 at s=1. For the SGM baseline, the framework is modified by replacing context xt with Gaussian noise, while for FM the denoising objective is replaced with the flow matching objective. The diffusion variance ϵ(s) is a tunable hyperparameter used in the SDE integral. The proof of Theorem 1 shows the density ρ_t satisfies the transport equation ∂_sρ + ∇·(bρ) = 0 with velocity b defined as an expectation.

Key Results
On synthetic datasets using Wasserstein distance, the SI (trig, linear) model achieves the lowest distance of 0.16 across 8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll. The DDPM (cosine) model performs poorly on Circles with Wasserstein distance of 0.258 compared to SI (trig, linear) at 0.16. The SGM model achieves 1.10 Wasserstein distance on 8gaussians, while SI (trig, linear) achieves 0.52. On the real-world Solar dataset, the SI model achieves a CRPS-sum of 0.359±0.06, outperforming FM (0.419±0.027) and SGM (0.364±0.029) while matching DDPM (0.359±0.061). On the Exchange dataset, the SI model achieves a CRPS-sum of 0.083±0.005, beating DDPM (0.084±0.023) and SGM (0.071±0.05). On the Traffic dataset, the FM model achieves the best CRPS-sum of 0.038±0.002, while SI is 0.080±0.007. On the Wiki dataset, the SI model achieves a CRPS-sum of 0.133±0.002, outperforming FM (0.15±0.002) and DDPM (0.15). The SI model outperforms or matches all generative baselines on three out of four real-world forecasting datasets. Compared to the pure recurrent baseline Vec-LSTM, the SI model (CRPS-sum 0.083±0.005 on Exchange) substantially improves upon Vec-LSTM (0.391±0.017). On the Wiki dataset, FM fails to capture the data distribution, with a CRPS-sum of 0.15 versus SI's 0.133±0.002. Figure 4 demonstrates that the SI model makes precise predictions and captures uncertainty even when the scale of different dimensions (137 total) varies significantly. The model's 90th confidence interval is shown for 6 of 137 dimensions on the Solar dataset, indicating well-calibrated uncertainty. The median prediction line is visible at 100 units for some dimensions, illustrating centered forecasting. Different gamma-interpolant combinations (sqrt, trig, quad) all achieve good results in modeling the target distribution.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The success of the model implies that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction, more so than pure autoregressive prediction. The RNN-plus-SI architecture shows that temporal dependency (captured by the RNN) and cross-feature distribution (captured by SI) can be decoupled into two complementary modules. The generative approach succeeds because the future time point's distribution is proximate to the current time point's, which is a characteristic of continuous time series data. Theorem 1 generalizes stochastic interpolant theory to arbitrary joint distributions with extra control features, proving the theoretical validity of the conditional generation framework. The model is described as a  The work suggests that stochastic interpolants offer a more stable alternative to flow matching by learning the vector field directly rather than the score, potentially simplifying inference. The result on Wiki where FM fails but SI succeeds suggests that the SDE-based interpolation is more robust to complex, multimodal distributions than direct flow matching. The framework opens a path for future developments in dynamic field where RNNs and diffusion models are combined for generative time series modeling.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors state they were unable to obtain satisfying results when searching over flow matching hyperparameters on real datasets. On the Traffic dataset, the FM model outperforms the SI model (0.038±0.002 vs 0.080±0.007), representing the only case where SI does not win. The loss values become larger when s is close to two ends, necessitating the use of importance sampling which may introduce bias or variance. The inference requires solving an SDE integral, which adds computational overhead compared to direct RNN inference, though the authors argue the RNN's efficiency partially offsets this. The model relies on the assumption that ρ_0 = ρ_1, which may not hold for time series with strong trend or seasonality that changes the marginal distribution over time. The authors note that they use a fixed RNN architecture for all generative baselines, which may not be the optimal parameterization for each specific model type. The paper does not report the specific computational time or memory requirements, leaving the true  The code is only promised for the camera-ready version, limiting reproducibility for the current preprint. The analysis in the appendix is referenced but the full content is not available in this preprint, limiting validation of the theorem proofs.

Claims
Recurrent Interpolants effectively combine RNN computational efficiency with diffusion-model probabilistic quality for time series forecasting. The model achieves CRPS-sum 0.359±0.06 on Solar, outperforming or matching all diffusion-based baselines. The SI model beats the pure RNN baseline Vec-LSTM by over 50% on the Exchange dataset. The model captures uncertainty across 137 variate dimensions with well-calibrated 90th confidence intervals. The SI model outperforms FM on the Wiki dataset where FM cannot capture the distribution. The FM model achieves better CRPS-sum (0.038±0.002) than SI (0.080±0.007) on the Traffic dataset. The authors admit they could not find satisfying flow matching hyperparameters, limiting their conclusion about FM superiority. The framework could be extended to broader generative tasks beyond time series forecasting. The decoupling of temporal dependency and distribution modeling may inform future architecture design in both RNNs and diffusion models.
Stochastic interpolants are a theoretically sound and empirically competitive generative module for conditional time series prediction. Theorem 1 proves the extension to arbitrary joint distributions with control features. Multiple gamma-interpolant schedules all achieve good results, showing robustness to scheduling choices. Wasserstein distance on synthetic data confirms SI is in the same regime as DDPM and SGM. The SGM model's CRPS-sum of 0.364±0.029 on Solar is nearly identical to SI's 0.359±0.06, with overlapping confidence intervals. The authors note that the score function and velocity function need to be learned as neural networks, introducing approximation error. SI provides a plug-and-play generative module that can replace DDPM or FM in various conditional forecasting settings. The theoretical foundation supports use in high-dimensional settings where direct density estimation is intractable.

Data And Code Availability
The authors state they will publish the code for the camera-ready version of the paper. The synthetic data was sourced from existing repositories of Chen et al. (2021) and Lipman et al. (2022). No specific code repository link is provided in this preprint version.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors test three different gamma-functions for the SI model: sqrt, quad, and trig. Most gamma-interpolant function combinations are shown to achieve good results in modeling the target distribution on synthetic data. The models are evaluated across four real-world datasets, demonstrating cross-dataset generalization. The RNN is used as a fixed encoder for all generative baselines to isolate the performance of the field function module. The SDE integral is solved with a configurable diffusion variance ϵ(s). The authors note that the loss values increase near the interpolation ends, which they address with Beta-distribution importance sampling.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows three interpolant schedules: α(s), β(s), and γ(s), illustrating the deterministic and stochastic components. Figure 2 illustrates the time-Grad model architecture combining RNN and diffusion for conditional time series prediction. Figure 3 presents generated samples from DDPM, SGM, FM, and SI on synthetic two-dimensional datasets. Figure 4 demonstrates forecast paths on the Solar dataset showing median prediction and 50th/90th confidence intervals. Figure 5 shows the conditional time series prediction pipeline with RNN followed by diffusion module. Table 1 reports Wasserstein distance for all models across 8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll. Table 2 reports CRPS-sum for all models across Solar, Exchange, Traffic, and Wiki datasets.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Recurrent Interpolants framework: a hybrid architecture that uses an RNN to encode context into a fixed-size history prompt, enabling a computationally-efficient SDE-based generation of future time-step distributions using stochastic interpolants. 2. The strongest evidence is the empirical performance across four real-world multivariate datasets, where the SI model achieves state-of-the-art CRPS-sum on three of four datasets and substantially outperforms the pure RNN baseline (Vec-LSTM) while matching or exceeding DDPM and SGM. 3. The future path is the extension of the conditional stochastic interpolant framework to broader applications including multivariate distribution transport and integration with other generative models for long-horizon time series forecasting.

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid; Nicolò Pianta; Simone Bonizzoni; Piercarlo Mustarelli; Riccardo Ruffo
summary.field_subfield: Energy Chemistry / Aqueous Electrolytes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental research article reporting physicochemical and electrochemical characterization of a novel binary electrolyte system with electrode application
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive characterization of a binary aqueous electrolyte system comprising 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH₃COOK (KAc) and variable amounts of CH₃COONa (NaAc), with the highest concentration at 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc (7N20K). The electrolyte was evaluated for its thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties, demonstrating that the most concentrated composition (7N20K) achieves the optimal compromise between ionic conductivity and electrochemical stability. Key findings include a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C, a stability window extending up to 3 V under flooded-cell conditions with glassy carbon electrodes, and a Tg shifting toward higher temperatures as salt concentration increases, consistent with a transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior. The electrolyte was tested in a sodium-ion battery configuration using carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (NASICON) as a cathode material. The 7N20K-CLTP system achieved a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, an average charge efficiency of 96%, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles, with a remarkably low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. EIS analysis revealed a diffusion coefficient of approximately 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹ at room temperature and a diffusion activation energy of 0.48 eV. These results demonstrate that highly concentrated acetate binary systems can support reversible sodium-ion intercalation with improved kinetics and stability compared to diluted aqueous electrolytes, positioning the water-in-salt approach as a viable candidate for safe, low-cost aqueous sodium-ion battery chemistries.

The electrolyte was tested in a sodium-ion battery configuration using carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (NASICON) as a cathode material. The 7N20K-CLTP system achieved a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, an average charge efficiency of 96%, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles, with a remarkably low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. EIS analysis revealed a diffusion coefficient of approximately 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹ at room temperature and a diffusion activation energy of 0.48 eV. These results demonstrate that highly concentrated acetate binary systems can support reversible sodium-ion intercalation with improved kinetics and stability compared to diluted aqueous electrolytes, positioning the water-in-salt approach as a viable candidate for safe, low-cost aqueous sodium-ion battery chemistries.

Research Context
Conventional lithium-ion batteries using non-aqueous organic carbonate electrolytes suffer from low flashpoints, high melting points, and high viscosities that render them ineffective at lower temperatures. The non-aqueous organic electrolyte LiPF₆ is thermally unstable and decomposes in the presence of moisture to produce HF, which corrodes battery components. Aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety, low cost, and environmental friendliness, but their wide electrochemical stability window (ESW) is restricted to approximately 1.23 V. Kinetic extension of the ESW to 1.5 V using diluted salt solutions still cannot compete with organic counterparts in terms of energy density. The water-in-salt electrolyte (WISE) concept, pioneered by dissolving LiTFSI in water up to 21 mol kg⁻¹, enables a voltage window of 3 V due to low water activity and ion clustering. Fluorinated salts like LiTFSI exhibit severe oral, dermal, and chronic aquatic toxicity, while their limited availability and high cost practicaly nullify the advantages of super-concentration. Highly soluble and widely available salts such as CH₃COOK (KAc) and CH₃COONa (NaAc) represent cost-effective alternatives for water-in-salt electrolyte formulations. A fundamental understanding of the physicochemical properties of aqueous acetate binary systems at high concentrations is still lacking in the literature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a binary CH₃COOK/CH₃COONa system can maintain sufficient ionic conductivity and broad electrochemical stability at 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc plus 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc to enable practical sodium-ion battery operation. The authors hypothesize that the high acetate concentration will suppress the activity of water molecules, extending the electrochemical stability window while maintaining workable ionic transport and rheological properties. It is further hypothesized that the 7N20K composition, as the most concentrated in the series, will represent the best compromise between transport properties and the electrochemical stability window. The sodium-ion intercalation into carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (NASICON) was predicted to be reversible with good kinetic properties, evidenced by low activation energy and stable capacity over cycling. The study aims to confirm that the water-in-salt behavior (water-in-salt structure formation) is the underlying mechanism for enhanced ESW and the observed correlation between Tg, viscosity, and ionic conductivity.

Methodological Details
Four electrolytes were prepared by dissolving NaAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) and KAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) in high-quality Milli-Q water (conductivity σ = 6.7 μS cm⁻¹) under sonication. The KAc concentration was held constant at 20 mol kg⁻¹, while NaAc was varied at 1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹, yielding the compositions 1N20K, 2.5N20K, 5N20K, and 7N20K. A 1 M NaAc solution was prepared as a diluted benchmark for comparison. Carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (CLTP) was synthesized via a one-pot solvogel route using 1.78 g NH₄H₂(PO₄)₃, 3.51 g Ti(OC₄H₉)₄, 0.52 g CH₃COOLi·2H₂O, and 0.58 g C₆H₁₂O₆. The precursor mixture was stirred for 4 h at 55°C, dried at 100°C under vacuum, and calcined at 800°C for 6 h under argon flux in a tubular furnace with a ramp rate of 5°C min⁻¹ and gas flow of 50 ml min⁻¹. Pristine LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (LTP) was synthesized using the same route without the carbon source C₆H₁₂O₆ for comparative analysis. XRD analysis was performed using a Rigaku Miniflex 600 equipped with a Cu cathode, in a 2θ range of 10° to 80° with step size 0.02° and scan speed 1 deg min⁻¹. SEM characterization was conducted using a Zeiss Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity measurements were performed with an MCR Rheometer 102 (Anthon Paar) using a 50 mm parallel plate setup at shear rates of 10–300 s⁻¹ at temperatures of 10, 20, 30, and 40°C. DSC analysis was conducted with a DSC 1Star (Mettler Toledo) across a temperature range of -120°C to 90°C with a heating/cooling rate of 1°C min⁻¹. Conductivity measurements used EIS with a dip probe cell having two platinum foils, cell factor 1.04 cm⁻¹, frequency range 1 Hz to 200 kHz, and 25 mV amplitude, under N₂ flux from 5°C to 70°C. NASICON electrode slurries for organic electrolyte benchmarking were prepared in weight ratio 8:1:1 of active material, PVDF binder, and carbon black in N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone, cast on Al foils in R2032 coin cells. The active material loads in coin cells were ~2.4 mg cm⁻², ~2.7 mg cm⁻², and ~1.7 mg cm⁻² for Li, Na, and K cells, respectively. For aqueous electrolyte measurements, the NASICON electrodes were dip-coated onto carbon cloth current collectors, yielding an active material load of ~6 mg cm⁻². ESW estimation used flooded three-electrode flooded cells with glassy carbon working, platinum mesh counter, and double-junction SCE reference electrodes. GCPL measurements progressed through current rates of 0.1 C, 0.5 C, 1 C, 5 C, and 10 C, with 10 cycles at each, and 1 C defined as 136 mA g⁻¹ for two-ion insertion. EIS for kinetics was conducted at 20°C to 70°C in a 1 kHz to 100 kHz frequency range with 50 mV amplitude in a Faraday cage.

Procedures And Architectures
Electrolytes were prepared by dissolving NaAc and KAc in Milli-Q water under sonication, maintaining KAc at 20 mol kg⁻¹ and varying NaAc from 1 to 7 mol kg⁻¹. The CLTP synthesis followed a one-pot solvogel procedure: dissolution of phosphate precursor in ethanol, addition of Ti source, lithium and carbon sources, stirring at 55°C, drying at 100°C, grinding, and calcination at 800°C. DSC protocol: cooling from 30°C to -120°C at 1°C min⁻¹, 5-minute isotherm at -120°C, and heating to 90°C at 1°C min⁻¹ after 30-minute equilibration at 30°C. Viscosity shear tests were performed at steady-state with parallel plate geometry at 10, 20, 30, and 40°C across 10–300 s⁻¹ shear rates. Conductivity was measured via EIS in a climatic chamber under N₂ flux, with bulk ohmic resistance identified as the x-axis intercept of the high-frequency Nyquist plot. LSV for ESW determination used a threshold of 0.1 mA cm⁻² on a glassy carbon electrode, with the note that the small surface area and electrocatalytic nature may overestimate limits. GCPL was performed in flooded three-electrode cells, with the aqueous electrolyte measurements using a Pt foil as reference and counter electrodes in a flooded configuration. EIS for interface kinetics used a partially sodiated CLTP electrode; the measurement was interrupted during de-sodiation at the middle of the first plateau, with spectra collected at 10°C intervals. EIS spectra were analyzed to extract charge-transfer resistance at infinite temperature and activation energy through an Arrhenius plot. The diffusion coefficient was calculated from the Warburg coefficient using the formula incorporating the gas constant, surface area, Faraday constant, and concentration (12930 mol m⁻³). Walden plots were constructed by plotting molar conductivity against fluidity (η⁻¹) at multiple temperatures to assess ionicity. Kohlrausch's law analysis was applied to the 7N20K solution at 25°C to verify complete salt dissociation.

Key Results
DSC showed the glass transition temperature (Tg) below -70°C, cold crystallization exotherms (Tc) below -20°C, and melting endotherms (Tm) around 0°C for all samples. Increasing salt concentration shifted Tg to higher temperatures, and 1N20K and 2.5N20K showed no cold crystallization or melting endotherm, indicating they were frozen in the glassy state. 5N20K showed a cold crystallization event at -28.06°C and 7N20K at -33.70°C, with melting endotherms both around 0°C. The ionic conductivity of 7N20K reached 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C, comparable to organic electrolytes despite the high concentration. Ionic conductivity decreased monotonically with increasing concentration, following VTF behavior with a pseudo-activation energy (Ea) that increased with concentration. Viscosity followed an Arrhenius behavior over the measured temperature range and increased with concentration, without decreasing at any concentration, classifying acetates as structure-making salts. All electrolytes behaved as Newtonian fluids in viscosity measurements, as confirmed by Supplementary Figures S1–S4. The activation energy from viscosity measurements matched the Ea from conductivity and the Tg behavior, confirming correlated mechanisms for transport and rheology. Walden plots classified all electrolytes as quasi-ideal, and the 7N20K solution at 25°C followed Kohlrausch's law with a molar conductivity at infinite dilution of 52.90 ohm⁻¹ cm² mol⁻¹. The cathodic ESW increased significantly with salt concentration, suppressing hydrogen evolution and confirming reduced water activity. The anodic ESW expansion was not as significant as on the cathodic side, consistent with prior acetate electrolyte studies. In 7N20K/CLTP, sodium preferentially inserted into the NASICON structure despite sodium concentration being 2.85 times lower than potassium concentration. At the first cycle in 7N20K, CLTP delivered a cathodic capacity of 104 mAh g⁻¹ and anodic capacity of 84 mAh g⁻¹ (80% efficiency), while in 1 M NaAc these values were 96 and 36 mAh g⁻¹ (40% efficiency), respectively. At 1 C (136 mA g⁻¹), CLTP in 7N20K provided average anodic capacity of 68 mAh g⁻¹ with 99.0% average charge efficiency. Capacity retention after 60 cycles in 7N20K was 90%. EIS revealed a charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV at the NASICON/7N20K interface, indicating very good kinetic properties. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was approximately 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹, and the diffusion activation energy was 0.48 eV.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Tg shift to higher temperatures with concentration marks a transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior, where ions outnumber water molecules available for solvation. The water-in-salt structure formation means available water cannot effectively shell cations, promoting anion-cation interaction and modifying local hydrogen bonding without significant reassociation. Reduced water activity, evidenced by suppressed hydrogen evolution and Tg behavior, underlies the ESW expansion and improved interfacial stability. The quasi-ideal behavior on Walden plots confirms that acetate electrolytes maintain high dissociation even at extreme concentrations, supporting the Kohlrausch law applicability. The low charge-transfer activation energy (0.12 eV) indicates that the aqueous concentrated electrolyte optimizes the NASICON/electrolyte interface, reducing barriers to faradaic processes. The fact that carbon coating does not affect the crystal structure but preferentially accommodates Na⁺ suggests that in mixed Na⁺/K⁺ systems, Na⁺ is thermodynamically preferred in the NASICON lattice due to its smaller ionic radius. These results provide a proof-of-concept that highly concentrated aqueous acetate systems can rival organic electrolytes in both stability and kinetics for alkaline ion battery applications.

Contradictions And Limitations
The LSV ESW estimation used a glassy carbon electrode with small surface area and high electrocatalytic activity in a flooded cell, which the authors acknowledge may lead to overestimated decomposition limits. The temperature range explored for conductivity (5–70°C) and EIS (20–70°C) is relatively narrow, limiting full extrapolation of VTF and Arrhenius trends. Viscosity measurements could not be extrapolated to lower temperatures due to instrumental limitations, and the simple Arrhenius fit was used as a pragmatic alternative to the VTF equation. The paper reports only a proof-of-concept demonstration with a single electrode material (CLTP) and four electrolyte concentrations; broader compatibility with different NASICON chemistries and other anode materials is not tested. Long-term cycling beyond 60 cycles was not performed, and no post-mortem analysis of the electrode or electrolyte decomposition products was presented.

Claims
The 7N20K (7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc) electrolyte provides the optimal balance of ionic conductivity, rheological behavior, and electrochemical stability for sodium-ion battery applications among the tested concentrations. The conductivity reached 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C, comparable to organic electrolyte benchmarks. The cathodic ESW expanded with increasing NaAc concentration, suppressing hydrogen evolution. The lowest liquidus temperature (Tc at -33.70°C and Tm at 0°C) for 7N20K reduces risk of premature failure from salt crystallization during cycling. The anodic ESW expansion was not as substantial as the cathodic, limiting the positive voltage reach. This identifies the KAc/NaAc binary system as a viable cost-effective water-in-salt electrolyte candidate for aqueous sodium-ion batteries.
The NASICON/7N20K electrolyte interface exhibits excellent charge-transfer kinetics with a very low activation energy (0.12 eV) and good ion diffusion (10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹). EIS analysis yielded an activation energy of 0.12 eV for charge transfer at the NASICON/7N20K interface. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was approximately 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹. The diffusion activation energy of 0.48 eV indicates that diffusion can be easily improved by increasing temperature. The EIS was performed on a partially sodiated electrode with a single concentration, and temperature-dependence of the interface was not investigated at higher current rates. Low interfacial resistance at the electrolyte/electrode boundary enables fast charge/discharge rates in aqueous sodium-ion cells.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information is available free of charge, including shear stress vs shear rate curves, XRPD patterns, SEM images, and additional electrochemical characterization in organic electrolytes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A 1 M NaAc control electrolyte was tested to demonstrate the specific benefit of the WISE approach. A pristine LTP (no carbon coating) was synthesized in parallel to verify the role of carbon on electrochemical performance. All electrolyte samples behaved as Newtonian fluids, confirmed in Supplementary Figures S1–S4. EIS was performed in a Faraday cage to eliminate surrounding interference. The NASICON electrodes were characterized in benchmark organic electrolytes (1.0 M LiPF₆ in EC/DMC, 1 M NaClO₄ in PC/FEC, 0.8 M KPF₆ in EC/DEC) before aqueous testing.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 lists the electrolytes with compositional parameters, including molar concentrations and salt ratios. Table 2 reports molar conductivities, Ea values from viscosity and conductivity, T°, Tg values, and liquidus temperatures. Table 3 summarizes cathodic and anodic decomposition potentials for all samples against SHE. Figure 1 shows DSC curves of electrolytes, with concentration increasing from top to bottom. Figure 2a displays ionic conductivity vs. temperature; Figure 2b shows conductivity vs. concentration. Figure 3a presents viscosity vs. temperature (Arrhenius behavior); Figure 3b shows viscosity vs. concentration. Figure 4a presents Walden plots (molar conductivity vs. fluidity) showing quasi-ideal behavior; Figure 4b shows the Kohlrausch plot for 7N20K at 25°C. Figure 5 presents LSV profiles for electrolyte ESW against SHE. Figure 7a and 7b show potential profiles and capacity data for CLTP in 7N20K vs. 1 M NaAc. Figure 8 shows EIS Nyquist plots of the partially sodiated CLTP electrode at different temperatures. Figure 9 presents the Arrhenius plot of charge transfer resistance.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the 7N20K (7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc) binary aqueous electrolyte as a viable water-in-salt system combining 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ conductivity, 3 V ESW, and excellent Na⁺ intercalation kinetics into NASICON. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of macroscopic transport/thermal data (Tg shift, Arrhenius viscosity) and microscopic electrochemical data (0.12 eV charge transfer Ea, 90% capacity retention) all converging on a water-in-salt mechanism with suppressed water activity. 3. The future path is the expansion of the water-in-salt approach to broader anode/cathode combinations, optimization of carbon-coating protocols, and long-term cycling stability beyond 60 cycles for practical alkaline ion battery systems.

summary.title: Freeze-Float System for High-throughput Measurement of Ice Nucleation
summary.authors: Yuki Kamijo (The University of Tokyo); Ratmir Derda (University of Alberta)
summary.field_subfield: Atmospheric Science / Microfluidics / High-throughput Screening
summary.type_of_paper: Methodological and validation paper describing a system implementation
summary.executive_summary: This paper describes the development of a high-throughput screening (HTS) implementation of the freeze-float selection platform, expanding on a previous proof-of-concept to achieve higher throughput, greater accuracy, and improved temperature uniformity. The core methodology replaces manual repeat-pipetting with a Biomek® 3000 robotic liquid transfer system for automated parallel generation of uniform droplets in multi-well plates, eliminating manual manipulation steps. A key advancement is the incorporation of a VIA Freeze™ Research controlled-rate freezer (Asymptote), which replaces a generic constant-temperature freezer. The previous system, limited by the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil and a 1 cm² footprint containing up to 50 droplets, was expanded to 48 cryovials each containing up to 40 droplets, achieving a 38-fold throughput increase (~1920 droplets total). Polydispersity of the robotically generated droplets was quantified at 9.2%, corresponding to a predicted nucleation temperature dispersion of no more than ±0.09 °C. The controlled-rate freezer demonstrated a significant reduction in cell-to-cell thermal gradient: the KS test p-value improved from 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ under constant-temperature cooling to 0.31 under linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min, with overall interwell dispersion reduced by 36% (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73). Validation experiments with 1 mg/mL Snomax droplets confirmed freezing temperatures at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C under controlled cooling versus -7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the generic freezer, indicating better INA detection sensitivity. The authors conclude that while the robotic system enables high-throughput parallelization and the controlled-rate freezer ensures thermal uniformity, the droplet system's stability during transport is insufficient due to static-induced coalescence, precluding full integration into portable workflows.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes the development of a high-throughput screening (HTS) implementation of the freeze-float selection platform, expanding on a previous proof-of-concept to achieve higher throughput, greater accuracy, and improved temperature uniformity. The core methodology replaces manual repeat-pipetting with a Biomek® 3000 robotic liquid transfer system for automated parallel generation of uniform droplets in multi-well plates, eliminating manual manipulation steps. A key advancement is the incorporation of a VIA Freeze™ Research controlled-rate freezer (Asymptote), which replaces a generic constant-temperature freezer. The previous system, limited by the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil and a 1 cm² footprint containing up to 50 droplets, was expanded to 48 cryovials each containing up to 40 droplets, achieving a 38-fold throughput increase (~1920 droplets total). Polydispersity of the robotically generated droplets was quantified at 9.2%, corresponding to a predicted nucleation temperature dispersion of no more than ±0.09 °C. The controlled-rate freezer demonstrated a significant reduction in cell-to-cell thermal gradient: the KS test p-value improved from 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ under constant-temperature cooling to 0.31 under linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min, with overall interwell dispersion reduced by 36% (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73). Validation experiments with 1 mg/mL Snomax droplets confirmed freezing temperatures at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C under controlled cooling versus -7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the generic freezer, indicating better INA detection sensitivity. The authors conclude that while the robotic system enables high-throughput parallelization and the controlled-rate freezer ensures thermal uniformity, the droplet system's stability during transport is insufficient due to static-induced coalescence, precluding full integration into portable workflows.

Research Context
The previous publication reported a proof-of-concept freeze-float system using a 1 cm² geometry cuvette that accommodated up to 50 droplets at once. Thermal conductivity limitations of silicone oil prevented scaling the container footprint without introducing significant thermal lag. Setting more than 5-10 cuvettes in parallel produced non-uniform results with a difference of a few degrees between cuvettes. High-throughput screening in multi-well plates and droplet-based assays offer parallelization, but polydispersity in simple emulsion preparation can bias freezing measurements. A 1 mm versus 0.1 mm droplet size difference leads to a 2.3 °C mean freezing temperature offset due to the diameter-temperature relationship.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether automated droplet generation combined with controlled-rate cooling can extend the freeze-float system to higher throughput while maintaining or improving measurement accuracy. The hypothesis is that droplet freezing is a random nucleation process accelerated by ice nucleating entities, where stochasticity in freezing spectra necessitates large sample sizes for reliable temperature determination. A calculated confidence interval formula determined that more than 30 droplets are sufficient to observe a reliable freezing temperature at a 95% confidence level. The authors predicted that expanding the assay from 50 droplets to 1920 droplets across 48 vials would increase throughput by factor of 38. It was hypothesized that a constant linear cooling rate would reduce cell-to-cell thermal gradients compared to constant-temperature cooling in multi-well plates.

Methodological Details
The system was tested initially using a 96 deep well plate compatible with the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling machine. A silicone oil buoyant layer with 1% silicone surfactant and HFE-7500 cushion layer was used, consistent with the previous publication. The Biomek 3000 dispensed 30 × 1 μL droplets into each well at a standard rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The robot generated 40 uniform droplets per well across 96 wells, yielding up to ~3800 droplets simultaneously in ~15 minutes. Droplet uniformity was validated using 60 droplets with fluorescein dye in a 12-well plate, imaged with a ChemiDoc MP. Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m quantified polydispersity as the standard deviation of radii divided by mean radius. The standard deviation was 2.86 × 10⁻⁵ m and the mean radius was 3.10 × 10⁻⁴ m, yielding a polydispersity of 9.2%. For the controlled-rate experiment, 48 cryovials were used, each containing 50 μL HFE-7500, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, and 40 droplets (20 with 1 mg/mL Snomax plus fluorescein, 20 INA-free milli Q with Coomassie Brilliant Blue). The VIA Freeze™ Research controlled-rate freezer accommodated the 48 cryovials in an instrument-specific metal holder. A custom-made glass lid was equipped on the bench-top freezer to enable automated image recording by a generic digital camera. Static electricity from the Biomek 3000 was mitigated using an Auto-set Ion Pump, and wet filter paper was used during transport.

Procedures And Architectures
Automated droplet generation proceeded by dispensing 30 × 1 μL droplets into the silicone oil layer of a 96-well deep plate using the Biomek 3000. A multi-head dispenser option was noted as capable of further accelerating the droplet generation rate. For validation, 30 droplets containing 1 mg/mL Snomax with yellow fluorescein dye were prepared in a 96-deep well system. Droplets were imaged and their freezing/floating behavior was recorded to validate agreement with previous reports. The Python script KStest.ipynb calculated p-values using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to compare cumulative freezing temperature distributions of two samples. In the controlled-rate setup, the freezer provided linear cooling down to -0.5 °C/min with high precision. A metal cooling plate and sample holder were used to achieve homogeneous cooling through the vials. The freezing temperature was measured over time and recorded for each well.

Key Results
The Biomek 3000 generated 40 droplets per well in 96 wells (up to ~3800 droplets) in approximately 15 minutes at 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The polydispersity of the 60 robotically generated droplets was 9.2%, corresponding to a standard deviation of 2.86 × 10⁻⁵ m divided by a mean of 3.10 × 10⁻⁴ m. Based on the droplet diameter-temperature relationship, the radius variation translated to an expected nucleation temperature dispersion of no more than ±0.09 °C. In the 96-deep well plate under constant-temperature cooling at -28 °C, the cell-to-cell thermal gradient showed a Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-value of 4.4 × 10⁻⁷. Under linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min in the 96-deep well plate, the p-value improved to 0.31, but the freezing time range increased with means of 47.4 and 50.6 minutes between cells. In the Asymptote freezer with 48 cryovials, Snomax droplets froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C compared to the generic freezer value of -7.5 ± 0.97 °C. The well-to-well freezing time dispersion in the 96-deep well system was 1.6 (p = 0.31), whereas the Asymptote freezer showed 0.73 (p = 0.83). The Asymptote freezer demonstrated 36% lower overall interwell dispersion compared to the generic freezer system. The freeze-float system with 48 vials achieved a 38-fold increase in droplet throughput over the 1 cm² cuvette system.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduced p-value (4.4 × 10⁻⁷ to 0.31) and decreased standard deviation confirm that linear cooling minimizes the cell-to-cell thermal gradient inherent in multi-well plates. The controlled-rate freezer provided better detection sensitivity, as evidenced by the tighter confidence interval around the INA freezing temperature. The stochastic nature of heterogeneous nucleation means that large ensemble sizes (N > 30) are required to extract a reliable mean freezing temperature from the inherent distribution. The droplet freezing temperature is directly proportional to the logarithm of droplet radius, making volume uniformity critical for quantitative measurement.

Contradictions And Limitations
When the droplet system is moved over certain distances (e.g., between laboratories), static electricity caused by friction leads to droplet coalescence. The authors state it was not successful to fully combine the droplet generation system with transport due to these stability issues. While linear cooling reduced the thermal gradient (p = 0.31), it simultaneously increased the range of freezing times, with a mean difference of 3.2 minutes between cells. The manuscript does not report a complete error analysis or formal sensitivity analysis of the detection threshold beyond the KS test comparison.

Claims
Automated droplet generation with Biomek 3000 achieves sufficient monodispersity for freeze-float ice nucleation measurement at high throughput. The polydispersity was measured at 9.2%, translating to a predicted temperature dispersion of ±0.09 °C. The robot generated up to ~3800 droplets simultaneously in 15 minutes. INA droplets prepared by the robot showed freezing behavior in good agreement with the previous publication's manual experiments. Droplet stability during transport is insufficient due to static-induced coalescence. The authors explicitly state the system was not fully successful when transport was required. The system is viable for in-situ high-throughput screening within a laboratory setting but requires further engineering for transportability.
A controlled-rate freezer with linear cooling significantly improves thermal uniformity and INA detection accuracy compared to generic constant-temperature freezing. The interwell freezing time standard deviation was reduced from 1.6 (p=0.31) to 0.73 (p=0.83), representing 36% lower dispersion. The INA freezing temperature confidence interval improved from ±0.97 °C in the generic freezer to ±0.59 °C in the controlled-rate freezer. The KS test p-value improved from 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ to 0.31 under linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min. Linear cooling increased the range of freezing times compared to constant-temperature cooling. Precise linear cooling rate is critical for the stochastic model of heterogeneous nucleation measurement.

Data And Code Availability
Source code S1 (Droplet_Dispersion.m) is for the Matlab automated circle detection program used for polydispersity analysis. Source code S3 (KStest.ipynb) is a Python script for the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test comparison of freezing temperature distributions. No explicit data repository is mentioned; source codes are referenced as S1 and S3 within the publication.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors compared constant-temperature cooling (-28 °C) versus linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) to isolate the effect of cooling rate on thermal gradient. The 96-deep well plate was first tested before proceeding to the 48-cryovial system, validating the workflow step-wise. The comparison between generic freezer results (-7.5 ± 0.97 °C) and Asymptote freezer results (-7.1 ± 0.59 °C) serves as a practical validation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows the 96 deep well plate compatible with Biomek 3000. Figure 1C shows fluorescein-dye-labeled droplets in a 12-well plate imaged with ChemiDoc MP. Figure 1D-E displays the circle detection results from the Matlab program. Figure 2 shows the freeze-float validation experiment with 30 Snomax droplets. Figure 3 presents the KS test p-value results (4.4 × 10⁻⁷) for the 96-well plate under constant-temperature cooling. Figure 4 shows the Snomax freezing temperatures (-7.1 ± 0.59 °C) in the Asymptote freezer. Figure 5 displays the freezing temperature distribution in the Asymptote freezer. Figure 6 shows the overall 36% lower dispersion in the Asymptote freezer.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the expansion of the freeze-float ice nucleation detection system from a single-cuvette manual format to a 48-vial (~1920 droplets) automated format using Biomek 3000 robotics and a controlled-rate Asymptote freezer, achieving a 38-fold throughput increase. 2. The strongest evidence is the 36% reduction in interwell freezing time dispersion (standard deviation 0.73 vs 1.6; p = 0.83 vs 0.31) and the improvement of the INA detection temperature confidence interval from ±0.97 °C to ±0.59 °C under linear cooling. 3. The future path must address droplet stability during transport due to static-induced coalescence before the system can be fully deployed in distributed or mobile laboratory workflows.

summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.field_subfield: Organic Chemistry / Photoredox Catalysis and Flow Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports a continuous flow protocol merging homogenous organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology to perform radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinyl carbazoles and styrenes. The study addresses the limitations of conventional batch organophotoredox dimerization, which were characterized by excessive reaction times, cryogenic conditions, and relatively high catalyst loadings (typically 3 mol%). By migrating the transformation to a commercial continuous flow platform at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ flow rate, the authors achieved the 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) dimer in 79% isolated yield using only 0.1 mol% of the pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst, a significant reduction from the 3 mol% required in batch. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports a continuous flow protocol merging homogenous organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology to perform radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinyl carbazoles and styrenes. The study addresses the limitations of conventional batch organophotoredox dimerization, which were characterized by excessive reaction times, cryogenic conditions, and relatively high catalyst loadings (typically 3 mol%). By migrating the transformation to a commercial continuous flow platform at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ flow rate, the authors achieved the 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) dimer in 79% isolated yield using only 0.1 mol% of the pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst, a significant reduction from the 3 mol% required in batch. Furthermore, the authors expanded the substrate scope to 16 brominated vinyl carbazoles, 2 functionalized (2-chloro, 2-methoxy, 2-hydroxy), and 2 bis-arylated vinyl carbazoles, as well as two styrenes (4-methoxystyrene, styrene) and the natural product E-asarone. The continuous flow approach consistently reduced reaction times—from 5 days in batch to under 1 hour in flow—and removed the need for cryogenic conditions. Post-dimerization utility was demonstrated via Suzuki cross-coupling of bromocyclobutanes, and the methodology was applied to deliver the lignan natural product magnosalin in 40% yield from 10 mmol scale E-asarone. The paper concludes that merging organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow provides a more efficient, scalable, and environmentally friendly synthetic route to cyclobutane functional materials and natural products.

Research Context
Vinyl carbazole (2) is a valuable monomer for conductive polymers and its dimer t-DCzCB serves as a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs. Naturally occurring styrenes like E-asarone can be seen as precursors to the anti-inflammatory lignan magnosalin through biomimetic light-induced dimerization. Cyclobutanes are synthesized via radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition of an electron-rich alkene radical cation intermediate. Prior work by Wang and coworkers using Fe(III) salts, Ledwith using Fe(III)/Ce(IV), and organomediated oxidation with Helquats achieved batch dimerization. Visible light photoredox catalysis with Ru- and Ir-complexes by Yoon showed effective dimerization at catalyst loadings of 0.025%. Nicewicz and coworkers reported dimerization using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst, but reaction times were excessive, cryogenic conditions were required, and loadings of 3 mol% were needed. Continuous flow technology offers improved irradiation of starting substrates and higher conversions in photochemical reactions. A heterogeneous photoredox fixed-bed flow process using polymeric carbon nitrides had been reported for magnosalin, but it was metal-free and not a homogenous small-molecule catalyst approach. The background gap is the lack of a homogenous organophotoredox/flow merged protocol that delivers functionalized carbazole host materials and natural products with minimal catalyst loading.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether merging homogenous organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology can deliver cyclobutane functional materials and natural products more efficiently than conventional batch chemistry. It was anticipated that continuous flow would reduce reaction times, eliminate cryogenic conditions, and allow lower catalyst loadings compared to the batch organophotoredox protocol of Nicewicz. A specific hypothesis was that a 0.1 mol% loading of the organophotoredox catalyst would suffice in flow, nearing the efficiencies of Ru-based photoredox systems. The authors hypothesized that functionalized vinyl carbazoles could be synthesized via a vinylation strategy rather than electrophilic aromatic substitution of the parent t-DCzCB scaffold to expand the available functional group scope. It was predicted that continuous flow would resolve issues of background oxidation and reversibility that plagued the batch dimerization of VCZ at low flow rates/extended residence times. A secondary hypothesis was that electron relays (anthracene or diethylaniline) could suppress undesired polymerization of styrenes during the dimerization.

Methodological Details
The study compared continuous flow versus batch reaction conditions on commercially available vinyl carbazole (2). A commercial, off-the-shelf continuous flow platform was used for its ease of use and availability. Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB employed 3 mol% of the pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst (10) in deoxygenated acetone at cryogenic temperatures. Optimization of the flow synthesis used HPLC analysis with p-terphenyl as internal standard. The flow reaction was performed at 1.00 mmol of 2 at 0.4 M in acetone. The expanded substrate scope included 16 brominated t-DCzCB substrates synthesized via Obora's vinylation method. Vinyl carbazoles (12a–24a) were synthesized in moderate to good yields, with the exception of 1-bromo-9vinylcarbazole (15a) which gave very low yields. For the expanded substrates, the flow dimerization concentration was reduced to 0.2 M in acetone. Styrene substrates included 4-methoxystyrene (27), styrene (29), and E-asarone (3). Electron relays: 0.25 equivalents of anthracene or diethylaniline were used for styrenes. Post-dimerization utility was tested using Suzuki cross-coupling with 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid. The study did not report random seeds, specific reactor geometry, or detailed NMR integration for all assignments.

Procedures And Architectures
The batch dimerization of VCZ (2) followed the Nicewicz protocol with 3 mol% organophotoredox catalyst 10 in deoxygenated acetone at cryogenic temperatures. Continuous flow optimization probed flow rates (0.5, 2, 5, 0.1 mL.min⁻¹), catalyst loadings (0.1, 1, 2, 4.5 mol%), and wavelengths (405, 420, 450 nm). The optimal flow condition for t-DCzCB (1) was 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min), 2 mol% catalyst 10, at 450 nm irradiation. Substrates 12a–17a were dimerized under batch and flow conditions to compare performance. 1-bromo-9vinylcarbazole (15a) was dimerized under both conditions but no cyclobutane product was detected by ¹H NMR. Continuous flow reactions for brominated substrates generally completed in under 1 hour, whereas batch required significantly more time. 2-chloro-, 2-methoxy-, and 2-hydroxy-9-vinylcarbazoles were dimerized solely under flow conditions. 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid was used in Suzuki coupling with 13b to give cyclobutane 25 in 75% yield. Bis(pinacolato)diboron was used in palladium-mediated borylation of 13b to give 26 in 36% yield. Styrene substrates were processed with electron relays (anthracene or diethylaniline) added to the starting solution before flow introduction. The flow reactor was a commercial off-the-shelf platform, the specific model of which is not stated.

Key Results
Batch dimerization of VCZ (2) to t-DCzCB (1) at 3 mol% catalyst gave 82% isolated yield, required deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended reaction times. Optimal continuous flow synthesis of 1 (0.5 mL.min⁻¹, 2 mol% catalyst, 450 nm) gave 98% isolated yield (entry 1 of Table 1). Increasing catalyst loading to 4.5 mol% (entry 2) gave 11% yield, which the text notes as a modest reduction to 90%. Reducing catalyst loading to 1 mol% (entry 3) gave 93% isolated yield. Lowering flow rate to 2 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 50 min) gave 79% yield at 2 mol% catalyst (entry 4). Further reducing flow rate to 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 100 min) gave 53% yield at 2 mol% catalyst (entry 6), with significant carbazole formation attributed to background oxidation by adventitious oxygen. At 10 mmol scale of 2, with only 0.1 mol% of 10 at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹, t-DCzCB (1) was obtained in 79% isolated yield (entry 11). Bromine-substituted 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (12a) gave 12b in 48% yield under batch conditions (5 days) versus 64% yield under flow at 0.2 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 50 min). 4-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (14a) gave improved isolated yields under flow conditions. 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (16a) gave 16b in 65% isolated yield under flow, while 2,7-dibromo-9vinylcarbazole (17a) had batch slightly outperforming flow. 2-chloro-9-vinylcarbazole (18a) dimerized to 18b in 61% yield, 2-methoxy-9-vinylcarbazole (19a) in 45%, and bis-enolether 21b from 20a in 25%. The 4-fluoroarylated vinyl carbazole 22a gave cyclobutane 22b in 65% yield, compared to 22% for 21a. 3,6-di-tert-butylcarbazole vinylation gave 23a in quantitative yields, subsequent dimerization gave 23b in 57% yield. 3,6-bisarylated 9-vinylcarbazole 24a gave cyclobutane 24b in 50% yield. Palladium-mediated Suzuki coupling of 13b with 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid gave cyclobutane 25 in 75% yield. Palladium-mediated borylation of 13b gave 26 in 36% yield. 4-methoxystyrene (27) gave dimer 28 in 44% isolated yield, improved with 0.25 eq. anthracene. Styrene (29) with diethylaniline gave pellucidin A in 22% isolated yield. E-asarone (3) dimerized on a 10 mmol scale to magnosalin (4) in 40% isolated yield. No cryogenic temperatures or extended reaction times were required for the flow styrene dimerizations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduction in yield at low flow rates (e.g., 53% at 0.1 mL.min⁻¹) is attributed to extended residence time and possible reversibility of the dimerization reaction. Formation of carbazole at low flow rates is attributed to background oxidation of 2 by adventitious oxygen within the flow system, increasing the likelihood of O₂ oxidation to N-formylcarbazole whose hydrolysis gives carbazole. The continuous flow protocol exploits the advantages of both organophotoredox catalysis (sustainable, metal-free, environmentally beneficial) and continuous flow (efficient irradiation, faster reaction times, scalability). The vinylation strategy for functionalized carbazoles overcomes the limitations of electrophilic aromatic substitution at the 3 and 6 positions, enabling a broader scope of host materials. The two enol ethers on bis-enolether 21b are described as synthetic handles for post-modification or polymerization, implying potential as monomer precursors. The demonstrated scalability (10 mmol scale for E-asarone, 1.00 mmol for VCZ) positions the methodology for practical application in producing functional materials and natural products.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report a specific random seed, train/test split, or detailed statistical analysis beyond the HPLC-verified isolated yields. 1-bromo-9vinylcarbazole (15a) could not be dimerized under either batch or flow conditions, with no cyclobutane detected by ¹H NMR, representing a clear substrate limitation. For 2,7-dibromo-9vinylcarbazole (17a), batch conditions slightly outperformed continuous flow, contrary to the general trend of flow superiority. The cyclobutane 21b from 21a was obtained in a moderate 22% yield due to poor solubility of 21a in acetone. The 10 mmol scale for E-asarone produced 40% yield, which is modest compared to the 79% yield for VCZ at 1.00 mmol scale. The specific model of the commercial continuous flow platform is not named, limiting reproducibility of flow parameters. The paper does not report degradation of the catalyst over repeated uses or the recyclability of the catalyst under flow conditions.

Claims
Merging organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow reduces catalyst loading from 3 mol% to 0.1 mol% for t-DCzCB synthesis. Batch synthesis required 3 mol% of catalyst 10, deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended reaction times. At 0.1 mol% catalyst loading and 0.5 mL.min⁻¹, t-DCzCB was obtained in 79% isolated yield on a 10 mmol scale. This catalyst loading is noted as being near the efficiencies of the Ru-based system reported by Yoon (0.025% loadings). The 79% yield at 0.1 mol% is lower than the 98% yield at 2 mol%, showing a trade-off between loading and yield. Lower catalyst loadings reduce costs and environmental impact, making the process more sustainable. The reduced loading positions the method as a viable alternative to metal-based photoredox systems.
Continuous flow reduces reaction times from days to under 1 hour for brominated vinyl carbazole dimerizations. 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (12a) required 5 days in batch but was completed in τ = 50 min under flow. Generally, under continuous flow reaction conditions completion could be attained in under 1 hour. The batch dimerization of VCZ required 'extended reaction times,' while flow achieved conversion in 20 minutes (τ = 20 min). The 10 mmol scale for E-asarone produced 40% yield, indicating that not all substrates achieve the same rate/efficiency under flow. Faster reaction times increase throughput and productivity in a production setting. Reduced time exposure limits potential side reactions and degradation pathways.
Continuous flow eliminates the need for cryogenic temperatures in the organophotoredox dimerization of vinyl carbazoles and styrenes. Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB required cryogenic temperatures. The continuous flow styrene dimerizations did not require cryogenic temperatures and could be completed in significantly shorter time periods. The batch dimerization of these substrate types required cryogenic temperatures, while flow conditions eliminated this requirement. The paper does not explicitly state the exact temperature of the flow reactor; only that cryogenic temperatures were not required. Ambient or elevated temperature operation simplifies reactor design and reduces operating costs.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The effect of catalyst loading was systematically probed: 4.5 mol% (90%), 2 mol% (98%), and 1 mol% (93%) gave diminishing returns above 2 mol%. Flow rate was varied (0.1 to 5 mL.min⁻¹) to probe reversibility, revealing that longer residence times (lower flow rates) led to lower yields. The absence of catalyst (entry 9) and the absence of irradiation (entry 10) confirmed that both components are necessary for dimerization. Two additional wavelengths (405, 420 nm) were probed as the catalyst 10 has UV absorbance, and both gave comparable yields to 450 nm. Electron relays (anthracene, 0.25 eq.) and (diethylaniline) were tested to suppress styrene polymerization, with anthracene greatly improving product outcome. The vinylation of 2-hydroxycarbazole to 20a in 62% yield allowed testing of chemoselective dimerization, yielding 21b in 25%.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the optimization study for t-DCzCB synthesis, showing entries 1–11 with yields (%) and catalyst loadings, flow rates, wavelengths, and residence times. Scheme 1 illustrates cyclobutane dimers as functional materials and natural products, including t-DCzCB, magnosalin, and their precursors. Scheme 2 depicts the radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism, with scheme 2A showing photochemical generation and scheme 2B showing Nicewicz's organophotoredox pathway. Scheme 3 shows the merged protocol: organophotoredox catalysis and continuous flow for cyclobutane synthesis. Scheme 4 shows the batch versus flow comparison for VCZ dimerization to t-DCzCB. Scheme 5 illustrates the brominated vinyl carbazole substrates and their dimerization under batch and flow conditions. Scheme 6 demonstrates the post-dimerization utility of bromocyclobutanes via Suzuki coupling and borylation. Scheme 7 shows the dimerization of styrenes and E-asarone with anthracene as an electron relay. Scheme 8 (labeled as [C] in the text) depicts the structure of the 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole derivative with the Ir-catalyst complex.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is merging homogenous organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow to achieve t-DCzCB in 79% yield at 0.1 mol% catalyst loading, eliminating cryogenic conditions and reducing reaction times from days to under 1 hour. 2. The strongest evidence is the systematic optimization of flow parameters (loading, flow rate, wavelength) demonstrating 98% yield at 2 mol% and the 10 mmol scale E-asarone dimerization to magnosalin in 40% yield, proving scalability. 3. The future path lies in expanding the substrate scope of functionalized carbazoles, utilizing the enol ether handles for post-modification, and potentially applying the method to more complex electron-rich styrenes for natural product synthesis.

summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan; Ken Yamazaki; Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba; Dhananjayan Vasu; Trevor A Hamlin; Darren J Dixon
summary.field_subfield: Synthetic Organic Chemistry / Total Synthesis
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports the 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a pentacyclic marine natural product isolated from Xestospongia sea sponges, enabled by a novel catalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition. The key step involves a prochiral ketone (4-aminocyclohexanone derivative) tethered to a β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin, which undergoes Michael addition catalyzed by Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst (9f) at 20 mol% loading with 20 mol% benzoic acid in dichloromethane, yielding the bicyclic nitroalkane (18) in 95% yield as a single diastereomer with >99% ee. This transformation concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, from an achiral starting material. The catalytic cycle, including the formation of a hemiaminal, imine, and enamine intermediate, was computationally probed using DFT calculations; the transition state (TS1) was identified with a ΔΔG‡ of 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹, predicting 99% ee in excellent agreement with experimental results. The reaction is highly exergonic (ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹), confirming its irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining nature. Following bicyclic core construction, the synthesis proceeds via oxidative lactamization (Iwabuchi conditions, AZADO/CuCl/2,2'-bipy/DMAP), a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone (Nicolaou's IBX/NMO, epoxidation with H₂O₂/NaOH, Wittig homologation with (methoxymethyl)triphenylphosphonium chloride and NaHMDS), and ring-closing metathesis (Grubbs 1st gen and Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd gen with p-benzoquinone). The synthetic strategy demonstrates that a single early chirality-inducing step can install all stereochemical information of the madangamine skeleton, proving the power of organocatalytic desymmetrization for generating high-value stereochemically-rich products.
