judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports the 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a pentacyclic marine natural product isolated from Xestospongia sea sponges, enabled by a novel catalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition. The key step involves a prochiral ketone (4-aminocyclohexanone derivative) tethered to a β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin, which undergoes Michael addition catalyzed by Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst (9f) at 20 mol% loading with 20 mol% benzoic acid in dichloromethane, yielding the bicyclic nitroalkane (18) in 95% yield as a single diastereomer with >99% ee. This transformation concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, from an achiral starting material. The catalytic cycle, including the formation of a hemiaminal, imine, and enamine intermediate, was computationally probed using DFT calculations; the transition state (TS1) was identified with a ΔΔG‡ of 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹, predicting 99% ee in excellent agreement with experimental results. The reaction is highly exergonic (ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹), confirming its irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining nature. Following bicyclic core construction, the synthesis proceeds via oxidative lactamization (Iwabuchi conditions, AZADO/CuCl/2,2'-bipy/DMAP), a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone (Nicolaou's IBX/NMO, epoxidation with H₂O₂/NaOH, Wittig homologation with (methoxymethyl)triphenylphosphonium chloride and NaHMDS), and ring-closing metathesis (Grubbs 1st gen and Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd gen with p-benzoquinone). The synthetic strategy demonstrates that a single early chirality-inducing step can install all stereochemical information of the madangamine skeleton, proving the power of organocatalytic desymmetrization for generating high-value stereochemically-rich products.



Research Context
The madangamine family of natural products isolated from marine sea sponges of the Xestospongia genus possess an architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. Three rings constitute a common diazatricyclic core (ABC rings) while the macrocyclic E ring is common except in madangamine F and the D ring differs in every member. Since their isolation, madangamines have attracted significant attention with numerous reported strategies to polycyclic core fragments. However there exist only two reports of total syntheses of members of the family and a single formal synthesis of madangamine A. The previous synthetic strategies by Amat in 2014 and Chida and Sato in 2017 did not utilize a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction to set the early stereochemistry. Intramolecular desymmetrizing variants that concurrently establish a quaternary carbon centre were unreported. A framework is needed to convert relatively simple achiral starting materials to high-value stereochemically-rich products.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a novel organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction of tri-substituted nitroolefin-linked cyclohexanones can be developed and applied to the total synthesis of madangamine E. The authors hypothesized that an enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral ketone to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin would efficiently construct a chiral bicyclic core. The hypothesis predicted the reaction would concurrently establish three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon stereocenter, and prove highly scalable. It was envisioned that this single chirality inducing step could install all the ensuing stereochemical information of the madangamine skeleton. The pathway and origins of enantioselectivity were predicted to be probeable using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The expected outcome was near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity comparable to or exceeding the best nitroolefin Michael addition reactions previously reported.

Methodological Details
The model substrate was methyl-substituted nitroolefin 7 selected as an ideal model for developing the enantioselective intramolecular Michael addition reaction. A range of chiral single enantiomer primary and secondary amine organocatalysts was investigated, including trans-cyclohexanediamine and proline-derived scaffolds. Reactions were performed in dichloromethane at 20 mol% catalyst loading in the presence of benzoic acid as a co-catalyst. The synthetic route to nitroolefin 7 was constructed in 3 steps from commercially available 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal via oxidative radical nitration. The synthetic route to nitroolefin 17 required a 5-step sequence: reductive amination, N-tosylation, oxidative cleavage, Henry reaction, dehydration, Michael addition, and selenoxide elimination. The installation of the butenyl chain was achieved by Michael addition of an organo-zinc-copper complex at 17 g scale, demonstrating scalability. Selenoxide elimination proceeded in 52% yield over 3 steps with E:Z ratio of 3.8:1 and required Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1, 0.033M) solvent mixture. The DFT calculations used a conformational search identifying 16 possible transition structures to locate the key C-C bond forming step. The final synthetic steps included ring-closing metathesis with Grubbs 1st generation and Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalysts and amide reduction with excess LiAlH4 in Et2O.

Procedures And Architectures
The key catalytic cycle begins with addition of the primary amine of catalyst 9f to ketone 7 forming hemiaminal Int1, followed by elimination of water to form imine Int2. Enamine Int3 is formed by tautomerization from imine Int2, and a conformational search of 16 transition structures was conducted. The intramolecular Michael addition proceeds through TS1, yielding iminium-nitronate species Int4, followed by hydrolysis through hemiaminal Int7 to furnish the product. Treatment of 17E with 20 mol% catalyst 9f and 20 mol% benzoic acid in dichloromethane provided bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield with >99% ee. The oxidative lactamization was carried out using AZADO, CuCl, 2,2'-bipyridine, and DMAP under Iwabuchi conditions with copper chloride. The two-step Z-selective olefination sequence used Nicolaou's IBX-NMO oxidation for dehydrogenation followed by epoxidation with hydrogen peroxide and aqueous NaOH. The Wittig homologation employed (methoxymethyl)triphenylphosphonium chloride and NaHMDS with a saturated aqueous NH4Cl quench at 60 °C for 3 hours. Ring-closing metathesis was performed under high dilution conditions at 40 °C with Grubbs 1st generation catalyst in CH2Cl2. The macrocyclic E-ring closure used Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in PhMe at 110 °C with co-catalytic p-benzoquinone and high dilution.

Key Results
Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f provided the desired bicyclic Michael adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. A simplified bifunctional primary amine catalyst 9e yielded 8 in 51% yield as a single diastereoisomer in 96% ee. The DFT-calculated ΔΔG‡ of 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ between TS1 and the second-lowest energy transition structure predicts 99% ee. The computed Michael addition is highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹, confirming its irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining nature. Treatment of 17E with catalyst 9f provided nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield with >99% ee as a single diastereomer on >5 g scale. The selenoxide elimination for nitroolefin installation proceeded in 52% yield over 3 steps with E:Z ratio of 3.8:1. The Wittig homologation yield was improved from 26% to 86% b.r.s.m 99% by incorporating a rigorous NH4Cl quench at 60 °C for 3 hours. RCM to close the D ring gave tetracyclic enone 26 in 82% yield with Grubbs 1st generation catalyst. The macrocyclic E-ring closure gave diamide 30 in 71% yield using Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst at 110 °C. The final double amide reduction afforded synthetic madangamine E in 72% yield using excess LiAlH4 in Et2O. All analytical data were highly consistent with that reported by Chida and Sato and the isolation team of Andersen.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The catalytic cycle is a cooperative push-pull mechanism stabilized by multiple hydrogen bonding interactions with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties in TS1. The observed mechanism (intramolecular protonation) differs from the unsaturated ester variant (intermolecular protonation) due to pKa differences: pKa = 17 (nitro) < 20 (thiourea) < 30 (ester). The deprotonation of the thiourea by the enolate is favorable, whereas deprotonation by the nitronate is unfavorable, determining the pathway. The early introduction of stereochemical information via a single desymmetrization reaction proves that a catalytic step can install all ensuing stereocenters in a complex natural product. The DFT-experimental agreement (99% calculated vs >99% experimental) validates the proposed mechanism and transition structure for nitroolefin Michael additions.

Contradictions And Limitations
Most tested catalysts (9a-9d, 9g-9k) failed to provide the cyclised product 8 and instead gave complex product mixtures. Amat's Wittig reaction of an octenoate phosphonium salt was largely unsuccessful despite extensive experimentation, with deprotonation out-competing functionalisation. The selenoxide elimination demonstrated strong dependence on solvent mixture, with Et2O:CH2Cl2 proving optimal. The spatial arrangement of the terminal alkenes in RCM precursor S8 prevented macrocyclisation. The reaction to install the butenyl chain via organocerium reagents was capricious and sensitive to the quality of the organocerium reagent. The yield of the Wittig homologation was low (26%) under standard conditions, requiring an optimized quench procedure to reach 86%.

Claims
The organocatalytic desymmetrization of tri-substituted nitroolefins establishes three stereogenic centers and a quaternary carbon from an achiral cyclohexanone in high yield and near-perfect selectivity. Catalyst 9f gave bicyclic adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. Treatment of 17E provided nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield with >99% ee on a >5 g scale. DFT calculates ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ predicting 99% ee in excellent agreement with experiment. The reaction is highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹ confirming it is the stereoselectivity-determining step. Most other tested catalysts gave complex product mixtures rather than the cyclised product. The simplified catalyst 9e gave lower yield (51%) and slightly lower ee (96%). This transformation enables the construction of sterically congested quaternary carbon centres that were previously inaccessible via conventional desymmetrization. The methodology can be applied to other beta,beta'-disubstituted nitroolefins for constructing bicyclic cores.
The 30-step synthesis of madangamine E is enabled by the early catalytic desymmetrization reaction, which sets all three stereocenters from a prochiral starting material. The synthesis was completed in 30 steps with all analytical data consistent with the known natural product. The desymmetrizing Michael addition installed the chiral bicyclic core as the first major stereoselective step. Relative and absolute stereochemical configurations of all three newly formed centers were confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Several steps in the sequence required optimization (e.g., Wittig homologation, RCM sequence, organozincate reagents). The E-ring RCM failed initially, requiring a reordered sequence and an elimination step. A single chirality-inducing step can replace multiple stereoselective operations, making the synthesis more efficient and atom-economical. The strategy demonstrates the utility of organocatalytic desymmetrization in total synthesis of high-value natural products.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The DFT conformational search examined 16 possible transition structures to identify the lowest-energy pathway. Computational testing with a nitro group versus an alpha,beta-unsaturated ester revealed a mechanism change: intramolecular protonation vs intermolecular protonation. The dihydrooxazine oxide intermediate IV and cyclobutane intermediate V were found to be unfavorable or energetically unstable. The O-protonation of nitronate VI via iminium proton transfer was found to not occur because the aci-nitro species is less electronegative at the alpha-position. The selenoxide elimination reaction showed strong dependence on the solvent mixture with Et2O:CH2Cl2 proving optimal. The RCM was sensitive to the spatial arrangement of terminal alkenes, failing with the original precursor and requiring reordering of elimination and RCM steps.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system of madangamine E with two nitrogen atoms. Figure 1B compares the madangamine E structure to Amat's madangamine D synthesis and Chida/Sato's madangamine A, C, and E syntheses. Figure 1C presents the retrosynthetic analysis of the pentacyclic skeleton of madangamine E. Figure 2A shows the previously reported enantioselective desymmetrising intramolecular Michael addition to alpha,beta-unsaturated esters. Figure 2B displays the catalytic cycle of the intramolecular Michael addition of nitroolefin 7 with catalyst 9f. Figure 2C shows the DFT-calculated reaction pathway with the transition state TS1 and intermediate structures. Figure 3 presents the DFT results including the transition state energy barriers. Figure 4A details the restructured synthetic route to nitroolefin 17. Figure 4B shows the application of the organocatalytic desymmetrization to the synthesis of madangamine E starting from nitroolefin 17.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a new organocatalytic desymmetrization of tri-substituted nitroolefins that installs three stereocenters (including a quaternary carbon) in a single step, enabling a 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E. 2. The strongest evidence is the nearly perfect stereochemical outcome (95% yield, >99% ee as a single diastereomer) of the key desymmetrization step, which is confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and validated by DFT calculations (ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹). 3. The future path lies in applying this organocatalytic desymmetrization to other substrate classes and in developing further macrocyclization strategies informed by the spatial organization effects observed during the E-ring RCM.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the dielectric response of molecular-scale nanocomposites comprising silver nanoparticle (mNP) inclusions in a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix. Using Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) within the Quantum Espresso code combined with the Modern Theory of Polarization, the authors model how nanoparticle morphology—specifically size (8 to 32 atoms), shape (rod-like vs. disk-like), and orientation relative to an external electric field—modulates the dielectric permittivity (ε_r). MgO was selected as the matrix due to its cubic structure, isotropic polarization, and manageable bandgap (7.8 eV) for computational treatment. Eight nanoparticle geometries (three rod-like, five disk-like) were characterized, with matrix extension of 2 Mg-O layers beyond inclusion edges to minimize periodic image interference. Key findings demonstrate that dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% occur as inclusion sizes vary from 8 to 32 atoms, with disk-like inclusions (disks 332, 432, 442) exhibiting >70% enhancement relative to the matrix at similar volume loadings. Born effective charge (BEC) mapping reveals that the dielectric enhancement is driven by localized induced fields at the mNP-matrix interface, with parallel orientation producing extended positive polarization fields and perpendicular orientation inducing depolarization regions that never decay to bulk values. The 2D disk nanoparticles (421, 441) show decreased polarization in both directions due to restricted electron motion in the z-direction. The work establishes that at molecular nanoparticle scales (<30 atoms), morphology governs the quantum polarization response, and the induced field reach is physically extended in parallel configurations but strongly screened in perpendicular ones, with perpendicular depolarization fields sometimes dominating and lowering the average dielectric constant below the pure matrix value. The authors propose that the small nanoparticle size limits conduction and leakage issues while providing a highly tunable platform for high-κ dielectric engineering.

Research Context
The demand for new high-κ dielectric materials is driven by energy storage and processing power limits of traditional single-phase materials. Nanocomposite (NC) materials combining a dielectric matrix with inclusions are proposed to expand the tunable dielectric range for transistors, super-capacitors, and quantum computing. Traditional Si/SiO₂ gate materials face current leakage and tunneling effects at few-nanometer scales, necessitating higher-permittivity alternatives like hafnium oxides. Molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) with up to 100 atoms bridge the gap between single-atom dopants and traditional metallic nanoparticles while avoiding band structures and high-electron density percolation issues. mNPs are essentially sources of highly polarizable electron density requiring quantum mechanical treatments to model local polarization effects. Prior work by the same group on Ag₈/MgO NCs revealed that interfacial effects produced greater than expected polarization response. Effective medium approximations are suitable for macroscale mixtures but do not provide insight into quantum response and local field effects at the nanoscale. Direct DFT has been used for doped materials, but a complete treatment of quantum polarization of the mixed material was not attempted until recently.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how the size, shape, and orientation of molecular-scale silver nanoparticle inclusions in MgO affect the overall dielectric capacity of the nanocomposite. The authors hypothesize that at mNP scales of <30 atoms, morphology greatly alters how inclusion electrons behave and affect atomic-scale polarization. A specific hypothesis is that asymmetric inclusions (rods, disks) will bring on dielectric enhancements larger than expected based on simple volume ratios. It is predicted that parallel orientation relative to the applied field will enhance polarization more than perpendicular orientation due to freer electron mobility along the field axis. The study aims to quantify the threshold at which exponential dielectric growth transitions to a more metallic-like behavior.

Methodological Details
The MgO matrix was chosen for its cubic crystal structure, isotropic polarization, and low number of polarizable d-electrons. The bulk dielectric constant of MgO is reported as 8-9.8 with a bandgap of 7.8 eV. Three rod-like inclusions and five disk-like inclusions were modeled, built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice. The matrix extended 2 Mg-O layers beyond the edge of the inclusion in each direction to prevent periodic image interaction. Inclusion sizes ranged from 8 to 32 atoms for the various geometries. The volume loading of inclusions to matrix was kept between 3-5% in numbers of atoms. Calculations used the Quantum Espresso code versions 6.0 and 6.6 with a plane wave-basis set using the LDA functional. Mg atoms used Bachelet-Hamann-Schluter norm-conserving pseudopotentials; O and Ag used Rappe-Rabe-Kaxiras-Joannopoulos ultra-soft pseudopotentials. The total energy convergence was set to 10⁻⁸ and the force threshold to 10⁻⁴. Wavefunction cutoff was 50-60Ry and charge density cutoff was 560Ry. The Brillouin zone was sampled at the Γ point with periodic boundary conditions. Electron masses were initially 300 a.u. and increased to 450 a.u. after damped minimizations. A static electric field of 0.001 a.u. was applied along the z-axis for polarization calculations. No thermostat was applied and temperatures were not controlled; test runs at 200-600K showed negligible temperature effects. The Avogadro software was used for model building. The electronic structure calculation followed a six-step procedure: initial minimization, damped dynamics for ions and electrons, and a lattice-vector relaxation step.

Procedures And Architectures
The electronic structure was relaxed using CPMD with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization for initial electron minimization followed by damped dynamics steps. An additional lattice-vector relaxation step removed stress from the cell induced by the inclusion. The polarization calculation followed a three-step procedure: damped dynamics (ionic polarization), electronic structure relaxation in-field (electronic polarization), and fully-relaxed static polarization. The low-frequency dielectric constant was computed as ε_r = 1 + 4π(P_e_damped - P_e_relax) / ε_field. The Born effective charge tensor was calculated by comparing forces under zero-field and static polarization conditions. Force calculations were normalized to the bulk matrix to isolate the effect of the nanoparticle. Mathematical corrections for polarization jumps (quantum of polarization effects) were applied during post-processing for asymmetric/low-symmetry systems. During zero-field damped dynamics and structure minimization, the simulation cell size and volume were continuously updated for stress relaxation. The polarization calculation was performed using the method described by Umari and Pasquarello. Electronic polarization and BECs were calculated in the clamped-ion step of the procedure.

Key Results
Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms. The prior Ag₈/MgO NC study showed an ≈30% increase in ε_r at ≈4% mNP volume ratio. Rod-like inclusions (Rod224) showed a polarization increase of approximately 9.23 for parallel orientation, greater than for perpendicular orientation. Disk-like inclusions (disks 332, 432, 442) exhibited more than 70% enhancement in ε_r over matrix permittivity at similar volume loading to rod-like inclusions. Disk442 showed a polarization increase of more than twice compared to Rod223, despite having twice the x,y dimensions. The 2-dimensional disk nanoparticles (421, 441) showed a decrease in polarization in both directions compared to the bulk. The distortion (stress) of the crystal structure extended only to the nearest neighbors, up to approximately 3 angstroms from the mNP edge. In the parallel configuration, the induced polarization field was stronger and had a further physical reach in the direction of the applied field. In the perpendicular configuration, the BEC converged to matrix values (+2, -2) over a short distance, indicating a smaller field and lower average dielectric constant. In some cases, the perpendicular depolarization response in the matrix dominated the overall polarization, making the calculated dielectric constant lower than for the pure matrix. Disk-shaped mNPs particularly suffered from severe screening rings that interacted with neighboring inclusions. The bandgap was expected to be significantly lower than experimental due to LDA functional and inclusion-introduced states. The density of states in the vicinity of the Fermi level was dominated by NP states, suggesting DFT performance would mirror its nanoparticle behavior rather than bulk behavior. The BEC maps showed depolarization (red/yellow) in the equatorial region where effective ionic charge was less than in the absence of the external field.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dielectric enhancement is driven by localized induced fields at the matrix-inclusion interface rather than uniform volume effects. The shape of the nanoparticle dictates the spatial distribution and reach of the induced polarization field. In parallel orientation, more electrons are available to mobilize along the field axis, inducing a higher polarization for longer distances. The perpendicular depolarization field is extended over large regions of the cell and never decays to bulk values, implying strong screening. The 2D disk nanoparticles show decreased polarization because inclusion electrons are not free to move in the z-direction. The BEC plots resemble an induced field on the nanoparticle with moving electrons throughout the simulation, producing areas of higher and lower force. The interfacial effect is considered the most important for isolation and exploitation in dielectric engineering. The exponential growth of polarization with disk size suggests a threshold where the inclusion begins to behave more metallic, though computational constraints limit the study size.

Contradictions And Limitations
The LDA functional is expected to underestimate the bandgap significantly, and the exact magnitude is not reported. The calculated dielectric constants are volume averages and do not account for surface charge and edge effects of a real material. The study could not reach the size threshold where the disk behaves more metallic due to computational constraints. The perpendicular depolarization response can dominate and reduce the dielectric constant below that of the pure matrix, a reversal of the expected enhancement. The paper does not report a random seed, specific train/test splits (as it is a DFT study), or detailed demographic information. The exact value for the bandgap is noted as a placeholder (?) in the text, indicating the value was not specified in this manuscript version. The paper notes that for larger nanoparticles, Wannier function convergence failed due to high delocalization and movement of Wannier centers.

Claims
Morphology (size, shape, orientation) of molecular-scale silver nanoparticles in MgO governs the dielectric response, enabling tuning of ε_r by 30-100%. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed across inclusion sizes of 8-32 atoms. Disk-like inclusions (332, 432, 442) showed >70% enhancement over matrix permittivity at similar loadings to rods. The 2D disks (421, 441) showed decreased polarization in both directions, confirming shape dependency. In some perpendicular configurations, the dielectric constant drops below that of the pure matrix, reversing the enhancement expectation. The exact threshold at which disk behavior becomes metallic was not reached due to computational limits. These results suggest a pathway for designing tunable high-κ dielectrics by controlling nanoparticle geometry. The small nanoparticle size limits conduction and leakage while enabling large permittivity gains.
The dielectric enhancement is primarily an interfacial phenomenon driven by localized induced fields rather than bulk polarization. BEC maps show that induced forces are mainly felt by atoms at the matrix-nanoparticle interface. The distortion of the crystal structure only extends to nearest neighbors (≈3 Å) from the inclusion edge. The perpendicular depolarization field is extended over large regions of the cell, indicating non-local effects. The 2D disks show a polarization decrease, which is a negative rather than positive interfacial effect. Encapsulation of mNPs by the matrix allows for isolation and exploitation of these interfacial effects. Control of direction and loading is critical for maintaining dielectric enhancement.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Test runs with thermostats between 200-600K confirmed that temperature effects on geometry were negligible. The matrix was extended by 2 Mg-O layers in all directions to verify that NP-induced distortion did not extend to neighboring cells. Wannier function convergence was attempted but failed for nanoparticles larger than 8 atoms due to delocalization. The BEC calculations used force normalization to the bulk matrix to isolate the nanoparticle contribution. The %loading was kept between 3-5% in numbers of atoms while ensuring sufficient matrix to separate periodic images.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows an example nanocomposite with a Ag₁₂ inclusion in MgO matrix. Figure 2 and 3 display three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions on an ideal Ag fcc lattice. Figure 4 illustrates the six-step polarization calculation procedure. Figure 5 shows polarization steps using QuantumEspresso with step numbering. Figure 6 presents mathematical corrections for polarization jumps during post-processing. Figure 9 shows smeared Born effective charge plots of normalized charges for a 224 rod-like inclusion. Figure 7 (referenced) and the density of states indicate NP states dominate near the Fermi level. Table 1 presents ε_r values for Ag/MgO NCs with rod-like and disk-like inclusions. The paper references Figure 5(a) showing increased force along polarization direction and Figure 5(b) showing opposite effect.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a first-principles quantification of how nanoparticle morphology (size 8-32 atoms, rod vs. disk shapes, parallel vs. perpendicular orientation) dictates the dielectric response in metal-oxide nanocomposites. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation of >70% dielectric permittivity enhancement for disk-like inclusions relative to the matrix at similar volume loadings, driven by localized induced fields at the interface. 3. The future path involves extending the framework to other matrix materials (SiO₂, HfO₂), other transition metal inclusions (Cu, Co, Fe), and studying interactions between multiple inclusions to build a robust understanding of quantum polarization effects.

summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Ivan Saika-Voivod (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Styliani Consta (The University of Western Ontario)
summary.field_subfield: Computational Chemistry / Biophysical Chemistry; Molecular Dynamics of supercooled water nanodroplets and ion distribution
summary.executive_summary: This study provides direct computational evidence that supercooled aqueous nanodroplets develop a heterogeneous radial structure featuring a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water surrounded by a higher-density, more disordered subsurface. The authors perform molecular dynamics simulations of single Na+ and multiple Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from N = 100 to N = 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The central finding is that at 200 K (supercooled conditions), the single Na+ ion is expelled from the droplet's center and resides in the subsurface region (within approximately 0.1 nm of the peak in Voronoi-based water density), whereas at 300 K, the radial ion distribution is nearly uniform, consistent with an electrostatic confinement model. The authors also introduce a novel analytical reference model describing the energy of a charged dielectric droplet as the sum of electrostatic and surface energies, predicting a harmonic potential—termed 'electrostatic confinement'—that centers the ion at the droplet's center of mass. This model successfully predicts the room-temperature behavior but fails at supercooling, where the heterogeneous core structure dominates. Multiple ions (5 and 8 Na+ per droplet) similarly exhibit subsurface localization at 200 K, with non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann theory failing to explain the distribution. The authors note that for the smallest droplet (N = 100), the tetrahedral core does not form, and the ion resides one or two layers from the surface, consistent with prior work by Voth et al. The study suggests implications for native mass spectrometry, Rayleigh fission, and atmospheric chemistry, positioning this work as a starting point for understanding ion distribution in supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecular conformations.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study provides direct computational evidence that supercooled aqueous nanodroplets develop a heterogeneous radial structure featuring a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water surrounded by a higher-density, more disordered subsurface. The authors perform molecular dynamics simulations of single Na+ and multiple Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from N = 100 to N = 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The central finding is that at 200 K (supercooled conditions), the single Na+ ion is expelled from the droplet's center and resides in the subsurface region (within approximately 0.1 nm of the peak in Voronoi-based water density), whereas at 300 K, the radial ion distribution is nearly uniform, consistent with an electrostatic confinement model. The authors also introduce a novel analytical reference model describing the energy of a charged dielectric droplet as the sum of electrostatic and surface energies, predicting a harmonic potential—termed 'electrostatic confinement'—that centers the ion at the droplet's center of mass. This model successfully predicts the room-temperature behavior but fails at supercooling, where the heterogeneous core structure dominates. Multiple ions (5 and 8 Na+ per droplet) similarly exhibit subsurface localization at 200 K, with non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann theory failing to explain the distribution. The authors note that for the smallest droplet (N = 100), the tetrahedral core does not form, and the ion resides one or two layers from the surface, consistent with prior work by Voth et al. The study suggests implications for native mass spectrometry, Rayleigh fission, and atmospheric chemistry, positioning this work as a starting point for understanding ion distribution in supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecular conformations.

Research Context
The spatial distribution of ions in droplets plays a decisive role in chemical reactivity in atmospheric and man-made aerosols. Man-made aerosols include spray-based ionization methods used in native mass spectrometry and droplets as micro-(nano-) reactors for chemical synthesis. In thunderclouds and electrosprays, droplets are highly charged, carrying a small charge determined by at most a few excess ions. Many experiments have used Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance (FT-ICR) mass spectrometry where dominant evaporative cooling of clusters over heating has been reported, with temperatures estimated at 130 K-150 K for 50-70H2O molecules. Supercooled droplets play a critical role as preservation environments of peptide conformations sprayed from the bulk solution. Most computational studies are for clusters at room or elevated temperature; there are relatively few computational studies of supercooled clusters due to the fact that they are notoriously challenging to equilibrate. Voth and co-workers previously investigated a single Na+, Cl-, and H in the temperature range of 100 K-450 K and found ions excluded from the cluster interior below freezing temperature. The distribution of multiple ions and biological molecules at supercooling is still completely unknown. Recent computational work revealed an anomalous, inverted radial density profile emerging for N ≥ 200 molecules at low temperature, with a low-density core with relatively good tetrahedral ordering surrounded by a high-density subsurface. The hypothesis that the low-density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate ion distribution from room temperature could not be explored in earlier research because small cluster sizes precluded the formation of the low-density core.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how the heterogeneous radial structure of supercooled aqueous nanodroplets (a low-density tetrahedral core and high-density subsurface) affects the spatial distribution of single and multiple Na+ ions compared to room temperature. The authors hypothesize that the low-density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate the ion distribution from that at room temperature, a phenomenon not observable at room temperature or in droplets smaller than N = 200 where the core does not form. A secondary hypothesis is that the spatial distribution of multiple ions at supercooling will differ from the prediction of the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which serves as the reference model for room-temperature distributions. The model predicts that a single ion in a charged dielectric droplet should be subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, an effect named 'electrostatic confinement' (EC). The model predicts that the electrostatic confinement is more pronounced at low temperature, high charge, small radius, and intermediate values of the dielectric constant. The model predicts the ion position distribution at 300 K but is expected to deviate at supercooling due to the influence of the low-density core. For multiple ions, the authors investigate whether the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation (solved for spherical geometry) can predict the ion distribution in supercooled droplets.

Methodological Details
The study uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Na+ ions in aqueous nanodroplets at three temperatures: 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K, representing standard and supercooled conditions. Droplet sizes vary from N = 100 H2O molecules (diameter ≈ 1.8 nm) to N = 1100 (diameter ≈ 4.0 nm). Simulations are performed using GROMACS v4.6.1 with the TIP4P/2005 water model. Na+ ion parameters are taken from OPLS-AA, with charge +1e. Each nanodroplet is placed in a periodic cubic box of length L large enough to avoid interaction between the droplet and its periodic images. The cutoff length for Coulomb and Lennard-Jones interactions is L/2, much larger than the droplet diameter, to reproduce long-range electrostatic interactions. Simulations are carried out in the canonical ensemble (constant N, V, T) with temperature controlled by a Nosé-Hoover thermostat with time constant 0.1 ps. Equations of motion are integrated with the leap-frog algorithm with a time step of 2 fs. For single Na+ runs at N = 360 and N = 776 at T = 200 K, the ion is placed at the surface for most runs and at the center for two runs to test equilibration. All multiple Na+ ion runs start with ions near the droplet center of mass. Equilibration time is estimated from convergence of ion density profiles ρion(r) from surface- vs. center-initiated runs; for N = 776, convergence is achieved after 400 ns. For N = 1100, the equilibration time is assumed longer by a factor of τ1100/τ776 ≈ 2. Structural quantities reported as a function of radial distance include water density ρ(r), Voronoi-based density ρv(r), tetrahedral order parameter qT(r), and distance to fifth O neighbor d5(r). The tetrahedral order parameter is defined with a cutoff radius of rcut = 0.35 nm and a spherical shell width of ∆r = 0.05 nm. Voronoi cells are computed for O sites only; H sites are ignored, and the density is averaged over configurations. The analytical reference model considers the energy as the sum of electrostatic and surface energies of a deformable droplet.

Procedures And Architectures
The analytical reference model expresses the energy related to ion distance from the droplet COM (∆E1) as a harmonic potential: ∆E1 = 1/2 K(ε) r^2, where K(ε) is the spring constant. The spring constant K(ε) has its maximum value at ε = 1 + √3 ≈ 2.73. The Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution of ion positions is used to derive the expectation value of r^2, giving the geometric confining effect. For high charges, cyclic peptide models are used to generate effective multi-charge ions, and DNA/RNA strands are cited as other examples. The relaxation time τ is determined from the neighbor correlation function, with values providing an estimate for ion-inclusive simulations. For pure water nanodroplets at low T, Voronoi cells are computed for all O sites, and the total volume V(r) and number N(r) of O sites within each shell of radius r are found. The non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation is solved for a spherical geometry to obtain the ion distribution as a reference model. The ion decay towards the droplet COM at 300 K is fitted to 0.42 exp(-(1.14 - x)/1.2) for 776 molecules and 0.40 exp(-(1.37 - x)/1.3) for 1100 molecules, with λPB ≈ 1.2 nm and 1.3 nm respectively. The NPB reference uses a water dielectric constant of 75, yielding λPB ≈ 0.8, which is comparable to the droplet radius. The 300 K data for the N = 776 droplet are fitted to Eq. 6 (the electrostatic confinement equation) using dashed lines in figures.

Key Results
At high temperature (300 K for N ≥ 200; 260 K for N ≤ 200), ρ(r) of pure water droplets shows a flat interior and sigmoidal decay at the interface, while Voronoi density ρv(r) is monotonically decreasing or flat with r. At low temperature (200 K), significant layering appears for all nanodroplet sizes, with an increase in density as r increases towards the surface, characteristic of supercooled water. At 300 K, the single Na+ radial distribution ρNa(r) is approximately uniform in the droplet interior and decays within the subsurface, consistent with the electrostatic confinement model. At 200 K, the Na+ ion peak is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in ρv(r) for N ≥ 200, meaning the ion resides in the highest-density subsurface region. For N = 100 at 200 K, ρNa(r) is peaked just below 0.3 nm, coinciding with a local minimum in ρ(r), suggesting layering plays a significant role in small droplets. At 200 K and 300 K, the N = 776 droplet shows ρv(r) with a monotonic increase towards a subsurface peak at 200 K and a monotonic decrease at 300 K. The tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) is approximately constant at 300 K but shows a significant decrease at 200 K coinciding with the subsurface density peak. The d5(r) parameter shows a more disordered structure (larger d5) in the vicinity of the subsurface density peak at 200 K. The N = 776 droplet at 200 K confirms ions (single or multiple) prefer the relatively disordered high-density subsurface to the relatively ordered low-density tetrahedral core. For 5 Na+ ions in the N = 776 droplet at 200 K, the ion density shifts to have a peak at approximately the same radial position as for the single ion case. For 8 Na+ ions in the N = 1100 droplet at 200 K, two peaks are observed at 0.52 nm (one ion) and 1.5 nm (multiple ions), indicating expulsion from the core. At 300 K, multiple-ion distributions are almost uniform with an incipient broad maximum in the outer layers, consistent with the NPB prediction. For the N = 100 droplet at 200 K, the Na+ lies one or two layers in from the cluster surface, and the core lacks tetrahedral organization because water molecules around the COM are affected by the ion's solvation shell. The geometric confining effect at 300 K for a 1000-water droplet with a single charge is estimated to be 12 Å in excursion from the center.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The heterogeneous solvent structure in supercooled droplets—a tetrahedral, low-density core and a disordered, high-density subsurface—differentiates ion distribution from room temperature. The Na+ ion tends to reside in the highest-density environment because the dielectric constant increases with density at constant temperature and polarization factor. The surface layer, while at very high density, does not provide a good solvation environment for the ion. The electrostatic confinement model predicts a harmonic potential that correctly describes the ion position at 300 K but fails at 200 K because the low-density core alters the local dielectric landscape. The distribution of multiple ions at 200 K cannot be explained by the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation because the tetrahedral core structure invalidates the continuum dielectric assumption. For the smallest droplet (N = 100), the core lacks tetrahedral organization due to the ion's first solvation shell affecting water molecules near the COM, and the droplet is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations. The model can be extended by including ion size and hydrophobic effects, serving as a reference framework for future simulation comparison. The expulsion of ions to the subsurface may impact Rayleigh fission and ion evaporation mechanisms in native mass spectrometry, as conical deformation (key for ion emission) could be hindered by the low-density core at supercooling. The study is anticipated to be the starting point for investigating ion structure in supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve peptide and macromolecule conformations for ion mobility-mass spectrometry.

Contradictions And Limitations
The electrostatic confinement model's prediction that the ion is centered at the droplet COM is violated at 200 K, where the ion is expelled to the subsurface. The authors note that for N = 100 at 200 K, the assumption that the ion peak should be uniform in the interior (where ρv(r) is constant) is contradicted by the fact that ρNa(r) peaks below 0.3 nm, indicating layering effects. The NPB prediction for ion decay at 300 K is qualitative rather than quantitative because shape fluctuations in droplets of up to a few thousand molecules are significant. For the N = 100 droplet at 200 K, direct visual inspection reveals the ion resides one or two layers from the surface, which is consistent with Voth et al. but the cluster lacks a tetrahedral core, limiting generalizability to the smallest droplets. The model does not include ion size or hydrophobic effects, and the authors acknowledge these as necessary extensions. The authors state that results for r < 0.2 nm are noisy due to poor statistics, making characterization of the innermost region difficult. The assumption that multiple-ion relaxation time is shorter and single-ion simulations provide upper bounds on relaxation times is not independently verified in the paper. The study does not report random seeds, specific error estimates, or statistical significance tests beyond convergence checks. The authors note the droplet of N = 100 is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations than larger droplets, which may affect the interpretability of the ion position.

Claims
At 200 K, a single Na+ ion in a supercooled aqueous nanodroplet (N ≥ 200) is expelled from the droplet center and resides in the high-density subsurface region rather than at the center of mass. The Na+ ion peak is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in ρv(r) for N ≥ 200 at 200 K. At 200 K, ρv(r) shows a monotonic increase towards a subsurface peak, and the ion peak coincides with this subsurface maximum. The tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) shows a significant decrease at 200 K coinciding with the subsurface density peak, confirming the disordered subsurface location. At 200 K, the N = 776 droplet shows ρNa(r) peaked at the subsurface rather than centered at r = 0. The ion density when five Na+ ions are present also has a peak at approximately the same radial position as for the single ion case at 200 K. For N = 100 at 200 K, ρNa(r) peaks just below 0.3 nm rather than being uniform as a constant ρv(r) in that region would suggest, indicating layering overrides the density effect in the smallest droplet. For r < 0.2 nm, statistics are difficult to obtain and results are quite noisy, limiting certainty about the innermost region. The ion distribution at supercooling is not described by the electrostatic confinement model, requiring a new theoretical framework that accounts for heterogeneous solvent structure. The expelled ion position may affect Rayleigh fission and conical deformation, impacting ion emission in electrospray sources.
The electrostatic confinement model, which predicts a harmonic potential centering a single ion at the droplet's center of mass due to electrostatic-surface energy competition, correctly describes the room-temperature radial ion distribution but fails at supercooling. At 300 K, the Na+ radial distribution is consistent with the electrostatic confinement model. The model's harmonic potential form is derived from the electrostatic and surface energy sum of a deformable droplet. The spring constant maximum at ε ≈ 2.73 corresponds to the predicted behavior for water droplets. The simulated ion decay at 300 K matches the NPB exponential decay predictions qualitatively. The model explicitly fails at 200 K, where the low-density core alters the local electrostatic landscape and expels the ion to the subsurface. The authors note that the model can only be extended further by including ion size and hydrophobic effects to be fully predictive. The model serves as a reference analytical framework for comparing with simulation data across different systems. The model's limitations at supercooling highlight the need for theory that incorporates local solvent structure rather than continuum dielectric properties.
Multiple Na+ ions in supercooled nanodroplets are expelled from the core to the subsurface, and their distribution cannot be explained by the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation. For 8 Na+ in N = 1100 at 200 K, two peaks appear at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm, with the multiple-ion peak in the subsurface. The multiple ions are expelled from the drop's core and show a maximum at the same location as the single ion. The NPB prediction for ion decay (λPB ≈ 0.8) is comparable to the droplet radius, so the effect is only qualitative. The ion distributions at 200 K show a decay that cannot be analyzed using the NPB. The appearance of two peaks for 8 ions at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm does not indicate a metastable state, as one ion can exchange with others. At 300 K, the multiple-ion distributions are almost uniform, consistent with the NPB prediction. The failure of continuum dielectric theory at supercooling suggests that local solvent organization dominates over global electrostatic fields. This has implications for atmospheric chemistry and the study of ion mobility-mass spectrometry of supercooled droplets.
For the smallest droplet (N = 100) at 200 K, a tetrahedral core does not form, and the Na+ ion resides one or two layers from the surface, consistent with prior single-ion cluster studies. The cluster of N = 100 does not show a tetrahedrally organized core. The central H2O molecules participate in the immediate solvation of the Na+, preventing core tetrahedrization. The Na+ lies one or two layers in from the cluster surface. This is in agreement with those of Voth et al. for the location of the Na+ ion in cluster of 100 H2O molecules. The droplet is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations than larger droplets. The layering effect at N = 100 means ρNa(r) peaks below 0.3 nm, contradicting the uniform-interior prediction of constant ρv(r). The absence of the tetrahedral core in N = 100 limits the generalizability of the subsurface expulsion mechanism to the smallest droplets. The agreement with Voth et al. validates the simulation approach but highlights that small-cluster-specific effects limit the broad application of the supercooling observation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Convergence of ion density profiles was verified by comparing surface- vs. center-initiated runs at 200 K for N = 360 and N = 776; convergence was reached after 400 ns for N = 776. The relaxation time τ was estimated from the neighbor correlation function to guide simulation length; for N = 1100, equilibration is assumed longer by a factor of τ1100/τ776 ≈ 2. For multiple ions, the relaxation time is presumed shorter, and single-ion simulations are taken as upper bounds. The analytical model predictions for electrostatic confinement were validated at 300 K against simulation data and contrasted at 200 K. The geometric confining effect at 300 K was estimated at 12 Å for a 1000-water droplet with a single charge, indicating the effect is significant. The NPB analysis of multiple-ion decay at 300 K was noted as qualitative due to significant shape fluctuations in droplets of this size. The Voronoi-based density ρv(r) was used instead of total density ρ(r) to decouple the Voronoi-volume effect from the layering undulations, providing a clearer interpretation of the subsurface peak. The tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) was cut off at its minimum (1.6 nm) because the subsequent increase in the surface region is not indicative of real tetrahedral order.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the electrostatic confinement spring constant K(ε) as a function of the relative dielectric constant, with its maximum at ε ≈ 2.73. Figure 2 shows the distribution of the center of mass of a charged cyclic peptide (charge 8e+) in a 3.8 nm droplet at 300 K, showing the geometric confinement. Figure 3 displays radial density profiles ρ(r) and Voronoi density ρv(r) for pure water droplets, and Na+ density ρNa(r) at 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K, showing the subsurface peak at 200 K. Figure 4 shows a detailed comparison of the N = 776 droplet at 200 K and 300 K, including water structure, ion density for single and 5 ions, and tetrahedral order parameters. Figure 5 displays the radial distributions of multiple ions (5 and 8 Na+) in droplets of 776 and 1100 H2O molecules at 300 K and 200 K, showing subsurface expulsion at 200 K. Table 1 lists the system sizes (N = 100, 360, 776, 1100) at T = 200, 260, 300 K, the mean number of molecules in the cluster, and the relaxation time τ. Figure S2 (SI) shows 

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that supercooled aqueous nanodroplets form a tetrahedral, low-density core and a disordered, high-density subsurface, which expels Na+ ions from the center to the subsurface at 200 K, while at 300 K the ion distribution remains nearly uniform due to electrostatic confinement. 2. The strongest evidence is the spatial coincidence of the Na+ ion peak (within 0.1 nm) with the subsurface peak in Voronoi-based water density ρv(r) at 200 K, supported by corresponding decreases in the tetrahedral order parameter and increases in d5, across multiple droplet sizes (N = 360, 776, 1100). 3. The future path is to extend this study to include unstructured peptides and ion complexes in supercooled droplets, examine the impact of ion expulsion on Rayleigh fission and conical deformation in ion emission, and connect these findings to native mass spectrometry of macromolecules and atmospheric chemistry.

summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from high-throughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa (Max-Planck-Gesellschaft); Christopher Sutton (Max-Planck-Gesellschaft); Luca M Ghiringhelli (Max-Planck-Gesellschaft); Sandip De (BASF SE); Patricia Löser; Stephan A Schunk (BASF SE); Ansgar Schäfer (BASF SE); Matthias Scheffler (Max-Planck-Gesellschaft)

summary.type_of_paper: Research article reporting experimental and computational study
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates the application of the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical dataset to identify physicochemical constraints (SG rules) that exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance in the selective oxidation of propylene. By using high-throughput experimentation (HTE), 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were synthesized and tested. Ten composition-dependent physicochemical parameters derived from density-functional-theory (DFT) free-atom calculations, along with reaction temperature, served as candidate descriptive parameters. The HTE-measured oxygenate yield (acrolein and acrylic acid) was used as the target variable. The SGD analysis identified three key parameters associated with high yields: temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity. A specific subgroup containing only 1.2% of the data set (15 out of 1220 data points) exhibited an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%, approximately five times the global average of 4.83%, guided by the rule 280 ≤ T ≤ 300°C, phosphorus content > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. These SG rules were then used to predict performance in more complex four- and five-component catalyst systems, achieving oxygenate yields of 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively—roughly twice the highest value observed in the training set (26.85%). A subsequent SGD analysis on the four- and five-component data revealed different critical parameters (higher temperature ≥ 360°C, atomic radius difference, and electron affinity), demonstrating that while the approach generalizes to more complex compositions, the specific mechanistic constraints evolve with increased complexity. The paper concludes that SGD-HTE-theory is a suitable local-modeling approach for discovering exceptional materials when explicit atomistic modeling of full catalytic progressions remains impractical.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates the application of the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical dataset to identify physicochemical constraints (SG rules) that exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance in the selective oxidation of propylene. By using high-throughput experimentation (HTE), 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were synthesized and tested. Ten composition-dependent physicochemical parameters derived from density-functional-theory (DFT) free-atom calculations, along with reaction temperature, served as candidate descriptive parameters. The HTE-measured oxygenate yield (acrolein and acrylic acid) was used as the target variable. The SGD analysis identified three key parameters associated with high yields: temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity. A specific subgroup containing only 1.2% of the data set (15 out of 1220 data points) exhibited an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%, approximately five times the global average of 4.83%, guided by the rule 280 ≤ T ≤ 300°C, phosphorus content > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. These SG rules were then used to predict performance in more complex four- and five-component catalyst systems, achieving oxygenate yields of 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively—roughly twice the highest value observed in the training set (26.85%). A subsequent SGD analysis on the four- and five-component data revealed different critical parameters (higher temperature ≥ 360°C, atomic radius difference, and electron affinity), demonstrating that while the approach generalizes to more complex compositions, the specific mechanistic constraints evolve with increased complexity. The paper concludes that SGD-HTE-theory is a suitable local-modeling approach for discovering exceptional materials when explicit atomistic modeling of full catalytic progressions remains impractical.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis is governed by an intricate interplay of multiple processes including surface reaction networks and dynamic restructuring of the catalyst material under reaction conditions. While theoretical approaches attempt to address the complexity of heterogeneous catalysis, explicit atomistic modelling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) allows testing large amounts of materials, but utilizing the information obtained to decide on the next promising materials to investigate is not straightforward. As the number of possible materials is practically infinite and the number of good catalysts is very small, the direct approach is unlikely to identify the needed catalyst material. Detailed characterization of each material in large libraries is typically not feasible, hindering in-depth understanding of underlying processes governing reactivity. Distinct catalytic mechanisms might operate depending on materials and reaction conditions, and only very few situations result in good catalytic performance, leading to an unbalanced distribution between high-and low-performance scenarios. Global models trained to minimize expected average prediction error over all samples do not necessarily allow focused modelling of the most interesting materials and mechanisms. Alternative approaches for catalyst design are required to handle the sparse distribution of high-performance outcomes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach applied to a hybrid HTE and DFT dataset can identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and constraints associated exclusively with high catalytic performance. The SGD approach is hypothesized to identify rules (propositions and selectors) that reflect specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance rather than average behavior. The study specifically investigates materials based on ruthenium combined with tungsten and phosphorus as an alternative catalyst class for selective oxidation of propylene. The hypothesis is that composition-dependent electronegativity, phosphorus content, and temperature will emerge as key parameters describing high yields of acrolein and acrylic acid. The predicted outcome is that the identified SG rules will generalize to design more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition, achieving oxygenate yields exceeding those observed in the three-component training set.

Methodological Details
120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were synthesized and tested in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. The three-component catalysts were prepared on a SiO2 pseudo-liquid support and might present a disordered, possibly amorphous structure. At each catalyst composition, several reaction temperatures between 200°C and 400°C were examined. All reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors with a reaction feed of Ar, H2O, N2, O2 and propylene (C3H6) at molar rates 4.015, 4.015, 104.40, 20.08, and 1.57 mmol/h, respectively. The same mass of catalyst was used in all reactions so that contact time, in terms of volumetric flow per mass of catalyst, was kept fixed. The dataset for three-component materials comprises 120 compositions times multiple temperatures, resulting in 1220 total data points (Fig. 2A). For the four- and five-component materials, the subsequent HTE dataset contains 746 data points (Fig. 5A). 11 descriptive parameters derived from DFT-calculated free-atom properties were used: I, J, K, L, M, L, N, L, O, L, PQR and S, T, S, U (note: the text lists 11 but some notation is partially obscured in the source). Candidate descriptive parameters included temperature and ten parameters related to the composition and chemical nature of the catalyst materials derived from calculated freeatom properties. DFT calculations were performed using DFT-PBEsol with the FHI-aims code.

Procedures And Architectures
Properties were calculated for isolated atoms using DFT-PBEsol and the FHI-aims code, with detailed values available in the electronic supporting information (ESI). L PQR is defined as the radius of the highest-occupied state, and for a given catalyst composition, per-element free-atom properties are converted into system-specific properties by taking the composition-weighted average. The SGD approach starts with the generation of a pool of propositions (π), statements about the data that apply only to a portion of the data set. For continuous candidate descriptive parameters, the propositions are inequalities constraining their values. SGD identifies selectors (σ), i.e., statements formed by a number of propositions and the 'AND' connector (∧), that result in the selection of subgroups with the most outstanding distributions of target values. The quality function is defined as the product of coverage M(jk)/M(X) and the cumulative Jensen-Shannon divergence m/no between the distribution of target values in the SG and the whole data set. The coverage term controls the subgroup size and prevents very small SGs with little statistical significance from being selected. The quality function is maximized, and for the chosen SG, a cumulative Jensen-Shannon divergence of 0.693 was achieved among subgroups within 40% of the optimal value. The oxygenate yield target is defined as Eq. 1: yield = (molar rate outlet - molar rate inlet) / (molar rate inlet). Cross-validation was performed by training with randomly selected 90% of data points or by excluding data points with oxygenate yields lower than 3%.

Key Results
50% of the measured materials and conditions result in less than 2% oxygenates yield, and only 41 out of 1220 measurements are associated with oxygenate yields above 20%. The average oxygenates yield over the whole three-component data set is 4.83%, with a maximum value of 26.85%. The identified SG for the three-component data contains 15 data points (approximately 1.2% of the data set), all with high oxygenate yields. The average yield of oxygenates in this SG is 24.15%, approximately five times higher than the global average. The SG rules are 280 ≤ T ≤ 300°C, J K > 0.55 (phosphorus content), and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV (composition-weighted electronegativity). The highest yield of oxygenates achieved for the four-component catalyst with 0.35 molar fraction of tellurium is 60.19% at 400°C. The five-component catalyst containing ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium, and tantalum achieves the highest oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400°C. Both four- and five-component outstanding catalysts achieve oxygenate yields up to twice as large as those obtained with three-component materials (26.85%). The four- and five-component SGD analysis yields an SG with highest m/no of 0.355, containing 18 data points (approximately 2.4% of the 746-point dataset). The rules for the four- and five-component SG constrain three parameters: T ≥ 360°C, L˜+1 ≤ 1.001 Å, and VH < -1.593 eV. The composition-averaged electronegativity for the 59.60% yield five-component catalyst is 3.947 eV, which lies within the threshold defined by the SG rule. Cross-validation using 90% of data or excluding low-yield points produces similar thresholds (3.882 to 3.910 eV for lower bound, 3.989 to 4.031 eV for upper bound).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The temperature rule highlights that highest yields are observed at intermediate temperatures (280–300°C) within the tested range of 200–400°C. The phosphorus content rule suggests a relatively high phosphorus content (>0.55) is needed, potentially related to the dilution of metal active sites on a phosphate matrix. The electronegativity rule effectively limits the ruthenium content, as Ru is needed for propylene conversion but excessive Ru leads to combustion products. The SGD rules reflect the specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance rather than average behavior, identifying local rather than global mechanisms. The rules are interpretable and chemically meaningful, providing a rational design strategy for heterogeneous catalysts beyond simple composition enumeration. The shift to higher temperatures and different composition-dependent parameters in the four- and five-component data suggests that increased material complexity alters the operative catalytic mechanisms.

Contradictions And Limitations
The atomic structures of all tested catalysts are not known in detail, and the catalysts may present a disordered or possibly amorphous structure. Oxygen content is not known from the catalysts formulation nor measured for all materials, so it is not included in the material characterization. The SG rule on reaction temperature derived from three-component materials is not transferable to the four-component materials, which require higher temperatures (≥ 360°C). It is unclear if the SG rules can identify exceptional materials for arbitrary ruthenium content or for V_X and V^ elements with significantly different radii compared to tungsten. Different mechanisms may operate on materials with different atomic radii, so the SGD analysis might need new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space. The five-component analysis used only a limited selection of additional elements (Mo, Nb, Ta, Sb) and was not comprehensive.

Claims
SGD applied to HTE-plus-theory data can identify chemically meaningful rules for exceptional catalytic performance in sparse datasets. The identified SG contains only 15 out of 1220 data points (1.2%) but with five-fold higher yield. The rules (temperature, P content, electronegativity) have direct chemical interpretations. The approach successfully predicted four- and five-component catalysts with yields exceeding the training set. The temperature rule is not transferable across composition space (300°C vs ≥ 360°C). New parameters (L˜+1 and VH) are required for more complex compositions, suggesting mechanism shift. The approach enables rational catalyst design without explicit atomistic modeling of the full reaction network. SGD can guide the synthesis of catalysts not yet experimentally realized.
Increasing material complexity from three to five components leads to significantly higher maximum oxygenate yields under the same conditions. Three-component max yield is 26.85%. Four-component max yield is 60.19% at 400°C. Five-component max yield is 59.60% at 400°C. The five-component catalyst with 59.60% yield slightly underperforms the 60.19% four-component result. Simple composition extension (adding a fifth element) can more than double the maximum performance. The SG rules remain approximately valid for the 3.947 eV value even in the five-component case.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Cross-validation was performed by training with randomly selected 90% of the data points. Data points with oxygenate yields lower than 3% were excluded from training, yielding similar SG rules. Ranges of variation for minimum and maximum thresholds were found to be [3.882, 3.910 eV] and [3.989, 4.031 eV], consistent with the main results. The SGD analysis on four- and five-component data (746 data points) confirmed that rules change with composition complexity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the SGD approach workflow: pool of propositions, selectors, and quality function maximizing outstanding target value distributions. Figure 1B shows the three-component catalyst compositions on Ru, W, and P. Figure 1C displays the catalytic reactions for propylene oxidation to acrolein, acrylic acid, and combustion products. Figure 2A shows the propylene conversion versus oxygenate selectivity profiles, and Figure 2B shows the distribution of oxygenate yields. Figure 2C presents the SG rules on three descriptive parameters for the three-component data. Figure 2D and 2F show rules on phosphorus content and composition-averaged electronegativity, respectively. Figure 3B shows the ternary diagram of composition with the electronegativity rule and the composition map. Figure 4A presents the four-component catalyst map with electronegativity values and HTE results. Figure 4C and 4D show the experimental HTE results for four- and five-component catalysts. Figure 5A and 5B show the distribution of data points for the four- and five-component SGD analysis. Figure 5C presents the rules for the four- and five-component SG, constraining temperature, atomic radius difference, and electron affinity.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration that a subgroup-discovery SGD approach, when coupled with HTE and DFT, can extract interpretable, chemically meaningful rules that define exceptional catalytic performance in sparse, unbalanced datasets where global models fail. 2. The strongest evidence is that the identified SG rules correctly predicted four- and five-component catalysts achieving oxygenate yields of 60.19% and 59.60%, more than twice the training maximum of 26.85%, and that the five-component catalyst composition was captured within the predicted parameter window. 3. The future path involves performing SGD on new data covering unexplored portions of the materials space—specifically different ruthenium contents and elements with significantly different atomic radii—to extend the domain in which the SG rules can detect exceptional catalysts.

summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Agricultural Chemistry / Green Chemistry - Mechanochemical Synthesis of Fertilizers
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (experimental) with reverse logistics and green chemistry framework
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates a solvent-free, mechanochemical synthesis of potassium calcium phosphate bioceramics from eggshell waste (calcite, CaCO3) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) as a sustainable alternative to conventional fertilizers. The process leverages reverse logistics principles, converting food-industry biowaste into value-added soil conditioners without solvent waste or unwanted byproducts. High-energy ball milling at 400 rpm for 2 hours and 600 rpm for 2 hours produces a mixture of the new phosphate phases K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4, while further milling induces dehydroxylation to the CaKPO4 phase. The novel bioceramics exhibit superior nutrient management: phosphorus and potassium release kinetics in 2% citric acid and soil are substantially slowed compared to the precursor KH2PO4, while calcium bioavailability is increased relative to the precursor CaCO3. In soil release assays, the 2h/600 rpm sample demonstrated a progressive P release profile (15% recovery at 30 days) compared to the precursor (40% recovery) and served as a bioavailable Ca source (30.97 mg/kg after 30 days, ~8% recovery). The material subsequently converts to hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) under soil conditions, functioning as a long-term slow-release fertilizer effective at pH ~5. NMR and TGA analyses confirm the structural transformations, with 31P NMR revealing disubstituted phosphate signals consistent with KCaPO4 formation. A radial P diffusion assay showed the 2h/600 rpm sample performed intermediate between struvite (low diffusion) and KH2PO4 (extremely soluble), with 34% faster diffusion than struvite and 22% slower than KH2PO4 at 30 days. The study provides a first-of-its-kind mechanochemical protocol for calcium and potassium phosphate production from calcite and KH2PO4.
