The process leverages reverse logistics principles, converting food-industry biowaste into value-added soil conditioners without solvent waste or unwanted byproducts. High-energy ball milling at 400 rpm for 2 hours and 600 rpm for 2 hours produces a mixture of the new phosphate phases K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4, while further milling induces dehydroxylation to the CaKPO4 phase. The novel bioceramics exhibit superior nutrient management: phosphorus and potassium release kinetics in 2% citric acid and soil are substantially slowed compared to the precursor KH2PO4, while calcium bioavailability is increased relative to the precursor CaCO3. In soil release assays, the 2h/600 rpm sample demonstrated a progressive P release profile (15% recovery at 30 days) compared to the precursor (40% recovery) and served as a bioavailable Ca source (30.97 mg/kg after 30 days, ~8% recovery). The material subsequently converts to hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) under soil conditions, functioning as a long-term slow-release fertilizer effective at pH ~5. NMR and TGA analyses confirm the structural transformations, with 31P NMR revealing disubstituted phosphate signals consistent with KCaPO4 formation. A radial P diffusion assay showed the 2h/600 rpm sample performed intermediate between struvite (low diffusion) and KH2PO4 (extremely soluble), with 34% faster diffusion than struvite and 22% slower than KH2PO4 at 30 days. The study provides a first-of-its-kind mechanochemical protocol for calcium and potassium phosphate production from calcite and KH2PO4.

Research Context
Eggshells are important food industry wastes produced in millions of tons globally, currently disposed in landfills with no pretreatment, producing odors from microbial growth. Reverse logistics, as defined by Tibben and Lembke (2002), provides a framework for the collection and restitution of solid waste back into productive cycles. Existing mechanochemical methods for hydroxyapatite synthesis from eggshells typically use phosphoric acid solutions rather than powder phosphate salts. Previous studies by Chaikina et al. (2019) and Francis and Rahman (2016) have reported mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite but not the specific phosphate structures targeted here. As far as the authors know, no mechanochemical process has been reported for production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate and potassium calcium phosphate from calcite and KH2PO4. The authors note the importance of avoiding unnecessary economic losses and prioritizing environmental care in ecological fertilizer production.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a solvent-free mechanochemical process can synthesize calcium and potassium phosphate bioceramics from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4 for use as smart-release fertilizer. The authors hypothesize that the K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 phases will provide better nutrient management of P, K, and Ca when applied to soil. The material is expected to first release K and form hydroxyapatite, acting as an important P and Ca bioavailable source at pH ~5. It is predicted that the mechanochemical approach, producing no liquid or solid waste, will ensure huge savings during production compared to traditional methods. The authors propose that the produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, providing a delay in P and K bioavailability while improving Ca bioavailability. The study aims to validate that the mechanical energy is sufficient to break reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration to form the new structures.

Methodological Details
Eggshells were collected by the authors from their homes, washed with water, and dried at room temperature, with diameters between 1 and 10 mm before grinding. KH2PO4 was supplied from Vetec, and the authors assumed eggshells were mainly composed of CaCO3. The milling process used a Fritsch Pulverisette 7 high-energy ball mill with a 250 mL zirconia bowl and five zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 corresponded to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. Two experimental series were performed: first at 600 rpm for 15, 30, 1, 2, 3, 6, 12, and 24 min, and second at 100, 200, 400, and 600 rpm for 2 h. XRD was performed on a Shimadzu XRD 6000 with Cu Kα beam (λ = 0.1546 nm), 2θ range of 3-40°, scanning speed 2° min⁻¹, at 30 kV and 40 mA. DSC used a TA Q100 Controller with refrigerated cooling system in the 25°C-600°C range; TGA used a TA Q500 in synthetic air, 20-900°C at 10°C min⁻¹. 31P NMR MAS was performed on an Avance III HD Bruker, rotating at 10 kHz using HPDEC sequence with ADP as reference at 0.8 ppm. Nutrient content was determined by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 (8:1 v/v, 24 h at 250°C), followed by atomic absorption and colorimetric methods. For release essays, materials were pelletized at 5 bar pressure and standardized to 100 mg/L of P; one pellet was placed in 10 mL beaker immersed in 300 mL of 2% citric acid. Soil release essays used Petri dishes (diameter 8.6 cm) with 78 g dry sieved 2.0 mm soil (density 1.2 g·cm⁻³) and 15 mL deionized water for 70% WHC. Soil release for closer-to-real-conditions used plastic containers with 50 g sandy soil and 75% water saturation. P diffusion was analyzed via paper marking, scanning, and image processing with GNU Image Manipulation Program v.2.6.11. Phosphorus was quantified by colorimetric molybdenum blue; potassium and calcium by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy using a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T.

Procedures And Architectures
The milling process was initiated as a solvent-free mechanochemical activation, applying friction and impact forces to promote solid phase ion migration. The reaction mechanism involves breaking reagent bonds to form K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 among non-crystalline compounds and CO2 from CaCO3 decomposition. The theoretical non-stoichiometric reaction was proposed as: KH2PO4 + CaCO3 → CO2 + H2O + K3CaH(PO4)2 + CaKPO4. Samples milled for 2 h and 400 rpm and 2 h and 600 rpm were identified as the key experimental conditions for product formation. After milling, samples were calcined at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C to characterize solid fractions after each main mass loss mechanism. The P diffusion marking method used pre-treated paper to mark P diffusion in soil, with threshold color value on a 0-255 scale for image quantification. Aliquots of 1.2 mL were collected from 15 min to 30 days in citric acid to construct release kinetic models. Soil release experiments were conducted at 3, 7, 15, and 30 days under aerobic conditions. After each soil release period, solid residues were removed for XRD characterization; K and Ca were extracted by 0.05 M HCl and 1 M KCl, and P by Mehlich 1 method. A supplementary experiment suspended ground samples in water, dried, and characterized by XRD to confirm phase transition to hydroxyapatite.

Key Results
XRD patterns showed that milling at 2 h and 400 rpm produced K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF 22-1218) and CaKPO4 (PDF 33-1002) as the main phases. Below 2 h and 400 rpm, only reactant diffraction patterns were found, indicating no chemical reaction occurred. KH2PO4 TGA showed a residual mass of 89% consistent with the theoretical 87% for KPO3 formation after structural water loss. Eggshell TGA showed experimental residue of 56% versus theoretical 59% for calcite decomposition. Milled samples at 600 rpm showed three mass loss events centered at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C; at 420°C the phase converted to KCaPO4 (PDF 33-1002). 31P NMR of KH2PO4 showed a single signal at δ = 3.74 ppm; milled samples showed shifts at δ = 3.28 ppm (2 and 6 h) and δ = 2.82 ppm (24 h), plus a signal at δ = 0.74 ppm for disubstituted phosphate. A signal at δ ≈ -5 ppm (marked δ = -4.78 ppm) in the 2 h / 600 rpm sample was attributed to pyrophosphate formed by phosphate dimerization. In 2% citric acid, phosphorus and potassium release was slower for milled samples compared to KH2PO4, showing a substantial decrease in kinetic constants. In contrast, calcium release was extremely slow for eggshell CaCO3 but readily available from the milled phosphate phases, showing an opposite effect. In soil (Fig. 6), P release for KH2PO4 increased from 0 to 107 mg/kg after 3 days (40% of total), while the 2 h/600 rpm sample released 0 to 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days (15% of total). The P radial diffusion of the 2 h/600 rpm sample was 1.99 cm at day 2 and 22% slower than KH2PO4 (2.62 cm) at day 30. The P radial diffusion of the 2 h/600 rpm sample was 34% faster than struvite at 30 days. K release in soil reached around 100% for both KH2PO4 and 2 h/600 rpm after 30 days, with a slight decrease at 3 days for the milled sample. Bioavailable calcium in soil increased from 0 to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for the 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery. Hydroxyapatite (PDF 9-432) was identified in soil from 3 to 30 days, with the phase transition confirmed by XRD of water-suspended ground samples.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The mechanism involves mechanochemical activation, where mechanical energy breaks reagent bonds to promote solid phase ion migration and new structure formation. The slower release of P and K from milled samples relative to KH2PO4 confirms that the new phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4) act as smart-release fertilizers. The increased Ca bioavailability from milled phosphates compared to CaCO3 indicates the formation of more acidic-soluble Ca sources. Hydroxyapatite formation in soil under pH ~5 conditions explains the progressive P release and Ca accumulation, aligning with the literature on apatite solubility. The disubstituted phosphate NMR signal at δ = 0.74 ppm and the pyrophosphate signal at δ = -4.78 ppm suggest intermediate phosphorous chemical environments during phase conversion. The intermediate P diffusion profile (between struvite and KH2PO4) positions the bioceramic as a middle-ground release strategy suitable for specific management needs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The TGA of milled samples at 600 rpm does not show calcite decomposition below 700°C, suggesting low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade total calcite. The 2 h/600 rpm milled sample has an unclear phosphate phase after milling, only matching K3CaH(PO4)2 after thermal treatment at 280°C. The exact composition of the non-crystalline and minor phases is not quantified, limiting structural characterization. Kinetic constants for calcium release could not be directly compared between precursor and milled samples, hindering full statistical validation. The soil release assay used only 50 g sandy soil with 75% water saturation, which may not represent all soil types or conditions. The study does not report a random seed for the image thresholding, a replication parameter, or a statistical comparison of the P diffusion zones beyond visual description. The authors do not specify the exact mass or surface area of the eggshells used, only the diameter range.

Claims
A solvent-free mechanochemical process can synthesize potassium calcium phosphate bioceramics from eggshell calcite and KH2PO4 with no liquid or solid waste. The milling process was described as free of solvent and producing no liquid or solid waste. XRD confirmed the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 phases after 2 h milling. At 600 rpm, calcite decomposition was not fully observed below 700°C, indicating incomplete reaction of all precursors. The process eliminates solvent waste costs and waste streams, supporting green chemistry goals.
The produced K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 phases exhibit slower P and K release and faster Ca release compared to the precursors, acting as smart-release fertilizers. In 2% citric acid, P and K release was slower for milled samples than KH2PO4. Calcium release from the milled samples was faster than from eggshell CaCO3. In soil, 34% faster P diffusion than struvite and 22% slower than KH2PO4 confirms intermediate release. The slower release in soil compared to citric acid is attributed to hydroxyapatite formation, introducing a second-stage kinetic complexity. The material enables synchronized nutrient release, potentially reducing runoff and maximizing plant uptake.
Hydroxyapatite forms in soil under pH ~5 conditions, providing a long-term slow-release source of Ca and P. PDF 9-432 identified in soil from 3 to 30 days. Phase transition to hydroxyapatite was confirmed by XRD of suspended ground samples. Literature cited confirms hydroxyapatite as a slow-release fertilizer effective at pH ~5. The study notes that if faster release is needed, hydroxyapatite nanocomposites would be preferable. The product is suitable for acidic soils (pH ~5) where phosphorus fixation is typically a problem.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The milling parameters were systematically varied in time (15 min to 24 h) and speed (100 to 600 rpm) to determine minimum reaction conditions. Replicate pellets (triplicate) were used for citric acid release assays, with one pellet per 10 mL beaker. TGA/DSC calcination at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C served as ablation steps to isolate and identify specific phase transitions. The radial P diffusion was compared against two benchmarks: the extremely soluble KH2PO4 and the low-diffusion struvite. Hydroxyapatite phase confirmation was independently verified by suspending ground samples in water and re-characterizing by XRD. Soil release used 50 g sandy soil with 75% water saturation as a standardized test condition.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: XRD patterns showing K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 phases after 2 h milling at 400 rpm. Figure 2: TGA curves for KH2PO4, eggshell, and milled samples showing respective mass loss events. Figure 3: XRD patterns of milled samples calcined at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C to identify solid fractions. Figure 4: 31P NMR MAS spectra showing phase-specific chemical shifts from 3.74 to -4.78 ppm. Figure 5: Release kinetics of P and K in 2% citric acid, fitted to pseudo-first and pseudo-second order models. Figure 6: Soil release profiles for KH2PO4, 2 h/600 rpm sample, and Ca, with 107 mg/kg P at 3 days for KH2PO4 and 30.97 mg/kg Ca at 30 days for the milled sample. Figure 7: XRD identifying hydroxyapatite phase transition in soil from 3 to 30 days. Table S1: Nutrient content of samples and precursors determined by acid digestion and colorimetric/atomic absorption methods. Table S2: Chemical and physical soil properties including sand, clay, silt, WHC, OM, SB, CEC, and V%.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first reported mechanochemical protocol for synthesizing K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 bioceramics from eggshell calcite and KH2PO4 in a solvent-free, waste-minimizing green chemistry framework. 2. The strongest evidence is the dual-pronged validation: (i) spectroscopic and thermal confirmation of the new phosphate phases and hydroxyapatite transition via XRD, TGA, and 31P NMR, and (ii) release kinetics demonstrating a substantial delay in P/K bioavailability with simultaneous enhancement of Ca bioavailability relative to precursors. 3. The future path involves optimizing the process for specific soil-pH tailoring, developing nanocomposites (as suggested by the Giroto et al. 2017 work) to further modulate release rates, and scaling production within the reverse logistics framework of food-processing industries.

summary.title: Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6
summary.authors: Marcial Fernández Castro (Technical University of Denmark); Jean Truer (Technical University of Denmark); Espíndola Rodríguez (Technical University of Denmark); Jens Wenzel (Technical University of Denmark)
summary.field_subfield: Photovoltaics / Flexible Organic Solar Cells
summary.type_of_paper: Research article reporting original experimental results on slot-die coated OSCs
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the 'lab-to-fab gap' in organic solar cell (OSC) manufacturing by demonstrating slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 binary and PM6:Y6:PC61BM ternary active layers on flexible PET substrates using o-xylene (a green solvent) without additives. The work is conducted in open-air on a roll-platform-compatible homemade coater, addressing the industrial relevance that spin-coating lacks. The active layer coating was systematically optimized by screening slot-die head temperatures from 60 °C to 120 °C (all components kept at the same temperature) and concentration from 12 to 28 mg/mL. The optimal coating temperature was determined to be 100 °C, where the short-circuit current density reached a maximum and bimolecular recombination was minimized (S = 0.978, closest to unity), while 120 °C induced edge aggregation and reduced fill factor (42.2% vs. 47.10%). The AL thickness was screened from 101 nm to 217 nm; the peak Jsc of 17.3 mA/cm² at 154 nm and a maximum average PCE of 5.8% at 217 nm were reported. Introducing a small amount of PC61BM (ternary 1:1.1:0.1 ratio) increased average PCE to 6.7% with a champion efficiency of 7.2% and Jsc of 20 mA/cm², attributed to improved exciton dissociation (96.3%) and charge collection (77.7%). Encapsulated devices retained >99% initial efficiency after 1050 h dark storage (ISOS-D-1 protocol), confirming long-term stability under normal room conditions. The study serves as a direct precursor to roll-to-roll production, demonstrating that green solvent, additive-free, slot-die coating can yield ~7% PCE on flexible substrates without cleanroom requirements.

claims.description: Slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 on flexible PET substrates in open-air using o-xylene without additives can achieve PCE comparable to lab-scale devices (~6.3%) and establishes a viable path to roll-to-roll production.

Adding a small amount of PC61BM as a complementary fullerene acceptor in a ternary blend enhances both exciton dissociation and charge collection in slot-die coated flexible devices, raising PCE to 6.7% (7.2% champion).

The optimal coating temperature for the PM6:Y6 slot-die process is 100 °C, where a tradeoff between improved carrier collection (higher EQE) and morphology-induced aggregation (lower FF) is minimized.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the 'lab-to-fab gap' in organic solar cell (OSC) manufacturing by demonstrating slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 binary and PM6:Y6:PC61BM ternary active layers on flexible PET substrates using o-xylene (a green solvent) without additives. The work is conducted in open-air on a roll-platform-compatible homemade coater, addressing the industrial relevance that spin-coating lacks. The active layer coating was systematically optimized by screening slot-die head temperatures from 60 °C to 120 °C (all components kept at the same temperature) and concentration from 12 to 28 mg/mL. The optimal coating temperature was determined to be 100 °C, where the short-circuit current density reached a maximum and bimolecular recombination was minimized (S = 0.978, closest to unity), while 120 °C induced edge aggregation and reduced fill factor (42.2% vs. 47.10%). The AL thickness was screened from 101 nm to 217 nm; the peak Jsc of 17.3 mA/cm² at 154 nm and a maximum average PCE of 5.8% at 217 nm were reported. Introducing a small amount of PC61BM (ternary 1:1.1:0.1 ratio) increased average PCE to 6.7% with a champion efficiency of 7.2% and Jsc of 20 mA/cm², attributed to improved exciton dissociation (96.3%) and charge collection (77.7%). Encapsulated devices retained >99% initial efficiency after 1050 h dark storage (ISOS-D-1 protocol), confirming long-term stability under normal room conditions. The study serves as a direct precursor to roll-to-roll production, demonstrating that green solvent, additive-free, slot-die coating can yield ~7% PCE on flexible substrates without cleanroom requirements.

Research Context
OSCs have achieved peak efficiencies (>15%) on rigid substrates using PM6:Y6 non-fullerene acceptors with green solvents like o-xylene and without additives. A significant 'lab-to-fab' gap exists because spin-coating, the dominant lab technique, is unsuitable for upscaling and wastes material. Roll-to-roll compatible techniques like slot-die, blade, or spray coating are needed but few studies report OSCs using these methods on flexible substrates. Slot-die coating is preferred over blade coating for one-dimensional pattern coating with almost no material waste. PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) behavior, requiring heating during slot-die coating to maintain the solution in liquid state. To date, there was no reported PM6:Y6 device transferred to roll-processing on flexible substrates using slot-die coating.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether PM6:Y6 and ternary PM6:Y6:PC61BM OSCs can be fabricated via slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open-air using a green solvent without additives while maintaining high efficiency. The authors hypothesize that optimizing coating temperature, concentration, and AL thickness will reveal a performance plateau, and that ternary PC61BM addition will improve charge extraction. It is predicted that higher coating temperatures will enhance carrier collection (EQE) while excessively high temperatures above 100 °C will induce material aggregation and degrade fill factor. The hypothesis is that a fullerene acceptor (PC61BM) will generate an energy cascade between PM6 and Y6 LUMO levels, improving exciton dissociation and charge collection. The anticipated outcome is achieving PCE values comparable to lab-scale devices (~6-7%) on flexible, roll-compatible architectures, with sustained stability for industrial relevance.

Methodological Details
Active layer materials PM6 (batch YY19260CH100) and Y6 (batch DW7038S) were purchased from 1-Material Inc.; PC61BM (batch M111) from Ossila. ZnO nanoparticle ink (Sigma-Aldrich) and MoO3 pellets (Kurt J. Lesker Co.) served as the ETL and HTL, respectively. The flexible substrate is pre-patterned ITO-coated polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from FOM Technologies. The solvent used for all active layer inks was o-xylene (O-XY) with ≥ 98% purity purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. A homemade roll-coater was fabricated for slot-die coating using a syringe pump for flow control, a hot tube for the ink line, and a drum with controllable speed and heating. For the ZnO ETL coating: substrate temperature was 75 °C, flow rate 0.06 mL/min, drum speed 1.08 m/min, with annealing at 100 °C for 10 min in air. For the PM6:Y6 AL coating: temperature was screened at 60, 80, 100, 120 °C; concentration at 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 mg/mL; drum speed at 1.5 m/min; flow rate at 0.12 mL/min. The D/A ratio for the binary blend was fixed at 1:1. For ternary devices, two PC61BM ratios were tested: [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]. The device geometry is inverted: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. MoO3 HTL (10 nm) and Ag back electrode (150 nm) were thermally evaporated under vacuum at 2 × 10⁻⁵ mbar through a shadow mask. Up to 24 solar cells were fabricated per evaporation from a one-meter-long active layer; at least 8 devices were encapsulated. The approximate active area of devices is 0.8 cm², while the aperture defined by an Ossila shadow mask (E2002A1) is 0.3996 cm². J-V curves were measured with a Keithley 2400 source meter (50 mV step) under AM1.5G, 1000 W/m² illumination from a Fraunhofer-certified reference cell. EQE and absorbance (300-1100 nm, 5 nm steps) were measured with a QEX10 system calibrated with a Si photodiode. Thickness was measured with a DS95-50 AFM from DME in noncontact mode (5 × 5 µm² scans). Light intensity dependence measurements swept from 62.14 mW/cm² to 147.33 mW/cm² to extract S and recombination slopes. Averages for PV parameters are calculated from statistics of eight devices.

Procedures And Architectures
The device structure is an inverted Schottky architecture: glass/ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6(PC61BM)/MoO3/Ag. The ZnO nanoparticle ETL was deposited via slot-die coating on the PET/ITO substrate. The PM6:Y6 active layer was deposited using a temperature-controlled slot-die process where the head, syringe, drum, and tube were held at the same temperature for each condition. All coating parameters (temperature, concentration, drum speed, flow rate) were fixed during the temperature optimization phase. After coating, the active layer was exposed to the atmosphere; devices were characterized directly after evaporation without a separate post-deposition anneal. An activation step of -5 V with a maximum of 100 mA reverse bias current was applied before encapsulation. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue (EPXR) consisting of bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and Chissonox 221 monomers, with two glass slides protecting both sides. Curing was performed under UV light for approximately 5 min, with temperature reaching 66 ± 0.5 °C. For the ternary optimization, the PC61BM content was first tested at a [1:1:0.2] D:A:T ratio, then halved to [1:1.1:0.1] to find the optimal amount. Thickness was varied by changing the solution concentration, spanning a wide range from semi-transparent to opaque layers.

Key Results
The binary PM6:Y6 devices achieved an average PCE of 5.8% at the optimal thickness of 217 nm (24 mg/mL), with a champion efficiency of 6.3% and FF of 49.0%. At the optimal coating temperature of 100 °C, the short-circuit current density was maximized; at 120 °C, the average FF dropped to 42.2% (vs. 47.10% at 100 °C) due to edge aggregation. The EQE increased at higher coating temperatures, indicating better carrier collection, but the PCE trend saturated around 100 °C. Bimolecular recombination was minimized at 100 °C with S = 0.978 (closest to unity in the temperature optimization), while at 120 °C, edge aggregation created inhomogeneities. Trap-assisted recombination was found to be the dominant mechanism in all devices, with open-circuit voltage (VOC) slope values higher than kT/q. As AL thickness increased from 101 nm to 217 nm, average PCE increased; Jsc reached its maximum at 154 nm (17.3 mA/cm²) before decreasing slightly at 217 nm. The FF improved from 42.0% at 101 nm to 47.1% at 116 nm, with no further improvement at larger thickness, implying high performance even in thick layers. The ternary PC61BM blend [1:1:0.2] achieved Jsc values up to 20 mA/cm², representing a 12% increase over the binary device coated at the same conditions. The [1:1:0.1] ternary blend yielded the highest average PCE of 6.7% with an FF of 49.1% (vs. 47.3% for [1:1:0.2]). The champion efficiency for a ternary PM6:Y6:PC61BM device reached 7.2%. Exciton dissociation probability improved from 93.7% (binary) to 96.3% ([1:1:0.2]) and 95.7% ([1:1.1:0.1]). Charge collection probability improved from 69.6% (binary) to 77.7% ([1:1:0.2]) and 73.2% ([1:1.1:0.1]). After more than 1000 h of dark storage (ISOS-D-1), ternary devices retained 99.4% of their average initial PCE. Binary devices retained more than 97% of their initial average PCE after more than 1500 hours of storage. Some ternary devices showed improved performance after storage, indicating a complex aging behavior.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The higher PCE at 100 °C vs. 120 °C is attributed to a tradeoff: higher temperatures enhance EQE (carrier collection) but exceed the optimal drying rate, inducing edge aggregation and degrading FF. The optimal 100 °C temperature balances drying kinetics with morphology control, resulting in reduced bimolecular recombination (S closest to 1) without the need for extra thermal annealing. The improved performance of ternary devices is attributed to an energy cascade effect: the LUMO level of PC61BM (-3.7 to -3.9 eV) lies between PM6 and Y6, favoring better charge separation. The increase in exciton dissociation and charge collection efficiencies confirms that PC61BM provides additional energetically favorable donor/acceptor interfaces. The high trap-assisted recombination at open circuit, evidenced by VOC slopes > kT/q, is likely due to impurities from processing in open-air rather than cleanroom conditions. The result that thicker layers (217 nm) do not increase series resistance demonstrates that PM6:Y6 retains high performance even in thick-film geometries suitable for roll-to-roll processing.

Contradictions And Limitations
The optimal temperature choice was based on higher PCE and ease of coating rather than a clear trend in S values, indicating unresolved recombination dynamics. The high trap-assisted recombination (VOC slopes > kT/q) is a drawback inherent to open-air/no-glovebox processing, limiting the ultimate efficiency potential. The study does not report a cleanroom or glovebox fabrication environment, which likely introduces impurity-related recombination not fully characterized. The stability data is for dark storage only; operation under illumination (ISOS-D-1) was not tested. The paper does not report the exact humidity and temperature conditions during storage, only 'normal room conditions.' Random seed or specific repeatability data beyond the 8-device average is not explicitly detailed. The study does not report a train/test split, as all devices are from the same fabrication run. The paper does not report demographics or participant data as it is an experimental materials science study.

Claims
Slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 on flexible PET substrates in open-air using o-xylene without additives can achieve PCE comparable to lab-scale devices (~6.3%) and establishes a viable path to roll-to-roll production. Binary PM6:Y6 devices with 24 mg/mL (217 nm) achieved average PCE of 5.8% and champion of 6.3% on flexible PET. The coating was performed in open-air on a roll-platform-compatible homemade coater. No additives were used, and o-xylene (green solvent) was the sole solvent. After 1050 h dark storage, ternary devices retained 99.4% of their initial PCE. The 5.8% average PCE is still significantly below the >15% achieved on rigid substrates with the same materials. The trap-assisted recombination remains high, limiting maximum VOC and PCE. This work demonstrates that the 'lab-to-fab gap' can be partially bridged for the PM6:Y6 system using scalable, environmentally friendly processes. The methodology can be directly transferred to industrial roll-to-roll production lines.
Adding a small amount of PC61BM as a complementary fullerene acceptor in a ternary blend enhances both exciton dissociation and charge collection in slot-die coated flexible devices, raising PCE to 6.7% (7.2% champion). Jsc reached up to 20 mA/cm² in the [1:1:0.2] ternary blend. Exciton dissociation probability improved to 96.3% for [1:1:0.2] vs. 93.7% for binary. Charge collection improved to 77.7% for [1:1:0.2] vs. 69.6% for binary. The LUMO of PC61BM (-3.7 to -3.9 eV) is between PM6 and Y6, creating an energy cascade. EQEs show no specific photocurrent maximum attributable to PCBM due to its weak and broad absorption. The [1:1.1:0.1] ratio with less PC61BM actually showed higher average PCE than [1:1:0.2], complicating the optimal loading determination. Ternary strategy with minimal fullerene loading is a low-cost way to boost flexible OSC performance.
The optimal coating temperature for the PM6:Y6 slot-die process is 100 °C, where a tradeoff between improved carrier collection (higher EQE) and morphology-induced aggregation (lower FF) is minimized. At 100 °C, bimolecular recombination was minimized (S = 0.978). Above 100 °C, edge aggregation induced inhomogeneities that degraded FF to 42.2% (vs. 47.10% at 100 °C). The EQE increased with temperature, but PCE saturated around 100 °C. 100 °C eliminated the need for extra thermal annealing that was required for devices coated at 60 °C and 80 °C. There was no clear trend in S values across all temperatures, reducing the statistical confidence of the choice. The hot slot-die approach (matching substrate, drum, tube, and head temperatures) is a robust parameter-space design for non-fullerene acceptors.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The temperature optimization screened 4 head temperatures (60-120 °C) with corresponding drum/tube heating, demonstrating robustness across the temperature space. The concentration screening (12-28 mg/mL) and thickness screening (101-217 nm) served as ablation studies for AL morphology and absorption control. Two ternary ratios ([1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]) were tested to isolate the effect of PC61BM loading. Statistical averaging over 8 devices for each parameter point provides confidence against single-device variability. Light intensity dependence (Jsc vs. Pin) and VOC vs. ln(Pin) served as mechanistic validation of recombination claims. Dissociation (ηdiss) and collection (ηcoll) efficiency calculations from Jph-Veff curves provided independent verification of the ternary improvement. Annealing of encapsulated devices (120 °C, 3 min) improved JSC for low-temperature-coated devices (60, 80 °C) but not high-temperature ones, validating the morphology-temperature link.

Figure 1 shows the device architecture, the PM6:Y6 energy level alignment, and absorption spectra of donor/acceptor. Figure 2 displays J-V curves and EQEs of binary devices at different coating temperatures. Table 1 summarizes PV parameters (Jsc, Voc, FF, PCE) for PM6:Y6 devices at temperatures 60, 80, 100, 120 °C (8-device averages with SD). Figure 6 shows J-V curves and EQEs for binary vs. ternary devices, with Table S2 providing average parameters. Figure 7 is a box plot comparing binary and ternary device PV parameters directly. Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration of PM6:Y6 slot-die coated flexible OSCs in open-air using a green solvent without additives, achieving ~7% PCE (6.7% average, 7.2% champion) on a roll-platform compatible architecture. 2. The strongest evidence is the systematic temperature optimization showing S = 0.978 (minimal bimolecular recombination) at 100 °C and edge aggregation above this, combined with ternary PC61BM increasing exciton dissociation to 96.3% and charge collection to 77.7%. 3. The future path is the direct transfer of this parameter-optimized, roll-platform compatible, green-solvent protocol to industrial roll-to-roll production, aiming to fully bridge the lab-to-fab gap for PM6:Y6-based organic photovoltaics.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the synthesis and characterization of a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs)—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—prepared via facile demethylation and oxidative treatment of phenolic precursors in air. These open-shell radicals exhibit rich resonance structures with delocalized unpaired electrons, leading to extremely high spin concentration and nearly total quenching of radiative decay. Cyclic voltammetry confirms high electrochemical reversibility over 15 cycles in dichloromethane, with negligible degradation. ESR spectroscopy reveals large paramagnetic signal intensities upon demethylation, confirming efficient radical generation. The highest-performing molecule, TPA-TPA-O6, exhibits a broad absorption spectrum from 300 to 2000 nm in powder state, a black powder appearance, and a photothermal conversion of 25 °C to approximately 210 °C within 60 seconds under 0.8 W cm⁻² laser irradiation at 808 nm. At 1.0 W cm⁻², the temperature reached 250 °C within 60 seconds. In a solar-driven water evaporation system using an interfacial heating foam (PU+TPA-TPA-O6), the material achieved a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun illumination (1.0 kW m⁻²). Seawater desalination was also demonstrated with significant reduction of all four primary ions. The materials are highly soluble in green solvents (ethanol, DMSO), contrasting with conventional high-performance photothermal materials that are solvent-insoluble. The work provides a novel design strategy for stable, low-cost organic small-molecule photothermal materials.

Research Context
Open-shell organic radicals have attracted attention for applications in optoelectronics, magnets, photothermal, thermoelectric, and spintronic materials due to their unique properties. Narrow optical band gaps can be achieved through chemical modification and structural control in radical systems. Comparing with inorganic, 2D framework, and conjugated polymer photothermal materials, organic small molecules have been relatively overlooked. Inorganic materials contain nondegradable metals posing in vivo safety issues; 2D frameworks suffer from poor synthesis reproducibility and high cost. Traditional small molecules like porphyrins and cyanine dyes face cumbersome synthesis and poor photothermal stability. Open-shell radicals with high photothermal efficiency and air stability are rarely reported in previous work. Preparing airstable organic conjugated radicals is challenging due to intrinsic high reactivity with oxygen. Stable neutral radicals are the basis for radical chemistry theory and the prerequisite for multifunctional applications.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether aromatic nitric acid radicals can be prepared as stable neutral open-shell species without steric protection groups and exploited for photothermal conversion. The hypothesis posited that rich resonance structures, including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures with delocalized unpaired electrons, would provide thermal, electrochemical, and air stability. It was hypothesized that the high spin concentration would enhance nonradiative decay, making these materials superior photothermal convertors. Four specific star-shaped architectures were designed by introducing triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene cores to test structure-property relationships. The predicted outcome was that the core's electron-donating capability would dictate the radical character, band gap, and photothermal performance. The ultimate application goal was to demonstrate solar-driven water evaporation and seawater desalination exceeding previous organic small-molecule benchmarks.

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials were synthesized: TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8, using triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene cores. Synthesis proceeded via facile demethylation followed by oxidative treatment of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. Characterization employed cyclic voltammetry (CV) in dichloromethane with 0.1 M nBu₄NPF₆ supporting electrolyte at a scan rate of 0.1 V/s. The saturated calomel electrode served as reference, with the Fe⁺/Fe couple (0.27 V) as an internal standard. For film measurements, methoxy-substituted precursors were dissolved at 5 mg/mL in dichloromethane, and target radical compounds were coated on carbon-glass electrodes. UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy measured absorption spectra in both DMSO solution and solid-state film form. Photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) tests were conducted to measure fluorescent emission in both solution and film. Electron spin resonance (ESR) was performed at a constant sample amount of 0.02 mmol to characterize radical spin concentration. Conductivity measurements were performed on all demethylated counterparts to evaluate electronic transport. Photothermal property evaluation used an 808 nm laser with power 0.8 W cm⁻² for laser-on tests and IR thermal camera monitoring. An interfacial heating system was established using commercially available white polyurethane (PU) porous foam as support. The PU foam was loaded with 30 mg of TPA-TPA-O6 via impregnation in solution and drying at 80 °C. Water evaporation was tested under 1 sun illumination (1.0 kW m⁻²) with mass change monitored over continuous irradiation. Seawater desalination was tested, monitoring four primary ions: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺. HOMO and LUMO energy levels were calculated based on CV data.

Procedures And Architectures
The four ANAR architectures utilize a star-shaped geometry: TPA-TPA-O6 (triphenylamine core), TPA-TPZ-O6 (triazine core), TPA-PY-O8 (pyrene core), and Spiro-O8 (spiro fluorene core). Cyclic voltammetry was performed for 15 cycles in dichloromethane to assess electrochemical stability. The absorption of TPA-TPA-O6 in DMSO solution was compared to the film absorption, showing a red shift and a tail extending to 825 nm in the solid state. PL spectra were recorded, showing fluorescent emission between 450 and 570 nm for precursors, while radicals exhibited no fluorescence in film. HOMO energy levels of the demethylated radicals were recorded as -4.90, -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV for TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8, respectively. The PLQYs of demethylated radicals were measured at 0.1%, 0.9%, 1.0%, and 0.3% for TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8, respectively. For laser photothermal tests, TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 were irradiated for 60 s at 808 nm with 0.8 W cm⁻². For TPA-TPA-O6, the temperature rose from 25 °C to approximately 210 °C within 60 s at 0.8 W cm⁻². The laser power was increased to 1.0 W cm⁻², raising the temperature to approximately 250 °C within 60 s. Ten cycles of laser on/off were performed for TPA-TPA-O6 to assess photothermal stability. The PU foam was impregnated with TPA-TPA-O6 solution and dried at 80 °C to obtain brownish-black foam. The foam diameter was 2.0 cm with 30 mg loading of TPA-TPA-O6.

Key Results
The powder absorption of TPA-TPA-O6 extends from 300 to 2000 nm upon aggregation, enabling broadband sunlight harvesting. The film absorption of TPA-TPA-O6 shows a typical radical red-shifted tail in the 400-825 nm range compared to the methoxy precursor. The PLQY of all demethylated radicals dropped below 1%, indicating nearly total quenching of radiative decay. The ESR signal intensity of TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 was significantly enhanced relative to TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8, reflecting higher radical concentration. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited a temperature rise from 25 °C to approximately 210 °C within 60 s under 808 nm laser irradiation at 0.8 W cm⁻². At 1.0 W cm⁻² laser power, TPA-TPA-O6 reached approximately 250 °C within 60 s, with the temperature rapidly returning to ambient upon laser turn-off. The equilibrium temperature of the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam (30 mg loading) reached 81.2 °C under 600 s continuous irradiation of 1.0 kW cm⁻². Under 1 sun illumination (1.0 kW m⁻²), the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam reached 45 °C after 1 h, which is approximately 10 °C higher than the bare PU foam. The water evaporation rate was measured at 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and the solar-to-vapor efficiency was 89.41% under 1 sun illumination. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited excellent photothermal stability over ten laser on/off cycles with negligible performance degradation. All four primary seawater ions (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺) were significantly reduced after desalination, with values lower than typical membrane-based methods. The HOMO energy levels of demethylated radicals were -4.90, -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV for TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8, respectively, showing enhancement relative to methoxy precursors.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The black color of TPA-TPA-O6 powder and its broad 300-2000 nm absorption are interpreted as a direct consequence of the high concentration of delocalized radical spin. The superior photothermal performance of TPA-TPA-O6 is attributed to the radical-promoted nonradiative decay, where the large spin concentration forces electronic relaxation via non-radiative pathways rather than fluorescence. The HOMO level dictates the ease of oxidation; lower HOMO levels in triazine and pyrene-core radicals make them less prone to radical generation, leading to weaker ESR signals. The results demonstrate that a strong donor-acceptor conjugation effect in star-shaped radical architectures simultaneously reduces the optical band gap and determines the paramagnetic property. The radical-based design strategy provides a path for producing low-cost, high-yield photothermal materials that avoid the expensive raw materials and complex synthesis of existing organic benchmarks. The materials show high solubility in green solvents (ethanol, DMSO), suggesting their advantage over conventional solvent-insoluble high-performance photothermal materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 exhibited relatively poor photothermal conversion, partially attributed to possible protonation forming hydroxyl groups. The study does not report specific quantitative metrics for the seawater desalination ion reduction (only  The paper mentions the equilibrium temperature of PU+TPA-TPA-O6 can reach 81.2 °C under 600 s but the water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ is measured under 1 sun (1.0 kW m⁻²), leaving the exact intensity conditions of the 1.293 measurement slightly ambiguous. No specific quantification of the  The comparison with the highest-efficiency pure organic system (CR-TPE-T) lists disadvantages including expensive raw materials, complex synthesis, and difficulty in purification, but does not provide absolute cost or yield numbers for the benchmark.

Claims
TPA-TPA-O6 is a top-performing organic small-molecule photothermal material with solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun. The water evaporation efficiency reached 89.41% and the rate was 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹. The temperature reached 250 °C within 60 s at 1.0 W cm⁻² laser power. The absorption extends to 2000 nm in powder state. The paper positions this as  No head-to-head direct comparison data with all reported organic materials is provided in the main text; the table is in Supporting Information. This design principle could lead to a new class of stable, low-cost photothermal materials for solar energy harvesting. The material enables practical applications in desalination, as confirmed by seawater ion reduction.
The aromatic nitric acid radical structure with delocalized unpaired electrons provides inherent air, thermal, and electrochemical stability without steric protection groups. CV curves showed negligible change after 15 cycles in dichloromethane. The radical species were prepared via oxidative treatment in air. HOMO levels were enhanced relative to methoxy precursors while maintaining stability. The radicals show a weaker signal intensity in ESR if the HOMO is too low (triazine/pyrene cores). Stable neutral radicals are the prerequisite for multifunctional applications including photothermal therapy and catalysis. This enables the use of open-shell radicals in practical environmental applications.

Data And Code Availability
The Supporting Information is available free of charge at http://pubs.acs.org.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Structure-property relationships were explored by varying the core from triphenylamine to triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene. CV was performed in both film and solution to assess chemical and electrochemical stability. The comparison of methoxy precursors vs. demethylated radicals in both absorption and CV confirmed that the radical state drives the unique properties. PLQY measurements in both dichloromethane solution and film corroborated the radical quenching mechanism. Laser photothermal tests were performed at two powers (0.8 W cm⁻² and 1.0 W cm⁻²) to establish the temperature-power relationship. Ten cycles of laser on/off were used to verify photothermal stability.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A, B, C shows the star-shaped ANAR structures with different cores (triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, spiro fluorene). Figure 2A-C presents the UV-Vis-NIR absorption spectra of the methoxy precursors and the demethylated radicals in solution and film form. Figure 3 shows the cyclic voltammetry curves for the four radical compounds after 15 cycles in dichloromethane. Figure 4A shows the ESR spectra confirming the radical signal increase upon demethylation. Figure 4B shows the photoluminescence spectra of all precursors and radicals. Figure 4D displays the photoluminescence quantum yields of the four radical compounds. Figure 5A-C shows the photothermal conversion temperature profiles under 808 nm laser irradiation at different powers. Figure 5B shows the IR thermal camera image of TPA-TPA-O6 powder during laser irradiation. Figure 6A shows the powder absorption spectrum of TPA-TPA-O6 from 300 to 2000 nm. Figure 6C shows the ten-cycle laser stability of TPA-TPA-O6. Figure 6D compares the absorption spectra of TPA-TPA-O6 in powder and dispersed states. Figure 6E shows the surface temperature of the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam compared to bare PU foam under 1 sun. Figure 6F shows the mass change curves for water evaporation efficiency and rate. Table S1 lists the HOMO, LUMO energy levels, PLQY values, and CV data for all precursors and radicals. Figure S14 shows the equilibrium temperature of the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam reaching 81.2 °C. Figure S16 shows the brownish-black PU foam after TPA-TPA-O6 loading. Figure S17 and Table S2 compare the water evaporation efficiency and rate with reported photothermal materials. Figure S18 shows the concentration of four primary seawater ions after desalination.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals that achieve nearly complete radiative decay quenching through high delocalized spin concentration, enabling the highest reported water evaporation efficiency (89.41%) for a pure organic small-molecule photothermal material. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of 89.41% solar-to-vapor efficiency (1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹) under 1 sun, 250 °C peak temperature in 60 seconds at 1.0 W cm⁻² laser power, and 2000 nm broadband absorption, all coupled with solvent solubility and low cost. 3. The future path is extending this radical design to enhanced planar architectures for photothermal conversion, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports a metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles, achieving yields up to 100% and 100% selectivity under ambient air at room temperature. The approach utilizes Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst at only 0.6 mol%, K3PO4 as a base, and 40 mM CTAB to form spherical micelles that house both the catalyst and substrates at the micellar Stern layer. The catalytic efficiency is attributed to a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with a time constant of 0.3 ps, mediated by the close proximity and aligned dipoles at the charged interface, alongside modulation of redox potentials. The methodology outperforms previously reported Ir-based and organic photocatalytic methods that required organic solvents, slower kinetics (24 h vs 4 h), higher catalyst loading, and in some cases, inert atmospheres. The broad substrate scope includes electron-rich and electron-deficient arylamines, and aerial O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant regenerating the photocatalyst via H2O2 formation. This is the first report of aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds using this specific micellar interface strategy, opening opportunities for sustainable azoaromatic synthesis.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are important organic molecules with potential in optical storage, molecular switches, and industrial applications. The traditional diazotization method produces unstable diazonium intermediates and unwanted waste. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed synthesis of azo compounds has been reported from anilines and nitroaromatics. Most prior methodologies suffer from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, high temperature, and/or inert atmosphere. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes suffers from poor product selectivity and requires an inert atmosphere. Ir-based photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics shows high selectivity but suffers from slow kinetics, moderate yields, high catalyst dose, and limited substrate scope. All earlier reports utilized organic solvents due to the low solubility of amine substrates in aqueous medium. Designing an efficient green catalytic route for azo synthesis in aqueous medium at ambient atmosphere is still of great importance.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics can be achieved in aqueous medium at ambient conditions with high efficiency. The authors hypothesize that the charged aqueous interface of micelles can host both photocatalyst and substrate, enabling a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer. It is hypothesized that the micellar scaffold brings the photocatalyst and substrate into close proximity, essential for bimolecular reactions at the interface. The hypothesis predicts that the charged interface will modulate redox potentials and align dipoles to facilitate product selectivity. The predicted outcome is excellent yields (up to 100%) and selectivity (100%) under ambient air with only 0.6 mol% photocatalyst. The mechanism is predicted to be a non-diffusive bimolecular quenching process driven by photoinduced electron transfer from the amine to the excited photocatalyst.

Methodological Details
The photocatalyst used is Eosin Y (EY), a common and low-cost organic photocatalyst bearing two negative charges at pH 7. Micellar surfactants screened included cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and triton X-100 (TX-100). The base used is K3PO4 (or alternatively KOH or DABCO) to facilitate proton abstraction. The optimized substrate was p-anisidine, and products were analyzed by GC-MS and NMR. CTAB forms spherical micelles at an optimized concentration of 40 mM as determined from HR-TEM measurements. The broad substrate scope includes electron-rich (anilines 1-7) and electron-deficient arylamines (9). Fluorescence quenching was monitored at 545 nm for EY@CTAB. Radical trap experiments used 1 equivalent of 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol (BHT) to intercept amine radicals. O2 sensing strips were used to detect H2O2 formation as evidence of aerial O2 involvement. Absorption spectra were recorded at 516 nm for the absorption peak of EY in water. Fluorescence lifetime measurements were performed in water and upon micellization.

Procedures And Architectures
The EY absorption peak at 516 nm in water exhibits a bathochromic shift of 9 nm with CTAB and 16 nm with TX-100 micelles. EY fluorescence is quenched in the presence of premicellar concentrations of CTAB and TX-100. EY fluorescence is enhanced 2.4-fold only in the presence of CTAB at 0.75-1.0 mM (near CMC). EY@CTAB fluorescence lifetime increases from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon micellization. Stability checks showed EY@CTAB remains stable with K3PO4, while EY@TX-100 suffers disassembly. The reaction is triggered by green light at wavelength 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. Blue light irradiation (previously reported) requires 6 h for 100% conversion. Stern-Volmer plots revealed a quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements provided a time constant of 0.3 ps for PET. Radical trapping: 1 equiv BHT added after 5 min irradiation with green light, then further irradiated for 4 h. The HR-MS peak for p-anisidine-BHT adducts appears at molecular weight 342.2399 g/mol. GC-MS measurements were used to determine conversion and yield.

Key Results
Within 4 h under green light at 525 nm, 100% conversion to the desired azo product was achieved using 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. The yield of 100% matches the selectivity of 100% as reported in the abstract. The dose of 0.6 mol% EY represents an 8.3-fold reduction compared to the previously reported catalyst loading in Ir-based POC. Electron-rich arylamines (1-7, Scheme 2a) all show 100% conversion within 4 h. p-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline show conversion yields of 98% and 95% respectively. Aniline substrate reaches 100% conversion under standard conditions. Lack of fluorescence quenching with p-nitroaniline indicates absence of electron transfer to EY*@CTAB. BHT trapping reduces azo conversion to ~5.0% after 4 h of irradiation. The Stern-Volmer quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1 supports a non-diffusive bimolecular process. The PET time constant of 0.3 ps is ultrafast, consistent with instantaneous quenching. CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM confirmed by HR-TEM. H2O2 detection by sensing strips confirms aerial O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The non-diffusive PET mechanism at the micellar interface is the primary driver for the enhanced catalytic efficacy. The micellar Stern layer, being the less polar hydrocarbon/aqueous interface, preferentially solubilizes arylamines compared to the aqueous bulk. The micellar surface charges and aligned dipoles dictate the interaction with charged molecules and facilitate product selectivity. The interfacial surface charges and confinement effect dramatically modulate chemical and photochemical reactions that would be inefficient in bulk medium. The mapped redox potentials indicate that oxidation of arylamines by EY* is thermodynamically feasible at the micellar surface regardless of substituents. PET precedes the proton abstraction step, as the presence of K3PO4 has no effect on SV plots or quenching rates. This is the first aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds at charged interfaces, opening new synthetic opportunities.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a ChemRxiv preprint and has not been peer-reviewed. Conversion yields for p-chloroaniline (98%) and p-bromoaniline (95%) are slightly lower than 100%, suggesting some limitation for highly electron-deficient substrates. Organic base (DABCO) gives slightly lower conversion yields compared to inorganic bases (K3PO4, KOH). The paper does not report an exact random seed or multiple independent replicates for the catalytic runs. The specific GC-MS conditions and NMR parameters are not detailed in the provided text. No explicit quantification of the 8.3-fold improvement in catalyst dose is provided with a reference value (the prior report is cited as [24]). The paper does not report a full characterization of all intermediate species formed.

Claims
A metal-free, aqueous-phase photocatalytic protocol achieves 100% conversion of arylamines to azoaromatics with 100% selectivity under ambient conditions using only 0.6 mol% Eosin Y. GC-MS confirmed 100% conversion to azo product within 4 h using 0.6 mol% EY at 525 nm. The selectivity is stated as 100% in the abstract. The electron-rich substrate scope (anilines 1-7) all reach 100% conversion within 4 h. p-chloroaniline (98%) and p-bromoaniline (95%) show slightly lower than 100% conversion. Blue light irradiation (6 h) requires longer time than green light (4 h). The method is applicable to both electron-rich and electron-deficient arylamines. This represents the first aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds via this interface strategy.
The catalytic boosting arises from a non-diffusive PET at the micellar CAI with a time constant of 0.3 ps, rather than diffusion-controlled quenching. Fluorescence up-conversion shows 0.3 ps time constant. The quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1 indicates non-diffusive quenching. BHT trapping reduces azo conversion to ~5.0%, confirming radical intermediate formation. The PET is instantaneous (a few picoseconds), making quantitative rate analysis challenging. The micellar interface can be used as a designed scaffold for bimolecular photoredox reactions.
Atmospheric O2 serves as a sacrificial oxidant to regenerate the photocatalyst by forming H2O2 as a byproduct. H2O2 sensing strips showed color change before and after irradiation, confirming O2 reduction. The reaction proceeds under ambient air atmosphere without inert atmosphere requirements. No explicit mechanistic study confirms H2O2 is the only byproduct or quantifies its concentration. The protocol avoids the inert atmosphere requirements that limit practical applicability of previous methods.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Micelle type ablation: CTAB showed strong interaction (bathochromic shift, fluorescence enhancement), SDS showed no interaction, TX-100 showed weaker interaction than CTAB. Base ablation: K3PO4 and KOH (inorganic) and DABCO (organic) all effective; DABCO gave slightly lower yields. Light wavelength: 525 nm (green) gave 100% in 4 h; blue light (previously reported) gave 100% in 6 h. Substrate scope: electron-rich (1-7) 100% in 4 h; p-chloroaniline (9) 98%; p-bromoaniline (9) 95%; p-nitroaniline showed no quenching. Radical trap: BHT (1 equiv) reduced conversion to ~5.0% after 4 h, validating the amine radical mechanism. pH/base: Proton abstraction is essential; reaction is feasible only in presence of base. Catalyst loading: 0.6 mol% EY compared to 8.3-fold lower than previous.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows bathochromic shifts of EY absorption peak at 516 nm in presence of CTAB (9 nm) and TX-100 (16 nm). Figure 1b shows fluorescence quenching of EY with premicellar CTAB and TX-100. Figure 1c shows enhanced fluorescence of EY at 0.75-1.0 mM near CTAB CMC. Figure 1d shows fluorescence lifetime increase from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. Figure 2b shows Stern-Volmer quenching plots; p-anisidine yields 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, p-nitroaniline shows no quenching. Figure 2c shows PET preceding proton abstraction step; K3PO4 does not affect SV plots. Figure 2d shows fluorescence up-conversion with 0.3 ps time constant. Figure S13 shows EY@CTAB fluorescence decrease with p-anisidine. Figure S14 shows K3PO4 has no effect on SV plots. Figure S15 shows HR-MS peak for p-anisidine-BHT adduct at 342.2399 g/mol. Figure S4 shows HR-TEM of spherical CTAB micelles at 40 mM. Figure S6 shows H2O2 sensing strips color change. Figure S5 shows blue light irradiation 6 h conversion. Table 1 summarizes optimized reaction conditions for p-anisidine to 1,2bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene. Table S1 lists photophysical behavior of EY with CTAB, SDS, TX-100. Table S2 lists fluorescence lifetime data. Table S3 tabs quenching parameters for other arylamines. Table S4 shows PET vs proton abstraction comparison. Scheme 1 compares previous (Ir-based) vs present (EY-micelle) POC approaches. Scheme 2 shows broad substrate scope of 9 arylamines. Scheme 3 shows BHT radical trapping procedure.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first metal-free, aqueous-phase photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at micellar charged aqueous interfaces, achieving 100% conversion in 4 h with 0.6 mol% Eosin Y under ambient air. 2. The strongest evidence is the ultrafast 0.3 ps PET time constant confirmed by fluorescence up-conversion, the 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1 quenching rate constant supporting non-diffusive kinetics, and BHT radical trapping confirming the amine radical mechanism. 3. The future path involves extending this CAI-based photocatalytic platform to broader substrate classes, heterogeneous or flow systems, and potentially other bimolecular photoinduced electron transfer reactions in aqueous media.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a universal post-preparation strategy for enhancing the photoluminescence (PL) intensity of all four monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) compounds—MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2—through coating with simple paraffin (a hydrocarbon). Prior to this work, PL enhancement strategies were fragmented: sulfur-based compounds (MoS2, WS2) benefited from p-type doping (F4TCNQ, TFSI) or superacids, while selenium-based compounds (MoSe2, WSe2) had limited and non-universal strategies (oleic acid, hydrohalic acid, or substrate separation by floating/ion insertion). The authors developed a paraffin coating method exploiting paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient to induce spontaneous fluctuation and desorption of the monolayer TMDC from the substrate, thereby removing the substrate effect that limits optical performance. Quantitative PL enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold were observed for MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 from as-exfoliated flakes, respectively. Raman spectroscopy confirmed a negative in-plane strain (-0.72 cm⁻¹ Eʹ shift) and a positive out-of-plane shift (1.03 cm⁻¹ Aʹ), correlating with decreased carrier concentration. Time-resolved optical microscopy revealed spontaneous, time-dependent monolayer deformation and bundling, while bulk flakes remained stationary. When surrounded by bulk flakes, the monolayer was constrained, showing nonuniform enhancement (2.3× center/rim) and a 5–10 meV PL redshift attributed to strain-induced funneling. The work establishes a universal strategy applicable to all TMDCs and positions paraffin as a functional material for transparent, flexible optoelectronics.

Research Context
Transition metal dichalcogenides (MX2) are 2D semiconductors with a layer-thickness of only three atoms and direct band gaps at K and Kʹ points. Monolayer TMDCs exhibit poor photoluminescence intensity due to over-carrier concentrations, strains, and crystalline lattice defects. For n-type MoS2 and WS2, p-type doping with F4TCNQ or TFSI (superacid) enhances PL intensity by hundreds of times. In contrast, selenium-based compounds of MoSe2 and WSe2 have very limited PL enhancement strategies, with methods being compound-specific. No universal strategy has been found for improving the optical behavior across a large variety of two-dimensional semiconductor materials. A potential substrate-free approach via mechanical floating of monolayers was identified but lacked a post-preparation method.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a single post-preparation method can universally enhance PL intensity in all four monolayer TMDCs (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2). The authors hypothesize that coating with a simple hydrocarbon (paraffin) will induce a spontaneous fluctuation and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. The underlying mechanism is predicted to be strain generated by paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient, removing the substrate effect as the key factor. The authors predict that the substrate effect, characterized by electron doping, is the primary bottleneck limiting PL in all TMDCs. The expected outcome is remarkable PL enhancement across all four compound families, distinguishing the approach from compound-specific chemical treatments.

Methodological Details
The paraffin used has a melting point of 42–45 °C. The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance before coating. Samples were placed on a spin coater with the paraffin dropped onto them. A heat blower (hair dryer) was used to keep paraffin melted during spin coating to prevent immediate solidification. Monolayer WS2, MoS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 were all subjected to the paraffin coating process. PL enhancement was measured for monolayer WS2 on both Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates. Optical microscopy images and PL mapping images were used to characterize the morphological and optical changes. Raman spectra were acquired for Eʹ (in-plane) and Aʹ (out-of-plane) peak positions to quantify strain and carrier concentration. 30 samples of monolayer MoS2 were analyzed for statistical Raman data. Time-course imaging was performed at 0 hours, 2 hours, and further 1 hour at room temperature for MoS2 deformation tracking. A sample surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides was prepared to test confinement of monolayer deformation.

Procedures And Architectures
The paraffin was first melted at 80 °C and then dropped onto the TMDC sample positioned on a spin coater. To maintain the melted state during spin coating, an external heat blower was applied continuously. A simple casting method (not spin coating) was used to produce a thick, non-transparent film for separate experiments. Monolayers were observed via optical microscopy through the transparent paraffin film. PL spectra were collected from the paraffin-coated TMDCs, with both the full spectrum and normalized peak shapes analyzed. For the constrained sample, the monolayer was deliberately surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides before coating. The in-plane Raman Eʹ peak sensitivity to strain and out-of-plane Aʹ peak sensitivity to carrier concentration were exploited.

Key Results
For monolayer WS2 on Si/SiO2, PL enhancement of approximately 36 times was observed through paraffin coating. The normalized PL spectrum showed a decreased shoulder at the low-energy side, indicating reduced trion-derived PL. In MoS2, a remarkable PL enhancement factor of 215 was observed from the as-exfoliated state. WS2 showed a PL enhancement factor of 55. WSe2 showed a PL enhancement factor of 9. MoSe2 showed a PL enhancement factor of 50. Raman spectroscopy showed the Eʹ peak shifted negatively by 0.72 cm⁻¹ on average, indicating in-plane strain. The Aʹ peak shifted positively by 1.03 cm⁻¹ on average, indicating decreased carrier concentration in MoS2. The strained constrained monolayer showed nonuniform PL enhancement, with the center intensity 2.3 times greater than at the rim. The constrained monolayer peak position shifted 5–10 meV lower in energy at the center compared to the rim. Optical microscopy revealed spontaneous, time-dependent monolayer deformation and buckling while surrounding bulk flakes remained unchanged.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
PL enhancement is attributed to a combination of partial strain and deformation of the monolayer TMDC. The strain is induced by the volume change caused by the high thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin. The subsequent desorption of the monolayer TMDC from the substrate removes the electron-doping substrate effect. The constrained monolayer results indicate the funnel effect where nonuniform strain decreases the band gap locally. The paraffin-coated TMDC film is transparent, flexible, and biocompatible, extending the material's utility to optoelectronics. The approach is described as a universal engineering method applicable to other 2D layered materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
A thick film of paraffin achieved by simple casting resulted in a glassy, non-transparent appearance, limiting spectroscopic analysis. PL enhancement in the constrained sample was nonuniform (2.3× center vs rim), indicating spatial variability in effect. The PL peak shift of 5–10 meV in the constrained sample was only observed at the center, not uniformly. The authors note that the PL enhancement in sulfur-based TMDCs is especially applicable for trion suppression explanations. The paper does not report explicit statistics (error bars or multiple replicates) for the enhancement factors themselves. The specific thermal history and cooling rate during paraffin crystallization are not detailed, which may affect strain.

Claims
Paraffin coating is a universal post-preparation method that enhances PL intensity in all four monolayer TMDC compound families by removing the substrate effect. MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 showed PL enhancement factors of 215, 55, 9, and 50, respectively, from as-exfoliated states. PL enhancement was observed on both Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates, confirming the material-independent nature of the effect. The method was applied successfully to both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The magnitude of enhancement varies significantly between compounds (from 9× to 215×), suggesting compound-specific sensitivity. In the constrained sample, the enhancement was nonuniform, with the center 2.3× higher than the rim. This eliminates the need for compound-specific chemical treatments (e.g., superacids) for PL enhancement in TMDCs. The strategy extends to other 2D layered materials due to the fundamental mechanism of thermal-expansion-induced strain.
The mechanism of PL enhancement combines thermal-expansion-induced in-plane strain with desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. Raman spectra showed a negative Eʹ shift (-0.72 cm⁻¹) indicating in-plane strain and a positive Aʹ shift (1.03 cm⁻¹) indicating reduced carrier concentration. Optical microscopy confirmed time-dependent spontaneous deformation of the monolayer through paraffin penetration. The desorption of the monolayer removes the electron-doping substrate effect, a key bottleneck for TMDC PL. The constrained sample showed a red-shifted peak (5–10 meV) consistent with the funnel effect from wrinkle-induced strain rather than pure desorption. The effect is compound-dependent; selenium-based TMDCs show smaller enhancement (9× and 50×) compared to sulfur-based (215×, 55×). This mechanistically links PL enhancement to a mechanical/structural reconfiguration rather than a purely electronic/chemical one. The strain can be quantified and predicted using Raman spectroscopy of in-plane and out-of-plane modes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A control experiment with a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides tested the confinement of the monolayer deformation. The PL enhancement was verified on a different substrate (quartz) to rule out Si/SiO2-specific effects. The thick, non-transparent paraffin film (from simple casting) served as a control for optical transparency. Time-series imaging (0h, 2h, 2h+1h) tracked the temporal progression of spontaneous deformation. Raman spectra were collected from 30 statistical samples to confirm the Eʹ and Aʹ shift directions.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the experimental setup of paraffin melting, spin coating, and heat blower application. Figure 1b presents the PL spectra of paraffin-coated monolayer WS2 with approximately 36× enhancement. Figure 1c and 1d show PL mapping images of the paraffin-coated WS2 monolayer. Figure 2a displays the band gaps and emission wavelengths of as-exfoliated monolayer TMDCs. Figure 2b shows the PL enhancement factors for each original monolayer flake. Figure 3a-d show the time-course optical microscopy of monolayer MoS2 deformation at 0, 2, and 3 hours. Figure 3e shows the PL spectra of the deformed MoS2 sample with time-dependent peak upshift and enhancement. Figure 4 presents statistical Raman shifts of Eʹ and Aʹ peaks for 30 monolayer MoS2 samples. Table 2 reports the average Raman peak shifts: Eʹ by -0.72 cm⁻¹ and Aʹ by 1.03 cm⁻¹. Figure 5 shows a constrained monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides with nonuniform PL mapping. Figure 5b shows the PL peak position distribution across the constrained monolayer plane.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of a universal post-preparation strategy—paraffin coating—that enhances PL intensity in all four monolayer TMDC compound families (MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2) by removing the substrate effect through thermally induced strain and desorption. 2. The strongest evidence is the remarkable PL enhancement factor of 215 for MoS2 and the simultaneous confirmation by Raman spectroscopy (in-plane strain and decreased carrier concentration) alongside time-resolved optical microscopy of spontaneous, progressive monolayer deformation. 3. The future path lies in applying this method to other 2D materials and utilizing paraffin's transparent, flexible, and biocompatible properties for packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.

summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H2O2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod
summary.field_subfield: Catalysis / Heterogeneous Catalysis - Methane Partial Oxidation
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the successful continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure using a modified silica-supported bimetallic (Au-Fe) catalyst with 15% w/v H2O2 as the oxidant. The authors address the long-standing 'holy grail' problem of methane-to-methanol (M2M) catalysis by operating under benign conditions (atmospheric pressure, 80 °C) rather than the harsh high-pressure regimes typical of the field. The catalyst, termed AuFeHS, is prepared via modified deposition precipitation on hydrophobic silica, yielding atomic clusters of Fe (0.46 wt% Fe, 0.23 wt% Au) and Au nanoparticles (1.4-2.8 nm). In batch conditions (20 bar, 50 °C), the catalyst achieved 1666 mmol/gFe+Au methanol yield with 95% selectivity. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, methanol production was sustained for 7 hours, peaking at 224 mmol/gFe+Au. Co-feeding CO with methane switched selectivity from methanol to acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat yield in 4 hours). Mechanistic insights from XPS, XANES, EXAFS, in-situ IR, and solid-state NMR attribute activity to low-valent Fe(3-δ+) species stabilized by Au, with hydrophobic silica preventing water-induced site blocking and facilitating methanol desorption. Isotopically labelled CD4 experiments confirmed that the observed methanol originates from methane feed rather than catalyst degradation products.
