judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the successful continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure using a modified silica-supported bimetallic (Au-Fe) catalyst with 15% w/v H2O2 as the oxidant. The authors address the long-standing 'holy grail' problem of methane-to-methanol (M2M) catalysis by operating under benign conditions (atmospheric pressure, 80 °C) rather than the harsh high-pressure regimes typical of the field. The catalyst, termed AuFeHS, is prepared via modified deposition precipitation on hydrophobic silica, yielding atomic clusters of Fe (0.46 wt% Fe, 0.23 wt% Au) and Au nanoparticles (1.4-2.8 nm). In batch conditions (20 bar, 50 °C), the catalyst achieved 1666 mmol/gFe+Au methanol yield with 95% selectivity. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, methanol production was sustained for 7 hours, peaking at 224 mmol/gFe+Au. Co-feeding CO with methane switched selectivity from methanol to acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat yield in 4 hours). Mechanistic insights from XPS, XANES, EXAFS, in-situ IR, and solid-state NMR attribute activity to low-valent Fe(3-δ+) species stabilized by Au, with hydrophobic silica preventing water-induced site blocking and facilitating methanol desorption. Isotopically labelled CD4 experiments confirmed that the observed methanol originates from methane feed rather than catalyst degradation products.

Research Context
Methane is a major natural gas constituent and a potent greenhouse gas with significant calorific value. Storage and transportation of methane require compression to 10-100 atm, making chemical conversion desirable. Direct partial oxidation of methane to methanol is considered the holy grail problem in catalysis. The challenge lies in the fact that an activated C-H bond is so reactive it readily undergoes complete oxidation to CO2. Most existing methods require harsh reaction conditions and suffer from low product yields, limiting commercial viability. Previous single-atom catalyst reports (FeN4/GN-2.7, single Cr on TiO2, single Cu on ZSM-5) showed yields in the µmol range over hours. Continuous flow reports are limited, and those using O2 as oxidant show only frugal methanol conversion.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether methane can be partially oxidized to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures. The authors hypothesize that a bimetallic Au-Fe system on a hydrophobic silica support will overcome the stability and selectivity issues of monometallic catalysts. The hypothesis posits that hydrophobic silica will prevent water-induced site blocking, facilitate peroxide access to active sites, and promote methanol desorption. The hypothesis further predicts that co-feeding CO will switch selectivity from methanol to acetic acid through C-insertion. The expected outcome is that the atmospheric pressure continuous process will surpass high-pressure batch benchmarks in methanol and acetic acid production. The design principle rests on generating and stabilizing low-valent Fe sites through Au interaction for concurrent activation of CH4 and H2O2.

Methodological Details
The catalyst AuFeHS was prepared using a modified deposition precipitation (DP) method to disperse Fe atomic clusters on hydrophobic silica (HS) support. The optimum catalyst composition was determined to be 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au, confirmed by ICP-OES. The hydrophobic support was verified by contact angle analysis showing an angle of 118°. FeHS images from HRTEM showed no contrast difference characteristic of Fe particles, indicating atomic dispersion. Au nanoparticles were observed in the range of 1.3-3.0 nm (1.4-2.8 nm for size distribution) via TEM. The specific surface area of AuFeHS was 392 m²/g. Methane oxidation was initially screened in a batch reactor at 10 bar, with Fe loading fixed at 0.5 wt% and Au varied. Optimization of the continuous flow process confirmed 80 °C as the best temperature for effective conversion. The oxidant was 15% w/v H2O2. Isotope labelling with CD4 was used to rule out background reactions from the support. Product yields were quantified by GC using standard calibrations, and GC and NMR confirmed product identity.

Procedures And Architectures
The batch process operated at 10 bar CH4 and 10 bar H2O2 with AuFeHS catalyst. For CO co-feeding, conditions were 50 °C with a total pressure of 20 bar (15 bar CH4 : 5 bar CO). The continuous flow process was conducted in a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure for up to 7 hours. XPS was performed with electron flood gun data acquisition, requiring no charge correction. XANES spectra were measured at Fe K-edge along with Fe standards, and linear combination fitting was used for oxidation state determination. EXAFS was collected at both Fe K-edge and Au L3-edge with fitting ranges of 0-4 Å. In-situ IR with CO adsorption probed isolated metal atoms: 2105 cm⁻¹ for Au(0)-CO and 2175 cm⁻¹ for Auδ⁺-CO. Solid-state 29Si NMR identified Q2, Q3, Q4 and T2, T3 states in the silica. 23Na NMR with peaks at 7.32 ppm and -1.59 ppm confirmed the Si-O-Na framework. Pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR showed Lewis acid bands at 1449 cm⁻¹ and -OH deformation at ~1640 cm⁻¹.

Key Results
In batch conditions at 10 bar CH4, AuFeHS achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. The Fe-HS catalyst (0.5 wt% Fe) produced 285 mmol/gFe with 82% methanol selectivity. The Au-HS catalyst produced only 47.6 mmol/gAu methanol, demonstrating the synergistic effect. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, AuFeHS produced 224 mmol/gFe+Au methanol within 4 hours. The hourly production rate was 422 µmol·h⁻¹·gcat⁻¹ (or 0.42 mol·kgcat⁻¹·h⁻¹) at 4 hours. With CO co-feeding in batch, acetic acid was the main product with 3403 µmol/gcat yield in 1 hour at 50 °C (20 bar). In continuous flow with CO, 648 µmol/gcat acetic acid formed within 4 hours. The FeHS catalyst in continuous flow produced 24.2 mmol/gFe methanol. The AuHS catalyst in continuous flow produced 12 mmol/gAu methanol. AuFeHS on SBA-15 (hydrophilic) produced only 111 mmol/gFe+Au methanol, confirming the role of hydrophobicity. Fe-SBA-15 and Au-SBA-15 produced only 0.30 mmol/gcat and 0.15 mmol/gcat, respectively. XPS showed 85% Au(0) and 15% Auδ⁺ species with spin-orbit splitting of 3.7 eV. EXAFS fitting showed 72% Fe3O4 and 28% FeO in the AuFeHS sample. The first EXAFS peak at Fe K-edge appeared at ~1.5 Å, lower than Fe foil, indicating non-elemental Fe. The Au L3-edge first peak was above 2 Å, confirming elemental Au character. XPS confirmed Fe3⁺ species at 710.3 eV and FeOOH at 712.5 eV on FeHS. Low-valent Fe3-δ⁺ species appeared at 709.5 eV in AuFeHS, absent in FeHS. The CO2 selectivity with CO addition was 10%, compared to 5-6% without CO. Oxo-di-copper on carbon nitride produced 129.7 mmol·gCu⁻¹·h⁻¹ with 4% methanol selectivity.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The synergetic effect arises from Au stabilizing low-valent Fe3-δ⁺ species that simultaneously activate CH4 and H2O2. Low-valent Fe sites are the active centers for hydrogen peroxide activation, providing the OH moiety for CH3OH formation. The hydrophobic environment prevents moisture from blocking active sites and facilitates methanol desorption, preventing over-oxidation to CO2. The C-H sigma complex forms on acidic sites (Lewis acid sites), converts to CH3· on Fe3-δ⁺, then reacts with OH· to form methanol. Au nanoparticles serve as excellent CO oxidation catalysts, providing low-energy activation sites for CO adsorption. The Si-O-Na framework (incorporated during NaOH-assisted deposition) contributes to the surface environment and acidity. Tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is proposed as a general strategy for converting lower alkanes to oxygenates.

Contradictions And Limitations
The exact random seed, train/test split, or demographic data are not applicable as this is a chemical catalysis paper. The role of Na and Lewis acid sites in the overall POM reaction is noted as beyond the scope of the study. The content is not peer-reviewed as it is a ChemRxiv preprint. The authors acknowledge that tuning active Fe species is a way forward, implying the current modulation is not exhaustive. The paper does not report a specific reproducibility protocol or calibration standard for GC measurements beyond 'standard calibrations'. No degradation or deactivation testing over extended time beyond 7 hours is reported.

Claims
AuFeHS achieves highly selective partial oxidation of methane to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure with yields surpassing all previous reports. AuFeHS produced 224 mmol/gFe+Au methanol at atmospheric pressure, the best reported value. The batch methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity is one of the highest reported to date. The continuous flow yield of 422 µmol·h⁻¹·gcat⁻¹ is better than the previously reported 1.81 µmol·h⁻¹·gcat⁻¹ using O2. The acidic sites and bimetallic synergy are confirmed by IR, XPS, XANES, and EXAFS analyses. While superior to O2-based and high-pressure H2O2 systems, some Au-Pd colloidal particles report even better absolute yields but suffer from poor selectivity. The CO2 selectivity increases to 10% when CO is co-fed, indicating not perfect liquid oxygenate selectivity. The catalyst is not fully characterized for long-term stability beyond 7 hours. This opens a commercialization pathway for methane-to-oxygenates (M2O) technologies using H2O2 as a green oxidant. Bimetallic modulation of active species is presented as a tunable strategy for lower alkane oxidation.
Hydrophobicity and bimetallic synergy are essential for high performance; monometallic and hydrophilic supports fail to reach comparable yields. AuFe on SBA-15 yielded only 111 mmol/gFe+Au, vs 224 mmol/gFe+Au on hydrophobic silica. Fe-SBA-15 and Au-SBA-15 produced only 0.30 and 0.15 mmol/gcat, respectively. FeHS produced only 285 mmol/gFe with 82% selectivity, while AuFeHS reached 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. No directly contradicting data; all comparisons consistently support the hydrophobic/bimetallic requirement. Surface engineering of the silica support is as critical as the metal composition for this reaction class.
Co-feeding CO with methane switches the major product from methanol to acetic acid through C-insertion. In batch, acetic acid was the main product with 3403 µmol/gcat yield in 1 hour at 50 °C. In continuous flow, 648 µmol/gcat acetic acid formed within 4 hours with CO co-feeding. Methanol was the only other liquid oxygenate formed (166 µmol/gcat in batch). CO2 selectivity rose from 5-6% to 10% with CO addition, indicating some loss of mass balance to gas products. This offers a single-catalyst pathway to both methanol and acetic acid by simple oxidant-feed modification.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information is made available for free via the Internet at http://pubs.acs.org. The preprint is available via ChemRxiv with a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The role of the hydrophobic support was differentiated by comparing AuFe on HS with AuFe on SBA-15 (111 mmol/gFe+Au vs 224 mmol/gFe+Au). Monometallic AuHS and FeHS were tested and both underperformed AuFeHS, confirming synergy. The support alone (HS) produced no product, serving as a negative control. Control experiments verified no product formation without methane flow, oxidant, and catalyst. Nitrogen gas as feed instead of methane resulted in no products, confirming methane specificity.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1(a-e) shows HRTEM images, elemental mapping, and Au particle size distribution (1.4-2.8 nm) over FeHS. Fig. 2(a-c) shows XPS Fe 2p spectra for FeHS and AuFeHS with oxidation state assignments. Fig. 2(d) shows radial distribution functions from EXAFS at Fe K-edge. Fig. 3(a-d) presents catalytic activity, selectivity, and yield data for methanol and acetic acid under different conditions. Fig. 4(a-b) displays methanol production in continuous flow over 7 hours for various catalysts. Fig. 5(a-c) shows 29Si NMR spectra of HS, FeHS, and AuFeHS. Fig. S18-S19 show 1H, 2H, and 13C NMR spectra confirming CD4 labelling. Table S4 compares catalytic activity on HS vs. SBA-15. Table S5 shows temperature optimization and product yields for batch and continuous flow. Table S6 compares literature yields for methane partial oxidation with H2O2 as oxidant.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is achieving continuous-flow partial oxidation of methane to methanol (224 mmol/gFe+Au) and acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat) at atmospheric pressure using H2O2 over a bimetallic AuFe/hydrophobic-silica catalyst. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au batch yield with 95% selectivity, 0.42 mol·kgcat⁻¹·h⁻¹ continuous flow rate, and multi-technique confirmation (XPS, XANES, EXAFS, in-situ IR, NMR) of the low-valent Fe3-δ⁺ active species stabilized by Au on a hydrophobic support. 3. The future path lies in tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation for lower alkane oxygenates, exploring the role of Na and Lewis acid sites, and commercializing M2O technologies using green H2O2 oxidation routes.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study introduces a novel computational workflow for identifying and energetically ordering viable crystal structures with partially occupied sites, applied specifically to the cubic lithium lanthanum zirconium oxide (c-LLZO) solid electrolyte. The central problem addressed is the lack of consensus in experimental and theoretical literature regarding the ground-state Li occupancy of c-LLZO, with previously reported structures often lacking rigorous geometric and energetic justification. The authors developed a systematic methodology: first, they eliminated unphysical structures containing overlapping Li atoms based on a nearest-neighbor count (cutoff at 1.7 Å), then reduced the configuration space using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates, and finally ranked the remaining unique structures using a machine-learning-based multiple linear regression model trained on 1,235 single-point DFT calculations. The method reduced the combinatorial space from approximately 2.3 × 10^8 to ~2 × 10^6 unique structures. DFT was performed with ONETEP using the PBE GGA functional and an 830 eV cutoff. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. The workflow identified four lowest-energy structures within 0.026 eV (1 k_BT at 298 K) of the global minimum, all exhibiting an 8:48 24d:96h occupancy ratio. Geometry relaxations on 20 structures showed that Li atom movement from original sites correlates negatively with energy, further supporting the validity of the identified configurations. The authors demonstrate that many previously reported structures may be unphysical or unstable, and provide a freely accessible database of all generated structures to improve reproducibility in c-LLZO research.

Research Context
Solid electrolytes for Li-ion batteries promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs compared to liquid electrolyte cells. Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) is a prominent solid electrolyte candidate with the best interfacial stability against metallic Li. c-LLZO has two primary polymorphs: disordered cubic c-LLZO (space group Ia 3d) and ordered tetragonal t-LLZO, with Li diffusivity over two orders of magnitude smaller in the tetragonal phase. Despite intensive study, there is no consensus on the Li occupancy of the 24d and 96h sites in c-LLZO. Previous computational studies use one experimental value as a starting point to obtain an idealized unit cell, but the range of predicted structures in the literature indicates disagreement about the ground state. Without knowing if used structures are close to the ground state, calculated thermodynamic and observable properties may not be well described.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is: what is the energetically favourable ground-state Li configuration of c-LLZO, and can a systematic workflow identify and rank all possible occupancies? The authors intend to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell and order them energetically to ascertain the presence of a significant energy difference in choice of structure. They hypothesize that the geometric constraints on Li-Li distances will immediately limit the physically possible 24d:96h ratios and that some previously reported structures may not be feasible or stable. A secondary hypothesis is that structural properties, such as the 24d:96h ratio, are indicative of a structure's energy. The workflow is also designed to be extensible to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. The authors anticipate that a large portion of previously reported structures may not be feasible or stable when subjected to geometric constraints.

Methodological Details
The c-LLZO unit cell contains 120 total crystallographic sites with Li partially occupying 24d (tetrahedral) and 96h (tetrahedral/octahedral interface) sites. The stoichiometric composition requires 56 Li atoms to be distributed among these sites. The number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is 120 choose 56, approximately 7.4 × 10^34, making brute-force combinatorial methods unviable. A minimal Li-Li distance cutoff of 1.7 Å was imposed, motivated by a Li-dimer in vacuum calculation showing a minimum energy at ~2.7 Å and a large energy penalty at 1.7 Å. The geometric constraint implies: (1) a maximum of 48 out of 96h sites can be occupied simultaneously (each 96h site exists as a pair within 0.68 Å); (2) each 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites within 1.67 Å. The crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. (2019) were used as the framework for structure generation. Initial structure generation produced approximately 2.3 × 10^8 structures, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. Symmetry equivalence was handled by constructing upper triangular connectivity matrices of the Li sublattice and applying local sensitive hashing (LSH). LSH optimized pairwise comparison from O(N^2) to O(N), enabling symmetry checks on over 100 million structures. The validation of the symmetry method used the ASE python package's symmetry equivalence check on the two smallest ratios (12:44 and 13:43). Only approximately 1% of structures were symmetrically unique, reducing the count by a factor of approximately 100. The final configuration space was reduced to around 2 × 10^6 structures. Two subsets were used for DFT: (1) the 200 energetically lowest structures from COMPASSIII, (2) a random selection of approximately 1000 structures across the configuration space. In total, 1,235 single-point DFT calculations were performed. Data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio for the MLR model.

Procedures And Architectures
DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code, using the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional with a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV and CASTEP on-the-fly generated pseudopotentials. The ONETEP computational cost scales linearly with the number of atoms, as opposed to cubic scaling in conventional DFT. The DFT energies were paired with a numerical representation: a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interaction distances (a reformulation of the connectivity matrix). A multiple linear regression (MLR) model was trained to predict energies from these interaction-distance descriptors. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. Geometry optimizations were performed on the 20 lowest-energy structures using the BFGS algorithm, with transitions between 96h to 96h, 96h to 48g, and 96h to 24d sites. A Li-dimer in vacuum calculation used 30 single-point calculations in a large unit cell to prevent self-interaction, with the energy fit as a 3rd order polynomial. The Li-dimer energy minimum was found at approximately 2.7 Å, while the 1.7 Å calculation was compared against this baseline. The COMPASSIII forcefield, applied only to the Li-sublattice, ordered the 13:43 ratio with a correlation of 0.991 but overestimated the energy separation by 24d:96h ratio. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation.

Key Results
All structures were found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground-state structures. Four structures, all with 8:48 occupancy, are within 0.026 eV (1 k_BT at 298 K) of the lowest-energy structure found. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. The COMPASSIII forcefield, applied only to the Li-sublattice, ordered the 13:43 ratio with a correlation coefficient of 0.991. The 96h to 24d transition was observed only once during geometry relaxation, yielding a structure 0.58 eV lower than the optimized lowest single-point structure. There is a negative correlation between the mean distance Li atoms move from their crystallographic sites and the final optimized structure energy (Figure S7a). A weaker negative correlation was found between distance to a crystallographic site and energy (Figure S7b), indicating movement from original sites is preferable. The 24d:96h ratios are limited by the 1.7 Å cutoff: a maximum of 48 96h sites can be occupied, and each 24d site eliminates 4 96h sites. The symmetry reduction reduced the configuration space from approximately 2.3 × 10^8 to around 2 × 10^6 unique structures, by a factor of approximately 100. The most symmetric ratio appears to be 8:48, followed by 12:44, and finally 10:46, with a slight correlation between lower energy and higher symmetry.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results indicate that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature are predicting or working with structures that are not reflective of a real system due to unphysical Li-Li overlaps. The energetic preference to avoid 24d occupancy (demonstrated by increasing average energy with 24d occupancy) suggests that the 24d sites are less favourable than 96h sites. The four lowest-energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates, the same 24d configuration, and only slight variations in the 96h configuration. The workflow demonstrates that a combinatorial search with geometric pruning and ML-based ordering can rigorously identify the ground-state space of a partially occupied crystal, overcoming brute-force limitations. The method is extensible to other ion conductors with partially occupied sites, providing a template for systematic structural discovery in similar materials. The negative correlation between displacement from crystallographic sites and energy suggests that Li atoms in the ground state reside slightly off their idealized positions, which the geometric-constraint method alone may not fully capture.

Contradictions And Limitations
The energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions, which may be significant at higher temperatures. The method assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which the authors acknowledge as an approximation. A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry-optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. The COMPASSIII forcefield overestimated the energy separation between different 24d:96h ratios compared to ONETEP, an issue considered too large to surmount in this paper. The LSH method has high specificity and is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions. The MLR model is trained on 1235 structures, which may not capture all nuances of the full 2.0 × 10^6 configuration space. The assumption that the base LaZrO structure remains relatively unchanged with each Li configuration is a simplification. The symmetry of the structure, when included in the MLR model, made a negligible difference to overall results. The 48g site is not included because it is not reported in most refinements found.

Claims
The workflow can identify and rank all energetically favourable Li occupancy configurations of c-LLZO from a crystallographically predicted structure without brute-force enumeration. The combinatorial space was reduced from 7.4 × 10^34 to ~2.3 × 10^8 by geometric pruning, then to ~2 × 10^6 by symmetry reduction. The MLR model achieved a 0.9996 correlation on the test set, successfully ordering structures energetically. 19 of the 20 lowest structures share the same 8:48 ratio, and 4 are within 0.026 eV of the minimum. The MLR model is trained on only 1235 structures representing a small fraction of the ~2 million candidates. The COMPASSIII forcefield showed a pronounced energy separation discrepancy that was not surmounted. This enables unambiguous identification of the ground-state Li occupancy for c-LLZO, which was previously unassigned in experimental and theoretical works. The database of all structures improves accuracy and reproducibility in future c-LLZO computational research.
A large proportion of previously reported c-LLZO structures in experimental and theoretical literature are unphysical due to Li-Li overlaps. The geometric constraint (1.7 Å) reveals that many reported 24d:96h ratios cannot exist without a Li-Li interaction below the crystal ionic diameter. Table S2 shows that many theoretical studies use Coulombic energy alone, which is insufficient for energetic ordering. The authors note they cannot verify every specific previously reported structure, only those explicitly listed in their summary tables. Future c-LLZO computational studies should validate structures against the 1.7 Å Li-Li constraint before proceeding with thermodynamic property calculations.

Data And Code Availability
The structures generated in this work are published alongside the results in the supporting information, and all structures are provided in a freely accessible database. The two symmetry-checking scripts are provided with the database in the supporting information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The symmetry reduction method was validated against the ASE python package's symmetry equivalence check on the two smallest ratios (12:44 and 13:43). The LSH method was validated for both 13:43 and 12:44 ratios. The effect of geometry relaxation was tested on a small dataset of 20 structures. The COMPASSIII forcefield was tested on the 13:43 ratio (correlation 0.991) and on a wider range of structures (Figure S3) to assess its viability. The MLR model was tested by including structure symmetry as a predictor, which showed a negligible difference. The Li-dimer optimal distance was determined using 30 single-point calculations to ensure no self-interaction in a large unit cell.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the c-LLZO crystal structure with Li sites, Li-Li interaction distances (including the 1.7 Å cutoff), and the red region indicating impossible 24d:96h ratios. Figure 2b displays the occupancy ratios for the 20 lowest-energy structures, showing 19 at 8:48 and one at 9:47. Figure 3 illustrates the workflow for finding the 4 final structures and their unique identity numbers in the database. Table 1 lists the number of structures for each 24d:96h ratio for one unit cell. Table S1 lists all experimental papers reporting 24d and 96h site occupancies with methods (X-ray vs Neutron) and stoichiometry. Table S2 lists all theoretical studies reporting 24d:96h ratios and their structure generation methods. Figure S4 shows the Li-dimer energy vs distance fit with the 1.7 Å point highlighted. Figure S5 shows MLR energies compared to the order of the individual structure space group for each 24d:96h ratio. Figure S7a shows the negative correlation between mean distance moved of Li atoms and final optimized energy. Figure S7b shows the weaker negative correlation between distance to a crystallographic site and energy.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a systematic workflow that combines geometric Li-Li distance pruning, LSH-based symmetry reduction, and ML-based energetic ordering to identify the ground-state space of partially occupied crystals, applied to c-LLZO. 2. The strongest evidence is the MLR model achieving 0.9996 correlation on the test set, with four structures within 0.026 eV (1 k_BT) of the global minimum, all sharing the 8:48 24d:96h occupancy. 3. The future path involves extending the workflow to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals, and performing large-scale geometry optimization on the full configuration space to account for entropic contributions.

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology); Takahiro Muraoka (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Supramolecular Chemistry / Biomaterials and Regenerative Medicine
summary.executive_summary:
This Feature Article presents recent advances in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic dynamic bio-interfaces—the contact sites between and within cells where critical biological processes such as adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation occur. The authors highlight four major material families that emulate distinct bio-interfacial functions: (1) stiffness-controlled peptide hydrogels (A16G) and A16G-N-cadherin composites that mimic the extracellular matrix (ECM) to promote neonatal neuroblast migration in injured brains; (2) jigsaw-shaped peptide amphiphiles (JigSAP) capable of high-efficiency incorporation and sustained release of growth factors (VEGF) for neural regeneration; (3) redox-responsive peptide systems (JigSAP-IMI/MII) with point-mutation-controlled gel-sol transition kinetics; and (4) phospholipid nanosheets stabilized by metal-chelating self-assembling peptides for extended blood circulation, alongside photoresponsive molecular machines (AzoMEx) that trigger endocytosis-like vesicle fission for in vivo virus delivery.

The article demonstrates that by harnessing the principles of supramolecular self-assembly, materials can be engineered with tunable macroscopic properties (stiffness, release kinetics, stability, and dynamic deformation) that directly correlate with the morphology and function of their biological counterparts. Key quantitative results include: EGFP incorporation at 93 mol% vs 3 mol% for JigSAP-tagged versus untagged proteins; protein release of 39 mol% after 168 hours versus only 8 mol% for RADA16-tagged counterparts; and M13 phage infectivity retained across multiple organs (spleen: [25.6 ± 13.2] × 10^9 virions/mg) following blood administration. The authors conclude that bio-interface biomimicry via supramolecular chemistry offers powerful strategies for regenerative medicine and drug delivery, while noting that the field is still in its infancy with substantial future progress expected.

Key quantitative results include: EGFP incorporation at 93 mol% vs 3 mol% for JigSAP-tagged versus untagged proteins; protein release of 39 mol% after 168 hours versus only 8 mol% for RADA16-tagged counterparts; and M13 phage infectivity retained across multiple organs (spleen: [25.6 ± 13.2] × 10^9 virions/mg) following blood administration. The authors conclude that bio-interface biomimicry via supramolecular chemistry offers powerful strategies for regenerative medicine and drug delivery, while noting that the field is still in its infancy with substantial future progress expected.

Research Context
Bio-interfaces are sites of contact between molecules, cells, and tissues, regulating physiological actions through adhesion, signaling, and substance transportation. The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex protein network that regulates cellular functions like migration and differentiation, yet its dynamic reconstruction in injured tissue remains a challenge. Phospholipid bilayers form cellular and organelle membranes, enabling substance transportation (exocytosis and endocytosis) and membrane-mediated signal transduction. Prior biomimetic approaches for membrane-bound carriers like liposomes and micelles are limited by inherent instability and short circulation times in blood. Endocytosis-like membrane deformation synchronized with substance transport remains critically unexplored in biomolecular engineering. Recent supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology advances have made it possible to construct dynamic materials functionalizing bio-interfaces.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can self-assembling peptide hydrogels with tunable stiffness mimic the ECM structure and promote neuroblast migration in an injured brain? Can jute-shaped hydrophobic surfaces on peptide amphiphiles enable efficient incorporation and sustained release of full-length proteins? Can single-point methionine mutations in supramolecular peptides control the kinetics of stimulus-responsive gel-sol transitions? Can metal-chelating self-assembling peptides stabilize phospholipid nanosheets against dilution for extended blood circulation? Can a photoresponsive diazocine-based molecular machine induce endocytosis-like vesicle fission for in vivo delivery of large biomacromolecules like M13 phage? The central hypothesis is that self-assembly principles can create functional biomimetics with tunable physical properties that recapitulate the dynamic, transient interactions at native bio-interfaces.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes several self-assembling peptide scaffolds, including RADA16 (Arg-Ala-Asp-Ala), peptide amphiphiles bearing fatty acid chains, and diphenylalanine backbones. RADA16 forms supramolecular nanofibres through β-sheet-type hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions corresponding to the alternating hydrophilic/hydrophobic amino acid sequence. The peptide A16G (RADA16 with terminal alanine replaced by glycine) forms curved fibres seen on transmission electron microscopy. JigSAP consists of Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2, featuring the AXXXA motif and forming nanofibres with an average width of 3.2 nm and length of several µm. JigSAP was dispersed in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) at 1.0 wt% concentration for hydrogel formation. For membrane studies, DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets were formed at a 5:1 molar ratio and 5.0 wt% total concentration. Chol-MBP features the PHGGGPHGG Cu²⁺-binding motif derived from naturally occurring imidazole groups of histidine. AzoMEx molecular machines were embedded in DOPC-based giant unilamellar vesicles at [DOPC] = 180 µM and [AzoMex] = 20 µM. M13 phage was used at 22.6 × 10¹¹ virions/mL for incorporation assays. In vivo experiments involved neonatal mice neocortex injection, ischaemic stroke mouse models, and tail vein administration of fluorescence-labeled vesicles and nanosheets. Blood circulation was assessed via IV-CLSM of the earlobe vessels. Protein incorporation was quantified by CD spectroscopy and fluorescence imaging, and release by incubation at 37 °C. In vivo M13 phage distribution was confirmed by plaque assays of homogenized organ samples.

Procedures And Architectures
JigSAP self-assembly was characterized in silico by molecular dynamics simulations and in vitro by circular dichroism spectroscopy over 100 hours. Rheological analysis measured storage modulus G' and loss modulus G For AzoMEx, photoisomerization changes the diazocine ring conformation to move two cationic NMe3⁺ moieties, expanding the liposomal membrane. DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were formed by adding 2.0 equivalents of Cu²⁺ ions to the 5.0 wt% dispersion. Fluorescent Cy5-labeled DPPC vesicles and DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were filtered through a membrane with 200-nm pores before injection. For the M13 phage delivery, GUVs were coated with a block copolymer of poly(aspartic acid) and poly(ethylene glycol). 100 μL of GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp encapsulating M13 phages was injected tail vein in mice for organ distribution analysis. For the neuronal migration model, A16G and A16G-Ncad hydrogels were injected into the site of injured neonatal neocortex at low temperature. For the stroke model, ischaemic stroke was produced by distal middle cerebral artery occlusion.

Key Results
A16G hydrogels with A16G-Ncad showed significantly higher neuroblast migration rates in time-lapse imaging on culture dishes. In vivo, Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in the mixture of A16G and A16G-Ncad at the injury site, while being sparse in other treatments. JigSAP exhibited a remarkably high rigidity of 1.1 × 10⁴ Pa with strain-thinning rheological profiles. EGFP-JigSAP was incorporated at 93 mol%, compared to only 3 mol% for non-tagged EGFP. EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 showed 66 mol% and 55 mol% incorporation, respectively. JigSAP-incorporated EGFP-JigSAP showed 21 mol% release after 24 hours and 39 mol% after 168 hours at 37 °C. In contrast, EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 released only 5 mol% and 8 mol%, respectively, after 168 hours. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets maintained their structure upon dilution to 0.2 wt% after Cu²⁺ crosslinking, while spherical aggregates formed without Cu²⁺. IV-CLSM of the earlobe showed FL DPPC vesicles aggregated and clogged, while FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed. GUVDOPC/AzoMEx successfully incorporated M13 phages with 22.6 × 10¹¹ virions/mL, and they were transiently protected. After M13 phage administration, infectivity was retained in all organs: spleen [25.6 ± 13.2] × 10⁹, liver [18.3 ± 3.2] × 10⁹, kidney [1.3 ± 0.6] × 10⁹, heart [1.1 ± 0.5] × 10⁹, lung [0.5 ± 0.3] × 10⁹, and brain [0.2 ± 0.1] × 10⁹ virions/mg. Double-positive cells with laminin and EdU increased in the injured stroke area for VEGF-JigSAP and JigSAP treatments.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The A16G-Ncad scaffold mimics both the fibrous structure and dynamic adhesive function of endogenous radial glial fibres, providing a mechanistic basis for enhanced neuroblast migration. The jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces of JigSAP enable cooperative β-sheet dimerization that simultaneously drives nanofibre assembly and protein binding, resolving the incompatibility between incorporation and release. Strain-thinning rheology in JigSAP hydrogels indicates covalent-like mechanical integrity of supramolecular fibres, supporting robust tissue regeneration applications. Cu²⁺-mediated crosslinking of the PHGGG motif converts transient phospholipid associations into stable, dilution-resistant nanostructures, analogous to metal-stabilized biomembranes. The photoresponsive AzoMEx mechanism uncouples membrane deformation from substance transport, enabling controlled endocytosis-like fission for encapsulation of micrometer-scale cargo. Retention of phage infectivity across multiple organs after in vivo circulation demonstrates that supramolecular encapsulation can protect bioactives from immune clearance while permitting tissue distribution.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a feature article reviewing recent studies rather than presenting a new standalone experiment; quantitative details for all cited studies are not exhaustive. The M13 phage infectivity was measured 15 minutes after injection, which may not capture long-term viral persistence or clearance dynamics. Spleen and liver samples were diluted 10-fold before plaque assay, suggesting higher organ burden that may mask complete quantification. The study does not report specific random seeds, sample sizes for in vivo cohorts, or exact power calculations, which are important for generalizability. The AzoMEx mechanism is demonstrated at the molecular/vesicle level; its efficacy at the cellular scale and under complex physiological stresses is not fully validated here.

Claims
Self-assembling peptide hydrogels with tunable stiffness can mimic the ECM and promote endogenous neuroblast migration in the injured brain. A16G hydrogels with A16G-Ncad showed higher migration rates in time-lapse imaging on culture dishes. In vivo, Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in the mixture of A16G and A16G-Ncad at the injury site. The study reports only time-lapse imaging and a single in vivo example; long-term functional recovery data is not provided. This provides a non-cell-based strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy using fibrous self-assembly. Point mutations (A16G vs RADA16) demonstrate that conformational flexibility controls macroscopic stiffness in self-assembling peptides.
Jigsaw-shaped peptide amphiphiles enable both high-efficiency incorporation and sustained release of full-length proteins for tissue regeneration. EGFP-JigSAP was incorporated at 93 mol% versus 3 mol% for untagged EGFP. JigSAP showed 39 mol% protein release after 168 hours, versus 8 mol% for RADA16-tagged protein. VEGF-JigSAP injection in a stroke model increased double-positive (laminin/EdU) cells in the injured area. The release profile stagnates after 168 hours for JigSAP, while the 5V and RADA16 controls stagnate much earlier (after 48 hours). The JigSAP architecture demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release of various full-length growth factors. This resolves the incompatibility between incorporation and release that has challenged peptide-based materials.
Metal-chelating self-assembling peptides stabilize phospholipid nanosheets against dilution, enabling extended blood circulation and efficient in vivo delivery. Cu²⁺ addition preserved the nanosheet structure upon dilution to 0.2 wt%, while the control formed spherical aggregates. IV-CLSM showed FL DPPC vesicles aggregated while nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in blood vessels. The paper does not report biodistribution or clearance rates of the nanosheets; only circulation profile and M13 phage distribution are given. This provides a suitable carrier for whole-body delivery via blood administration, overcoming the instability of surfactant-phospholipid bicelles. The approach of incorporating a self-assembling peptide as a surrogate surfactant enables structural control that cannot be achieved with traditional surfactants.
A photoresponsive molecular machine can induce endocytosis-like membrane fission for encapsulation and in vivo delivery of micrometer-sized cargo. M13 phages were encapsulated and remained infective across all sampled organs after blood administration. IV-CLSM confirmed higher blood stability of encapsulated M13 phages compared to bare phages. The endocytosis-like fission is shown at the vesicle level; cellular-scale endocytosis and macrophage uptake/escape are not demonstrated. The AzoMEx-GUV technology could be applied to in vivo phage display for selection of peptides binding to ligands in living bodies. This decouples the membrane deformation trigger (photoisomerization) from the cargo loading event, enabling controlled entry.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The A16G/A16G-Ncad experiment included controls: A16G alone, and mixtures with A16G/Ncad (non-tagged), showing that the tag-peptide conjugate is necessary for migration. For protein incorporation, EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 served as alternative tag controls, showing intermediate efficiency (66 and 55 mol%) compared to JigSAP (93 mol%). For membrane stability, a control of DPPC/Chol-MBP without Cu²⁺ was used, demonstrating structural degradation upon dilution. For M13 phage delivery, both bare M13 phageCy5 and encapsulated M13 phageCy5-pAsp were compared in circulation and organ distribution.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities, highlighting ECM and phospholipid bilayers. Figure 2 shows: (a-c) A16G vs RADA16 hydrogel morphology, (d) A16G curved fibres by TEM, (f) MD simulation of fibre self-assembly. Figure 3 presents: (a) time-lapse imaging of neuroblast migration on hydrogels, (b) in vivo Dcx+ distribution in injured neocortex. Figure 4 details: (a-b) MD simulation of JigSAP assembly, (c) CD spectrum showing β-sheet transition, (d-e) rheology and modulus, (f) strain thinning, (g) CD of tagged proteins, (h-j) incorporation efficiency, (k) release profiles, (l-q) in vivo stroke model results. Figure 5 demonstrates: (a-b) gel-sol transition, (c-g) IMI vs MII variants with oxidative contrast, (h) redox responsiveness under physiological conditions. Figure 6 shows: (a) Chol-MBP design, (b) self-assembly mechanism, (c) TEM of diluted nanoparticles, (d) Cu²⁺-crosslinked nanosheets, (f-g) IV-CLSM of vesicles vs nanosheets. Figure 7 details: (a-d) AzoMex design, (e) M13 phage incorporation, (f) IV-CLSM circulation comparison, (l-n) IV-CLSM of encapsulated phages, (o-t) organ infectivity plaque assays.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that supramolecular self-assembly can engineer bio-interfaces with tunable stiffness, sustained protein release, structural stability, and dynamic deformation to recapitulate ECM and membrane functions for regenerative medicine. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative validation: 93 mol% incorporation versus 3 mol% for untagged proteins, 39 mol% sustained release, and retention of M13 phage infectivity across six organs ([25.6 ± 13.2] × 10⁹ virions/mg) after in vivo circulation. 3. The future path involves scaling these supramolecular bio-interface biomimetics from vesicle and culture-dish demonstrations to full-organ regenerative therapies and in vivo phage display methods for ligand selection.

summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires (NOVA School of Science and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Chemoinformatics / Computational Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: GUIDEMOL is a Python-based computer program developed to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors using the RDKit software library, accessible through a graphical user interface (GUI) built with the tkinter package. The application targets chemoinformatics users with no programming skills, including scientists and students, by providing easy access to RDKit tools. Beyond standard RDKit descriptors, GUIDEMOL implements 3D molecular structure representations: electrostatic potential grids (EP) and voxel encoding, which have gained attention for training deep learning neural networks. The GUI supports buttons for triggering calculations, checkbuttons for YES/NO options, radiobuttons for mutually exclusive choices, and entries for numeric input, all managed by the grid geometry manager. 3D molecular models are generated via MMFF94 optimization with 5000 maximum iterations. The RDKit version used is 2022.9.5. Available descriptors include RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA, and exact molecular weight. The EP grid uses Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges, while voxelisation supports atomic number, partial charge, and Wildman-Crippen molecular refractivity and logP contributions. A command-line interface (CLI) is also provided for 3D grid calculations. The source code is available under the three-clause BSD license at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol. claims.description: GUIDEMOL provides easy access to RDKit descriptors and 3D grid representations for users without programming skills.
3D molecular representations (EP and voxel) can be used for deep learning and 3D-QSAR.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based computer program developed to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors using the RDKit software library, accessible through a graphical user interface (GUI) built with the tkinter package. The application targets chemoinformatics users with no programming skills, including scientists and students, by providing easy access to RDKit tools. Beyond standard RDKit descriptors, GUIDEMOL implements 3D molecular structure representations: electrostatic potential grids (EP) and voxel encoding, which have gained attention for training deep learning neural networks. The GUI supports buttons for triggering calculations, checkbuttons for YES/NO options, radiobuttons for mutually exclusive choices, and entries for numeric input, all managed by the grid geometry manager. 3D molecular models are generated via MMFF94 optimization with 5000 maximum iterations. The RDKit version used is 2022.9.5. Available descriptors include RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA, and exact molecular weight. The EP grid uses Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges, while voxelisation supports atomic number, partial charge, and Wildman-Crippen molecular refractivity and logP contributions. A command-line interface (CLI) is also provided for 3D grid calculations. The source code is available under the three-clause BSD license at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol. The paper notes that some descriptors yielded inconsistent values across runs or operating systems with the same RDKit version.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors are central to QSPR/QSAR methodology used by scientists with varying levels of computer skills. Chemoinformatics is gradually permeating curricula in chemistry, biology and material science degrees, creating a demand for teaching software. Several programs calculate molecular descriptors: CDK (Java) with PaDEL and CDK Descriptor Calculator GUI; BlueDesc for ARFF/LIBSVM conversion; OCHEM web service; and ChemDes web service. Proprietary software options include MOE, VolSurf+, CORINA Symphony, ChemAxon Calculator Plugins, and alvaDesc. The open-source RDKit software implements a wide range of chemoinformatics tools used in machine learning. Mordred is a Python package for descriptor calculation, but it is primarily for command-line or web use. Python's tkinter package enables GUI development as the standard interface to Tcl/Tk. Prior work by Shi and Borchardt combined RDKit and tkinter to create JRgui for Joback and Reid group contribution descriptors. 3D molecular representations (electrostatic potentials, voxel grids) have gained attention for deep learning neural networks. 3D-QSAR and molecular similarity assessments have long used electrostatic potentials generated by point charges at atom centers. A gap exists for a minimalist, no-programming-required interface combining standard RDKit descriptors with 3D grid representations in a single Python GUI.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a Python GUI based on tkinter can provide easy access to RDKit molecular descriptor calculations and 3D grid representations for non-programmers. The paper hypothesizes that combining RDKit, tkinter, and 3D grid representation methods into a single application would facilitate chemoinformatics for scientists and students. The authors predict that a minimalist interface with various widget types (buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries) can support user configuration of both 3D structure generation and descriptor calculation parameters. The application aims to support both standard RDKit descriptors and the emerging 3D voxel/EP representations, making it relevant for both QSAR and deep learning applications. The hypothesis includes that a CLI would be necessary as a complementary access mode for 3D grid calculations. The paper expects that the software, released under a BSD license, would allow for easy extensibility to other descriptors or tasks.

Methodological Details
The study presents a single software application (GUIDEMOL) rather than a controlled experiment with participants or datasets. The software is built on the RDKit open-source library and the tkinter GUI toolkit. The GUI uses the tkinter grid geometry manager to arrange widgets: buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, and a scrollbar. File selection is implemented via the tkinter.filedialog module, and a log file registers successful processing and failures per molecule. 3D molecular models are generated using MMFFOptimizeMolecule with mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000. Pre-generation options include removing metals (MetalDisconnector), keeping the largest fragment (LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True)), and neutralizing (Uncharger). Hydrogen atoms are added via Chem.AddHs(), and optionally with addCoords=True to preserve original atom coordinates. Available 3D RDKit descriptors are: RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA, and exact molecular weight. The EP grid uses Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges calculated via AllChem.ComputeGasteigerCharges() or GetMMFFPartialCharge(). The EP calculation excludes atoms within 1 Å of the cube center and those beyond a user-defined cutoff distance. Voxelisation properties include atomic number, partial atomic charge (Gasteiger or MMFF), and Wildman-Crippen atomic contributions to refractivity and logP via _CalcCrippenContribs(). Output is saved in a csv file with the last columns containing molecule name and molecule ID number. The CLI uses the guidemol.py script with arguments for input/output files, grid type, atomic property, coordinates, cube size, cutoff/sigma, and grid dimensions. The RDKit version used is 2022.9.5. The source code is hosted at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause BSD license.

Procedures And Architectures
The GUI architecture follows a widget-based layout managed by the tkinter grid geometry manager. The 3D structure generation procedure follows: SMILES input → MetalDisconnector (optional) → LargestFragmentChooser (optional) → Uncharger (optional) → Chem.AddHs() → MMFFOptimizeMolecule (MMFF94, 5000 iterations). For descriptor calculation, the user selects descriptors via checkbuttons, and the software calls the corresponding functions in RDKit's rdMolDescriptors module. The EP grid generation procedure computes the potential EP at each cube c as the sum over partial charges q_i times inverse distance r_{ic}, excluding nearby atoms. The voxelisation procedure computes VoxG_c as the sum over atomic properties p_i weighted by a Gaussian exponential, with σ controlling the decay. The CLI procedure bypasses the GUI and invokes the grid calculation scripts directly, accepting command-line arguments for all configuration parameters. The CLI example shown uses -g pot for EP, -p Gasteiger, -cx 0 -cy 0 -cz 0, -r 0.5, -w 3, -sx 5 -sy 5 -sz 5, with input.sdf and output outfile.csv.

Key Results
The software successfully implements all RDKit 3D descriptors (RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA) through a unified GUI. Both EP and voxel grid representations are computable via the GUI with user-specified parameters (coordinates, cube size, cutoff/sigma). A CLI alternative for 3D grid calculations was successfully implemented, enabling non-GUI use. The author observed that for some molecules and certain descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or operating systems. A concrete reproducibility issue was identified with the 3D structure generated for the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The software produces a log file registering successful processing and failures for each molecule. The output format includes the molecule name and ID number in the final columns, ensuring traceability.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The combination of GUI and CLI with 3D grid outputs positions GUIDEMOL at the intersection of classical QSAR and modern deep learning applications in chemoinformatics. The reproducibility issue with GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors suggests that these RDKit 3D descriptors may depend on stochastic elements or uninitialized states in the underlying C++ implementation. The minimalist design, releasing under a BSD license, is intended to serve as a template for extending to other chemoinformatics tasks. By offering both Gasteiger and MMFF charge options, the software addresses two standard methods in 3D-QSAR for EP grid construction. The inclusion of Wildman-Crippen molecular refractivity and logP as voxel properties connects the tool to established physicochemical descriptor calculation methods.

Contradictions And Limitations
The author explicitly reports inconsistent results for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors across runs or operating systems despite using the same RDKit version (2022.9.5). The reproducibility issue was exemplified by the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br, though no quantitative difference is specified in the paper. The paper does not report any formal validation, benchmarking, or cross-validation experiments comparing GUIDEMOL output to standard tools or datasets. No performance metrics (execution time, memory usage) are reported for either the GUI or CLI paths. The software's applicability is limited to molecules compatible with RDKit's MMFF94 optimization and descriptor modules. The text does not specify which exact RDKit modules beyond rdMolDescriptors are involved for all descriptors. No test datasets or sample molecule counts are mentioned for validation purposes.

Claims
GUIDEMOL provides easy access to RDKit descriptors and 3D grid representations for users without programming skills. The GUI is built with tkinter widgets (buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries) for non-programmers. A log file records processing, simplifying user error tracking. The source code is released under a BSD license, making it open and extendable. The authors admit that some 3D descriptors yield inconsistent values across runs or OS with the same RDKit version. The reproducibility issue for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM may undermine reliability for some users. This reduces the barrier to entry for QSAR/QSAR methodology in educational and non-computational settings. The BSD license enables commercial adoption, potentially expanding the tool's reach beyond academia.
3D molecular representations (EP and voxel) can be used for deep learning and 3D-QSAR. EP and voxel grids can be computed with user-defined parameters. Wildman-Crippen contributions are implemented for logP and molecular refractivity. The paper notes that these representations have recently gained attention, implying the field is nascent and potentially less mature than traditional descriptors. GUIDEMOL can serve as a data preparation front-end for CNN-based molecular representation tasks. Users can toggle between Gasteiger and MMFF charges, a standard distinction in 3D-QSAR methodology.

Data And Code Availability
The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause BSD license.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The author identifies a robustness issue: different values obtained for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors across runs or operating systems with RDKit 2022.9.5. The example molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br demonstrates this inconsistency. No ablation studies comparing descriptor subsets or grid parameters are presented.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 is described as the GUIDEMOL interface showing various tkinter widgets arranged with the grid geometry manager. No tables or other figures are cited with quantitative data.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a Python/tkinter GUI that provides non-programmers easy access to RDKit molecular descriptors and 3D electrostatic/voxel grid representations for both QSAR and deep learning applications. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit demonstration of the reproducibility issue: GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors yielded different values across runs or OS with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) for the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. 3. The future path is indicated by the BSD-licensed, extensible code released at GitHub, which can be adapted for additional descriptors, other chemoinformatics tasks, and potential fixes to the reproducibility issues identified.

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang (Peking University); Tianzuo Li (Peking University); Jiyeon Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Dahye Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Lianjie Xu (Peking University); Yajie Liu (Peking University); Jongcheol Seo (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Wen-Bin Zhang (Peking University)
summary.field_subfield: Protein Engineering / Synthetic Biology / Topological Proteins
summary.type_of_paper: Research Article / Protein Design and Synthesis Report
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the design and cellular synthesis of cat-DHFR, a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase, representing the first instance of a single-domain protein with two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings. The approach diverges from conventional artificial topological protein synthesis, which typically requires exogenous entangling motifs and results in multidomain architectures. Instead, the authors employed a 'rewiring' strategy that exploited the spatially entangled relationships of the native DHFR fold as the entangling template. By splitting the wild-type DHFR at residues 88 and 89 (α-helix-C and β-sheet-5 boundary) and rewiring the connectivity into two closed rings using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-inteins, they synthesized cat-DHFR in E. coli BL21(DE3) without any in vitro reactions. The target molecule was purified by Ni-NTA and SEC chromatography, with topology verified by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, TEV protease digestion, ion mobility mass spectrometry (IMS-MS), and collision-induced dissociation (CID). Structurally, cat-DHFR retains the folded core but exhibits a slightly loosened secondary structure (reduced CD ellipticity) compared to the linear control. Catalytically, cat-DHFR maintains ~35% of the linear enzyme's activity (5 U/mg vs. 14 U/mg), with a ~5-fold increase in Km, ~38% kcat, and a ten-fold reduction in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km), and ~173-fold higher KD for DHF. Notably, cat-DHFR shows enhanced thermal resilience (87% vs. 74% activity in 5% DMSO). The work establishes a new paradigm in protein science: linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with near-identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability, opening a horizon for topological protein design without exogenous motifs.

claims.description: cat-DHFR is a single-domain protein catenane that retains folded structure and catalytic activity of the linear ancestor.
Rewiring the native DHFR fold as the entangling template eliminates the need for exogenous entangling motifs.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the design and cellular synthesis of cat-DHFR, a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase, representing the first instance of a single-domain protein with two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings. The approach diverges from conventional artificial topological protein synthesis, which typically requires exogenous entangling motifs and results in multidomain architectures. Instead, the authors employed a 'rewiring' strategy that exploited the spatially entangled relationships of the native DHFR fold as the entangling template. By splitting the wild-type DHFR at residues 88 and 89 (α-helix-C and β-sheet-5 boundary) and rewiring the connectivity into two closed rings using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-inteins, they synthesized cat-DHFR in E. coli BL21(DE3) without any in vitro reactions. The target molecule was purified by Ni-NTA and SEC chromatography, with topology verified by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, TEV protease digestion, ion mobility mass spectrometry (IMS-MS), and collision-induced dissociation (CID). Structurally, cat-DHFR retains the folded core but exhibits a slightly loosened secondary structure (reduced CD ellipticity) compared to the linear control. Catalytically, cat-DHFR maintains ~35% of the linear enzyme's activity (5 U/mg vs. 14 U/mg), with a ~5-fold increase in Km, ~38% kcat, and a ten-fold reduction in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km), and ~173-fold higher KD for DHF. Notably, cat-DHFR shows enhanced thermal resilience (87% vs. 74% activity in 5% DMSO). The work establishes a new paradigm in protein science: linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with near-identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability, opening a horizon for topological protein design without exogenous motifs.

Research Context
Natural protein domains function as autonomous modules with limited topological diversity due to linear polypeptide chain constraints. Scarce natural topological proteins suggest unconventional topologies could enhance protein stability relative to linear counterparts. Recent advances in 'assembly-reaction' synergy have enabled synthesis of star, cyclic, lasso, and protein catenane proteins. Existing artificial topological proteins typically contain multiple domains, complicating the study of topological effects on structure-property relationships. A single-domain topological protein would exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology and provide an unusual scaffold for further engineering. Preparing single-domain topological proteins remains challenging even for the simplest catenane or Hopf link. DHFR has been shown to tolerate rethreading and loop manipulation while maintaining folding and function, making it a viable model system. The need for an exogenous entangling motif as a template may be eliminated by exploiting spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a single-domain protein can be rewired into a catenane topology without collapsing the fold and while preserving catalytic function. The authors hypothesize that using the original DHFR fold itself as the entangling template enables synthesis of single-domain protein catenanes with identical composition to the linear wild-type. The specific prediction is that the cat-DHFR molecule will retain enzymatic activity, fold properly, and exhibit altered physical and thermodynamic properties due to conformational restriction. The hypothesis extends that the reduced catalytic activity of the catenane can be restored or surpassed by directed evolution, similar to other structural variants. A computational hypothesis was formulated that specific cleavage sites identified by Gaussian linking number (GLN) would reveal the entangling core needed for catenane formation.

Methodological Details
The model enzyme DHFR was derived from Escherichia coli, which catalyzes 7,8-dihydrofolate reduction to 5,6,7,8-tetrahydrofolate in the presence of NADPH. The wild-type DHFR structure (PDB: 4KJJ) was used as the starting point for virtual loop splitting and GLN matrix analysis. The cleavage site was identified at the boundary between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5, corresponding to residues 88 and 89. The design adopted residues 1–88 as ring I and residues 89–159 as ring II, yielding a cat-DHFR with GLN of +1.120. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. Two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs were used for ring closure to ensure simultaneous cyclization. The gene cassette included two DHFR segments as entangling template, two split-intein pairs, and a TEV protease recognition sequence in the first ring. A linear DHFR with identical amino acid composition (l-DHFR) was designed as the control, bearing extra amino acids at N- and C-termini. Genes were synthesized and sub-cloned into pMCSG19 (cat-DHFR) and pET21a (l-DHFR) vectors. Plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Protein expression was carried out at 16°C for 20 hours to ensure proper folding and complete intein reaction. Proteins were purified under native conditions using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography, followed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC). Catalytic activity was assayed by monitoring absorbance at 340 nm at 25°C. Binding affinities were determined using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). The samples were tested in 5% DMSO to evaluate solvent tolerance.

Procedures And Architectures
The molecular design proceeded by virtually cleaving the wt-DHFR backbone at all unstructured loops and calculating GLN matrices for each split. The split yielding the largest GLN (+0.726 for the intermediate segment) indicated the potential entangling core. New loops were designed with distinct lengths to ensure proper crossing and reconstitution efficiency. A retrosynthetic analysis (Figure 1a) guided the placement of cyclization motifs and circular permutation. The rewired loops were designed to be at least 16 residues long to bridge the split structural motifs. In the control l-DHFR, extra amino acids were placed at the N- and C-termini to account for intein residues without altering the DHFR sequence. SDS-PAGE analysis showed a single band at ~22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at <20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The SEC overlay revealed cat-DHFR eluting as a broader peak at a larger retention volume than l-DHFR. Far-UV CD spectra showed reduced positive ellipticity at ~200 nm and negative peak between 210 and 230 nm for cat-DHFR. The TEV protease digestion experiment involved pre-programmed cleavage in the first ring, converting cat-DHFR to linear and cyclic fragments. Ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) and collision-induced dissociation (CID) were applied to characterize topology through CCS values and fragment ions.

Key Results
cat-DHFR was successfully synthesized and purified from E. coli, yielding a major band at less than 20 kDa on SDS-PAGE, reflecting its compact concatenated form. The SEC overlay confirmed that cat-DHFR elutes as a broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume than l-DHFR, consistent with a dynamic compact structure. CD spectra showed that cat-DHFR retains a folded structure but with substantially reduced ellipticity peaks at ~200 nm and 210–230 nm compared to l-DHFR, indicating loosening of secondary structure. The near-UV CD spectrum of cat-DHFR exhibited positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to l-DHFR, confirming the folded core remains intact. The TEV protease digestion converted cat-DHFR into a linear fragment and a cyclic fragment, confirmed by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS. IMS-MS and CID revealed that the topological topology was consistent with a catenane structure. The catalytic activity of cat-DHFR was ~5 U/mg compared to ~14 U/mg for l-DHFR. The previously reported rethreaded DHFR variant showed no reducing activity at all, highlighting the significance of cat-DHFR retention. The Km of cat-DHFR was approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The kcat of cat-DHFR was about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of cat-DHFR was reduced by an order of magnitude relative to l-DHFR. The KD for DHF was ~173-fold larger for cat-DHFR than l-DHFR. The KD for NADPH was ~14-fold larger for cat-DHFR than l-DHFR. The KD for the product THF was increased by ~3.6-fold for cat-DHFR. In 5% DMSO, cat-DHFR preserved 87% activity versus 74% for l-DHFR. A construct with split-intein pairs on the same side of DHFR yielded only ~33% catenane with considerable single-ring side products. The shortest linker yielded only about one-fifth the output (~12 mg/L) of the longest linker.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The retention of folded structure, albeit slightly looser, confirms that the native fold provides the necessary scaffold for catenane formation. The reduced catalytic activity and increased Km are attributed primarily to compromised affinity for substrate and cofactor, rather than a complete loss of fold. The 5-fold increase in NADPH-saturated Km, contrasted with the 173-fold increase in unliganded KD, suggests NADPH binding significantly enhances DHF affinity in cat-DHFR. The mechanical interlocking imposes conformational restriction that enhances thermal resilience (87% vs. 74% in DMSO). The study demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into single-domain concatenated counterparts with almost identical chemical composition and well-preserved function. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science: structural topology as a tunable dimension for protein engineering independent of linear sequence constraints. The approach is generally robust before the linker becomes too short, as even the shortest linker yielded detectable catenated products.

Contradictions And Limitations
No crystal structure of cat-DHFR could be obtained due to unsatisfactory purity, disordered linkers, or reduced substrate binding affinity. Topological proof is indirect, relying on proteolytic digestion, IMS, and CID rather than atomic-resolution structural data. The approach requires extensive optimization of loop length, sequence, and intein orientation to achieve high-yield expression and efficient catenane formation. The reduced catalytic activity (5 U/mg vs. 14 U/mg) and ten-fold reduction in catalytic efficiency indicate that the catenane topology is not neutral to function. The broader SEC peak and SDS-PAGE mobility for cat-DHFR suggest a dynamic or polydisperse population rather than a single homogeneous species. The study was confined to a single protein (DHFR) and a single catenane topology; generalization to other folds or topologies is not established.

Claims
cat-DHFR is a single-domain protein catenane that retains folded structure and catalytic activity of the linear ancestor. Cat-DHFR purified as a single major band on SDS-PAGE, confirmed by LC-MS mass accuracy. CD spectra confirmed folding with only minor loosening of secondary structure. The protein was converted to linear and cyclic fragments upon TEV cleavage, confirming the concatenated topology. The protein exhibited ~35% of the control's catalytic activity (5 U/mg vs. 14 U/mg). No crystal structure was obtained, leaving the exact atomic-resolution catenane geometry unconfirmed. The SEC profile shows a broad peak, suggesting conformational dynamics or slight heterogeneity in the catenate. Catalytic efficiency was reduced by an order of magnitude, indicating a functional cost to the topology. Linear proteins can be converted to single-domain catenanes with identical composition and well-preserved function. This opens a new structural dimension for protein engineering, where topology is decoupled from linear sequence. The catenane topology confers enhanced thermal resilience, potentially useful for industrial enzyme applications.
Rewiring the native DHFR fold as the entangling template eliminates the need for exogenous entangling motifs. The design used split-DHFR segments themselves as the entangling template for catenane formation. No exogenous entangling motif was added to the DHFR sequence. The strategy relies on exploiting spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures. The method still requires two pairs of orthogonal split-inteins and circular permutation as artificial constructs. The approach is not completely template-free, as the split sites and rewired loops are externally engineered. The strategy could be applied to any protein domain with a sufficiently intertwined fold. Further optimization may reduce the burden of circular permutation and intein orientation requirements.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The same-side intein orientation construct yielded only ~33% catenane with considerable monocyclic by-products, demonstrating the necessity of circular permutation for steric separation. Testing different linker lengths (L2 of ring II) showed that shorter linkers reduce intein reconstitution and favor monocyclic by-products, with the shortest yielding only ~12 mg/L of culture. Despite yield reduction at shorter linker lengths, catenated products remained detectable, suggesting method robustness. The design choice of residues 23–24 for ring closure was identified as most efficient among multiple possible loop-region sites.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the retrosynthetic design of cat-DHFR with the split site, circular permutation, intein placement, and TEV protease site. Figure 1b illustrates the gene cassette containing the two DHFR segments, intein pairs, and TEV site. Figure 1d presents the Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix used to identify the entangling core. Figure 2a shows SDS-PAGE of purified cat-DHFR and l-DHFR, with cat-DHFR running at <20 kDa. Figure 2b shows the SEC overlay comparing cat-DHFR and l-DHFR retention profiles. Figure 2c shows LC-MS spectra confirming the molecular identities of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure 2d shows far-UV CD spectra indicating retained but loosened folding in cat-DHFR. Figure 2e shows TEV protease digestion confirming the conversion of cat-DHFR to linear and cyclic fragments. Figure 4c shows kinetic curves of DHFR activity monitored at 340 nm. Figure S1 presents the GLN matrices for split DHFR (GLN +0.726) and cat-DHFR (GLN +1.120). Figure S2 shows the near-UV CD spectrum of cat-DHFR confirming a folded core. Figure S3a–d shows the comparison of same-side vs. opposite-side intein orientation and ring-closure site optimization. Figure S4 shows the effect of L2 linker sequence and length on catenane yield. Table 1 presents kinetic parameters (Km, kcat, kcat/Km) and ITC binding constants (KD).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and cellular synthesis of the first single-domain protein catenane, achieved by rewiring a native protein fold as an entangling template without exogenous motifs. 2. The strongest evidence is multi-technique topological confirmation combining LC-MS mass accuracy, TEV-mediated topology verification, IMS-MS/CID for CCS and fragment ion analysis, and CD spectroscopy confirming a folded core. 3. The future path involves applying this template-free topology engineering to other protein domains, and using directed evolution to restore the ~35% catalytic activity of cat-DHFR to linear-control levels.
