judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a robotic platform designed to automate sequential electrochemical rate data collection for CO2 electroreduction, addressing the heavy data requirements of cohesive kinetic analysis that preclude traditional manual Tafel and reactant-order analyses. The authors demonstrate the system by investigating CO2RR to CO at three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). Key findings reveal that common linearization strategies yield incomplete or uninterpretable results due to non-ideal behaviors; specifically, bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences are non-linear and potential-dependent across all three catalysts. For CoPc and CoTPP, bicarbonate inhibition attenuates at more reductive potentials, while for FePc it is amplified. These behaviors are explained through models invoking electrolyte poisoning (bicarbonate adsorption on unoccupied sites) and potential-dependent mixed rate control between bicarbonate-dependent and independent pathways. The robot enables up to ten sequential electrolyses with varying electrodes, electrolytes, gas compositions, and voltages in a single lab effort, with data automatically uploaded to an SQL database. Comparison with literature for CoPc showed that robot-collected rates were up to ten times lower and CO Faradaic efficiency (FE) was typically under 30%, yet kinetic trends were preserved. The work concludes that complex reaction mechanisms—previously uncaptured by traditional Tafel analysis—are prevalent across this class of catalysts, and that opposing kinetic observations in the literature may be reconciled by differences in the operating condition range probed.

Research Context
Reaction kinetics analysis in electrocatalysis has traditionally relied on linearized rate data, assuming experimental handles can be factored separately on log-log or semi-log graphs. This is the basis for typical Tafel and reactant order dependence analyses which require highly simplifying assumptions. Coverage effects, mixed rate control, and side reactions can all lead to rate behavior difficult to analyze using linearization. Since elementary charge transfer steps display an order of magnitude change in equilibrium constant with only 59 mV of voltage difference, surface coverages could drastically change within a few hundred millivolts. Cohesive kinetic analyses, more common in heterogeneous thermocatalysis, interrogate correlations between variables using large volumes of data over wide reaction conditions. In electrocatalysis, these analyses have already highlighted complex kinetic phenomena underpinning the CO2 reduction reaction. A meta-analysis of reported Tafel data showed that Tafel slopes do not show a strong preference for commonly interpretable values such as 120, 60, or 40 mV/dec. One barrier for implementing cohesive kinetic analysis is its heavy data requirement, which can entail months of intensive manual experimentation subject to human error. Most strategies for automation in electrocatalysis are tailored towards high-throughput catalyst or condition screening, not kinetic analysis. A strategy involving sequential electrochemical testing and online product quantification of well-controlled reaction conditions within geometrically well-defined reactors would be ideal for automating kinetic analysis.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a robotic platform can automate the collection of electrochemical rate data for kinetic analysis that exceeds the capacity of traditional linearization methods. The authors hypothesize that complex reaction mechanisms not amenable to Tafel and order dependence analyses are prevalent across this class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts. Specifically, the study tests whether bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences change with applied potential at CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. The hypothesis extends that phenomena such as electrolyte poisoning, mixed control, and coverage effects can explain the observed kinetic behaviors. The study predicts that CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism, while FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. The authors also anticipate that CoPc and CoTPP show voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition attenuation, while FePc shows amplification, distinguishable by their respective electrosorption and coverage physics. The work seeks to illustrate that non-idealities are widespread and that the robot can produce data robust enough to compare with and extend previous literature findings.

Methodological Details
CoPc catalysts from Sigma Aldrich were dissolved in DMF and drop-casted onto calcined Toray060 carbon paper electrodes at loadings of 5.98 x 10^−11 mol/cm². CoTPP (Frontier Scientific) and FePc (Sigma Aldrich) were dissolved in carbon black-containing DMF solutions and drop-casted at loadings of 5.11 x 10^−10 and 8.04 x 10^−10 mol/cm² respectively. Carbon black was used for less active catalysts to help increase loading while avoiding aggregation. All catalysts were tested at low loadings where aggregation was not expected to be an issue. Electrolytes were prepared from stock solutions of 0.5 mol/L Na2CO3 and 1 mol/L NaClO4, bubbled overnight with CO2 and stored. Electrolyte solutions had overall 1 mol/L ionic strength prepared by mixing stock solutions in volumetric ratios to achieve desired bicarbonate concentrations. Electrolyses were queued in batches of ten, with all ten runs using the same electrolyte composition per batch. The Pt wire counter electrode resided in the cell body and was not often removed. The leak-free Ag/AgCl reference electrode was calibrated against a saturated calomel electrode every day and swapped every 1-3 days. The cell assembly is a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell with a 10 mm diameter carbon paper working electrode. A 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire counter electrode was inserted on the opposite side of the cell body. All data files, including electrolyses and reference calibrations, were automatically uploaded to an SQL database. A Python script output average current, partial CO current, and partial H2 current as a function of operating condition to an Excel document. The robot enables up to ten electrolyses for a single effort spent in the lab. The robot closes the cell body, pumps electrolyte through the 'electrolyte in' port, initiates gas flow, waits, applies voltage, and performs online product quantification. A gas chromatograph connected to the 'gas out' port confers online detection of CO and H2.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot consists of a single cell body housing reference and counter electrodes, with a line of ten cell pan pairs each housing a carbon paper working electrode. The cell body moves horizontally to sequentially perform electrochemistry on each cell pan and vertically to open and close onto any given cell pan. Two electrolyte configurations are possible: each cell pan with its own individual electrolyte or one common reservoir; the common reservoir option was employed. The cell body is rinsed after the completion of a full set of ten electrolyses by moving onto a wash station and pumping milliQ water in and out for several cycles. The common reservoir electrolyte was freshly bubbled with CO2 before each batch of ten runs. The robot operates by: (1) closing cell body onto cell pan, (2) pumping electrolyte in, (3) initiating gas flow, (4) waiting a few minutes, (5) applying voltage, (6) initiating online product quantification, (7) pumping electrolyte out to a waste container, and (8) opening the cell. Upon completion of each experiment, the robot uploads run information and associated data files to an SQL database. The cycle repeats after the cell body robot wash sequence and manual cleaning of the used cell pans. Users load working electrodes into cell pans, desired electrolyte into vials/reservoir, and electrolysis specifications into an Excel queue file before the robot automates the sequence.

Key Results
For CoPc, the CO2 order dependence appeared quite ideal, with a simple first-order dependence within error for both potentials shown. For CoTPP, the apparent order in CO2 was slightly below one and appeared to slightly decrease at more reductive potentials, characteristic of surface saturation effects. For FePc, the apparent CO2 order was more attenuated at less reductive potentials and the curves for the two potentials intersected. At CoPc and CoTPP, the apparent dependence on bicarbonate is most negative at less reductive potentials and becomes positive at more reductive potentials. For FePc, greater bicarbonate inhibition occurs at more reductive potentials. The newly measured rates towards CO production for CoPc were up to ten times lower than previously reported in a classic three-compartment cell. Faradaic efficiencies toward CO for CoPc were typically under 30%, which was lower than expected. Across all runs, an average of only c.a. 60% Faradaic efficiency was attributable to CO and H2 formation, with the remainder presumably lost to oxygen reduction. Relatively high FEs toward HER were observed, typically around 30 to 60%. Bicarbonate and CO2 order dependencies were observed to be non-linear and/or change with different applied potentials across all three catalysts. Previously reported kinetic trends in CO production for CoPc were preserved despite the lower rates and FE, and the new data was well-correlated with previous work.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Bicarbonate inhibition models invoke adsorption of bicarbonate onto an unoccupied catalyst site to form a bicarbonate-poisoned surface species with positive electrosorption valency. For CoPc and CoTPP, the model combines bicarbonate poisoning with potential-dependent mixed control between bicarbonate-dependent and bicarbonate-independent pathways. At more reductive potentials in CoPc and CoTPP, the local poisoning equilibrium shifts away from the poisoned species, decreasing inhibition, while the bicarbonate-dependent pathway attains a greater degree of rate control, leading to an apparent positive dependence. For FePc, bicarbonate inhibition is stronger at more reductive potentials; this is explained by invoking the most abundant reactive intermediate as a species prior to the unoccupied site. Alternatively, apparent bicarbonate inhibition can be explained by mixed control between two catalytic pathways, where high coverage of a bicarbonate-dependent intermediate causes attenuated bicarbonate dependence in one pathway and diverts flux away from the other. For FePc, flux towards the on-cycle poisoning species increases with more reductive voltages, leading to the opposite trend compared to CoPc and CoTPP. CO2 order attenuation in CoTPP is explained by accumulation of the surface species, with higher coverage at more reductive potentials leading to further attenuation. For FePc, the intersecting CO2 order curves imply that at low CO2 partial pressures, voltage inhibits the reaction, but at higher pressures, the CO2-dependent step becomes faster and the pathway becomes productive. These behaviors can only be explained by models invoking explicit catalyst poisoning or accumulation of a bicarbonate-dependent reactive intermediate, rather than mechanisms typically invoked for CO2RR at immobilized tetrapyrroles. The work suggests that ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in the literature might be reconciled by differences in the operating condition range probed. The study demonstrates that complex reaction mechanisms not interpretable via common Tafel or order dependence analyses are quite prevalent across this class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts.

Contradictions And Limitations
The cell is an undivided compartment without a membrane, allowing crosstalk between working and counter electrodes where oxygen evolved at the counter electrode can crossover and lead to parasitic oxygen reduction reaction. Across all runs, only c.a. 60% Faradaic efficiency was attributable to CO and H2, with the remainder presumably lost to oxygen reduction. The newly measured rates for CoPc were up to ten times lower than previously reported, and CO Faradaic efficiencies were typically under 30%, which differed from literature values. The model fits are conceptual and only qualitatively capture the observed trends; they do not quantitatively fit all experimental data via statistical goodness-of-fit metrics. The counter electrode was Pt rather than carbon-based to preclude attributing adventitious anode oxidation products to CO2RR, but metal crossover from Pt to copper was noted as a potential issue in other systems. CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte rather than fed directly to or through the working electrode, which may have unexpected influence over measured kinetics even in non-transport-limited regimes. The robot was tested with a common reservoir configuration; whether contamination would occur with sequential uses across different catalysts is not fully addressed beyond the stated expectation that it would not. The work acknowledges that the flow configuration could have unexpected influence over measured kinetics, even in ostensibly non-transport-limited regimes. The cell body cleaning was performed after each set of ten runs, and the user must manually clean the used cell pans.

Claims
The robot platform enables flexible, automated, and sequential electrochemical rate data collection that is more time-and-labor-efficient than manual protocols. The robot automates up to ten sequential electrolyses with different electrodes, electrolytes, gas compositions, and voltages in a single lab effort. All data files and reference calibrations are automatically uploaded to an SQL database, reducing manual handling. The system uses a Python script to output averaged current, CO current, and H2 current to Excel for analysis. Cell pans must still be manually cleaned after each set of ten runs. The Ag/AgCl reference electrode must still be calibrated daily and swapped every 1-3 days, requiring human intervention. Automation can accelerate and standardize kinetic analysis workflows, which were previously hindered by heavy manual data requirements. The workflow can be extended to include a membrane for anode-cathode separation and alternative electrolyte/gas flow configurations.
Non-ideal reaction rate data, manifested as non-linear and potential-dependent bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences, are prevalent across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. Across all three catalysts, bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences were observed to be non-linear and/or change with different applied potentials. Two distinct bicarbonate trends were observed: attenuation at more reductive potentials for CoPc and CoTPP, and amplification for FePc. Co2 order dependence for FePc showed intersecting curves for different potentials, indicating voltage-dependent inhibition at low pressures. For CoPc, the CO2 order dependence appeared quite ideal, with simple first-order dependence within error for both potentials shown. The models provide only conceptual and qualitative explanations and do not quantitatively fit all experimental data. Complex reaction mechanisms not captured by traditional Tafel analysis are widespread in this class of electrocatalysts. Ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in literature may be reconciled by differences in the operating conditions probed.

Data And Code Availability
All experimental data reported in this work (xlsx) is available. The preprint is available at https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-h0zh1, license CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Supporting information includes reagent information, detailed experimental protocols, supplemental data, and additional discussion. The paper notes that content has not been peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. A Python script is used to process the data from the SQL database to Excel. Data are also provided in the Supplemental Information (xlsx) including aggregated rates and selectivities.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data robustness was first evaluated by collecting kinetic data for CoPc and comparing it against previously reported literature results for CoPc. The newly measured rates were up to ten times lower and CO FEs typically under 30%, yet previously reported kinetic trends were preserved. Two electrolyte configurations were tested: each cell pan with individual electrolyte and one common reservoir; the common reservoir option was employed for this work. The cell body was rinsed after each set of ten electrolyses in the common reservoir configuration, with the expectation that no contamination would occur as products were gas-phase. The Ag/AgCl reference electrode was calibrated daily and swapped every 1-3 days to maintain reference stability. The Pt counter electrode was chosen over carbon to preclude attributing adventitious anode oxidation products to CO2RR.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the overall robot design with a single cell body and ten cell pan pairs. Figure 1B illustrates the cell assembly analogous to a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell with electrolyte in/out and gas in/out ports. Figure 1C shows the cell body moving horizontally and vertically to sequentially operate on each cell pan. Figure 2A-C shows the bicarbonate dependence curves for CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc at different potentials. Figure 2D-E show generalized models of bicarbonate poisoning with positive electrosorption valency for CoPc and FePc respectively. Figure 3A-C shows the CO2 order dependence curves for CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. Figure S7 and S8 show the rate comparison between the new robot-collected CoPc data and previously reported literature data. Figure S10A shows the CO Faradaic efficiencies across all runs. Figure S5 shows the overall Faradaic efficiency closure. Figure S9 shows aggregated rates towards CO and H2 for all three catalysts. Figure S10 shows selectivities towards CO and H2 for all three catalysts.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robotic platform that enables flexible, sequential electrochemical rate data collection for up to ten conditions in a single lab effort, automatically uploading data to an SQL database for cohesive kinetic analysis. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation of non-linear and potential-dependent bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc, explained by models of electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent mixed rate control that were not interpretable via traditional Tafel analysis. 3. The future path involves incorporating a membrane for anode-cathode separation, alternative electrolyte and gas flow configurations, and software to automatically enumerate mechanisms and suggest the most informative experimental conditions.

summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada, M Ondráček, M Lamanec, A Gallardo, A Jiménez-Martín, B De La Torre, P Hobza, P Jelínek
summary.field_subfield: Surface Science / Chemical Physics / Scanning Probe Microscopy
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in a halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon—on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The authors investigate 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and compare it to anthracene (An) on an Au(111) surface. The π-hole, predicted theoretically as a consequence of strong electron-withdrawing substituents (Cl, F) that reverse the quadrupole moment of the aromatic π-system from negative to positive, is visualized as a characteristic bow-tie pattern of local contact potential difference (LCPD) in the central region of the FCl-An molecule. KPFM measurements, complemented by total energy density functional theory (DFT) calculations, simulations using the Probe Particle model, and symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT0) energy decomposition, confirm the π-hole's existence and demonstrate its functional role in molecular surface adsorption. The presence of the π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppresses charge induction at the molecule/metal interface, and results in a larger adsorption height (360 pm vs 330 pm) and weakened induced electrostatic interaction. The self-assembly of FCl-An and An forms a rhombic periodic structure (one An, two FCl-An per unit cell) stabilized by attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between fluorine atoms, σ-holes on chlorine, and positive hydrogen atoms. This work establishes KPFM as a viable tool for mapping submolecular charge distributions and opens new avenues for studying how internal charge asymmetries govern non-covalent interactions and chemical properties in molecular systems.

claims.description: The π-hole predicted theoretically in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons can be directly visualized experimentally on a single molecule using KPFM.
The presence of the π-hole increases the adsorption height of the molecule on a metallic substrate by weakening the electrostatic interaction.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in a halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon—on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The authors investigate 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and compare it to anthracene (An) on an Au(111) surface. The π-hole, predicted theoretically as a consequence of strong electron-withdrawing substituents (Cl, F) that reverse the quadrupole moment of the aromatic π-system from negative to positive, is visualized as a characteristic bow-tie pattern of local contact potential difference (LCPD) in the central region of the FCl-An molecule. KPFM measurements, complemented by total energy density functional theory (DFT) calculations, simulations using the Probe Particle model, and symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT0) energy decomposition, confirm the π-hole's existence and demonstrate its functional role in molecular surface adsorption. The presence of the π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppresses charge induction at the molecule/metal interface, and results in a larger adsorption height (360 pm vs 330 pm) and weakened induced electrostatic interaction. The self-assembly of FCl-An and An forms a rhombic periodic structure (one An, two FCl-An per unit cell) stabilized by attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between fluorine atoms, σ-holes on chlorine, and positive hydrogen atoms. This work establishes KPFM as a viable tool for mapping submolecular charge distributions and opens new avenues for studying how internal charge asymmetries govern non-covalent interactions and chemical properties in molecular systems.

Research Context
Non-covalent interactions, including dispersion and electrostatic forces, govern chemical processes such as protein stability and DNA base stacking. The electrostatic component is highly directional and its nature is intimately linked to the internal charge distribution within the molecule. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) possess an electron-rich conjugated π-system that generates a negative quadrupole moment. Substituting peripheral hydrogens with electronegative substituents like fluorine or chlorine reverses the π-bond system to electron-deficient, making the quadrupole moment positive. This π-electron-deficient cavity is called a π-hole, and its existence was predicted exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations. A direct experimental observation that would clearly prove the existence of the π-hole has been lacking so far. Scanning probe microscopy (SPM) with functionalized probes has enabled spatial resolution of σ-holes, suggesting its applicability to π-holes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the π-hole predicted theoretically in halogen-substituted PAHs can be directly visualized experimentally on a single molecule. The authors hypothesize that Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM), which resolved the σ-hole, is also the ideal imaging tool for real-space observation of the π-hole system. They specifically test FCl-An, where the π-hole is predicted, against anthracene (An), where no such hole should exist. The hypothesis extends to whether the π-hole affects the adsorption behavior, specifically through changes in ionization potential and induced electrostatic interactions at the substrate interface. They predict that the π-hole will manifest as a submolecular LCPD variation (bow-tie pattern) and increase the molecule's adsorption height above Au(111).

Methodological Details
The study employs two molecular species: 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An, C14F8Cl2) and anthracene (C14H10, An). Molecular self-assembly was grown by simultaneous sublimation of the two compounds via two Knudsen cells in UHV at room temperature on Au(111) for 15 s. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by repeated cycles of Ar+ sputtering (1 keV) and annealing at approximately 800 K. Experiments were conducted at a temperature of 4.2 K using a commercial STM/nc-AFM microscope (Createc GmbH). Pt/Ir tips were sharpened by focused ion beam (FIB) and further cleaned by gentle indentation (~1 nm) in the bare metallic substrate. nc-AFM used a qPlus sensor with a resonant frequency of ≈30 kHz and stiffness of ≈1800 N/m, operated in frequency modulation mode with an oscillation amplitude of 200 pm. KPFM LCPD maps were obtained from a 64x80 pixels rectangular grid of size 3 nm x 5 nm, using the same CO-functionalized tip for both species. Each KPFM data point was acquired in approximately 3 seconds, with each parabola containing 600 points. LCPD fitting used a parabolic expression over the bias range of (-150, 400) mV. Theoretical calculations used DFT with the PBE functional and Tkatchenko-Scheffler Van der Waals correction, with a 6x6 unit cell surface supercell. For individual molecules, hybrid PBE0 functional and tight basis sets were employed. SAPT0 was performed on a cluster model with one molecule and a gold surface represented by 38 gold atoms in a (111) orientation. Molecular orbital calculations used MP2/cc-pVTZ geometries, and SAPT0 used cc-pVDZ and cc-pwCVDZ-PP basis sets. All KPFM/AFM images were simulated using the Probe Particle model with a CO-terminated tip and a CO lateral spring constant of 0.25 N/m.

Procedures And Architectures
The self-assembly was grown simultaneously by sublimating An and FCl-An at RT in UHV on Au(111). STM images at 4.8 K identified large-scale ordered molecular islands with both species alternating periodically. nc-AFM with a functionalized CO tip in constant height mode resolved two different molecular species within the assembly. The rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell was determined by comparing experimental nc-AFM images with DFT-calculated theoretical images. KPFM LCPD maps were generated by fitting frequency shift vs. bias spectroscopies at every grid point to a parabolic expression. The LCPD value (bias at parabola maximum) and Δf* (maximum frequency shift) were extracted and plotted in (x, y) grids. Tip-sample height was chosen close to the Δf minima on both molecules to ensure absence of tip relaxation and enhance contrast. Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy was acquired above the central benzene unit of both molecules to determine adsorption height differences. Spectroscopy over the bare Au(111) surface enabled relative height determination above the substrate. KPFM simulations were performed using the optimized supramolecular structures obtained from DFT calculations via the PP-AFM code. A dipole-like charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å² was assumed for the CO tip termination in KPFM simulations. The electrostatic potential and electrical polarizability maps were derived from DFT electron densities to generate simulated KPFM images. Symmetry-adapted perturbation treatment (SAPT0) was performed using PSI4 for interaction energy decomposition on cluster models. Molecular orbitals were calculated for MP2/cc-pVTZ optimized geometries to compare electronic structures.

Key Results
nc-AFM images clearly distinguished two different molecular species in the self-assembly, with FCl-An systematically imaged brighter than An due to a topographic effect. The supramolecular assembly was resolved as a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules in the unit cell. The arrangement is dictated by attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between negatively charged fluorine atoms, the σ-hole on chlorine, and positively charged hydrogen atoms. KPFM LCPD maps showed a submolecular bow-tie pattern in the central part of FCl-An, reproducing the characteristic σ-hole signature. The LCPD variation matches the distribution of the electrostatic potential calculated for a free-standing FCl-An molecule. Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy revealed a 30 pm difference between the Δf-z minima of An and FCl-An, directly related to adsorption height difference. Relative adsorption heights above Au(111) were measured at 330 pm for An and 360 pm for FCl-An. These experimental values match DFT-calculated adsorption heights of 325 pm and 351 pm, respectively. More significant induced electron density was observed in the An/Au(111) interface compared to FCl-An/Au(111), consistent with the An HOMO being closer to the Fermi level. In the An molecule, the π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppressing charge density induction at the molecule/metal interface. The induction energy (electrostatic interaction between permanent and induced charge multipoles) is larger for An than for FCl-An. SAPT0 decomposition showed the attractive interaction dominates the dispersion energy in all cases, with induction being a critical differentiator. The π-hole signature is entirely absent in the KPFM images of anthracene (An), providing a negative control. The LCPD data exhibited no significant distortion from parabolic behavior within the (-150, 400) mV bias range for either molecule.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole is fundamentally a consequence of the strong electron-withdrawing effect of Cl and F substituents, which modulate charge transfer from the π-system locally. The positive π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule, raising the energetic cost of charge transfer to the metal surface. The larger adsorption height of FCl-An (360 pm vs 330 pm) is a direct physical consequence of the π-hole reducing the electrostatic binding energy at the interface. The bow-tie pattern in KPFM images represents the spatially inhomogeneous local contact potential arising from the anisotropic submolecular charge distribution. This demonstrates that submolecular charge asymmetries govern not just intramolecular properties but also inter- and intermolecular interactions, including supramolecular self-assembly. The findings support the use of KPFM as a general tool for mapping submolecular charge distributions in organic molecules.

Contradictions And Limitations
KPFM contrast is highly dependent on tip-sample distance; far distances yield no intramolecular features, and very short distances generate tip relaxation artifacts. The AFM images themselves do not provide direct evidence of the π-hole, as they show only a relatively similar carbon skeleton contrast and topographic brightness differences. The adsorption height comparison relies on a 30 pm difference, which is within the sensitivity range but requires careful assignment of tip positions. The DFT calculations used a lightweight setup (PBE, no k-grid) necessitated by large supercells, which may compromise accuracy for electronic structure details. SAPT0 calculations were performed on a cluster model rather than a full slab, introducing a model dependency, though results were validated against slab calculations. The CO tip lateral spring constant was fixed at 0.25 N/m in simulations; actual experimental value may vary with environment. The study focuses on a single molecular species and a single substrate; generalizability to other substituted PAHs or metals is not directly tested. The LCPD maps are interpreted through parabolic fitting over a finite bias range; the true behavior outside (-150, 400) mV is unconstrained.

Claims
The π-hole predicted theoretically in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons can be directly visualized experimentally on a single molecule using KPFM. The KPFM LCPD map of FCl-An reveals a bow-tie submolecular variation in the central region. This LCPD pattern matches the calculated electrostatic potential of a free-standing FCl-An molecule. The KPFM signature is entirely absent in the control measurement of anthracene. KPFM simulations reproduce the experimental submolecular variation accurately. AFM images alone show similar carbon skeleton contrast for both species and do not resolve the π-hole. The bow-tie pattern is an interpretation of LCPD data; the exact physical mapping to the π-hole is indirect. KPFM is established as a viable tool for resolving submolecular charge asymmetries in organic molecules. The visualization confirms the electronic structure predictions from quantum calculations at the single-molecule level.
The presence of the π-hole increases the adsorption height of the molecule on a metallic substrate by weakening the electrostatic interaction. An has an adsorption height of 330 pm, while FCl-An has 360 pm. The DFT-calculated heights are 325 pm and 351 pm, supporting the experimental values. The induction energy is larger for An than for FCl-An in SAPT0 decomposition. More significant induced electron density is observed at the An/Au interface. The 30 pm difference is relatively small, and the agreement with DFT is only reasonable rather than exact. The presence of chlorine atoms does not influence the adsorption height, suggesting the effect is purely through the π-hole. The π-hole directly influences the physical adsorption of molecules on surfaces, affecting contact resistance and charge transfer. The electrostatic component of the dispersion-dominated surface interaction is a non-negligible term for molecular surface science.

Data And Code Availability
The paper references the FHI-AIMS code for DFT calculations and the PP-AFM code for KPFM simulations. The KPFM data processing was done using WSxM software. SAPT0 calculations were performed using the PSI4 quantum chemistry program. The orbital and electrostatic potential calculations were carried out by the ORCA package.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The absence of submolecular resolution in Δf* images (at compensated LCPD) for both molecules confirms the choice of tip-sample height. The KPFM images do not exhibit intramolecular features at far tip-sample distances, as shown in the distance dependence study. The nc-AFM/STM images at 4.8 K confirm the supramolecular assembly structure independently of KPFM/AFM imaging. The mere deposition of An alone does not produce self-organized structures, supporting the role of FCl-An. DFT and SAPT0 calculations give very similar adsorption energies, validating the cluster model against the slab model. Hybrid PBE0 functional with tight basis was used for free-standing molecules, yielding nearly identical geometries to PBE/light basis.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematics showing the negative quadrupole moment of PAHs and the positive quadrupole moment of halogen-substituted species. Figure 2: STM (4.8 K), nc-AFM, and theoretical images of the self-assembled molecular islands on Au(111), showing the rhombic unit cell. Figure 2d: Schematic of attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between F, Cl, and H atoms. Figure 3: KPFM LCPD maps of FCl-An and An, with (a) calculated electrostatic potential, (c, f) simulated KPFM images, and (d) experimental KPFM image. Figure 4: Force-distance spectroscopy (a) and calculated induced electron densities (b, c) comparing An and FCl-An on Au(111). Figure 6: Constant-height AFM images showing the emergence of submolecular contrast on FCl-An molecules. Table S2: DFT and SAPT0 adsorption energy decomposition for An, FCl-An, and Au(111). Table S3: SAPT0 energy decomposition for the three molecules.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole on a single halogen-substituted PAH molecule using KPFM, confirming a long-standing theoretical prediction. 2. The strongest evidence is the bow-tie submolecular LCPD pattern in FCl-An that matches both DFT-calculated electrostatic potential and Probe Particle KPFM simulations, coupled with the 360 pm vs 330 pm adsorption height difference confirmed by force-distance spectroscopy and SAPT0. 3. The future path lies in applying KPFM and similar functionalized SPM techniques to map submolecular charge asymmetries in other organic systems, influencing supramolecular design, sensor development, and electronic material design.

summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.field_subfield: Computational Chemistry / Machine Learning for Materials Science
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents the first ranking of solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) candidate structures in lithium-ion batteries generated via a multitask machine learning force field (MLFF) model. The authors combine a QRNN model trained on DFT reference data with enhanced reaction sampling techniques (AFIR and NEB) and a multitask learning scheme that incorporates a general organic chemistry dataset (SPICE) to bridge the gap between classical force fields and expensive DFT simulations. Using wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD and PBE-D3 as reference levels, they generated thousands of candidate geometries through OPLS4 molecular dynamics with reaction templates, annealed them at 400 K and 1000 atm, and ranked the resulting structures by mean potential energy. The study is constrained by the lack of experimental validation metrics (density, diffusivity, etc.) for the specific SEI compositions, necessitating validation against surface reaction barriers instead. The authors demonstrate that multitask learning with an external organic chemistry dataset expands model capacity without degrading performance on the target battery dataset. The most stable candidate was identified from the 33-added-Li+ subgroup, and bond-count analysis revealed that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with stability, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with lower stability. This work serves as a methodological proof-of-concept for using MLFFs to explore complex redox-reactive interphase materials, with implications for future automated SEI design through multiple electrolyte formulation comparisons.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the first ranking of solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) candidate structures in lithium-ion batteries generated via a multitask machine learning force field (MLFF) model. The authors combine a QRNN model trained on DFT reference data with enhanced reaction sampling techniques (AFIR and NEB) and a multitask learning scheme that incorporates a general organic chemistry dataset (SPICE) to bridge the gap between classical force fields and expensive DFT simulations. Using wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD and PBE-D3 as reference levels, they generated thousands of candidate geometries through OPLS4 molecular dynamics with reaction templates, annealed them at 400 K and 1000 atm, and ranked the resulting structures by mean potential energy. The study is constrained by the lack of experimental validation metrics (density, diffusivity, etc.) for the specific SEI compositions, necessitating validation against surface reaction barriers instead. The authors demonstrate that multitask learning with an external organic chemistry dataset expands model capacity without degrading performance on the target battery dataset. The most stable candidate was identified from the 33-added-Li+ subgroup, and bond-count analysis revealed that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with stability, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with lower stability. This work serves as a methodological proof-of-concept for using MLFFs to explore complex redox-reactive interphase materials, with implications for future automated SEI design through multiple electrolyte formulation comparisons.

Research Context
The SEI is a complex passivating layer combining organic and inorganic components that allows batteries to function by protecting electrodes. Key questions about SEI, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them, remain unanswered. Pure density functionals underestimate reaction barriers, and hybrid functionals struggle with metals and scale poorly for periodic systems. No existing method is fully applicable to the task of simulating the SEI system. Traditional force fields have fixed functional forms that make them difficult to fit for complex systems like the SEI. MLFFs promise atomistic simulation accuracy with DFT-level precision and classical force field sampling speeds.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a multitask MLFF trained on DFT data of electrolyte, salt, and SEI components can accurately rank candidate SEI structures. The authors hypothesize that multitask training with an external organic chemistry dataset (SPICE) can expand model capacity without degrading performance on battery-specific tasks. They predict that the SEI simulator method can generate plausible geometries that are thermodynamically relaxable and rankable. The underlying assumption is that MLFFs trained on DFT references can capture the redox reactivity characteristic of SEI formation. The study hypothesizes that the latent space of MLFF models contains unused capacity applicable to broadening chemical scope.

Methodological Details
Reference level for non-periodic systems is wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD; periodic is PBE-D3 in plane-wave basis. PBE-D3 was also used for a random subset of non-periodic systems to improve multitask information exchange. Atomic partial charges from GFN1-xTB were selected as the best compromise between accuracy and convergence for charge labels. Initial SEI geometries were generated via the SEI Simulator using OPLS4 MD with reaction templates at intervals. Each system started with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, totaling 7416 atoms. Four levels of added Li+ were defined: 5, 12, 23, and 33 ions per box, arising from 40 MD iterations. Enhanced reaction sampling used Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) on the QRNN energy surface. The SPICE dataset (H, Li, C, O, F, P elements) was added via multitask learning to shape the latent space. Hidden layers of size 256, 224, and 192 were used; batch size was 64; weight decay was 1e-3 for the final model. Periodicity in DFT used 40 Ry cutoff, 3x3x3 k-point mesh for bulk, 3x3x1 for surfaces, in Quantum Espresso via Schrodinger.

Procedures And Architectures
A QRNN model with multitask learning was trained simultaneously on GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and SPICE wB97X-D3BJ heads. The loss function comprised energy, atomic force, and charge mean squared error for each theory level per batch. Adamax optimizer was used with decoupled weight decay at a learning rate of 2e-3. 1% of the data was used as validation set, selected uniformly at random. The final model was an exponential moving average averaging every 10 batches with alpha = 0.001. Hidden layer widths were doubled when adding disparate data to increase capacity. Decoupled weight norms were applied with norms not included in the optimizer. Each system ran with a unique random seed for packing and MD to ensure diverse configuration sampling. Candidates were annealed using NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each using the reactive QRNN model. Ranking was performed by calculating mean potential energy over a 20 ps MD trajectory at 300 K and 1 atm.

Key Results
Adding the SPICE dataset resulted in no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE and only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. The QRNN models gave stable dynamics at 400 K and 1000 atm, which is not typical for MLFFs under extreme conditions. P-F and Li-O bonds were associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds were associated with less stable ones. The best candidate was defined as the lowest-energy structure from the 33-added-Li+ subgroup predicted by wB97X-D3BJ. The GFN1-xTB head encompassed all data, periodic and non-periodic, for the final model. The highest weight decay of 3e-3 reduced reaction barrier heights relative to reference barriers. The lowest energy SEI candidate was identified from the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The latent space of MLFF models contains unused capacity that can be applied to broadening chemical applicability through multitask learning. This is the most complex redox-reactive system simulated using an MLFF or any method of comparable accuracy to date. MLFFs enable a quantitative understanding of lithium-ion battery interphases, serving as an impetus for development of machine learning models for battery materials. By calculating Li+ diffusivity and mechanical properties as a function of starting formulation, detailed optimization of SEI chemistry becomes possible.

Contradictions And Limitations
Experimental validation metrics such as density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus do not exist for any SEI composition. Only a single electrolyte formulation (1M LiPF6 in EC) was used, limiting the scope to this specific chemical system. The model was validated against surface reaction energy barriers rather than thermodynamic or transport properties. The high weight decay (3e-3) reduced the height of reaction barriers relative to reference barriers, necessitating a compromise to 1e-3. The scope of the model is still small compared to what is required for full SEI characterization.

Claims
A multitask MLFF can model the complex redox reactions of SEI and rank candidate structures by energy. QRNN models produced stable dynamics at 400 K and 1000 atm during NPT annealing. Mean potential energies over 20 ps MD at 300 K and 1 atm provided a comparable ranking across candidate sets. Bond-type correlations (P-F/Li-O vs C-O/Li-F) consistent with chemical intuition were captured. Validation against surface reaction barriers is indirect and does not prove accuracy for relaxed thermodynamically relevant structures. No direct comparison to experimental SEI data is possible. Enables first quantitative ranking of SEI structures to guide future ML applications. Sets a precedent for combining enhanced sampling with MLFFs for complex redox systems.
Incorporating a general organic chemistry dataset (SPICE) via multitask learning does not degrade battery-specific model performance. PBE-head validation RMSE showed no increase when adding SPICE data. Hybrid-head RMSE increased by only 8% despite greatly increased data scope. The latent space has unused capacity for broadening chemical applicability. The SPICE data was not used for prediction on SEI systems; its impact on the SEI-head directly is not quantified. Recommends supplemental organic datasets for future MLFF development. Broadens MLFF applicability beyond the original chemical domain.

Data And Code Availability
The SEI candidate structures (seed*.pdb), energies (energies.csv), initial 1M LiPF6 in EC solution, and plotting scripts are available at https://figshare.com/s/e842ae88023902700e12.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two weight decay values (3e-3 and 1e-3) were tested; 3e-3 produced smoother surfaces but underestimated barrier heights. GFN1-xTB, GFN2-xTB, and GFN0-xTB were tested for atomic partial charges; GFN1-xTB was selected for best compromise between accuracy and convergence. Early stopping validation showed little effect, attributed to insufficient model capacity to overfit. Reaction templates were applied at intervals in the SEI simulator MD, with 40 iterations total.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the 7416-atom system with 700 EC molecules, 52 Li+, and 52 PF6- ions. Table 1 reports validation against the best available surface reaction energy barriers. Figure 4 shows bond counts versus total system energy for the most lithiated SEI candidate set (33 added Li+).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first multitask MLFF-based ranking of candidate SEI structures generated via enhanced reaction sampling, demonstrating that such models can capture complex redox-reactive systems. 2. The strongest evidence is the stable dynamics under extreme NPT conditions (400 K, 1000 atm) and the identification of bonding trends (P-F, Li-O stabilization) that correlate with energy, combined with multitask validation metrics. 3. The future path involves comparing multiple electrolyte formulations, testing other architectures (Nequip, MACE, CHGNet), and extending the dataset with amorphous metalorganic MD data.

summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime; Galina Lebedev; Jackline Abo-Nassar; Sally Marzouk; Moshe Inbar; Murad Ghanim; Radi Aly
summary.field_subfield: Agricultural Entomology / Plant Biochemistry / Natural Pesticides
summary.type_of_paper: Original research - bioassay and histological study of plant extracts against insect pests
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the biological activity of crude and fractionated extracts from Ajuga iva against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major pest of cotton, maize, rice, and other crops. The authors hypothesize that phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) and clerodane diterpenes present in A. iva leaves interfere with larval development, molting, and metamorphosis, acting as antifeedants and hormonal disruptors. The experimental design employed three concentrations of crude leaf extract (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl) on first and third instar S. littoralis larvae. Key findings demonstrate a dose-dependent increase in mortality: first instar mortality rose from 5% in controls to 85% at 250 µg/µl. Third instar larvae exhibited significantly reduced larval weight gain (LWG) and relative growth rate (RGR), with RGR dropping by 0.05 and 0.20 g/g per day on days 6 and 8 at the highest concentration. Pupation was suppressed: none of the treated larvae completed development to adult moths, showing instead short limbs, small heads, and incomplete pupation of only stomach and chest. Histological analysis via DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed that 250 µg/µl treatment caused smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei, reduced actin filament amount, and histolysis of gut epithelium with apoptosis. A cross-over experiment confirmed that feeding on extract at any time point caused irreversible developmental decline. A limitation noted is the inability to test commercial standards at the same concentrations as the plant-derived compounds due to cost. The study supports the use of phytoecdysteroids as promising green pest control agents in integrated pest management (IPM) programs.

claims.description: Crude A. iva leaf extract containing phytoecdysteroids significantly reduces mortality and growth of first and third instar S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner.
The phytoecdysteroid fraction from A. iva recapitulates the major developmental inhibitory effects of the crude extract, confirming these compounds as the primary active agents.
The mechanism of action involves gut histolysis, actin cytoskeleton disruption, and inability to reach the critical weight for pupation.

top_influential_citations.Aly et al. (2011): This paper provided the established protocol for phytoecdysteroid extraction and purification from A. iva and demonstrated that a 5 µg/ml dose of pure A. iva ecdysterone reduced fecundity and fertility in Oligonychus perseae.

top_influential_citations.Kubo (1997): Kubo's work on Ajuga remota extracts containing 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone inhibiting ecdysis in Bombyx mori established the precedent for Ajuga phytoecdysteroids as insecticides.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the biological activity of crude and fractionated extracts from Ajuga iva against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major pest of cotton, maize, rice, and other crops. The authors hypothesize that phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) and clerodane diterpenes present in A. iva leaves interfere with larval development, molting, and metamorphosis, acting as antifeedants and hormonal disruptors. The experimental design employed three concentrations of crude leaf extract (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl) on first and third instar S. littoralis larvae. Key findings demonstrate a dose-dependent increase in mortality: first instar mortality rose from 5% in controls to 85% at 250 µg/µl. Third instar larvae exhibited significantly reduced larval weight gain (LWG) and relative growth rate (RGR), with RGR dropping by 0.05 and 0.20 g/g per day on days 6 and 8 at the highest concentration. Pupation was suppressed: none of the treated larvae completed development to adult moths, showing instead short limbs, small heads, and incomplete pupation of only stomach and chest. Histological analysis via DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed that 250 µg/µl treatment caused smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei, reduced actin filament amount, and histolysis of gut epithelium with apoptosis. A cross-over experiment confirmed that feeding on extract at any time point caused irreversible developmental decline. A limitation noted is the inability to test commercial standards at the same concentrations as the plant-derived compounds due to cost. The study supports the use of phytoecdysteroids as promising green pest control agents in integrated pest management (IPM) programs.

Research Context
S. littoralis is a globally significant pest affecting cotton, maize, rice, alfalfa, potato, tomato, ornamentals, and orchard trees. Current insect control relies primarily on insecticides that pose risks to human health and the environment. Plant-derived organic insecticides, particularly alkaloids, terpenoids, phenols, and steroids, exhibit high toxicity against agricultural pests. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroid analogs of insect molting and metamorphosis hormones. They are present in 5-6% of plant species, generally at higher concentrations than in arthropods. Phytoecdysteroids can mimic insect 20-hydroxyecdysteroid, bind ecdysone receptors, and cause abnormal larval development, feeding deterrence, and death. Previous studies on Ajuga remota extracts containing 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone inhibited ecdysis in Bombyx mori, causing larval death. A. iva extracts had shown high activity against Oligonychus perseae, with pure extracted ecdysterone at 5 µg/ml significantly reducing fecundity and fertility. Clerodane diterpenes in Ajuga species also possess potential insect antifeedant and repellent activities. The authors previously identified high contents of three phytoecdysteroids and two clerodanes in A. iva growing in Israel.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central hypothesis is that crude A. iva leaf extract containing 20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone interferes with molting, metamorphosis, and antifeedant activities in insects. The primary research question asks whether A. iva crude leaf extract affects S. littoralis larvae. A second question addresses whether phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude extract and commercial standards have different effects on the larvae. A third question investigates whether phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut. The authors predicted that S. littoralis larvae would show increased mortality, reduced growth, and suppressed pupation when fed treated leaves. It was predicted that the effects would be dose-dependent, with higher concentrations yielding more pronounced results. The authors hypothesized that gut cell destruction would underlie the reduced larval weight gain and eventual death. The study aimed to evaluate whether A. iva extracts could serve as promising pest-control agents.

Methodological Details
S. littoralis larvae were sourced from the Agricultural Research Organization, Department of Entomology, African cotton leafworm colony reared on castor bean leaves. First and third instar larvae were used for all bioassays. Young and mature leaves and stems of A. iva were collected after blooming (July-November), oven-dried at 55°C for 3-4 days, and homogenized. A. iva crude extracts were prepared by soaking 24 g of leaf and stem powder in 240 ml of 100% MeOH. The extract was shaken at 2500 rpm for 1 h, centrifuged at 112 g for 10 min, filtered, and concentrated under vacuum. Three concentrations of crude leaf extract were prepared: 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl. First instar assay: 10 larvae per treated castor bean leaf in a petri dish, fed for 3 days at 25°C. Control leaves were treated with double-distilled water and Tween 20. The data for first instar mortality represent 11 replicates of 10 larvae each. Third instar assay: larvae fed for 4 or 8 days at 25°C; 1 or 10 larvae per leaf. Four treatment groups for third instars: (1) crude extract for 4 days then 4 days fresh, (2) crude then purified phytoecdysteroid fraction, (3) crude then control, (4) control then crude. Pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days after the larval feeding period. Relative growth rate (RGR) was calculated as (ln W2 - ln W1) / (t2 - t1). The RGR experiment used n = 20 replicates per treatment. Larval weight gain (LWG) data are the result of 10 replicates of 10 larvae each. Gut morphology analysis: larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude extract for 7 days were used. Guts were dissected in 1X PBS, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min. Slides were stained with 0.1% phalloidin in PBST for 30 min and DAPI for visualization. Images were captured under Leica confocal microscope (SP8) and Olympus IX 81. Statistical analysis was performed with IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows.

Procedures And Architectures
Phytoecdysteroids were purified from A. iva by flash chromatography on silica gel (TLC), yielding 20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone. TLC plates were GF-254 silica gel, 0.25 mm, 20×20 cm. LC-TOF-MS analysis was used to confirm compound identities in crude extract at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl. For first instar treatment: 1.2 g dried extract dissolved in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20 for 250 µg/µl; 0.83 ml of 250 µg/µl dissolved in 3 ml ddH2O for 100 µg/µl; 0.67 ml of 100 µg/µl dissolved in 3 ml ddH2O for 50 µg/µl. The pure phytoecdysteroid mixture was obtained by fractionating the crude extract as described by Aly et al. (2011). Commercial standards were used only at maximum concentration of 100 ppm each for a control comparison. The cross-over design tested: (1) 250 µg/µl crude for 4 days then 250 µg/µl purified fraction for 4 more days. Larval gut dissection involved 30 min fixation, 30 min washing in 0.1% Triton X-100, three washes in PBST, 30 min phalloidin incubation. Mounting in DAPI used 20 mM Tris-HCl, 0.9 M NaCl, 0.01% SDS, 30% formamide. Larvae were exposed to three concentrations per treatment in the main experiment. Significance was determined by t-test for first instar, mixed-model ANOVA (repeated measures until day 4, two-way from day 4) for RGR, Friedman test for survival, repeated measures ANOVA for LWG. All statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Error bars represent the standard error of the mean (SEM).

Key Results
First instar S. littoralis mortality at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl of crude extract reached 25%, 65%, and 85%, respectively. Control first instar mortality (treated with water) was 5%. Third instar larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude extract showed reduced LWG with F3.104 values of 20.334, 17.246, and 13.007 (p < 0.001) compared to control. All crude extract concentrations significantly decreased third instar RGR compared to control. At 250 µg/µl, RGR decreased by 0.05 g/g per day on day 6 and by 0.20 g/g per day on day 8 compared to control (F3.16, 18 = 12.641, p < 0.001). All concentrations reduced third instar larval survival after 11 days (X²₃ = 6.221, p = 0.038). At 250 µg/µl crude extract, none of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days; at 100 and 50 µg/µl, none survived more than 10 days. In the sequence where larvae were first fed on control then on crude extract, RGR was affected after day 5 (F3.16, 18 = 7.310, p < 0.001) and continued to decrease with no survivors (X²₃ = 9.282, p = 0.021). When the sequence was reversed (crude then control), RGR significantly decreased on days 2-4 with F values of 4.595, 3.608, and 8.113 (p = 0.034, 0.02, 0.001) for 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl, respectively. The purified phytoecdysteroid mixture at 250 µg/µl significantly reduced RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) compared to control. Few larvae survived on leaves treated with the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (X²₃ = 11.305, p = 0.04). No significant effect was observed when S. littoralis was fed on castor bean leaves treated with 100 ppm of the mixture of three commercial ecdysteroids for 8 days. Larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude extract for 8 days had smaller nuclei with abnormal shape: nuclei moved to cell edges and were thinner than normal. In guts treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract or purified phytoecdysteroids, actin filaments were smaller and their amount was reduced compared to normal organization. None of the larvae fed 250 µg/µl crude extract or purified phytoecdysteroid fraction for 8 days were able to complete development and pupate after 15 days. Incomplete pupae showed short limbs, small heads, decreased weight, and only stomach and chest pupated, considered nonpupation. None of the dying larvae completed development to adult moths.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dose-dependent mortality and growth inhibition support a mechanism involving phytoecdysteroid-mediated disruption of the molting cycle. The sequence experiments (control then crude and crude then control) demonstrate that once growth is impaired by the extract, the damage is irreversible, supporting a cumulative toxic effect. The purified phytoecdysteroid fraction recapitulated most of the crude extract's effects, indicating that these compounds are the primary active agents. Histological evidence of smaller actin filaments and smaller nuclei supports the notion that phytoecdysteroids disrupt cytoskeleton integrity and cellular structure. The authors propose that the observed effects on pupation are a consequence of reduced larval weight preventing larvae from reaching the threshold for pupation, combined with hormonal imbalance. Phytoecdysteroids may act as ecdysial agents, inducing two head capsules and developmental anomalies during metamorphosis, consistent with previous findings in other lepidopterans. The data suggest that A. iva could be a valuable component in IPM programs for cotton leafworm control, reducing pesticide-related risks. The comparison with commercial standards at 100 ppm versus 250,000 ppm highlights the much higher potency of the plant-derived compounds.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors could not use commercial standards at the same concentrations as the plant-derived compounds because they were very expensive and not feasible as a control treatment. Clerodanes were not fractionated from the crude extract due to difficulty in calibrating the protocol and high cost of commercial standards. S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg, unlike Pieris brassicae, suggesting species-specific sensitivity. The commercial mixture of three ecdysteroids at 100 ppm showed no significant effect, but the authors note this is very low compared to the 250,000 ppm in the extract. The study did not directly measure endocrine levels in vivo; the mechanism is inferred from histological and developmental data. The larval survival data did not follow a normal distribution, requiring the use of the Friedman test rather than parametric methods. The authors acknowledge that external ecdysteroid detoxification is a primary mechanism for insects to overcome toxicity, but they do not directly measure detoxification rates in S. littoralis.

Claims
Crude A. iva leaf extract containing phytoecdysteroids significantly reduces mortality and growth of first and third instar S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner. First instar mortality reached 85% at 250 µg/µl compared to 5% in control. Third instar larvae showed reduced LWG with F3.104 values of 20.334, 17.246, and 13.007 at the three concentrations. RGR decreased by 0.05 and 0.20 g/g per day on days 6 and 8 at 250 µg/µl. None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 to 10 days at the highest concentration. S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by commercial 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg, indicating a threshold effect. The commercial mixture at 100 ppm showed no significant effect, though this is well below the 250,000 ppm of the extract. A. iva extracts could serve as a green pesticide against S. littoralis. Phytoecdysteroids may be beneficial in IPM programs. The dose-dependent effect suggests that treatment levels can be optimized for maximum efficacy.
The phytoecdysteroid fraction from A. iva recapitulates the major developmental inhibitory effects of the crude extract, confirming these compounds as the primary active agents. Purified fraction at 250 µg/µl significantly reduced RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001). Few larvae survived on the purified fraction leaves (X²₃ = 11.305, p = 0.04). Gut histology showed smaller actin filaments and abnormally shaped nuclei with the purified fraction, similar to crude extract. The crude extract still retained some additional activity, suggesting other minor compounds or synergistic effects beyond the three phytoecdysteroids. The three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone) are the key bioactive constituents. Further development could focus on optimizing the extraction of this specific fraction.
The mechanism of action involves gut histolysis, actin cytoskeleton disruption, and inability to reach the critical weight for pupation. Gut cells showed histolysis, destroyed microvilli, and formation of vacuoles with clear signs of apoptosis. Phalloidin staining showed reduced actin filament amount and smaller size in treated larvae. Larvae were unable to complete development because they did not reach the threshold weight for pupation. The authors hypothesize that the gut destruction could be a consequence of phytoecdysteroid titers rather than the primary event. Targeting the insect gut epithelium may be a viable pathway for phytoecdysteroid-based pesticides. The cytoskeletal integrity of the larval gut appears highly sensitive to phytoecdysteroids.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The cross-over design (control-then-crude vs crude-then-control) confirmed that developmental arrest was irreversible and not a temporary suppression of growth. The purified phytoecdysteroid fraction treatment served as a biological ablation, demonstrating that the three phytoecdysteroids are sufficient to produce most of the crude extract's effects. Pupation was evaluated for 15 days after the larval feeding period, providing a comprehensive developmental timeline. Multiple concentrations (50, 100, 250 µg/µl) were tested, establishing a dose-response relationship. Larval gut histology was assessed at 7 days post-treatment, capturing peak developmental disruption.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows TLC profiles comparing RFR values of A. iva phytoecdysteroids with commercial ecdysteroid spots. Figure 2a displays first instar mortality percentages at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl compared to control. Figure 2b shows reduced LWG for third instar larvae at the three crude extract concentrations. Figure 3a displays RGR decline over time, with reduced RGR as early as day 2. Figure 3b shows third instar survival at 11 days. Figure 4a-c shows RGR in the sequential cross-over treatments. Figure 5a-b shows RGR and survival for the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction treatment. Figure 6a-i shows DAPI and phalloidin staining of larval guts, illustrating normal vs abnormal actin and nuclei. Figure 7 shows incomplete pupae from treated larvae, with 7b and c showing nonpupated forms.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that crude A. iva leaf extract, containing a specific mixture of three phytoecdysteroids, significantly impairs development, growth, and survival of S. littoralis larvae through irreversible developmental arrest and gut histolysis. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of dose-dependent mortality (85% at 250 µg/µl), RGR collapse (0.20 g/g/day reduction), complete pupation failure, and histological proof of actin cytoskeleton destruction and gut cell apoptosis. 3. The future path involves further development of A. iva as a green pesticidal agent in IPM, potentially optimizing the specific phytoecdysteroid fraction, and investigating mechanisms of insect ecdysteroid detoxification.

summary.title: Sorry, we're open: Golden Open Access and inequality in the natural sciences
summary.authors: Russell J Gray
summary.field_subfield: Bibliometrics / Scientometrics; Open Access Publishing in Natural Sciences
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the relationship between Article Processing Charges (APC), Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and publisher country within the ecosystem of Golden Open Access (GOA) natural science journals. The author collected metadata from 237 vetted open-access natural science journals, extracting APCs, IF, EF, citation counts, and publisher countries. Using R statistical software with packages including scholar, quantmod, dplyr, reshape2, and ggplot2, the study applied Pearson's correlation coefficient to analyze linkages between cost and impact metrics. The findings reveal statistically significant positive correlations across all dimensions: APC was positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < .001), EF (r = 0.303, p < .001), and citability (r = 0.323, p < .001). Furthermore, the majority of publishers with the highest APCs and impact metrics are located in developed countries, while mean APC for the analyzed sample was $1344.27 USD with a mean IF of 2.855, mean EF of 0.017, and mean citability of 5925.92. The discussion situates these findings within the broader critique of GOA, arguing that the current system creates a two-tier research ecosystem where high-impact, high-cost journals serve as gatekeepers of prestige and citations, effectively penalizing researchers from developing countries and unaffiliated independent scientists. The author further contextualizes these findings through personal experience with Research4Life funding barriers and links the trends to global inequality, biodiversity conservation research disparities, and the rise of independent researchers. The paper concludes that the GOA transition perpetuates systemic inequality, promoting a false association between journal cost and scientific reliability while restricting exposure for important but underfunded research.
