judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the relationship between Article Processing Charges (APC), Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and publisher country within the ecosystem of Golden Open Access (GOA) natural science journals. The author collected metadata from 237 vetted open-access natural science journals, extracting APCs, IF, EF, citation counts, and publisher countries. Using R statistical software with packages including scholar, quantmod, dplyr, reshape2, and ggplot2, the study applied Pearson's correlation coefficient to analyze linkages between cost and impact metrics. The findings reveal statistically significant positive correlations across all dimensions: APC was positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < .001), EF (r = 0.303, p < .001), and citability (r = 0.323, p < .001). Furthermore, the majority of publishers with the highest APCs and impact metrics are located in developed countries, while mean APC for the analyzed sample was $1344.27 USD with a mean IF of 2.855, mean EF of 0.017, and mean citability of 5925.92. The discussion situates these findings within the broader critique of GOA, arguing that the current system creates a two-tier research ecosystem where high-impact, high-cost journals serve as gatekeepers of prestige and citations, effectively penalizing researchers from developing countries and unaffiliated independent scientists. The author further contextualizes these findings through personal experience with Research4Life funding barriers and links the trends to global inequality, biodiversity conservation research disparities, and the rise of independent researchers. The paper concludes that the GOA transition perpetuates systemic inequality, promoting a false association between journal cost and scientific reliability while restricting exposure for important but underfunded research.

Research Context
The availability of journal articles has increased due to platforms like Sci-Hub and ResearchGate, nullifying previous paywall systems for capital generation. High-impact journals have transitioned to mandatory open access, known as Golden Open Access (GOA), to maintain profitability. While open-access science appears genuine, the costs associated with publishing create a problematic system where reliability and importance are conflated with expense. Researchers from developing countries are forced to pay full Western prices for high-impact 'Mega-Journals' to gain exposure and credibility. The alternative is publishing in lower IF journals, predatory journals with low-quality peer review, or compromising article quality. High-impact journals generate exposure through increased citations, accelerating researcher careers, making costs a barrier for those without available funding. The author notes that publication fees continue to increase despite the transition from print to digital formats.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether publication costs (APC) are linked to journal impact factor (IF), eigen factor (EF), and citability within natural science open-access journals. The author also examines whether the country of journal publisher correlates with cost, citability, IF, and EF to locate potential disparities. The implicit hypothesis is that higher publication costs correlate positively with journal impact and visibility metrics, and that developed countries host journals with higher performance indicators. The study aims to determine the implications of these trends on inequality within the global scientific community regarding the GOA framework. The author hypothesizes that the system rewards publishers in developed countries and penalizes researchers from developing countries and independent scientists.

Methodological Details
Data was acquired from the Directory of Open Access Journals, containing journal name, APC, country of publisher, and currency records. The raw dataset contained n = 14275 records. A subset of n = 1047 journals with topics relative to biological sciences was queried using keyword data including ecology, conservation, agriculture, species, forest, etc. Journals with an IF > 40 were excluded to eliminate medical and engineering overlap; excluded journals were related to oncology, medical, and engineering. The final vetted dataset consisted of n = 237 open-access, natural science journals. Mean APC for the final sample was $1344.27 USD. Mean IF was 2.855, mean EF was 0.017, and mean total citation count (citability) was 5925.92. Currency standardization was performed converting all currencies to USD for comparison. The author notes a personal experience of being rejected from Research4Life funding multiple times despite co-authors from eligible developing countries. The author was from the United States with no current institutional affiliation, meaning no accompanying financial benefits and no access to >1000 USD for publication fees.

Procedures And Architectures
R statistical software was used for all data analyses. The scholar package (Keirstead, 2016) was used to generate impact factors using journal name strings. The quantmod package (Ryan et al. 2019) converted all currencies to USD for standardization. The dplyr package (Wickham et al., 2015) and reshape2 package (Wickham, 2012) were used for data cleaning and selection. The ggplot2 package (Wickham et al., 2016) was used for data visualizations. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to analyze potential correlation between APC, IF, EF, and citability. Functions from the ggpubr package (Kassambara, 2020) facilitated the statistical analysis. A linear trend analysis was conducted between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC. The country of each journal publisher was cross-examined against APC, IF, EF, and citability. The data subsetting process involved keyword filtering for biological science topics from the original Directory of Open Access dataset.

Key Results
APC was found to be significantly positively correlated with IF at Pearson correlation r(237) = 0.391, p < .001. APC showed a highly significant positive correlation with EF at Pearson correlation r(237) = 0.303, p < .001. APC showed a highly significant positive correlation with citability at Pearson correlation r(237) = 0.323, p < .001. A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC. Journal publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability. The mean APC of the analyzed n = 237 journals was $1344.27 USD. The mean IF was 2.855. The mean EF was 0.017. The mean total citation count (citability) was 5925.92. The data supports that with increasing publishing costs, impact (IF), importance (EF), and citation count increase concurrently.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results indicate that research published in journals from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure, while journals from developing countries are less likely to generate profit and credibility. Expensive APC in prestigious journals are not linked to the actual reliability of the research published in them, according to Brembs (2018). The Impact Factor of prestigious journals creates a false perception of reliability in the research they publish. The GOA system paradoxically rewards journals for publishing more manuscripts, generating more capital, which gives rise to predatory journals and editorial complacency. Higher-ranking institutions have greater access to expensive, higher-impact journals, while lower-ranking institutions are forced into less expensive or closed-access outlets. Independent researchers with no institutional affiliation face increasingly narrow options, and their count has risen over the past decade. Most biodiversity hotspots are in the tropics, meaning the vast majority of conservation research is conducted in tropical regions. Research from tropical regions historically includes authors from developed countries even when the institutions are in developing nations. Foreign authors from developed countries nullify eligibility for Research4Life APC assistance, forcing authors to seek low-impact, hybrid, or predatory journals. The author argues that prestige and costliness of journal publications are false equivalents of reliable science.

Contradictions And Limitations
The bibliography is not provided in the source text, precluding a full assessment of cited works' validity. The study is a single-author descriptive/correlational analysis, which limits the ability to establish causality between APC and impact metrics. The exclusion of journals with IF > 40 was necessary due to medical/engineering overlap but may omit naturally high-impact natural science journals if they exist. The sample is limited to open-access natural science journals (n = 237), not the full spectrum of natural science publishing including closed-access and hybrid models. The analysis relies on metadata from a single source (Directory of Open Access Journals), which may have incomplete or inconsistent data across all records. The author's personal experience with funding rejection is anecdotal and not generalizable to all researchers facing APC barriers. No information is provided regarding the geographic distribution of the n = 237 journals by country or continent, making the 'developed vs. developing' comparison less granular. No random sampling was conducted; the dataset represents the entire Directory of Open Access Journals corpus (n = 14275) filtered by keywords, introducing potential selection bias.

Claims
Higher APC in GOA natural science journals is positively and significantly correlated with Impact Factor, Eigen Factor, and citability. APC was positively correlated with IF at r = 0.391, p < .001. APC was highly positively correlated with EF at r = 0.303, p < .001. APC was highly positively correlated with citability at r = 0.323, p < .001. A linear trend was confirmed across all three metrics in relation to APC. The correlations are moderate (r ranging from 0.303 to 0.391), suggesting that APC explains only a portion of the variance in impact metrics. The author acknowledges that expensive APC are not linked to reliability of the research itself. Cost functions as a barrier to visibility, creating a tiered system where only well-funded researchers can access high-impact outlets. The false equivalence between journal cost and scientific quality is reinforced by the system.
Developed country publishers host journals with significantly higher APCs, IFs, EFs, and citability compared to developing country publishers. Publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability. The mean APC of $1344.27 is relatively high for an open-access journal average, suggesting developed country dominance in high-cost brackets. The majority of journals with the highest metrics are from developed countries. The source does not provide the absolute number of journals from developed vs. developing countries or specific country-level means. No quantitative comparison of the actual APC distribution between developed and developing country groups is reported in the text. Research published in journals from developing countries is less likely to generate profit and credibility. The concentration of high-impact journals in developed countries exacerbates global scientific inequality.
Research4Life eligibility criteria for APC funding assistance are inaccessible to researchers from developed countries, even when collaborating with eligible developing-country authors. Once an international collaborator from a developed country is named, eligibility for financial assistance becomes void. The author personally experienced this: co-authors from eligible developing countries could not receive funding because the author (from the US) was a co-author. The research on the critically endangered Sumatran elephant could not be published in GOA journals due to the >1000 USD APC barrier. This is a single anecdotal case and the paper does not provide systemic data on how many researchers are affected by this specific rule. The paper does not analyze whether other funding mechanisms exist that circumvent this Research4Life rule. Important conservation research may fly under the academic radar due to APC funding constraints. Authors may be forced to remove co-authors to gain access to publication funds, compromising research integrity.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The exclusion of journals with IF > 40 was a sensitivity check designed to remove medical and engineering overlap and isolate natural sciences. Excluded journals (oncology, medical, engineering) were re-checked via keywords to ensure no natural science journals were inadvertently removed. The use of Pearson's correlation is appropriate for assessing linear relationships, but does not address non-linear dependencies. Currency standardization to USD was performed, which is a robustness measure against multi-currency bias in the original dataset.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the linear trend between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC, and indicates that publishers from developed countries have higher metrics. The text reports the mean values directly: APC ($1344.27), IF (2.855), EF (0.017), citability (5925.92) for the n = 237 sample.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is empirical evidence that APC is positively correlated with IF, EF, and citability in GOA natural science journals, revealing that high publication costs are rewarded with higher academic prestige and visibility, creating a tiered research ecosystem that disadvantages underfunded researchers and developing-country institutions. 2. The strongest evidence is the consistent, statistically significant positive correlation across all three impact metrics (IF, EF, citability) with APC (all p < .001), combined with the finding that the majority of high-APC, high-impact journals are concentrated in developed countries. 3. The future path requires structural reform of APC funding eligibility (e.g., amending Research4Life criteria), a shift from cost-based prestige models to reliability-based evaluation, and the development of more inclusive publication environments that do not penalize researchers by geographic location or institutional affiliation.

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Genomics / Molecular Diagnostics (SARS-CoV-2 detection and sequencing)
summary.executive_summary: This paper describes the development and validation of a highly sensitive multiplex PCR-based method for detecting and sequencing the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. The authors address the limitation of standard RT-PCR, which was reported to identify only 47–59% of true positive cases due to low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or mutations at primer binding sites. The developed assay employs two overlapping pools of 171 and 172 primer pairs (343 pairs total) targeting the entire 29,903bp SARS-CoV-2 genome with an average amplicon length of 99bp and 76±10bp gaps between adjacent amplicons. Mathematical modeling predicted a detection limit of 1.15 copies at 95% probability for one pool, and 0.29 copies when both pools are used. Validation with plasmids containing S and N gene sequences spiked into human cDNA demonstrated library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids, with quantification covering a dynamic range of 1 to approximately 1,000 copies, and 96% amplicon recovery at 14 copies. The method was applied to 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL, achieving 95–99% genome coverage at 100X depth for the majority of samples. Mutations were detected by two independent algorithms, with true intra-host mutations requiring ≥20% allele frequency. The D614G mutation was identified in 11 of 13 specimens. A parallel multiplex PCR-based metagenomic method using random hexamer-adapters achieved 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery at only ~0.6M total reads per library, with no additional host depletion. The paper demonstrates that the multiplex PCR approach is more sensitive than RT-PCR, tolerates viral mutations, and provides full-genome mutational surveillance, while the metagenomic variant enables discovery of novel or emerging isolates at moderate sequencing depth.

The metagenomic multiplex PCR method enables full-genome SARS-CoV-2 recovery at moderate sequencing depth without host depletion.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes the development and validation of a highly sensitive multiplex PCR-based method for detecting and sequencing the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. The authors address the limitation of standard RT-PCR, which was reported to identify only 47–59% of true positive cases due to low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or mutations at primer binding sites. The developed assay employs two overlapping pools of 171 and 172 primer pairs (343 pairs total) targeting the entire 29,903bp SARS-CoV-2 genome with an average amplicon length of 99bp and 76±10bp gaps between adjacent amplicons. Mathematical modeling predicted a detection limit of 1.15 copies at 95% probability for one pool, and 0.29 copies when both pools are used. Validation with plasmids containing S and N gene sequences spiked into human cDNA demonstrated library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids, with quantification covering a dynamic range of 1 to approximately 1,000 copies, and 96% amplicon recovery at 14 copies. The method was applied to 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL, achieving 95–99% genome coverage at 100X depth for the majority of samples. Mutations were detected by two independent algorithms, with true intra-host mutations requiring ≥20% allele frequency. The D614G mutation was identified in 11 of 13 specimens. A parallel multiplex PCR-based metagenomic method using random hexamer-adapters achieved 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery at only ~0.6M total reads per library, with no additional host depletion. The paper demonstrates that the multiplex PCR approach is more sensitive than RT-PCR, tolerates viral mutations, and provides full-genome mutational surveillance, while the metagenomic variant enables discovery of novel or emerging isolates at moderate sequencing depth.

Research Context
RT-PCR, the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, was reported to detect only 4–8 copies of virus at 95% confidence intervals in laboratory conditions. Despite its prevalence, RT-PCR only identified 47–59% of true positive cases, with 75% of RT-PCR-negative results later found positive by other assays. The discrepancy was attributed to low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or mutations spanning primer binding sites, mandating more robust methods. The SARS-CoV-2 genome is 29,903bp (NC_045512.2), while standard RT-PCR amplicon lengths are around 78–158bp. Mathematical modeling of RT-PCR with 99% efficiency showed it could only detect 4.8 copies at 95% probability, explaining the ~47–56% detection rate in known positive samples. Standard multiplex PCR had demonstrated 99% median coverage, 99.8% specificity for Hantaan orthohantavirus and Plasmodium falciparum, suggesting its applicability to SARS-CoV-2. A metagenomic approach for SARS-CoV-2 identification was recently described, motivating a parallel multiplex PCR-based metagenomic variant.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question was whether a multiplex PCR strategy targeting hundreds of SARS-CoV-2 genome regions could achieve higher sensitivity than RT-PCR and tolerate viral mutations. The authors hypothesized that simultaneous amplification of multiple regions would increase the frequency of occurrence in the mathematical detection model, lowering the limit of detection. It was predicted that the multiplex PCR LOD would be independent of the viral genome size, consistent with the RT-PCR model finding. A second hypothesis was that combining two overlapping pools of primer pairs would yield a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The authors further hypothesized that a random hexamer-based multiplex PCR metagenomic method could recover >96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome at moderate sequencing depth (~0.6M reads per library). They predicted that even with comparable molar ratios of viral targets to human haploid genomes, the viral genes would be preferentially amplified due to more 'random' base composition.

Methodological Details
The authors designed a panel of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers targeting the SARS-CoV-2 genome, with an average amplicon length of 99bp. A second pool of 171 multiplex PCR primer pairs was designed such that their target regions overlapped with the gaps between the first pool's regions, providing full genome coverage. Amplicons spanned the entire genome with an average 76±10bp gap between adjacent amplicons. For mathematical modeling of RT-PCR, 100bp amplicon length and a 30kb SARS-CoV-2 genome size were used with an assumed 99% amplification efficiency. The SARS-CoV-2 genome is NC_045512.2 with 29,903bp. For the multiplex PCR model, the authors assumed 6% amplification efficiency in a single-strand cDNA molecule and 80% successful targeted region amplification, based on reported recovery of 79% of variants from 600 amplicons. Two plasmids containing the full S and N gene sequences of SARS-CoV-2 were used as validation templates, totaling 28 expected amplicon targets. Plasmids were spiked into cDNA generated from human total RNA and diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy. Copy numbers were precisely determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) using a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. Thirteen nasopharyngeal swab specimens previously diagnosed positive by RT-PCR were used for full-genome amplification; viral loads ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL. The metagenomic method used random hexamer-adapters for amplification, Paragon Genomics' background removal reagent, and reverse transcription reagents for RNA-to-cDNA conversion. The metagenomic validation used 4,500 copies of N and S gene-containing plasmids spiked into 10 ng of human gDNA, representing approximately 3,300 haploid genomes.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow involved a secondary PCR step to amplify multiplex PCR products, during which sample indexes and NGS sequencing primers were added. PCR products were first analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize potential positives before NGS sequencing. The validated library was sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform. Mutation detection was performed by two independently developed algorithms, and only mutations detected by both methods were reported. Mutations with allele frequencies (%AF) >60% were considered empirically true; %AF ≥20% was the cutoff to eliminate noise from PCR and sequencing. For the metagenomic method, random hexamer-adapters amplified DNA/cDNA, non-specific products were removed by a background removal reagent, and human gDNA was not depleted by additional means. CleanPlex libraries were sequenced at approximately 1,000 paired-end reads per amplicon for standard mutation detection. Sub-sampling to 150,000 and 100,000 total reads per library (equivalent to 437 and 291 reads per amplicon, respectively) was performed to test sensitivity.

Key Results
Mathematical modeling of RT-PCR with 99% efficiency predicted a detection limit of 4.8 copies at 95% probability. The single 172-amplicon panel was modeled to detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Combining both overlapping pools of primers resulted in a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. In validation with plasmid spiking, library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies, demonstrating a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies. The yield of libraries started to saturate when the copy number reached 1,700. RT-PCR detection of a single S gene target rapidly dropped at 2.85 copies, in contrast to the multiplex PCR performance. The observed experimental probability to detect 1.1 copies was 56%, significantly higher than the predicted 12% based on the assumed 6% amplification efficiency. At 14 copies of plasmid, approximately 96% of amplicons were recovered; at 2.8 copies, 77% were recovered; and at 0.6 copies, 37% were recovered. Of the 13 specimens sequenced, about 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies, and 98–99% coverage at 100X was achieved for 22 to 675,885 copies at an average sequencing depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon. One genome from the 5,000-copy sample showed lower coverage at 96% for 100X, attributed to poor sample quality from processing or handling. At 150,000 total reads per library, at least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X; at 100,000 total reads, 86% coverage was achieved. At 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X. The D614G mutation, a G-to-A base change at position 23,403, was found in 11 of the 13 specimens. In the metagenomic validation with 4,500 copies of N and S gene-containing plasmids, 16% of recovered bases (13% of recovered reads) were within the viral N and S genes. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered in the metagenomic assay. Only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified in the metagenomic assay. After further optimization, 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered in the metagenomic method.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The multiplex PCR approach increases the frequency of detection by simultaneously targeting hundreds of regions, making it more sensitive than single-target RT-PCR and tolerant of mutations. The experimental detection of 1.1 copies at 56% probability versus the predicted 12% suggests the actual multiplex PCR amplification efficiency for single-stranded cDNA is higher than the assumed 6%. The 75% of RT-PCR-negative results later found positive by other assays can be partially explained by the predicted 26% detection probability of RT-PCR for a single copy. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of 13 specimens, confirming the mutation's spread and presence in the analyzed isolates. The 0.08% human chromosomal amplification versus preferential viral and mitochondrial amplification suggests random hexamers deselect the human genome while favoring more 'random' base composition regions. The 10-fold depth range of recovered bases in the metagenomic assay is a routine observation with the authors' multiplex PCR technology, implying that increasing sequencing depth alone may not further improve coverage.

Contradictions And Limitations
The assumed 6% amplification efficiency for multiplex PCR of single-stranded cDNA was not validated by UMI-labeled counting, leaving the true efficiency uncertain. No UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification, meaning intra-host mutations cannot be definitively distinguished from PCR or sequencing artifacts. Copy numbers and sequencing depth should be cautiously considered when mutations have low %AF, as low input and low depth may introduce false intra-host mutations. In the 13 specimens, one genome showed only 96% coverage at 100X (from a 5,000-copy sample), attributed to poor sample quality rather than method failure. The metagenomic method requires verification and validation of detection of SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses/respiratory viruses before clinical use. The authors note that the D614G mutation was found in 11 of 13 specimens, but the exact geographic origin of the 13 specimens is not detailed beyond 'close communities.'

Claims
The multiplex PCR method is significantly more sensitive than standard RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection and sequencing. Mathematical modeling predicted a detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability when both primer pools are used. Experimental validation showed 96% amplicon recovery at 14 copies of plasmid, compared to RT-PCR rapid drop at 2.85 copies. The assay produced clean characteristic target peaks of defined sizes, allowing direct identification by electrophoresis. The authors caution that 75% of RT-PCR-negative results were later found positive by other assays, suggesting RT-PCR still has substantial limitations in clinical settings. No UMI was used, making intra-host mutation calls uncertain at low copy numbers and depths. This method could be used for routine clinical diagnosis, potentially reducing the need for repeated testing. The dual-pool approach allows for full-genome mutational surveillance of the virus.
The metagenomic multiplex PCR method enables full-genome SARS-CoV-2 recovery at moderate sequencing depth without host depletion. 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered at ~0.6M total reads per library. 16% of recovered bases were within viral N and S genes, significantly higher than the 0.08% human chromosomal amplification. This coverage surpassed the recommended 50% threshold for drafting a genome. The 10-fold coverage range was noted as a routine finding, suggesting that simply increasing sequencing depth may not improve coverage. Metagenomic methods generally require very high sequencing depth and are economically prohibitive for routine diagnostic use. The method could identify novel or emerging pathogens at moderate sequencing depth of approximately 1 million reads. The approach could theoretically detect any sequence in a specimen, broadening its utility beyond SARS-CoV-2.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two independently developed mutation detection algorithms were used, and only mutations detected by both were reported. A %AF ≥20% threshold was selected based on mutation profiles from synthetic SARS-CoV-2 RNA controls from Twist Bioscience. Sub-sampling to 150,000 and 100,000 total reads per library (437 and 291 reads per amplicon) was performed to confirm that 1,000 reads per amplicon provided sufficient data for mutation detection. The uniformity of amplicon recovery was assessed using log10 distance to the mean amplicon number, with the high coverage manifested by superior uniformity. The metagenomic method was optimized iteratively to reach 96% genome recovery.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the RT-PCR mathematical model predicting 4.8 copies at 95% probability, and the probability of 26% for detecting one copy. Figure 1B displays the design of the two overlapping primer pools (172 and 171 pairs) with 99bp average amplicon length and 76±10bp gaps. Figure 1C shows the predicted detection limits: 1.15 copies for one pool and 0.29 copies for both pools. Figure 1D illustrates the full workflow from multiplex PCR to secondary PCR and NGS. Figure 4F shows shorter gaps in SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial regions. Figure 4G shows optimized 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a multiplex PCR method targeting 343 SARS-CoV-2 genome regions that is more sensitive than standard RT-PCR and enables full-genome mutational surveillance. 2. The strongest evidence is the mathematical prediction of a 0.29-copy detection limit and experimental validation showing library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 plasmid copies with 96% amplicon recovery at 14 copies. 3. The future path includes expanding the panel to detect other respiratory viruses, applying the metagenomic variant to identify novel pathogens at moderate sequencing depth, and cautioning interpretation of intra-host mutations at low viral load and depth.

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.field_subfield: Molecular Biology / Translation Biology / Ribosome Biochemistry
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the translational properties of Ribo-T, a tethered Escherichia coli ribosome in which the 30S and 50S subunits are covalently linked via short RNA linkers. The central question is whether this structural constraint impairs translational accuracy—specifically in reading frame maintenance (frameshifting), stop codon recognition, and translation initiation—or whether the ribosome can maintain fidelity despite the inseparable subunits. The authors employed the pCL99 dual reporter system in E. coli BL21 (DE3) to measure translational output of the lacZ-luc fusion gene under various SD sequence and recoding signal conditions. 

Key findings demonstrate that: (1) Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to the SD sequence during programmed -1 frameshifting, maintaining efficiencies equivalent to wild-type ribosomes across IS911 (13% vs 13%), IS3 (33% vs 33%), and dnaX (43% vs 45%), confirming that SD-ASD base pairing is not required for this event. (2) However, for +1 frameshifting, Ribo-T ribosomes show a dramatic impairment, with efficiency reduced from 33% to 2% (p < 8.9×10⁻⁹), indicating that the SD-dependent stimulatory mechanism for +1 frameshifting is lost. (3) Translation initiation is impaired: Ribo-T ribosomes use the Ribo-T-specific SD sequence four-fold less efficiently than wild-type ribosomes use the wild-type SD, and the authors demonstrate that initiation occurs via internal 70S loading rather than scanning. (4) Stop codon readthrough is increased, with Ribo-T showing readthrough rates of 0.07% (UAG), 0.26% (UGA), and 0.04% (UAA), compared to 0.013%, 0.11%, and 0.01% for wild-type, respectively. The authors conclude that covalent subunit tethering modifies ribosome dynamics, specifically at the H44 helix, impairing SD-dependent elongation and initiation while maintaining -1 frameshifting fidelity, with a slight increase in termination error.

This work contributes to the understanding of ribosome flexibility, challenging the hypothesis that mutual subunit mobility is strictly essential for translocation and suggesting that structural constraints on H44 orientation govern the SD-dependency of both elongation and initiation steps.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the translational properties of Ribo-T, a tethered Escherichia coli ribosome in which the 30S and 50S subunits are covalently linked via short RNA linkers. The central question is whether this structural constraint impairs translational accuracy—specifically in reading frame maintenance (frameshifting), stop codon recognition, and translation initiation—or whether the ribosome can maintain fidelity despite the inseparable subunits. The authors employed the pCL99 dual reporter system in E. coli BL21 (DE3) to measure translational output of the lacZ-luc fusion gene under various SD sequence and recoding signal conditions. 

Key findings demonstrate that: (1) Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to the SD sequence during programmed -1 frameshifting, maintaining efficiencies equivalent to wild-type ribosomes across IS911 (13% vs 13%), IS3 (33% vs 33%), and dnaX (43% vs 45%), confirming that SD-ASD base pairing is not required for this event. (2) However, for +1 frameshifting, Ribo-T ribosomes show a dramatic impairment, with efficiency reduced from 33% to 2% (p < 8.9×10⁻⁹), indicating that the SD-dependent stimulatory mechanism for +1 frameshifting is lost. (3) Translation initiation is impaired: Ribo-T ribosomes use the Ribo-T-specific SD sequence four-fold less efficiently than wild-type ribosomes use the wild-type SD, and the authors demonstrate that initiation occurs via internal 70S loading rather than scanning. (4) Stop codon readthrough is increased, with Ribo-T showing readthrough rates of 0.07% (UAG), 0.26% (UGA), and 0.04% (UAA), compared to 0.013%, 0.11%, and 0.01% for wild-type, respectively. The authors conclude that covalent subunit tethering modifies ribosome dynamics, specifically at the H44 helix, impairing SD-dependent elongation and initiation while maintaining -1 frameshifting fidelity, with a slight increase in termination error.

This work contributes to the understanding of ribosome flexibility, challenging the hypothesis that mutual subunit mobility is strictly essential for translocation and suggesting that structural constraints on H44 orientation govern the SD-dependency of both elongation and initiation steps.

Research Context
Ribosomes are evolutionary conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes that function as two separate subunits in all kingdoms of life. The 30S subunit contains 16S rRNA and 21 proteins for decoding, while the 50S contains two rRNAs with 33 proteins for peptide bond formation. A ribosome with tethered subunits, in which the two subunits were covalently linked in a single entity, was recently engineered in Escherichia coli. Ribo-T was shown to be functional and able to sustain cell growth, although doubling times were slower (107 min vs 35 min for wild-type). The rate of protein synthesis with Ribo-T catalysis was only 50% that with wild-type ribosomes. Cell viability depends on a balance between rapid protein synthesis and accurate decoding of genetic information. Recoding events such as frameshifting and stop codon readthrough are powerful tools for investigations of translation accuracy. Prior to this work, the translational properties of Ribo-T had not been systematically characterized across different recoding and initiation contexts.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether tethered ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes during programmed frameshifting. The authors asked whether Ribo-T ribosomes terminate translation accurately at stop codons. A third question was whether Ribo-T ribosomes translate messenger RNA accurately, specifically regarding SD sequence recognition. The hypothesis was that covalent attachment of the two subunits modifies the properties of the ribosome, altering its ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly. Specifically, the authors predicted that SD-dependent recoding events would be affected because the SD-ASD interaction is essential for both -1 and +1 frameshifting. For initiation, the authors anticipated that Ribo-T ribosomes would be less efficient at using SD sequences to assemble at the start codon due to tethering constraints. For termination, the hypothesis was that reduced ribosomal mobility might impair release factor binding, increasing stop codon readthrough. The overall prediction was that the tethered structure would have specific, rather than general, translational consequences.

Methodological Details
The experiments were performed with the E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain (Invitrogen) with and without the poRibo-T2 vector carrying Ribo-T ribosomal DNA. The ASD sequence of Ribo-T 16S rRNA was altered from wild-type (5'-UCACCUCCUUA-3') to an orthogonal sequence (5'-UCAUUGUGGUA-). The bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system was used, carrying the lacZ-luc fusion gene under the T7 promoter with streptomycin resistance and the CloDF13-derived CDF replicon. Target sequences for translation accuracy were inserted by oligocloning into the MscI restriction site of pCL99 at the junction between lacZ and luc genes. Cloned double-stranded oligonucleotides were obtained by hybridizing two complementary oligonucleotides after heating for 5 min at 100°C. For wild-type ribosomes, constructs used a lacZ gene carrying a wild-type SD sequence AGGAGG. For Ribo-T ribosomes, corresponding constructs used a mutated SD sequence CACCAC upstream from lacZ, complementary to the 3' end of Ribo-T 16S rRNA. In Ribo-T strains, both wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes are present, but only Ribo-T ribosomes can initiate lacZ translation because of the orthogonal SD. Crosstalk between wild-type ribosomes and the orthogonal mRNA was checked and found to be too low to affect results. Translational efficiency was calculated as the ratio of luciferase activity to β-galactosidase activity for the target, divided by the ratio for the corresponding in-frame construct. The median value was calculated for at least six independent experiments. Significance of differences was determined using Student's t-tests. For the intergenic analysis, the 46-nucleotide E. coli lacZ-lacY sequence was used, with the SD sequence promoting initiation at lacY.

Procedures And Architectures
Three programmed -1 frameshifting sites were selected: IS911 (stem-loop), IS3 (pseudoknot), and dnaX (stem-loop) from insertion sequence elements. For +1 frameshifting, the site from the E. coli prfB gene (UGA C termination context) was selected. For stop codon readthrough, the stop codon sequence of the mtmB1 gene from Methanosarcina barkeri, which promotes pyrrolysine insertion, was used. The dual reporter constructs were verified by sequencing after construction. In the -1 frameshifting experiment, the reverse modification replaced the dnaX SD with a Ribo-T-specific SD (dnaXRibo-T) to test SD dependence. In the +1 frameshifting experiment, the WT SD was replaced with the Ribo-T SD sequence to test whether SD recognition could restore activity. For the initiation experiment, the lacZ-lacY SD sequence was modified by either deleting the SD or replacing it with the Ribo-T SD. A stable stem loop structure was inserted immediately downstream from lacZ as a roadblock to rule out scanning-mediated initiation. Readthrough quantification compared Ribo-T against wild-type for all three stop codons (UAG, UGA, UAA). The Ribo-T construct was the poRibo-T2 vector carrying the Ribo-T ribosomal DNA. The study used the E. coli strain BL21 (DE3) from Invitrogen for all experiments.

Key Results
Ribo-T ribosomes showed 13% -1 frameshifting at IS911, identical to wild-type (p = 0.54), confirming SD-independence of -1 frameshifting. For IS3, both WT and Ribo-T showed 33% frameshifting (p = 0.77). For dnaX, WT showed 43% and Ribo-T showed 45% frameshifting (p = 0.77). Replacing dnaX SD with a Ribo-T SD reduced WT frameshifting to 11% (p = 1.7×10⁻³) but left Ribo-T unchanged at 45% vs 44% (p = 0.85), confirming Ribo-T SD-insensitivity. WT ribosomes showed 33% +1 frameshifting on the prfB sequence, consistent with previous reports. Ribo-T ribosomes showed only 2% +1 frameshifting (p < 8.9×10⁻⁹), representing a ~94% relative decrease. Replacing the WT SD with Ribo-T SD did not restore Ribo-T +1 frameshifting (1.8%, p = 0.56) but reduced WT +1 frameshifting to 0.6% (p = 1.6×10⁻⁵). In the absence of Ribo-T, removing the SD upstream of luc produced almost no luciferase activity. With wild-type SD, high luciferase activity was obtained, confirming SD-dependence of initiation. With Ribo-T SD, no statistically significant difference in luciferase activity was observed (p = 0.04 vs no SD), confirming WT ribosomes cannot use the Ribo-T SD. In the presence of Ribo-T, luciferase induction was increased by a factor of four (p = 4.7×10⁻⁴) when Ribo-T SD was present, indicating Ribo-T can use the alternative SD. When the Ribo-T SD was placed in front of the lacZ start codon, luciferase was four times stronger than with no SD (p = 9.8×10⁻⁶), similar to WT SD. The roadblock stem loop had no effect on luc initiation (p = 0.22), confirming initiation by internal 70S loading rather than scanning. Ribo-T readthrough rates were 0.07% (UAG), 0.26% (UGA), and 0.04% (UAA) compared to WT rates of 0.013%, 0.11%, and 0.01%. All readthrough differences were statistically significant: p = 4.7×10⁻⁷ (UAG), p = 5×10⁻³ (UGA), p = 2.5×10⁻⁴ (UAA).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Ribo-T ribosomes do not use SD sequences to promote frameshifting, whether at elongation (-1 frameshifting) or initiation (translation startup). The SD-ASD interaction is essential for +1 frameshifting as it causes E-site tRNA release and destabilizes the ribosome; Ribo-T's inability to sense SD abolishes this. The tethering of subunits via helix 44 (H44) likely modifies the orientation of the ASD sequence, preventing normal SD recognition. The slow growth phenotype (doubling time 107 min vs 35 min) and 50% protein synthesis rate are consistent with decreased SD-dependent initiation rates across many genes. The slight increase in stop codon readthrough suggests the covalently linked A-site is less able to bind termination factors, consistent with restricted ribosomal dynamics. These findings support the view that ribosomal subunit mobility is at least partially dispensable for core translational functions. The results highlight greater-than-expected flexibility of the ribosome architecture.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper notes that Ribo-T doubling times were slower (107 min vs 35 min), which was attributed to slower rRNA biogenesis rather than impaired Ribo-T activity. The authors note that no natural stop codon readthrough sequence has ever been identified in E. coli, requiring use of an archaeal sequence for the assay. The study does not report whether tethered ribosomes would be efficient in eukaryotes, where the initiation mechanism differs. Crosstalk between wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes was checked, but the paper notes it was too low to affect results; however, precise quantification of crosstalk is not provided. The mechanism by which Ribo-T ribosomes initiate translation in the absence of an SD sequence remains unclear. The paper does not provide random seed values for replicates or specify exact temperature and media conditions for all experiments. No high-resolution structural data (e.g., cryo-EM) for Ribo-T were generated in this study to directly test the H44 orientation hypothesis.

Claims
Ribo-T ribosomes maintain -1 frameshifting efficiency equal to wild-type ribosomes regardless of whether an SD sequence is present or recognized. IS911 efficiency was 13% for both WT and Ribo-T (p = 0.54). IS3 efficiency was 33% for both (p = 0.77). dnaX efficiency was 43% (WT) vs 45% (Ribo-T) (p = 0.77). Replacing dnaX SD with Ribo-T SD kept Ribo-T efficiency at 45% vs 44% (p = 0.85) but dropped WT to 11% (p = 1.7×10⁻³). For +1 frameshifting, Ribo-T efficiency was severely impaired (2% vs 33%, p < 8.9×10⁻⁹), showing the effect is context-specific. The SD-ASD interaction is not required for -1 frameshifting but is critical for +1 frameshifting, revealing different molecular requirements for the two events. Tethering does not disrupt the slippery sequence recognition or the pause-inducing element for -1 frameshifting.
Ribo-T ribosomes are impaired in stop codon recognition, displaying increased readthrough at all three stop codons compared to wild-type. UAG readthrough: 0.07% (Ribo-T) vs 0.013% (WT), p = 4.7×10⁻⁷. UGA readthrough: 0.26% (Ribo-T) vs 0.11% (WT), p = 5×10⁻³. UAA readthrough: 0.04% (Ribo-T) vs 0.01% (WT), p = 2.5×10⁻⁴. The impairment is described as 'slight' (0.07% vs 0.013%), and the authors note the readthrough assay uses an archaeal stop codon sequence rather than a natural E. coli one. The covalently linked A-site may be less dynamic or less accessible to release factors. The structural constraint of subunit tethering perturbs the coordinated motion required for efficient termination.
Ribo-T ribosomes use SD sequences inefficiently during both translation initiation and programmed elongation. Ribo-T could use the Ribo-T SD but at only 1/4 the efficiency of WT using WT SD (p = 4.7×10⁻⁴). WT ribosomes could not use the Ribo-T SD (p = 0.04 vs no SD), confirming the SD is orthogonal to WT. Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to SD presence during -1 frameshifting (no change in efficiency). Ribo-T cannot use SD for +1 frameshifting (2% vs 33%). Initiation of luc occurs via internal 70S loading, not scanning (roadblock test, p = 0.22). Some mRNAs in prokaryotes are devoid of SD sequences, indicating SD is neither necessary nor sufficient for initiation. The study does not resolve the exact mechanism by which Ribo-T initiates without an SD. The decreased initiation rate across genes likely contributes to the 50% protein synthesis rate and slow growth of Ribo-T cells. The H44 helix orientation in Ribo-T is the proposed structural basis for impaired SD-dependent processes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The reverse experiment (replacing dnaX SD with Ribo-T SD) confirmed Ribo-T SD-independence for -1 frameshifting (45% vs 44%, p = 0.85). The replacement of WT SD with Ribo-T SD in the +1 frameshifting assay failed to restore Ribo-T activity (1.8% vs previous, p = 0.56) but abolished WT activity (0.6% vs 33%, p = 1.6×10⁻⁵), confirming the SD was the reason for WT frameshifting. A stable stem-loop roadblock was inserted downstream of lacZ to ablate scanning-mediated initiation; the lack of effect (p = 0.22) confirmed internal 70S loading. The authors note that Ribo-T doubling times were slower (107 min vs 35 min) but attribute this to slower rRNA biogenesis rather than impaired Ribo-T activity. Crosstalk between WT and Ribo-T ribosomes was checked and found too low to affect the results. The translational efficiency calculation used the median value for at least six independent experiments.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the three programmed -1 frameshifting sites from IS911, IS3, and dnaX insertion sequences with their respective structures. Figure 2A presents -1 frameshifting efficiencies at IS911 (13% WT vs 14% Ribo-T, p=0.54), IS3 (33% vs 33%, p=0.77), and dnaX (43% WT vs 45% Ribo-T, p=0.77). Figure 2B shows the reverse experiment: replacing dnaX SD with Ribo-T SD, demonstrating WT frameshifting dropped to 11% while Ribo-T remained at 45% vs 44% (p=0.85). Figure 3A shows the +1 frameshifting site from prfB with WT frameshifting efficiency of 33%. Figure 3B shows Ribo-T +1 frameshifting at only 2% (p < 8.9×10⁻⁹) versus WT at 33%. Figure 3C shows the SD-swap experiment for +1 frameshifting: Ribo-T at 1.8% (p=0.56) and WT dropped to 0.6% (p=1.6×10⁻⁵). Figure 4A shows the initiation assay: no SD vs WT SD vs Ribo-T SD upstream of luc, with WT SD giving high luciferase activity. Figure 4B shows in Ribo-T strains: WT SD vs Ribo-T SD vs no SD, with Ribo-T SD giving 4-fold higher induction (p = 4.7×10⁻⁴). Figure 4C shows the Ribo-T SD swap experiment: Ribo-T SD upstream of lacZ versus no SD, showing 4-fold higher luciferase activity (p = 9.8×10⁻⁶). Figure 4D shows the roadblock stem loop experiment: with and without roadblock, demonstrating no effect on luc translation (p = 0.22). Figure 5 presents stop codon readthrough for UAG, UGA, and UAA, showing Ribo-T readthrough rates 0.07%, 0.26%, and 0.04% compared to WT rates of 0.013%, 0.11%, and 0.01%. Table 1 lists the target sequences tested for translation accuracy, including SD sequences and frameshifting sites for all constructs.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is that covalent tethering of ribosomal subunits abolishes SD-dependent recoding (+1 frameshifting) and translation initiation but preserves SD-independent -1 frameshifting and cell viability, revealing the H44-mediated SD-ASD interaction as the molecular determinant of tethering effects. 2. The strongest evidence is the multi-parameter demonstration across four recoding/initiation contexts: -1 frameshifting (no effect), +1 frameshifting (~94% reduction), SD-dependent initiation (4-fold reduction), and stop codon readthrough (4–8-fold increase), all confirmed by SD-swap experiments and statistical significance. 3. The future path is to obtain a high-resolution structural determination of Ribo-T to resolve the proposed H44 orientation modification hypothesis, and to investigate whether tethered ribosomes would behave similarly in eukaryotes with different initiation mechanisms.

summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak; Laura Serra-Saurina; Raquel Rabionet Janssen; Laura Domènech; Mattia Bosio; Francesc Muyas; Xavier Estivill; Georgia Escaramís; Stephan Ossowski
summary.field_subfield: Bioinformatics / Statistical Genetics
summary.type_of_paper: Methodological with benchmark and application study
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces BATI, a novel Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) for the association of rare genetic variants with complex phenotypes in case-control studies. While existing rare variant association studies (RVAS) struggle with low statistical power in small-to-medium cohorts, BATI enables the simultaneous integration of individual and variant-specific features—both categorical and numeric—as covariates within a fully specified hierarchical Bayesian GLMM. The methodological framework utilizes INLA, a non-sampling-based numerical approximation for latent Gaussian models, which offers substantial computational speed and accuracy advantages over Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) for genome-wide applications. BATI was evaluated against five established RVAS methods (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, and HBMR) on semi-synthetic breast cancer risk cohorts constructed from thousands of real WES datasets (1000GP, ExAC, Exome Project, Iberian cohort) combined with ClinVar-derived risk variants. Key results demonstrate that BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios where risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance, while competing methods show near-zero power. At 0.01% TIER and 0.5% variance explained, BATI identifies all risk genes at 0.1% TIER with over 80% power, whereas Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently fail on BRCA2, and HBMR fails on BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2. The method was implemented within the rvGWAS framework and applied to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, identifying eight candidate predisposition genes including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The authors conclude that BATI provides a flexible, powerful alternative to existing methods, particularly when biological context (functional annotations) is leveraged, and propose ∆DIC-based model selection for inference.

Research Context
Rare variants are believed to contribute substantially to the etiology of complex diseases and may explain missing heritability. However, traditional genome-wide association studies lack power for rare variants because few individuals carry the alternative allele at single positions. Previous RVAS methods aggregate variants into functional units (genes, promoters, pathways) to increase statistical power. Burden tests are powerful only when effects are unidirectional (all protective or all deleterious). Variance-component methods (SKAT, C-alpha) and their combination (SKAT-O) address heterogeneous effects. MiST proposed a mixed-effects test considering variant characteristics but restricted inference to a score test under the null because full model estimation with multiple integration was computationally intensive. Prior benchmark studies used artificial cohorts based on HapMap statistics, lacking realistic noise and functional variant distributions. Existing RVAS benchmarks have been restricted to small genomic regions, limiting generalizability to exome-wide association tests. Simulated variant data lacks the complexity and noise-level of real data, leading to overly optimistic performance estimates.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA can integrate both categorical and numeric variant characteristics as covariates while maintaining computational feasibility for genome-wide scans. The hypothesis is that incorporating individual and variant-specific features (e.g., functional annotations, damage scores) as covariates within a fully estimated GLMM via INLA will increase statistical power relative to existing methods. A secondary hypothesis is that the gain in power will be most pronounced when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function variants, reflecting the known biological architecture. The authors also hypothesize that BATI can cope with complex population structure and confounders in realistic cohorts. The predicted outcome is that BATI will substantially outperform established methods on realistic, semi-synthetic cohorts, particularly at low variance-explained (VE) settings.

Methodological Details
The study developed semi-synthetic breast cancer risk cohorts combining thousands of real WES datasets with known risk variants. Two large datasets served as the simulation basis: 1000GP (with half of samples randomly assigned as cases) and the Iberian cohort (one-third cases, two-thirds controls). Risk variants were queried from ClinVar and annotated as exonic or splicing, with MAF threshold set at 0.01 in EVS, 1000GP, or ExAC. Ten random cohort splits were used to generate comparable TIER thresholds (5%, 0.1%, 0.01%) across all methods. Benchmark testing involved 100 simulations of risk variants for each of 8 risk gene architectures. The Iberian cohort simulation included 1,810 total individuals (1,167 cases vs. 1810 total), while the 1000GP simulation had 1,810 total. The rvGWAS framework integrates QC, interactive filtering, stratification detection, functional variant annotations, and six RVAS tests. The framework supports rare variant association for genes or any other biological unit such as promoters. The R-INLA implementation used version 17.06.20 for model estimation. The benchmark study used S = 10 random shuffling datasets for robust ΔDIC threshold estimation. For the Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia application, the framework was applied to WES data, identifying eight candidate genes.

Procedures And Architectures
BATI is implemented as a hierarchical Bayesian GLMM using the R-INLA package for posterior estimation. The model assumes a phenotype Y_i from the exponential family: logit(p_i) = X_t_iα + (G_t_i Z)ω + G_t_iδ, where variant-specific effects are random and patient/variant characteristics are fixed. INLA is a non-sampling-based numerical approximation procedure that estimates latent Gaussian Markov random field models. Model selection is based on the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC), comparing H₀: η_i = X_t_iα with H₁: η_i = X_t_iα + (G_t_i Z)ω + G_t_iδ. Type I error thresholds are determined by randomly assigning individuals to cases or controls under the null and generating the empirical distribution of ΔDIC. For more robust thresholds, S random datasets are shuffled, and the median of S ΔDIC thresholds is used. The rvGWAS framework allows integration of four commonly used RVAS tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST) as well as two Bayesian alternatives (HBMR, BATI). BATI can efficiently and flexibly integrate a large number of categorical and numeric characteristics of genetic variants as covariates. The benchmark used TIER thresholds of 5%, 0.1%, and 0.01%, derived as p-value equivalents from ΔDIC distributions. In the breast cancer cohort, ClinVar risk variants were introduced into the VCF files of cases only.

Key Results
At 0.01% TIER and 0.5% VE, all methods except BATI show power close to 0, while BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes (median power of 55%). At 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, BATI calls most genes and at 0.1% TIER all genes with >80% power. Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently fail to call BRCA2 (both missense and LoF versions) at 0.5% VE. HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 already at 0.1% TIER. At 2% VE and 0.01% TIER, all methods except MiST identify all risk genes. In the Iberian cohort (smaller size: 1,167 vs 1,810), BATI's performance is stable while most other tests perform slightly worse. The power plots at 0.5% VE are very similar for Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O, indicating they share the same strengths and weaknesses. MiST failed to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER thresholds in the realistic WES benchmark. The Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia application identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. Estimated ΔDIC thresholds are highly similar across all 10 randomized case-control splits (Supplementary S6 Fig).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI outperforms existing methods because it leverages both categorical and numerical variant characteristics as covariates, providing biological context to the statistical model. The gain in power is most pronounced when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function variants, suggesting that functional annotation is a key moderator of RVAS performance. INLA's non-sampling approach enables inference on the full model with complex random effect structures that were computationally infeasible with MCMC or required score-test approximations (MiST). The semi-synthetic design (real WES noise + real ClinVar variants) addresses the 'overly optimistic' benchmark artifact of pure simulations, making the findings more relevant for clinical applications. Combining Burden-and SKAT-type methods with completely different approaches (like BATI) is recommended to compensate for shared weaknesses. BATI's flexibility in covariate integration represents a paradigm shift from fixed-form RVAS tests toward customizable Bayesian genetic models.

Contradictions And Limitations
The Iberian cohort has a smaller size (1,167 vs 1,810 total individuals), which makes most tests perform slightly worse, although BATI remains stable. BATI is shown to perform at least as good as other methods when testing genes containing mostly missense variants, implying its relative advantage is limited to specific genetic architectures. The paper notes that at 0.01% TIER only 2 genes (out of ~20,000) are expected as significant by chance, introducing a ceiling on what can be reliably detected. The benchmark is restricted to 8 breast cancer risk genes and one CLL application, limiting generalizability across all disease types. MiST performs poorly on the realistic WES cohorts due to likely zero-inflated p-values from inappropriate handling of low variant counts, which is a methodological limitation of the original MiST. No explicit random seed or specific software version for the data generator is provided beyond the R-INLA version. The comparison with HBMR only uses the 8 risk genes and does not test HBMR's variant-detection-error correction functionality directly in the benchmark.

Claims
BATI substantially outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic, semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts, particularly at low variance-explained settings. At 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes while all other methods show near-zero power. At 0.5% VE and 0.1% TIER, BATI calls all genes with >80% power, surpassing all competing methods. BATI remains stable in the smaller Iberian cohort while other methods degrade. The 100-simulation gene-wise power analysis confirms consistent superiority across multiple architectures. BATI's relative advantage is reduced for genes containing mostly missense variants, where it performs at least as well as other methods. At 2% VE, the performance gap narrows, with all methods except MiST identifying all risk genes. Clinicians can use BATI with greater confidence for detecting risk genes with subtle phenotypic effects in WES data. The rvGWAS framework provides a ready-to-use pipeline for geneticists to apply BATI to their own datasets.
Integrating functional variant characteristics as covariates in a Bayesian framework provides measurable gains in statistical power. BATI achieves >80% power at 0.1% TIER even at 0.5% VE, whereas without covariates, power would be substantially lower. The semi-synthetic approach with real functional annotations (ClinVar) reveals method-specific power dynamics that pure simulations miss. The magnitude of the gain depends on the specific genetic architecture; some genes show only marginal improvement. Future RVAS methods should prioritize flexible covariate integration rather than rigid functional assumptions.

Data And Code Availability
The BATI test is implemented as part of the 'Rare Variant Genome Wide Association Study' (rvGWAS) framework, which supports whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing data. The semi-synthetic cohorts were constructed from real WES datasets including 1000GP, ExAC, Exome Project, and the Iberian cohort, making the underlying data available through established repositories. No explicit code repository URL or data access protocol is mentioned in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors performed 10 random cohort splits to generate comparable TIER thresholds, demonstrating robustness of the threshold estimation across different randomizations. The Iberian cohort (smaller sample size) was used as a secondary validation, confirming BATI's stability across cohort sizes. 100 simulations per gene were performed to characterize power under different genetic architectures. The power plots at 0.5% VE showed very similar patterns for Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O, suggesting their underlying statistical mechanisms are analogous in low-VE regimes. No explicit ablation of specific variant characteristics (e.g., removing damage scores vs functional annotations) is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 shows gene-wise power plots for the 1000GP cohort across 100 simulations per gene, with TIER thresholds (5%, 0.1%, 0.01%) marked. Table 2 provides quantitative power estimates across all methods for each of the 8 risk gene architectures at different TIER levels. Supplementary S6 Figure shows the ΔDIC thresholds across all 10 randomized case-control splits, demonstrating similarity. Supplementary S8 Figure presents results for the Iberian cohort, showing BATI's stability at low VE. Supplementary S4 Table lists the TIER thresholds for all methods, derived from the ΔDIC distributions. Supplementary S9 Figure provides gene-wise power plots for the Iberian cohort.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BATI, a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA that enables full-model inference with integrated categorical and numeric variant covariates, outperforming all existing methods at low variance-explained settings on realistic semi-synthetic cohorts. 2. The strongest evidence is that at 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, BATI achieves power near 100% (median 55%) for three risk genes while all competing methods show near-zero power, and at 0.1% TIER it calls all genes with >80% power. 3. The future path involves extending BATI's flexible covariate integration to larger cohorts, other disease types, and further enhancing the rvGWAS framework for clinical genetic analysis.

summary.title: A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors
summary.authors: Nishi Kumari, Ayush Upadhyay, Kishan Kalia, Rakesh Kumar, Kanika Tuteja, Rani Paul, Eugenia Covernton, Tina Sharma, Vinod Scaria, Anshu Bhardwaj
summary.field_subfield: Drug Discovery / Virology / Computational Chemistry
summary.type_of_paper: Data curation and prioritization study (knowledgebase development)
summary.executive_summary: This paper describes the systematic curation and combined-evidence prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs) to address the lack of approved treatment for Nipah virus, a pathogen with over 75% case fatality rate. The authors developed the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK), a LAMP-based web platform containing 182 entries (98 unique small molecule inhibitors, 125 total small molecule entries, with 57 being peptides or incomplete). Data was sourced from PubMed and Google using a scoring system (0–10) on 838 papers, followed by manual curation by a two-team verification system. The study computed 1875 descriptors per compound using PaDel and performed comparative analysis against 2,346 FDA-approved compounds and 4,644 Enamine antivirals. A two-pronged prioritization strategy was applied: (1) robustness of the assays used to identify the compounds, and (2) drug-likeness filtering using DruLito (Lipinski, Veber, MDDR-like, Ghose, BBB, CMC-50, QED) and PAINS. Of 98 unique small molecule NVIs, 34 showed structural similarity to 76 FDA drugs. DruLito filtering was highly restrictive, with only 2 of 91 compounds passing all filters except CMC. The independent assay-robustness screen prioritized 11 NVIs, of which NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and showed overlap with FDA-approved physicochemical ranges. CIC0032 exhibited the best activity among the shortlisted three. Clustering using Jarp revealed 90 clusters, with 84 singletons (93.3%), confirming high chemical diversity. IC50/EC50 values ranged from 0.47 nM to 7,562,710 nM. The NVIK platform supports text, structure, and complex query searches (SMILES, SDF, MOL, JSME drawing), near-neighbor identification (NNeib 5.12.0), clustering (Jarp 6.0.2), and CIRCOS/Cytoscape visualizations. The work is positioned as a centralized resource aligned with WHO's priority disease R&D blueprint.

claims.description: The NVIK platform provides a systematically curated, validated knowledgebase of Nipah virus inhibitors that outperforms existing scattered datasets.
A combined evidence strategy of assay robustness and drug-likeness prioritization successfully identifies actionable NVIs for drug development.
