judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes the systematic curation and combined-evidence prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs) to address the lack of approved treatment for Nipah virus, a pathogen with over 75% case fatality rate. The authors developed the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK), a LAMP-based web platform containing 182 entries (98 unique small molecule inhibitors, 125 total small molecule entries, with 57 being peptides or incomplete). Data was sourced from PubMed and Google using a scoring system (0–10) on 838 papers, followed by manual curation by a two-team verification system. The study computed 1875 descriptors per compound using PaDel and performed comparative analysis against 2,346 FDA-approved compounds and 4,644 Enamine antivirals. A two-pronged prioritization strategy was applied: (1) robustness of the assays used to identify the compounds, and (2) drug-likeness filtering using DruLito (Lipinski, Veber, MDDR-like, Ghose, BBB, CMC-50, QED) and PAINS. Of 98 unique small molecule NVIs, 34 showed structural similarity to 76 FDA drugs. DruLito filtering was highly restrictive, with only 2 of 91 compounds passing all filters except CMC. The independent assay-robustness screen prioritized 11 NVIs, of which NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and showed overlap with FDA-approved physicochemical ranges. CIC0032 exhibited the best activity among the shortlisted three. Clustering using Jarp revealed 90 clusters, with 84 singletons (93.3%), confirming high chemical diversity. IC50/EC50 values ranged from 0.47 nM to 7,562,710 nM. The NVIK platform supports text, structure, and complex query searches (SMILES, SDF, MOL, JSME drawing), near-neighbor identification (NNeib 5.12.0), clustering (Jarp 6.0.2), and CIRCOS/Cytoscape visualizations. The work is positioned as a centralized resource aligned with WHO's priority disease R&D blueprint.

Research Context
Nipah virus is a negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus causing severe disease with a mortality rate of 50–100%. The first outbreak occurred in Malaysia (1998–1999) followed by annual outbreaks in Bangladesh and India (2001–present). NiV causes cell-to-cell fusion forming multinucleated cells called syncytia, influencing pathogenicity. Currently there is no known treatment for Nipah disease, and WHO has listed NiV on its R&D Blueprint priority diseases. Broad-spectrum antiviral ribavirin showed contradictory results with reduction of mortality below 50% at best. Despite reports of NVIs from screening large libraries, no systematic evaluation of reported compounds has been performed. Existing databases (IRD, ViPR) contain limited or no information focused on Nipah virus inhibitors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to systematically curate, characterize, and prioritize Nipah virus inhibitors from heterogeneous literature data. The authors hypothesize that a combined-evidence approach—merging assay robustness with drug-likeness parameters—can identify the most promising NVIs for further development. The study predicts that filtering through DruLito and PAINS, combined with independent assay-robustness ranking, will narrow the candidate pool to actionable druglike molecules. A specific predicted outcome is that structural similarity to FDA-approved compounds can guide repurposing or scaffold identification. The hypothesis also includes that clustering analysis will reveal chemical diversity and potential common pharmacophore features across molecular weight ranges.

Methodological Details
Inhibitors were collected from PubMed and Google using the query 'Nipah' with keywords in abstract/title. A total of 838 papers were initially considered for data-mining. A scoring system was applied: 10 for confirmed inhibitor info in abstract, 5 for potential info, 4 for peptides, 0 for no relevance. Papers with scores 4–10 were manually curated by a team to create the NVIK sheet. Data quality was ensured by a separate curation team re-performing curation; errors were marked Red and verified Green. Data curation was done manually and stored in an NVIK-Open resource Sheet as a crowdsourcing platform. Each entry was tagged with the contributor's email ID. The platform was developed using LAMP (Linux-Apache-Mysql-PHP) server technology with PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS. Near neighbors were identified using NNeib version 5.12.0. Clusters were obtained using Jarp version 6.0.2 based on (1-Tanimoto coefficient) with a dissimilarity threshold of 0.15. A total of 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. Physicochemical properties depicted in CIRCOS were defined with 98 inhibitors and a band width of 1000. Comparison was made against 2,346 FDA-approved compounds and 4,644 Enamine nucleoside-like antivirals. The database contains 182 entries, of which 125 were small molecule entries (98 unique) and 57 were peptides or incomplete. EC50/IC50 values ranged from 0.25 nM to 7,562,710 nM for 182 entries.

Procedures And Architectures
NVIK is accessible via a web platform at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah since May 2018. Three search options are available: Simple Search (text-based), Query Builder (logical operators AND/OR), and Structure Search. Structure Search supports SMILES, SDF, and MOL formats plus a JSME in-browser compound drawing tool. Browsing allows inspection of molecular weight, XLogP, TopoPSA, HBD, HBA, and rotatable bonds. Drug-likeness was evaluated via DruLito screening using eight filters: Lipinski, MDDR-like, Veber, Ghose, BBB, CMC-50, and QED (weighted/unweighted). The PAINS filter was applied to each compound to study toxicity profiles. Compound network diagrams (CND) were made using Cytoscape to visualize clusters. Customized CIRCOS was used to represent relationships among physicochemical properties of NVIs. The combined evidence approach first ranked NVIs by assay robustness, then applied DruLito and PAINS filtering, and finally compared to FDA/Enamine properties.

Key Results
The NVIK database contains 182 total entries, of which 98 are unique small molecule NiV inhibitors. EC50/IC50 values for 70 of 98 unique inhibitors were obtained, ranging from 0.47 nM to 7,562,710 nM. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters, with 84 singletons (93.3%) and 14 non-singletons (15.5%). In total, 34 NVIs showed structural similarity to 76 FDA-approved drugs. Example: NVIC0097 (5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine) showed structural similarity to four FDA molecules: Adenosine, Vidarabine, Fludarabine, and Ademetionine. DruLito filtering: only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except the CMC filter. The independent assay-robustness evaluation prioritized 11 NVIs for further study. Of these three shortlisted compounds (NVIC0025, NVIC0032, NVIC0048), NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and displayed a high degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges. NVIC0032 exhibited better activity among the three and had considerable overlap with FDA-approved physicochemical properties. GS-441524 (531.202 g/mol) was identified as a near neighbor of GS-441524 ("NUC") (291.267 g/mol), suggesting common structural features. Most compounds in NVIK are cyclic in nature. For the majority of NVIs, the distribution of all six Lipinski/Veber properties was similar to FDA-approved drugs. The platform allows submission of new inhibitors, as stated in the conclusions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high number of singleton clusters (93.3%) indicates the NVIK library is chemically diverse, offering multiple scaffolds for further development. Near-neighbor relationships across different molecular weight ranges suggest common structural features responsible for antiviral activity against NiV. The combined evidence strategy (assay robustness + drug-likeness) provides a more robust prioritization framework than either metric alone. The structural similarity to FDA drugs suggests potential for repurposing or identifying safe scaffolds for anti-Nipah development. The identification of compounds with both bioactivity and drug-like properties (NVIC0048, NVIC0032) provides validated starting points for medicinal chemistry.

Contradictions And Limitations
57 of 182 entries were either peptides or lacked complete information, limiting the scope of the small-molecule analysis. EC50/IC50 values were only obtained for 70 of 98 unique inhibitors, leaving 28 without quantified activity data. The DruLito filter was highly restrictive: only 2 of 91 compounds passed all filters except CMC, suggesting most reported NVIs are not druglike. The ranking of 'top 10' NVIs is mentioned in the conclusion but the specific ranking list is not fully detailed in the text. The authors note studies are planned to assess efficacy of remdesivir over time, indicating the status of some antivirals is still preliminary. The scoring system for paper selection (10, 5, 4, 0) introduces subjectivity in what constitutes 'confirmed' inhibitor information. The platform relies on crowdsourcing for data submission, which requires continuous verification to maintain data quality.

Claims
The NVIK platform provides a systematically curated, validated knowledgebase of Nipah virus inhibitors that outperforms existing scattered datasets. NVIK contains 182 entries, 98 unique small molecule inhibitors, with 98% of which have structure data. Two teams independently verified curation, with errors marked in Red and Green. The platform supports complex queries, structure searches, and crowdsourced submissions. 93.3% of NVIs are in singleton clusters, demonstrating extreme chemical diversity. Only 70 of 98 unique inhibitors have quantitative EC50/IC50 data. 57 entries are not complete small molecules (peptides or partial info). The platform enables the community to contribute and access NVI data in a seamless manner, accelerating anti-NiV R&D. Compounds may be utilized for antiviral activity against other viruses beyond Nipah.
A combined evidence strategy of assay robustness and drug-likeness prioritization successfully identifies actionable NVIs for drug development. 11 NVIs were prioritized based on assay robustness alone. NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and showed FDA-property overlap. NVIC0048 displayed a high degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges. Only 2 of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except CMC, indicating most NVIs fail druglike criteria. This multi-pronged approach reduces the false-positive rate in compound selection for NiV inhibitors.

Data And Code Availability
The data is publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah and was made accessible since the inception of the project (May 2018). The platform includes a submission form for users to submit new compounds. Compounds are mapped to Pubchem/Chemspider IDs wherever possible for linkage to external databases.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A separate team re-performed curation independent of the initial team to ensure data quality. Errors in the curation sheet were marked in 'Red' and only marked 'Green' once verified by both teams. Each entry was tagged with its contributor's email ID for traceability. The assay robustness prioritization was performed independently of the drug-likeness filtering. Comparison against FDA-approved compounds (2,346) and Enamine antivirals (4,644) serves as a reference baseline.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the unique fields in the database and the major fields for browsing. Table 1 shows the predefined data structure for the NVIK sheet. Figure 2 depicts the overall distribution of physicochemical properties, the compound network diagram, and the near neighbors among NVIs. Figure 3 compares physicochemical properties of NVIs with FDA approved compounds (2,346) and Enamine antivirals (4,644). Figure 4 shows the DruLito filter results, where only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except CMC. Table 2 shows the comparison of prioritized NVIs with FDA approved compounds for molecular weight, HBD, HBA, rotatable bonds, XLogP, and TopoPSA.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the creation of the NVIK platform, a curated knowledgebase of 182 Nipah virus inhibitor entries with a two-pronged prioritization strategy combining assay robustness and drug-likeness filtering. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of NVIC0048 and NVIC0032 as NVIs that pass multiple DruLito filters and show overlap with FDA-approved physicochemical properties, validated by independent assay-robustness ranking and structural similarity to FDA drugs. 3. The future path involves continuous crowdsourced curation of new NVIs, further chemical scaffold development, and potential application of prioritized NVIs against other viruses beyond Nipah.

summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang; Leping Zhang; Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.field_subfield: Hematology / Cancer Genomics - 3D Genome Architecture
summary.type_of_paper: Original research article reporting integrated Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq analyses of 18 T-ALL patient samples
summary.executive_summary: This study provides the first integrated 3D genome and transcriptome analysis of newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients. By performing BL-Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq on 18 T-ALL patient samples and 4 healthy T cell controls, the authors demonstrate that 3D genome organization at the compartment, TAD, and loop levels hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% (996/3392) of differentially expressed genes were associated with 3D genome alterations, with a further estimate indicating 3D genome alterations associate with ~45% of upregulated genes. The study identified 34 novel translocations in noncoding regions and 44 translocation-mediated loops forming new interchromosomal interactions. A key finding is the identification of translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking, where genes like TLX3 hijack enhancers from BCL11B and TRB, driving ectopic T-ALL-associated transcription factor expression. Furthermore, the study characterized the HOXA cluster (11 genes) dysregulation, revealing that T-ALLs with HOXA overexpression are heterogeneous entities; specifically, ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression (associated with the 5' TAD) is linked to DN and ETP phenotypes and poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALLs. The authors also identified CDK6 as a potential therapeutic target. The findings highlight the critical role of 3D genome architecture in T-ALL etiology, differentiation blockade, and prognostic stratification, with JAK-STAT pathway mutations enriched in HOXA11-A13+ cases.

claims.description: 3D genome organization hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to T cell differentiation trajectory.
Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusion drive ectopic T-ALL-associated transcription factor expression.
Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is an independent predictor of poor overall survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALL and is enriched for JAK-STAT pathway mutations.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study provides the first integrated 3D genome and transcriptome analysis of newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients. By performing BL-Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq on 18 T-ALL patient samples and 4 healthy T cell controls, the authors demonstrate that 3D genome organization at the compartment, TAD, and loop levels hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% (996/3392) of differentially expressed genes were associated with 3D genome alterations, with a further estimate indicating 3D genome alterations associate with ~45% of upregulated genes. The study identified 34 novel translocations in noncoding regions and 44 translocation-mediated loops forming new interchromosomal interactions. A key finding is the identification of translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking, where genes like TLX3 hijack enhancers from BCL11B and TRB, driving ectopic T-ALL-associated transcription factor expression. Furthermore, the study characterized the HOXA cluster (11 genes) dysregulation, revealing that T-ALLs with HOXA overexpression are heterogeneous entities; specifically, ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression (associated with the 5' TAD) is linked to DN and ETP phenotypes and poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALLs. The authors also identified CDK6 as a potential therapeutic target. The findings highlight the critical role of 3D genome architecture in T-ALL etiology, differentiation blockade, and prognostic stratification, with JAK-STAT pathway mutations enriched in HOXA11-A13+ cases.

Research Context
While 3D genome alterations have been demonstrated to play important roles in tumorigenesis and hematological malignancies, how such alterations provide key insights into T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia patients remains largely unknown. Prior work had identified 3D genome alterations in cancer generally, but no comprehensive integrated analysis of 3D genome architecture and transcriptome changes had been performed in newly diagnosed T-ALL. The etiology of T-ALL development and its classification into ETP and non-ETP subtypes based on differentiation stall points had not been mechanistically linked to chromosomal 3D organization.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question asks how 3D genome alterations and differentially expressed genes in newly diagnosed T-ALL patients interrelate to drive T-ALL development and differentiate subtypes. The authors hypothesized that 3D genome organization at compartment, TAD, and loop levels, along with gene expression profiles, could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. A specific hypothesis was that the chromosomal organizations of T-ALL represent different "frozen stages" of T cell development, where ETP ALL samples stall at the early T progenitor stage and non-ETP ALLs at later differentiation stages. The study further hypothesized that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusion events drive ectopic transcription factor activation, leading to specific pathogenic gene expression profiles of T-ALL subgroups. A secondary question investigated whether HOXA-positive T-ALLs represent a homogeneous clinical entity and what specific HOXA genes contribute to poor prognosis.

Methodological Details
Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under a protocol approved by the ethics committee of the Institute of Hematology at Peking University. Leukemia blast cells were prepared by density-gradient centrifugation of bone marrow samples and further purified (CD19-CD14-CD235-CD45+CD7+) by FACS analysis for both RNA-seq and Hi-C library preparations. Four peripheral blood samples from healthy donors were obtained under approval from the Peking University ethics committee. T cells from healthy donors were purified using the EasySep Direct Human T Cell Isolation Kit. RNA-seq libraries were prepared with TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2, generating paired-end reads with an average depth of 15 million read pairs. Hi-C was performed on one million cells per sample according to the BL-Hi-C protocol. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq reads were mapped to hg19 using Bowtie2 with default parameters. Raw RNA-seq data for the Houcy and Jurkat cell lines were downloaded from the GEO database and analyzed alongside patient samples. DESeq2 was used to identify differentially expressed genes with FDR <0.01 and fold change >2. CTCF motif detection was performed using FIMO with a 20 bp motif from the Homer database in Loucy and Jurkat CTCF peaks.

Procedures And Architectures
Reads were aligned to hg19 with TopHat v2.1.0; duplicates were removed, and FPKM normalization was performed using HTSeq. Juicer was used to generate merged Hi-C contact matrices, and Knight-Ruiz (KR) normalization was applied for compartment and TAD analyses. Compartments were calculated under 100 kb resolution with the over 70% sample majority rule. TAD boundaries were calculated by the insulation score method on pooled 40 kb Hi-C matrices of healthy controls, ETP, and non-ETP samples. The domain score was calculated by dividing intra-TAD interactions with all interactions connected to the corresponding TAD. Loops were called using HiCCUPS, and differential loop detection was adapted from Douglas et al. with loops split into distance ranges of > or < 150 kb. hic_breakfinder was adapted to detect translocations; chimeric reads from BL-Hi-C data were treated as single ends with 5-20 kb resolution for breakpoint refinement. Translocation-mediated loops were manually recorded using Juicebox after loop detection tools could not reliably identify them. GREAT was used to analyze loop anchor biological processes, and DAVID was used for KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. ChIP-seq analysis of the HOXA+ Loucy cell line was used to correlate increased loop interactions with H3K27ac histone mark gains.

Key Results
Approximately 29% (996/3392) of DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. 3D genome alterations were associated with nearly 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL (estimated after eliminating overlapping upregulated DEGs). Among the estimated 45%, 56% could be directly related to structural alterations, while the remaining 44% could be due to structure alteration-mediated dysregulated transcription factors. The CDK6 locus exhibited a strong intra-TAD interaction and its expression was upregulated in all T-ALL samples. 46 translocations were identified in 14/18 T-ALL samples, of which 34 were novel events and 26 were interchromosomal. Among 78 unique breakpoints, 47% were in noncoding regions and 66% were in the stable A compartment. 44 new loops were formed between translocated chromosomes (translocation-mediated loops), with nearly 78% of CTCF-motif-bearing loops linked to pairs of convergently orientated CTCF motifs. The 3D genome landscape separated ETP ALL from non-ETP ALL samples, and further analysis identified 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops in ETP samples. A strong positive correlation (Pearson's correlation coefficient 0.685) was found between gene expression changes and the combined p-value of loop strength and D-score changes. Approximately 20% and 16% of upregulated genes in ETP and non-ETP ALL, respectively, harbored chromatin structure changes. Translocation-mediated fusion events could be detected in 5/7 HOXA-positive samples without HOXA translocation. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity alone or in combination was associated with poor overall and event-free survivals in young adult and pediatric T-ALLs. In multivariate analysis, HOXA13+ status served as an independent predictor for overall survival of pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. HOXA11-A13+ cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes and a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The chromosomal organization of T-ALL may represent different "frozen stages" of T cell development, providing a structural framework for the lineage differentiation blockade observed in leukemia. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusion events activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors ectopically, blocking normal differentiation at specific developmental stages. The partition of HOXA genes into two TADs with different boundary usage (C11/13 for 5' TAD, C7/9 or C10/11 for 3' TAD) explains how specific fusion events control a defined subset of HOXA genes. CTCF binding sites serve as insulators, preventing hijacked enhancers from influencing genes in the opposing TAD, thereby constraining the phenotypic output of translocations. The finding that JAK-STAT pathway mutations are enriched in HOXA11-A13+ cases suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit the subtype currently incurable by standard treatments. 3D genome alterations, in addition to oncogenic driver mutations, play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and regulating T-ALL development.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study reports no significant difference between healthy controls and HOXA-negative cases in the 12 HOXA interaction regions, limiting comparison of enhancer-gene interactions in healthy vs. malignant states. The analysis of HOXA gene expression was performed in a relatively small subset (7 samples without HOXA translocation plus 3 HOXA-T cases), which may limit generalizability of the TAD boundary usage findings. Sample 093 was identified as a unique case falling between ETP and non-ETP ALL, indicating that the binary classification of ETP vs. non-ETP may not capture all inter-stage transitional states. The association between HOXA13+ and survival was observed in a cohort from a companion paper, and the direct linkage to 3D genome architecture requires further validation in larger cohorts. The exact mechanism by which the various fusion proteins recruit DOT1L and activate the HOXA cluster epigenetically beyond the 3D genome level is not fully detailed.

Claims
3D genome organization hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to T cell differentiation trajectory. PCA and hierarchical clustering of both 3D genome features and transcriptome changes showed high consistency in separating ETP and non-ETP samples. ETP samples arrested at the immature LMPP to Thy1 stages, while non-ETP samples were at the Thy2 to Thy4 stages. Loop-based hierarchical clustering matched T-ALL subtypes signified by chromosomal translocation-mediated dysregulation. Sample 093 fell between ETP and non-ETP ALL with significant TCR rearrangement, suggesting intermediate phenotypes that do not cleanly fit the binary classification. The chromosomal structure of T-ALL may serve as a diagnostic or prognostic stratification tool reflecting developmental arrest points.
Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusion drive ectopic T-ALL-associated transcription factor expression. TLX3 hijacked enhancers from BCL11B via translocation-mediated loops in ETP, TLX, and TAL subtypes. Most hijacked enhancers are from genes normally expressed during T cell development (BCL11B, TRB), leading to ectopic T-ALL transcription factor activation. Fourteen out of eighteen samples harbored translocations with 44 translocation-mediated loops. Not all genes in the HOXA cluster showed ectopic expression; only HOXA11-A13 were associated with immature phenotypes and poor outcomes. The hijacking mechanism provides a structural basis for how T-ALL-associated transcription factors are activated and differentiation is blocked.
Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is an independent predictor of poor overall survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALL and is enriched for JAK-STAT pathway mutations. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity was associated with poor overall and event-free survivals. HOXA13+ status served as an independent predictor in multivariate analysis. HOXA11-A13+ cases had a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations. TAL1/2 positivity was mutually exclusive from HOXA positivity and associated with better survival. HOXA9 expression, previously used as a biomarker, was not associated with poor survival in this study. TLX positivity had no association with outcome. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit the HOXA11-A13+ subgroup, which is currently incurable by standard treatments.

Data And Code Availability
Raw RNA-seq data for the Houcy and Jurkat cell lines were downloaded from the GEO database. Supplementary Tables and Supplementary Figures (including Tables 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and Figures 1a-h, 2a-h, 4a-d, 5a-h, 6a-h) contain supporting data. The authors mention a companion paper for outcome information but the specific data/code access policy is not detailed in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
TAD boundary calculation was performed on pooled 40 kb Hi-C matrices to ensure consistency across conditions. Loop detection was split into two distance ranges (> or < 150 kb) to minimize potential bias. Differential TAD boundaries required a t-test FDR <0.01 and a difference higher than 50% quantile of the overall difference. Differential domain scores required a t-test FDR <0.01 and fold change higher than 70% quantile. Differential loop calling required FDR <0.1. The analysis used HOXA-negative samples as a common denominator to calculate differential interaction intensities for the 12 HOXA enhancer regions. ChIP-seq analysis of the HOXA+ Loucy cell line was used to correlate increased loop interactions with H3K27ac mark gains, providing orthogonal validation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a: PCA and hierarchical clustering showing transcriptome changes consistent with 3D genome structural changes. Figure 1c: Bar plots showing upregulated (red) and downregulated (blue) DEGs associated with compartment, domain score, and loop changes. Figure 2a: PCA separating ETP ALL from non-ETP ALL based on loop-level 3D genome landscape. Figure 3a: Hi-C maps showing 46 translocations in 14/18 samples with red lines indicating translocation-mediated loops. Figure 4a: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering based on HOXA gene expressions separating HOXA-positive samples into 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups. Figure 5: Visualization of translocation-mediated new loops between the 5' HOXA cluster and active enhancers of BCL11B and ERG. Figure 6: Survival curves demonstrating HOXA13+ status as an independent predictor and JAK-STAT pathway mutation enrichment. Supplementary Table 5: Precise breakpoint locations for 46 translocations at single base-pair resolution. Supplementary Table 6: Translocation-mediated loops with genes and promoter overlaps annotated. Supplementary Table 4: Genes associated with ETP and non-ETP loop-associated expression changes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first integrated 3D genome and transcriptome characterization of T-ALL, demonstrating that chromosomal architecture hierarchically classifies subtypes and that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking drives ectopic transcription factor activation. 2. The strongest evidence is the consistent alignment of 3D genome structural changes with transcriptome changes (PCA and hierarchical clustering), the identification of 44 translocation-mediated loops with 78% CTCF motif conservation, and the multivariate independent association of HOXA13+ with poor survival. 3. The future path involves validation of JAK-STAT pathway mutations and HOXA13 status as therapeutic targets in larger cohorts, refinement of 3D genome diagnostic markers, and exploration of the loop extrusion mechanism in T-ALL.

summary.title: ProNetView-ccRCC: A web-based portal to interactively explore clear cell renal cell carcinoma proteogenomics networks
summary.authors: Selim Kalayci; Francesca Petralia; Pei Wang; Zeynep H Gümüş
summary.field_subfield: Bioinformatics / Network Visualization / Computational Oncology
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces ProNetView-ccRCC, an open-access, interactive web-based network exploration portal designed to visualize and navigate phosphopeptide co-expression networks derived from the Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) phosphoproteomics data. The CPTAC project has performed large-scale proteogenomic characterization of multiple cancer types, including ccRCC, generating gene/protein regulatory networks that capture higher-order molecular regulatory structures. However, these networks present significant challenges for visual communication due to their large dimensions and complicated topologies. The authors developed ProNetView-ccRCC using a 3D network exploration interface built on the Three.js framework for WebGL, incorporating 3D layout algorithms from the iCAVE desktop tool. The portal visualizes a network of 3,614 genes comprising 20,976 phosphopeptides across 103 ccRCC samples, with 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules identified via the Glay clustering algorithm. Users can interactively rotate, zoom, query specific genes (e.g., ERG), view neighbors, explore pathway enrichments (via Fisher Exact test), and query associations between phosphopeptide abundance and clinical variables such as tumor grade, age, gender, and FDR cut-offs. The tool requires no additional plugins and runs on all modern web browsers. The paper demonstrates the portal's functionality through example queries (ERG, Angiogenesis module, pathway exploration) and integrates with the ProTrack multi-omics tool for heatmap visualization, aiming to facilitate hypothesis generation for the cancer research community.

claims.description: ProNetView-ccRCC provides an intuitive and customized 3D exploration environment that overcomes the limitations of static 2D network visualizations for CPTAC co-expression networks.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces ProNetView-ccRCC, an open-access, interactive web-based network exploration portal designed to visualize and navigate phosphopeptide co-expression networks derived from the Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) phosphoproteomics data. The CPTAC project has performed large-scale proteogenomic characterization of multiple cancer types, including ccRCC, generating gene/protein regulatory networks that capture higher-order molecular regulatory structures. However, these networks present significant challenges for visual communication due to their large dimensions and complicated topologies. The authors developed ProNetView-ccRCC using a 3D network exploration interface built on the Three.js framework for WebGL, incorporating 3D layout algorithms from the iCAVE desktop tool. The portal visualizes a network of 3,614 genes comprising 20,976 phosphopeptides across 103 ccRCC samples, with 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules identified via the Glay clustering algorithm. Users can interactively rotate, zoom, query specific genes (e.g., ERG), view neighbors, explore pathway enrichments (via Fisher Exact test), and query associations between phosphopeptide abundance and clinical variables such as tumor grade, age, gender, and FDR cut-offs. The tool requires no additional plugins and runs on all modern web browsers. The paper demonstrates the portal's functionality through example queries (ERG, Angiogenesis module, pathway exploration) and integrates with the ProTrack multi-omics tool for heatmap visualization, aiming to facilitate hypothesis generation for the cancer research community.

Research Context
Recent advances in molecular profiling technologies enable large-scale integrative proteomic and genomic (proteogenomic) studies of cancers. The National Cancer Institute's Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) has performed comprehensive proteogenomic characterizations of tumor samples from breast, colon, ovarian, and kidney cancer patients. Co-expression networks derived from proteomics and phosphoproteomics data reveal regulatory relationships between proteins and posttranscriptional modifications (PTMs), bringing new insights on pathway dysfunctions driving tumor progression. While these networks contain rich information for identifying active pathways and oncogenic drivers, they are challenging to visually communicate due to their large dimensions and complicated topologies. These networks are best visually explored together with associated information between gene/protein activities, biological pathway annotations, and clinical outcomes. Current network data visual exploration tools are mainly used for visually communicating networks as static 2D images in print publications and are not well suited for user-initiated interactive network explorations. A centralized platform customized for CPTAC co-expression networks and associated meta-data is necessary to make these resources readily available to the cancer research community.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central challenge is to effectively visualize and navigate the resulting network models that capture higher-order structures in proteogenomic profiles. There is a pressing need for a new open community resource tool for intuitive visual exploration, interpretation, and communication of gene/protein regulatory networks by the cancer research community. The paper hypothesizes that a web-based interactive portal can provide an intuitive and customized exploration environment for phosphopeptide co-expression networks and other analysis results from CPTAC ccRCC study. A 3D network exploration interface was hypothesized to enable quick and easy interactions with the ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network as well as 30 functional network modules and their associated meta-data. Users were expected to be able to conveniently query for association between abundance of each phosphopeptide in the network and clinical variables such as tumor grade. The portal was intended to facilitate researchers from a wide spectrum of computational skill levels to conduct their own analyses and share/communicate results.

Methodological Details
The network characterizes the co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC. The network was derived using a random-forest based network construction algorithm based on phospho-peptide level data of 103 ccRCC samples. The network displays association among genes based on phosphopeptide level data with two genes being connected if at least two phosphopeptides mapping to the two genes are associated to each other. The overall network comprises 3,614 genes, as well as 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules. Network modules were derived by using the Glay clustering algorithm. 30 modules containing at least 20 genes were identified and each was presented as a different module network. For each module network, pathway enrichment analysis was performed via Fisher Exact test and overrepresented pathways were incorporated as associated meta-data. For intuitive exploration, ProNetView-ccRCC enables interactive explorations in 3D by building on the Three.js framework which provides an interface for WebGL. Network layouts were calculated using 3D layout algorithms within iCAVE, a desktop-based tool developed earlier for stereoscopic and immersive exploration of networks. Multiple client-side Javascript libraries (D3.js, dataTables.js, JQuery, etc.) were utilized to handle various user interaction events in real time. For the styling of web interface elements, Bootstrap v3.3.7 was primarily utilized integrated with custom styling. The portal utilizes only standard libraries and does not require the use of any additional plug-ins, running on all modern web browsers.

Procedures And Architectures
The landing page provides the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network and links it to functional network modules. Users can interactively explore the large and dense topology in 3D by rotating and zooming in/out the view. Six modules within the network were significantly associated with biological pathways and highlighted using different coloring of nodes. Searching for the oncogene ERG (associated with VEGF response) highlights the corresponding node in red and identifies it as member of the Angiogenesis enriched module network. The query returns a list of genes whose phosphopeptides were directly connected to ERG and provides association with tumor grade and other phenotypes. Clicking on a module name displays a snapshot of that module network; node sizes are proportional to the number of connections. Hovering over a node displays the gene name of the phosphopeptide, and clicking on the node displays associated gene-level meta-data in a separate panel. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes within the same module and maps to 5 different peptides. The Heatmap link directs users to ProTrack, which provides a web-based interface to explore ccRCC multi-omics data through interactive heatmaps. Users can construct a simple query for genes with similar association to tumor grade by specifying phenotype (grade) and FDR cutoff value (FDR=20%). The portal displays and provides interactive exploration capabilities for any pathway enriched in a network module, with pathways sorted by p-values. Clicking a pathway name returns the list of associated genes (e.g., BRCA1, CDC20, CDK1, etc.) in a textbox and highlights them in red in the network exploration panel.

Key Results
The network comprises 3,614 genes representing the co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides. 30 functional network modules containing at least 20 genes each were identified using the Glay clustering algorithm. Six modules were significantly associated with biological pathways, as validated by Fisher Exact test. For the oncogene ERG, the association with tumor grade yielded a p-value: 0.003 and FDR: 0.118. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes within the Angiogenesis enriched module and maps to 5 different peptides. The portal allows filtering genes by phenotype and FDR cutoff, with example FDR=20% demonstrated in the use case. The interactive table lists enriched pathways sorted by p-values for each module. The tool runs on all modern web browsers without the need for any additional plugins or libraries.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
ProNetView-ccRCC addresses the gap between rich proteogenomic network information and effective visual communication by providing an interactive 3D exploration environment. The tool enables users to understand the phosphopeptide network in the context of markers of user interest, helping guide hypothesis generation for future studies. By integrating pathway enrichment meta-data, clinical phenotype querying, and multi-omics heatmap visualization, the tool contextualizes network topology within biological and clinical frameworks. The ability to query specific genes and view their immediate neighbors directly supports identifying oncogenic drivers and active pathway members within a complex network. The tool is intended to facilitate researchers from a wide spectrum of computational skill levels to conduct their own analyses on the rich CPTAC ccRCC network data.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report any formal validation, usability testing, or user evaluation metrics; no performance benchmarks are provided. The network was constructed using a random-forest based algorithm; the specific hyperparameters and model details beyond the algorithm type are not fully reported. The number of samples (103 ccRCC) and number of phosphopeptides (20,976) are fixed from the CPTAC data; the paper does not report sensitivity analyses for network stability. The tool integrates with the ProTrack tool, but no quantitative performance or accuracy metrics for this integration are provided. No mention of computational runtime for layout generation or 3D rendering performance on different hardware is provided.

Claims
ProNetView-ccRCC provides an intuitive and customized 3D exploration environment that overcomes the limitations of static 2D network visualizations for CPTAC co-expression networks. The tool uses Three.js for 3D WebGL rendering and iCAVE 3D layout algorithms to handle large dense topologies. Users can rotate and zoom in/out to explore the 3,614-gene, 20,976-phosphopeptide network. 30 modules are available as separate network views with proportional node sizing. No user study, survey, or quantitative usability metric is reported to verify whether the interface is actually 'intuitive' for researchers. Performance of 3D rendering with ~3,600 nodes is not quantified across different devices or browsers. Successful adoption would enable rapid hypothesis generation and more effective communication of network results by non-expert researchers. The tool could serve as a model for other CPTAC cancer types and other proteogenomic consortia.

Data And Code Availability
The portal is an open-access freely available resource at http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/. The paper does not explicitly state whether the underlying network construction code, web application source code, or specific data files are individually distributable.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network layout. Figure 1B shows links to functional network modules with six modules highlighted by pathway association. Figure 1C demonstrates the query for ERG, its highlighted status, and associated p-value/FDR values. Figure 2A displays a snapshot of the Angiogenesis enriched module network (module 26). Figure 2B shows node-clicking behavior displaying gene-level meta-data and connections. Figure 2C shows the query interface for phenotype (grade) and FDR cutoff. Figure 2D shows the results of the phenotype query with highlighted nodes. Figure 3A displays the interactive table of enriched pathways for module 18. Figure 3B shows pathway-specific gene highlights in the network panel.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is ProNetView-ccRCC, an open-access 3D interactive web portal that enables visual exploration of a 3,614-gene, 20,976-phosphopeptide co-expression network with 30 functional modules and clinical meta-data integration. 2. The strongest evidence of utility is demonstrated via the ERG example query, where a p-value: 0.003 (FDR: 0.118) and 11 direct connections in the Angiogenesis module were retrieved through the interactive interface. 3. The future path involves facilitating hypothesis generation for researchers with varied computational skills, potentially extending the portal to other CPTAC cancer types and proteogenomic networks.

summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee; Anabel Eckerling; Boaz Israeli; Gali Yanovich; Ella Rosenne; Suzana Fichman-Horn; Ido Ben Zvi; Liat Sorski; Ronit Satchi-Fainaro; Tamar Geiger; Erica K Sloan; Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu
summary.field_subfield: Cancer Biology / Metastasis Research / Systems Oncology
summary.type_of_paper: Original Research Article with In Vivo Animal Model and Retrospective Patient Data
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first animal model demonstrating spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT) in breast cancer, identifying the PT-derived secretome as a critical mediator of early metastatic growth. Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells expressing highly sensitive luciferase transduced into luciferase-mCherry vectors, the authors established a system to monitor micro-metastases in real-time within BALB/c nu/nu mice. Upon PT excision (average volume 80 mm³), a dramatic 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal was observed within 24 hours (p<0.0001), and metastases entered a latent state with no signal increase for 50 days, confirmed by H&E staining. Regression was significantly more prominent in small (10⁶ photons/s) versus large (10⁷ photons/s) metastatic foci (p<0.000). Tumor-conditioned medium (CM) was shown in vitro to enhance cell viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and endothelial tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo supplementation of the secretome via osmotic minipumps (providing approximately 1/8 of in vivo production) reduced regression by 10-fold compared to serum-free controls (p<0.005), confirming that PT-secreted factors support survival of distant metastases. Human cytokine array and mass spectrometry proteomic analysis (2,600 proteins identified; 359 extracellular factors) narrowed down four key mediators: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. Simultaneous in vivo neutralization of these four factors with mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies completely blocked metastatic progression in the presence of PT (p<0.0001). Retrospective analysis of the public TCGA provisional dataset for lung adenocarcinoma confirmed that high protein levels of these four factors correlated with poor survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The authors conclude that the PT secretome promotes early metastatic stages through shared pathways of angiogenesis, apoptosis regulation, focal adhesion, and metalloprotease regulation, and that the perioperative period offers a therapeutic window to control minimal residual disease by neutralizing these pro-metastatic factors.

claims.description: Primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of micro-metastases mediated by elimination of the PT-derived secretome.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF are key PT-secreted mediators promoting metastatic growth, and their neutralization arrests progression.

summary.ethical_considerations: All procedures were approved by Monash University or Tel-Aviv University Animal Ethics Committees.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first animal model demonstrating spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT) in breast cancer, identifying the PT-derived secretome as a critical mediator of early metastatic growth. Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells expressing highly sensitive luciferase transduced into luciferase-mCherry vectors, the authors established a system to monitor micro-metastases in real-time within BALB/c nu/nu mice. Upon PT excision (average volume 80 mm³), a dramatic 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal was observed within 24 hours (p<0.0001), and metastases entered a latent state with no signal increase for 50 days, confirmed by H&E staining. Regression was significantly more prominent in small (10⁶ photons/s) versus large (10⁷ photons/s) metastatic foci (p<0.000). Tumor-conditioned medium (CM) was shown in vitro to enhance cell viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and endothelial tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo supplementation of the secretome via osmotic minipumps (providing approximately 1/8 of in vivo production) reduced regression by 10-fold compared to serum-free controls (p<0.005), confirming that PT-secreted factors support survival of distant metastases. Human cytokine array and mass spectrometry proteomic analysis (2,600 proteins identified; 359 extracellular factors) narrowed down four key mediators: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. Simultaneous in vivo neutralization of these four factors with mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies completely blocked metastatic progression in the presence of PT (p<0.0001). Retrospective analysis of the public TCGA provisional dataset for lung adenocarcinoma confirmed that high protein levels of these four factors correlated with poor survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The authors conclude that the PT secretome promotes early metastatic stages through shared pathways of angiogenesis, apoptosis regulation, focal adhesion, and metalloprotease regulation, and that the perioperative period offers a therapeutic window to control minimal residual disease by neutralizing these pro-metastatic factors.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, yet this approach has been suggested to accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease through surgical-procedure-triggered processes. Alternatively, various case studies report spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis, particularly in breast and lung cancers, though the mechanisms remain elusive. Proposed mechanisms include surgical trauma, vascular insufficiency, or elimination of PT-derived stimulating factors, but no animal model of spontaneous regression exists to test these hypotheses. The realization that cancer is a systemic disease with continuous crosstalk between the PT, microenvironment, and distant organs stresses the need to study PT-metastasis interactions. The gap is that no model has been able to detect and study the early-stage regression of micro-metastases into latent foci, limiting mechanistic understanding.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of distant micro-metastases and whether this is mediated by elimination of PT-secreted factors. The authors hypothesize that PT-derived factors support survival and growth of distant micro-metastases, and that their removal by surgery induces regression. They further hypothesize that regression is stage-specific, more prominent in small metastatic foci where autocrine self-sufficiency is insufficient. The secondary hypothesis is that specific secreted mediators (cytokines, growth factors) can be identified and their blockade will mimic PT removal and arrest metastasis. The clinical hypothesis is that high levels of these secretome factors correlate with poor patient survival in lung adenocarcinoma.

Methodological Details
MDA-MB-231 HM cells (a highly metastatic triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma variant) were transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% glutamax, 4.5g/L D-glucose, and 110mg/L sodium pyruvate at 37°C and 5% CO₂. Eight-week-old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were injected with 2×10⁵ cells in 20 μl PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad under 2% isoflurane anesthesia. PT volume was calculated by (length × width²)×0.5; metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging using an IVIS spectrum apparatus after i.p. injection of 150 mg/kg D-luciferin sodium. Once metastatic foci reached a total count of 10⁶ photons/s (~3-4 weeks post-injection), the PT (average size 80 mm³) was excised. Sham surgery involved an identical incision with the PT untouched; complete PT removal was verified by bioluminescence imaging. Tumor-cell-conditioned medium (CM) was produced by incubating ~80% confluent cells in serum-free medium for 24 h at 37°C, 5% CO₂. CM was collected from ~30 million cells, filtered through 0.45 μm, and concentrated by 3 kDa Amicon filters to 100 μl/mouse, stored at -20°C. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with CM or SM and implanted i.p. immediately following tumor excision. The amount of secretome released by the minipump was estimated at ~1/8 of the amount produced in vivo by the ~80 mm³ primary tumor. Adhesion studies used IncuCyte imaging at 20 min intervals for 8 hours; apoptosis used AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD with flow cytometry after 24 h. Tube formation used 50 μl BME in 24-well plates with HUVEC reconstituted in CM or SM, imaged for 24 h. Human Cytokine Array (R&D Systems, Proteome Profiler TM Array, ARY022) compared 10² soluble proteins in CM, plasma from PT-bearing mice, post-excision mice, and controls. Mass spectrometry used LC-MS on an Easy-nLC1000 and Q-Exactive Plus with 140 min linear gradient; peptides digested with LysC/Trypsin. MaxQuant and LFQ algorithms were used; FDR of 0.01 applied to peptide and protein levels against a decoy database. Enrichment analysis used Gene Ontology annotations from UniProt (Fisher exact test, FDR <0.02); String database and Cytoscape for PPI networks. Mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies (R&D Systems) for IL-8, Serpin E1, PDGF-AA, and MIF were injected once daily (1 μg/mouse) for two days. Isotype control was mouse IgG1 (Clone #11711); H&E staining used 6 μm sections with 4% paraformaldehyde fixation. Statistical tests included repeated-measures or factorial ANOVA, Fisher's PLSD for pairwise, and Student's t-test; significance set at 0.05, two-sided.

Procedures And Architectures
The cancer model employed a luciferase-mCherry reporter in MDA-MB-231 HM cells to enable sensitive in vivo tracking of metastatic progression. The orthotopic metastasis model in nude mice allowed spontaneous formation of metastases in lymph nodes and lungs 2-4 weeks post-injection. A critical intervention threshold was set at 10⁶ photons/s for metastasis detection before PT excision. The secretome replenishment was validated by estimating that 50×10⁶ secretome-producing cells in the ~80 mm³ PT generate ~8 times more secretome than the minipump per day. The proteomics pipeline followed a multi-step process: concentration, 1:1 urea mixing, LysC/Trypsin digestion, StageTip cleanup, and UHPLC-MS analysis. The MS method (top10) performed high-resolution MS followed by HCD fragmentation of 10 most abundant peaks per scan. The patient outcome analysis used the public TCGA provisional dataset via cBioPortal for lung adenocarcinoma. The antibody neutralization experiment required injection 24 h prior to tumor excision, and was performed at early metastatic stages (bioluminescence <10⁶ p/s).

Key Results
Upon PT excision, metastatic signal decreased by up to 100-fold within 24 h (p<0.0001), confirming dramatic regression in the early post-surgical window. The regression was not immediate; it developed over 24 h, and no in vivo bioluminescent signal increase occurred for 50 days post-excision. Microscopic malignant foci were confirmed via H&E on both day 1 and day 50 post-excision, verifying regression into latent foci. Regression was significantly less prominent in large metastases (10⁷ photons/s) compared to small metastases (10⁶ photons/s), p<0.000. In sham surgery (PT untouched), metastases continued to increase, while in PT excision mice they regressed, p<0.05, ruling out surgical trauma as the mechanism. CM-treated cancer cells showed enhanced viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and endothelial tube formation (p<0.0001) compared to SM controls. Mice supplemented with CM via minipumps showed 10-fold less regression than SM controls, p<0.005, demonstrating PT-secreted factors support metastasis survival. Human cytokine array identified 28 cytokines highly expressed in CM, 4 of which (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) were validated by ELISA. MS proteomics identified 2,600 proteins, of which 359 were annotated as extracellular factors by GO. Pathway enrichment of the 359 extracellular proteins revealed involvement in apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. Simultaneous in vivo neutralization of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely blocked metastatic progression, p<0.0001. No difference in regression was evident on post-excision day 1 between antibody and IgG groups, as excision removes all secreted factors from both. TCGA analysis revealed high protein levels of all four factors correlated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05) in lung adenocarcinoma patients.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results indicate the PT secretome plays a vital supportive role in metastasis through shared and distinct pathways of angiogenesis, apoptosis suppression, and EMT. The finding that larger metastases are self-sufficient suggests the PT-support mechanism is critical specifically during the early micrometastatic window. The absence of regression in sham surgery rules out surgical trauma and vascular insufficiency as primary drivers of spontaneous regression. The data suggest that spontaneous regression, though rare in humans, may occur in a substantial portion of patients but remain undetected due to low sensitivity for micrometastases. The study implicates the perioperative period as a therapeutic window to control minimal residual disease by blocking PT support for micrometastases.

Contradictions And Limitations
The tumor-conditioned medium minipump supplementation only provided ~1/8 of the in vivo secretome, so complete replenishment was not achieved. The antibody neutralization was performed only for two days at 1 μg/mouse, which may not fully capture chronic secretome-dependence. The TCGA dataset used is a  The study was limited to one syngeneic model (MDA-MB-231 HM in nude mice); generalizability to other tumors or immunocompetent models is untested. The exact prevalence of post-operative regression of micrometastases in human cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations. The four factors identified were the only ones blocked; other secreted factors are likely involved in supporting metastatic progression. No random seed or exact number of biological replicates per treatment arm is explicitly reported in the text.

Claims
Primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of micro-metastases mediated by elimination of the PT-derived secretome. 100-fold decrease in metastatic signal within 24 h of PT excision (p<0.0001). Metastases regressed significantly in excision mice but continued to increase in sham surgery mice (p<0.05). CM-treated cells showed enhanced viability, adhesion, and tube formation in vitro. CM supplementation in vivo reduced regression 10-fold (p<0.005). Regression was significantly less prominent in large metastatic foci (10⁷ photons/s) versus small foci (10⁶ photons/s), p<0.000. The minipump only provided ~1/8 of the in vivo secretome amount. The perioperative period could be exploited to control minimal residual disease by blocking PT support for micrometastases. This may explain the rare but validated clinical phenomenon of spontaneous regression following PT excision.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF are key PT-secreted mediators promoting metastatic growth, and their neutralization arrests progression. Four factors were identified by cytokine array and validated by ELISA and MS proteomics. Pathway enrichment revealed roles in apoptosis, angiogenesis, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. In vivo neutralization of all four antibodies completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). High levels of these factors correlated with poor survival in TCGA lung adenocarcinoma patients (HR=2.05).5 No difference in regression on post-excision day 1 between antibody and IgG groups, as excision removes all secretome factors. Only four factors were tested; other secreted factors likely also support metastatic progression. Identifying critical pro-metastatic factors per patient may enable individually tailored perioperative antibody combination therapy. Targeting these factors may counteract the metastasis-promoting effects of surgery and tilt the balance toward eradication.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The sham surgery served as an ablation/control to rule out surgical procedure effects; metastases continued to increase in sham mice (p<0.05). The serum-free medium (SM) served as the control for CM supplementation, showing that secretome factors alone drive the phenotype. The isotype control (IgG1 Clone #11711) was used in the antibody neutralization experiment to rule out non-specific IgG effects. Technical replicates were averaged and used to represent biological replicates throughout the study. The antibody neutralization experiment was performed at early metastatic stages (<10⁶ p/s) to isolate early-stage effects.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B shows the time course of metastatic signal decrease following PT excision (100-fold drop within 24 h, p<0.0001). Figure 1C shows no in vivo bioluminescent signal increase for 50 days post-excision. Figure 1D shows H&E stained lung and lymph node sections from day 1 and day 50 post-excision confirming latent malignant foci. Figure 1E shows the comparison of regression in small (10⁶) vs large (10⁷) metastatic foci (p<0.000). Figure 1F shows metastases regressing in PT excision mice but continuing to increase in sham surgery mice (p<0.05). Figure 2A-C shows CM-induced viability, adhesion, and tube formation in vitro. Figure 2D shows 10-fold less regression in CM-treated mice vs SM controls (p<0.005). Figure 3A shows PPI networks identifying pathways involved in early stages of metastasis. Figure 3B shows antibody neutralization of four factors completely blocking metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Figure 3C shows no difference in regression on post-excision day 1 between antibody and IgG groups. Figure 3D shows Kaplan-Meier survival curves and hazard ratio (2.05, p<0.05) for the four-factor TCGA cohort. Table S1 lists the 28 cytokines from the human cytokine array with exclusion criteria.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first animal model demonstrating spontaneous regression of micro-metastases upon primary tumor excision, establishing the PT-secretome as a crucial early-stage support for metastatic foci. 2. The strongest evidence is the in vivo neutralization of four key factors (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) completely arresting metastatic progression (p<0.0001), combined with 100-fold reduction in metastatic signal post-excision and validation in TCGA patient data. 3. The future path involves validating this phenomenon in other cancer types, syngeneic models, and immunocompetent settings, with the goal of developing perioperative, patient-specific neutralizing antibody combinations to control minimal residual disease.
