judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation triggers global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells detectable by Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy. The authors treated RAW 264.7 macrophages with 1 µM K3 ODN (CpG DNA) or 0.5 µg/ml LPS and monitored molecular dynamics at four time points (10 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h) using ATR-FTIR. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified PC-1 as accounting for 83% of variability, with the 1750–850 cm⁻¹ region containing the highest variation. CpG DNA stimulation induced a significant increase in nucleic acid content starting at 10 min and persisting through 6 h (p < 0.1), with the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ showing the strongest activation signal (p < 0.001) maintained until 2 h. Protein content (Amide I, 1639 cm⁻¹) increased significantly from 10 min to 2 h (p < 0.001) and subsequently declined. LPS-treated cells showed elevated total RNA up to 2 h post-stimulation, consistent with LPS inhibiting DNA synthesis and inducing cell cycle arrest. Both CpG and LPS increased triglyceride and cholesterol markers (C=O stretch near 1741 cm⁻¹) from 10 min, and fatty acid concentration (C–O symmetric stretch, 1400 cm⁻¹), indicating shared de novo lipogenesis. The study is the first to demonstrate FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality for monitoring macrophage activation dynamics via bulk molecular fingerprinting, providing a rapid, non-invasive alternative to omics techniques.

Research Context
ATR-FTIR spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful biomedical tool enabling non-destructive, rapid, and high-throughput analysis of biological systems where all macromolecular changes are captured in a single spectrum. The technique can reveal changes in conformation and concentration of nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids simultaneously, with peak area providing quantitative concentration data and specific frequencies revealing chemical bond nature. The use of the ATR unit allows samples to be placed directly on the crystal without preparation steps, and a very small sample amount is sufficient for good quality spectra. Macrophage cells at the front line of the immune system exhibit high structural and functional plasticity allowing them to inspect the body and respond to challenges. Bacterial DNA containing unmethylated CpG oligodeoxynucleotides triggers macrophage proliferation, pro-inflammatory cytokine production, Th1 reaction induction, B cell proliferation, and other immune-activating responses. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), comprising approximately 75% of the gram-negative bacterial cell wall surface, stimulates monocytes and macrophages to release biological response mediators including pro-inflammatory cytokines and platelet-activating factor. Both CpG DNA and LPS activate the same downstream pathways including MyD88 adaptor and NF-kB and AP-1 transcription factors. While trending omics techniques provide precise quantitative data on specific molecules, they require complex sample preparation that can alter chemical ratios and post-translational modifications. The simple, rapid, and non-invasive experimental setup using bulk FTIR analysis provides a broad view of nucleic acids, lipids, proteins, and other metabolites not readily accessible by other techniques. Despite known effects of CpG and LPS on the immune system, how these activations impact relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins has not been studied.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation in murine macrophages leads to global molecular changes in cells that are detectable by FTIR spectroscopy. The authors hypothesized that both CpG DNA and LPS would induce detectable, time-dependent alterations in the relative concentrations of nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids within the macrophage cells. The study aimed to use ATR-FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor the activation dynamics of murine macrophages upon stimulation with CpG DNA and LPS. A secondary hypothesis was that CpG DNA and LPS would elicit distinct temporal profiles of macromolecular synthesis, particularly in nucleic acid metabolism during early activation stages. The expected outcome was that PCA analysis could identify principal sources of variation between treatment groups, followed by targeted peak analysis of specific molecular biomarkers. The authors predicted that CpG DNA would induce RNA synthesis before DNA synthesis, whereas LPS would inhibit DNA synthesis entirely. The study also tested whether both CpG and LPS would stimulate lipogenesis, as suggested by prior evidence of shared fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis pathways in macrophage activation. The ultimate objective was to establish FTIR as a rapid, high-throughput screening tool for defining macrophage activation states and defining global molecular consequences of TLR signaling.

Methodological Details
Murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 2 mM L-glutamine. Sub-culturing in a 1/10 ratio was performed every 2–3 days to maintain logarithmic growth, with cells harvested and centrifuged at 1000 rpm (208 g) for 10 min. Cells were resuspended at a concentration of 2×10⁶/mL for experimental application. Three experimental groups were tested: control treated with 0.9% PBS, CpG-stimulated with 1 µM K3 ODN (endotoxin-free), and LPS-stimulated with 0.5 µg/ml LPS. Four time points post-treatment were used to evaluate activation kinetics: 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h. At each time point, samples were spun at 1000 rpm, media discarded, washed with 15 mL of sterile PBS, and spun again to remove organic compounds and growth medium. Each group was scanned in three independent replicates, and n=5 replicates were used in data analysis. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with a mild N₂ flux for 5 min to allow cells to settle on the crystal. The ATR crystal was a Diamond-ZnSe crystal attached to a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer. The spectral region of interest was 4000–650 cm⁻¹ at 25°C, with air background subtracted automatically and PBS spectrum subtracted manually. Data acquisition used 128 scans at 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution, with the ATR surface cleaned using a water-ethanol-water sequence. Post-processing included 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction at 3800–2750–1800–900 cm⁻¹ points. Normality was tested using Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests in GraphPad Prism 8.3. Peak assignment was done using center-of-weight measurements and literature comparison, with second derivative spectra used for side-peak band assignment. Concentration studies were carried out by integrating curves under peaks, and conformational alteration studies used bandwidth measurements at 75% peak height.

Procedures And Architectures
The spectral data matrix was constructed from raw IR readings at 0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed using Unscrambler 11.0 (Camo, NO) in the 3000–650 cm⁻¹ region. PCA used the spectra imported directly, without initial information input, as an unsupervised multivariate data analysis method. Two PCA outputs were analyzed: Scores Plots showing clusters of similar data and Loadings Plots showing sources of highest variation. Principal Component 1 (PC-1) accounted for 83% of the variability, while PC-2 accounted for 11%. The 1750–850 cm⁻¹ IR region was identified by Loadings Plots as having the most significant spectral variation among samples. The Scores Plots showed considerable clustering of samples according to treatment across both PC directions. PCA guided selection of peaks for detailed quantitative analysis, specifically the nucleic acid-phosphate vibration (1238 cm⁻¹), symmetric PO₂⁻ stretching (1085 cm⁻¹), and ribose vibration (915 cm⁻¹). Protein content was quantified using the Amide I peak at 1639 cm⁻¹ and Amide II peak at 1540 cm⁻¹. Lipid quantification focused on the ester C=O stretching vibration near 1741 cm⁻¹ (triglycerides and cholesterol) and the C–O symmetric stretching of fatty acid side chains at 1400 cm⁻¹. All group comparisons were performed with n=5 replicates, using statistical testing to determine significance of peak integration differences. The ATR surface was cleaned between scans using a water-ethanol-water sequence, then air-dried. Air background was automatically subtracted to remove H₂O and CO₂ interference, and PBS was manually subtracted. Each sample was scanned under identical conditions for reproducibility across all treatment groups and time points.

Key Results
PCA revealed that PC-1 explained 83% of the spectral variability, while PC-2 explained 11%, confirming that the primary source of variation was treatment-driven. The 1750–850 cm⁻¹ IR region exhibited the most numerous peaks with high variation among samples, guiding further peak selection. Scores Plots showed clear clustering of samples by treatment across both PC directions, validating the spectral data's quality. CpG DNA stimulation induced a significant increase in nucleic acid content (1238 cm⁻¹ peak integration) from 10 min to 6 h (p < 0.1*), though a potential DNA synthesis adaptation was expected to appear later. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ showed a significant increase from the first minutes (p < 0.001***) and was maintained until 2 h post-stimulation (p < 0.1*), indicating extensive RNA synthesis. LPS stimulation showed an increased concentration of total RNA up to 2 h post-stimulation, but no significant nucleic acid changes occurred after 6 h. CpG DNA treatment caused a significant increase in total protein content (Amide I, 1639 cm⁻¹) from 10 min to 2 h (p < 0.001***), followed by a decline. A similar protein increase pattern was observed upon LPS stimulation, but the initial increase was reduced compared to CpG DNA. The protein concentration began to decrease from the 2 h time point for both CpG and LPS treatment groups. Both CpG and LPS stimulated groups showed a very significant increase in triglyceride and cholesterol (C=O stretch near 1741 cm⁻¹) starting from the first minutes of stimulation. LPS stimulation elevated triglyceride and cholesterol concentration after 10 min, whereas CpG DNA stimulation showed effects from the very first minutes. A significant increase in fatty acid concentration (C–O symmetric stretching, 1400 cm⁻¹) was observed for both CpG and LPS groups, pointing to de novo lipogenesis. The RNA-specific peak (915 cm⁻¹) allowed definition of the macrophage activation state at the very first minutes of activation, filling a gap in activation biology.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The sequential appearance of RNA synthesis (10 min–2 h) followed by DNA synthesis (from 6 h) under CpG stimulation reflects a time-dependent macromolecular response to immune activation. The lack of significant nucleic acid changes after 6 h for LPS-treated cells is consistent with LPS-induced inhibition of DNA synthesis and cell cycle arrest. The transient protein increase followed by decline in CpG-treated cells aligns with bioinformatic evidence showing short-lived immune activation followed by dynamic suppression by IL-10, SOCS, and NF-kB inhibitors. The decrease in total protein content upon LPS stimulation is attributed to histone release, vesicle-mediated secretion, and ROS-driven oxidative protein degradation, though the exact degree remains unknown. The simultaneous increase in fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol in both activated groups suggests a shared de novo lipogenesis pathway mediated by a common metabolite like Acetoacetyl-CoA. CpG-induced lipogenesis modulates secretory activity by the ER and Golgi, which is essential for CpG-activated anti-tumor activity of macrophages in cancer cells. FTIR spectroscopy provides an aerial view of total protein fate and global macromolecular changes that are not readily accessible by specific omics techniques. Understanding the rules governing cellular responses to stimulatory motifs can foster the design of ODNs for therapeutic adjuvant uses. This study demonstrates that bulk molecular fingerprinting via ATR-FTIR can detect macrophage activation at the first minutes, potentially identifying activation states earlier than prior methods.

Contradictions And Limitations
The exact degree to which histone release, vesicle secretion, and oxidative degradation contribute to total protein loss under LPS remains unknown, limiting firm attribution of mechanisms. The authors acknowledge that a potential adaptation of DNA synthesis only becomes prominent after several hours, which may explain the overlap in nucleic acid signals. A limitation of IR spectroscopy is the absorbance of water, which superimposes signals from aqueous cell systems, though the ATR design and Fourier transform procedure mitigate this. The random seed or specific train/test splits for PCA are not reported, though the study is unsupervised and the data matrix was obtained directly from spectral readings. No specific demographic or genetic information on the macrophage source beyond being RAW 264.7 murine cells is provided. The study does not report explicit validation against gold-standard protein or lipid quantification (e.g., ELISA, MS), relying instead on internal consistency and literature alignment. The 128-scan acquisition at 2 cm⁻¹ resolution is a trade-off between signal-to-noise and speed that may affect the detectability of subtle molecular changes. The study identifies protein loss under LPS but notes that this pathway contributes at a certain unknown degree, marking a limitation in mechanistic attribution.

Claims
CpG DNA and LPS induce detectable global molecular changes in macrophages detectable by ATR-FTIR at first minutes of activation. Activation-induced nucleic acid changes were detected 10 min after treatment (Figure 2.A). The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ showed significant increase from the first minutes (p < 0.001***). PCA PC-1 explained 83% of variability, confirming treatment-driven differences. The study does not provide absolute quantification against external standards, so 'detectable' refers to relative spectral shifts. This establishes FTIR as a viable independent modality for monitoring macrophage activation dynamics. Rapid detection at first minutes enables earlier identification of activation states.
CpG DNA induces an initial RNA synthesis phase (10 min–2 h) followed by a DNA synthesis phase starting from 6 h, while LPS inhibits DNA synthesis. RNA-specific peak maintained significance until 2 h (p < 0.1*), while nucleic acid changes persisted to 6 h (p < 0.1*). LPS showed no significant nucleic acid changes after 6 h, consistent with anti-proliferative effects. LPS was shown to induce 263 genes, including those related to cell cycle repression. The distinction between RNA and DNA contributions to the 1238 cm⁻¹ peak relies on the time-course inference rather than direct separation. The time-course data validates the role of RNA as the primary early activation marker. The findings support the mechanism by which CpG activates macrophages via RNA-dependent pathways.
Both CpG and LPS stimulate de novo lipogenesis, indicated by concurrent increases in fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol. Very significant increase in C=O stretch near 1741 cm⁻¹ for both groups. Significant increase in fatty acid C–O stretch at 1400 cm⁻¹ for both groups. LPS showed a shared metabolite (Acetoacetyl-CoA) between fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis pathways in prior studies. LPS effect on triglycerides and cholesterol was delayed until after 10 min, unlike CpG which showed effects from first minutes. This identifies lipogenesis as a shared macromolecular consequence of TLR-9 and TLR-4 signaling. The pathway is essential for CpG-activated anti-tumor macrophage activity in cancer.

Data And Code Availability
The study protocol is available online, but specific spectral data and analysis code are not explicitly cited as accessible. The data analysis was performed using Unscrambler 11.0 (Camo, NO) software, which is a commercial proprietary package.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Three independent scans per sample were performed, with the average constituting a replicate (n=5 used in analysis). PCA served as the initial dimension reduction to identify significant variation regions, guiding subsequent targeted peak analysis. Second derivative spectra were used for side-peak band assignment to confirm peak identity beyond the main peak. The use of two independent stimuli (CpG and LPS) and four time points provides robustness across activation modalities and time scales. The 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction were applied consistently across all samples.

Key Figures Tables
Figure A1 presents a comprehensive spectrum of resting control RAW 264.7 cells and its second derivative in the 4000–650 cm⁻¹ region. Table A1 shows peak assignments based on literature, and Table A2 shows area integration measurements for peaks of interest. Table 1 lists all study groups with their specific concentrations and time points. Figure 1.A, 1.B, and 1.C show PCA scores and loadings plots revealing clustering by treatment and regional spectral variation. Figure 2.A shows the nucleic acid-phosphate vibration spectrum at 10 min post-treatment. Figure 2.B shows bar diagrams of peak integration values for nucleic acid content. Figure 2.C shows the RNA-specific ribose vibration peak at 915 cm⁻¹. Figure 3.A and 3.B show the amide I and amide II protein peaks. Figure 3.C shows protein integration data showing the 10 min–2 h increase and subsequent decline. Figure 4.D and 4.E show the ester C=O stretch near 1741 cm⁻¹ for triglyceride and cholesterol content. Figure 4.B and 4.C show the C–O symmetric stretching peak at 1400 cm⁻¹ for fatty acid concentration.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration that ATR-FTIR spectroscopy can function as an independent modality to monitor global macromolecular activation dynamics in murine macrophages, revealing sequential RNA and DNA synthesis, transient protein increase, and concurrent lipogenesis. 2. The strongest evidence is the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹, which shows highly significant elevation (p < 0.001) from the first minutes of CpG stimulation and is maintained until 2 h, pinpointing the early activation state window. 3. The future path includes mechanistic studies of the CpG DNA-induced protein loss and further investigation of lipid metabolism modifications as part of macrophage activation programs detectable by FTIR.

The method provides a fast, one-time quantification that informs biosecurity decisions, with potential extensibility to Nosema, European foulbrood, and invasive pests like small hive beetle and tracheal mites.

The diagnostic component is a dual-target qPCR assay (AFBduo) targeting the single-copy ftsZ gene for quantification and the multi-copy 16S gene for increased sensitivity, with an internal control for quality assurance. Analytical validation demonstrated high sensitivity (detection limit 4 copies per 10 µL) and excellent linearity over 7 orders of magnitude. Field evaluation across three cohorts (45 quarantine hives, 23 single-beekeeper quarantine hives, and pooled-swab trials) confirmed that entrance swab spore levels are comparable to whole-baseboard levels, rendering extensive sampling unnecessary. Statistical modeling identified a threshold of 565,000 spores or more, corresponding to a 95% probability of clinical AFB. Notably, one hive showed pre-clinical high spore levels in bees but undetectable levels on hiveware due to new hiveware, highlighting the need for longitudinal monitoring. The method provides a fast, one-time quantification that informs biosecurity decisions, with potential extensibility to Nosema, European foulbrood, and invasive pests like small hive beetle and tracheal mites.

Research Context
American Foulbrood caused by Paenibacillus larvae spores is highly destructive, remaining infectious for over 30 years and requiring only a few spores to infect a new larva. New Zealand hive numbers more than doubled since 2013, and infected hives rose from 0.21% in 2015 to 0.46% in 2021. Current AFB diagnosis relies primarily on visual inspection of thousands of brood cells per hive through a roping test, which is subjective and laborious. Prior testing methods required dismantling hives, multiple visits to retrieve passive samples, or installing collection sheets on baseboards. While qPCR is a preferred diagnostic tool, most applications have used it for rapid confirmation of culture isolates rather than leveraging quantitative data. Most prior molecular publications relied on the sole 16S gene, which offers high sensitivity but compromised specificity. The ability to detect relevant levels from a single entrance sample would permit more rapid hive sampling and quicker containment. Previous studies detected P. larvae in hive baseboard debris but required collection sheets and dismantling the hive twice.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a single entrance-region swab combined with dual-target qPCR can detect clinically significant P. larvae levels without hive dismantling. The authors hypothesized that entrance swab sampling provides comparable pathogen DNA to whole-baseboard sampling, removing the need for invasive inspection. A second hypothesis stated that quantitative spore levels from entrance swabs could differentiate infected from non-infected hives and identify pre-clinical infections. The authors predicted that the 16S gene would amplify 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ due to its multi-copy nature per bacterium. A predicted outcome was that spore levels in bees from the brood nest would exceed levels detected on hive entrance surfaces. The authors aimed to establish a quantitative threshold (spores per sample) that predicts clinical AFB status with high statistical confidence. A secondary hypothesis was that the sampling technique could extend to other bee pathogens and incursion pests.

Methodological Details
Samples were collected from five quarantine apiaries in East Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa, and South Canterbury regions from late 2018 to early 2020. The first cohort comprised 45 hives sampled up to 6 times; 8 showed clinical AFB ('roping' remains), and 6 were presumed infected. The second cohort involved 23 hives from one beekeeper in a quarantine apiary, four of which showed clinical AFB. Nurse bees were collected from brood frames in 50 mL sterile containers and frozen for euthanasia. 10 bees were used per sample for ease of handling and throughput, with the practical purpose being convenience. Sterile foam-tipped Puritan swabs were moistened with sterile water and swiped the whole baseboard or hive entrance for 3-5 seconds. Beekeepers were instructed to rotate swabs to ensure coverage of all swab surfaces. Swab heads were snapped into 2 mL microcentrifuge tubes and sent at ambient temperature via overnight courier. Genomic DNA extraction used the Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit with beadbeating in a Mini Beadbeater 16 instrument. Bees were homogenized in 3 mL DXL lysis buffer with 0.5 mm (2.4 g) and 2.3 mm (1 g) zirconia silica beads for 3 minutes. Incubation occurred at 65°C for 10 minutes with manual inversion every 3 minutes. Swab extraction used 0.5 mm (0.8 g) and 2.3 mm (0.3 g) zirconia silica beads with 800 µL DXL buffer for 3 minutes homogenization. For pooling, individual swabs were added to 500 µL DXL buffer, vortexed 10 seconds, and 60 µL eluate from up to twelve swabs was processed. A synthetic DNA standard (gBlock, IDT, Singapore) of 153 bp incorporated both amplicon sequences. Standard dilution range was 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL in a pooled DNA diluent from AFB-negative bees. Quantification used a DS-11 FX microvolume spectrophotometer for nanograms per µL measurement. Copy number calculation used: Copies = ng * Avogadro's constant copies/mole length of standard x 660 g/mole x 1x10^9 ng/g. Cq values were converted to spores using: Spores per swab or 10 bees = 10^ (Cq ftsZ - 3.48) x 50. Binary logistic regression was performed in Minitab; analysis of variance confirmed the correlation between entrance spores and clinical signs. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant.

Procedures And Architectures
The assay is a dual-target hydrolysis probe ('TaqMan') qPCR using a commercially available multiplex assay for P. larvae (Hall et al., 2021). The assay targets the single-copy ftsZ gene for quantification and the multi-copy 16S gene for added sensitivity. An internal control was included in an additional detection channel to confirm suitable quality DNA in the reaction. The 16S marker was used as a secondary target, amplifying 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ due to multiple copies per bacterium. The 153 bp synthetic standard was resuspended in TE buffer (pH 8) and quantified before dilution series. Pooled applications involved 8 or 12 swab eluates added to 500 µL DXL buffer, vortexed, then processed through the beadbeating pipeline. Remnant samples from positive pools were tested individually to identify specific infected hives. DNA yields from bees showed OD260/280 measurements between 1.8 and 1.9, indicating high purity. DNA yields from swabs were too low for spectrophotometer measurement but internal control Cq's confirmed suitable quality. Serial dilutions showed expected increase in Cq with decreasing concentration, indicating no significant inhibitors after extraction. The Foster method is a one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing.

Key Results
The AFBduo assay detected down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction for both targets, demonstrating high analytical sensitivity. The 16S target amplified with 96% efficiency and the ftsZ target with 94% efficiency in the multiplex. Linearity was excellent over 7 orders of magnitude with a correlation coefficient of r = 0.998. On P. larvae-positive bee, honey, and hive material, the 16S target amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ. In the first cohort, 8 of 45 hives showed clinical AFB (roping remains), while 6 more were presumed infected due to apiary prevalence. In the second cohort, 4 of 23 hives showed clinical AFB, with higher spore levels in both bee and entrance swab samples. The third cohort demonstrated that even in pools of twelve hive samples, single hives with higher AFB levels were clearly detectable. Statistical analysis by binary logistic regression and ANOVA showed a strong relationship (p = 0.00) between increasing spore levels and clinical signs. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more revealed a 95% probability of clinical signs being present in the hive. Entrance swab P. larvae levels were similar to whole-baseboard levels, indicating baseboard swabbing was not required for detection. Spore levels in bees from the brood nest area were highest. One hive (Hive 11) showed high bee spore levels but undetectable entrance swab levels, subsequently showing clinical signs at a two-week follow-up. In two cases (hives 11 and 12), the bees showed high spore levels while hiveware showed low or undetectable levels. The discrepancy was explained by new hiveware (< 2 weeks old) and colonies newly established from an unknowingly infected parent.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 16S copy number possibly varied among AFB isolates, so it could not be relied upon for quantification. Variability in Cq difference between the two markers among samples supports previous findings that copy number for diagnostic targets can fluctuate. Entrance swabs alone could clearly differentiate infected from non-infected hives, validating the non-invasive sampling approach. The ability to sample through the entrance removed the need to dismantle and disrupt the hive, a major operational improvement over prior methods. The method provides clinically significant information as to whether visual signs are likely present now or in the near future. The Foster method is a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing that provides actionable biosecurity data. The quantification aspect is critical because low levels of AFB are often not clinically relevant and such hives may never develop clinical symptoms. Preliminary work suggests the entrance swab samples can be used to test for other bee pathogens, including Nosema ceranae and European foulbrood. The method is extensible to biosecurity surveillance for incursion pests such as tracheal mites, tropical honey bee mites, and small hive beetle.

Contradictions And Limitations
The spore levels never increased during monitoring for many hives, and became undetectable in some low spore cases, limiting predictive confidence. The variability in Cq difference between markers among samples suggested 16S copy number was inconsistent across isolates. DNA yields from swabs were too low to be measured on the spectrophotometer, relying instead on internal control Cq's for quality assessment. Two hives (11 and 12) showed a discrepancy between high bee spore levels and low/undetectable hiveware levels, complicating interpretation. The study notes that further research is required to assess spore accumulation rate on hive surfaces and to refine clinical spore threshold levels. The statistical model required imputing data points by regression analysis for two clinical hives where spore numbers were skewed lower by new hiveware. The total number of data points for paired clinical analysis was limited to 26. The random seed, specific train/test split parameters, or demographic details of beekeepers are not reported.

Claims
The Foster method provides a non-invasive, one-time sampling technique that detects clinically significant AFB without hive dismantling. Entrance swab P. larvae levels were similar to whole-baseboard levels, rendering baseboard swabbing unnecessary. The 16S marker amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ, confirming the dual-target assay captures AFB signal. A spore level of 565,000 predicts 95% probability of clinical AFB. Entrance swabs differentiated infected from non-infected hives in the second cohort. Hive 11 showed high bee spore levels but undetectable entrance swab levels at sampling. Spore levels became undetectable in some low-positive cases, limiting monitoring utility. The method reduces beekeeper labor and hive disruption, enabling faster containment of infected colonies. The quantification provides a risk assessment of whether visual signs are imminent.
The dual-target qPCR assay (AFBduo) offers high analytical sensitivity and specificity with an internal control. The assay reliably detected down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction. Efficiency was 94% for ftsZ and 96% for 16S in the multiplex format. Linearity was excellent over 7 orders of magnitude with r = 0.998. The internal control confirmed suitable DNA quality in swab samples. The 16S copy number variability could not be relied upon for quantification. Swab DNA yields were too low for spectrophotometer quantification. The internal control reduces false negatives due to inhibitors. The dual-target approach addresses sensitivity/specificity tradeoffs identified in prior 16S-only assays.
The sampling method is extensible to detection of Nosema ceranae, European foulbrood, and invasive bee pests. Nosema ceranae has been detected through hive debris and qPCR with good correlation between bees and debris. Hive debris from a week-long collection was used to estimate European foulbrood loading. The technique could detect tracheal mites, tropical honey bee mites, and small hive beetle. No empirical validation for incursion pest detection was presented in this study. A single sampling workflow could provide biosecurity surveillance across multiple pathogens. The method would provide faster sampling than dismantling hives to extract hive debris.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Serial dilutions of extracted DNA showed the expected increase in Cq with decreasing concentration, confirming no inhibitors. The 16S marker amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ, confirming the multi-copy target sensitivity advantage. Comparing whole-baseboard vs. entrance-only swabs demonstrated comparable P. larvae and internal control DNA levels. Three cohorts (quarantine, single-beekeeper quarantine, pooled-swab) provided independent replication of the findings. Pooling swab eluates into groups of eight and twelve was tested as a practical optimization. Remnant samples from positive pools were re-tested individually to identify specific infected hives. The discrepancy in Hive 11 was explained by new hiveware (< 2 weeks old), validating the methodology when hive history is known.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the progression of P. larvae levels in three colonies, with converted Cq data as spores per 10 bee or swab sample. Table 2 compares nurse bee and entrance swab spore levels in 23 hives from one beekeeper's quarantine apiary. Table 3 presents results of pooled swab extractions with remnant individual tests. Table 4 compares P. larvae and internal control DNA levels between whole-baseboard and entrance swabs. Supplementary Figure 4 shows the analysis of variance confirming the correlation between entrance spores and clinical signs. Supplementary S1 lists the standards and their resulting Cq values.

Three Takeaways
1. The Foster method enables rapid, non-invasive detection of clinically significant AFB levels through a single hive-entrance swab, eliminating the need to dismantle hives or collect baseboard debris. 2. The dual-target qPCR assay with ftsZ quantification and a 565,000 spore threshold predicts clinical AFB with 95% probability, validated across multiple independent cohorts and analytical checks. 3. The method is extensible to other bee pathogens and invasive pests, providing a unified sampling workflow for beekeeping biosecurity.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map prediction method that leverages unsupervised transformer language model features (ESM-1b attention maps) instead of homologous sequence evolutionary profiles. The motivation stems from the fact that MSA-based methods fail for proteins with few or no homologs, and generating evolutionary profiles is computationally intensive. The methodology constructs an ensemble of six 12-layer ResNet models (Duta et al. version) trained on diverse input feature combinations: one-hot amino acid encoding, SPOT-1D-Single structural features, and ESM-1b attention maps from either the last layer or all layers. Training data was curated from ProteinNet, reduced to 34,691 proteins after homology filtering (HHblits, e-value < 0.1) and sequence length trimming (< 500 residues). Validation was performed on 88 proteins, and independent testing on SPOT-2018 (669 proteins) and CASP14-FM (15 free modeling targets) was conducted. Key results show: a 15% F1-score improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM; 48.7% and 48.5% F1-score improvements over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact, respectively, on proteins with no homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 set. The method is 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU and 42 times faster on GPU. The paper concludes that ESM-1b features significantly enhance single-sequence predictors, providing a viable alternative to evolutionary-profile methods for genomic-scale applications, constrained by the 1024-residue window of ESM-1b.

Research Context
Protein contact map prediction is essential for accurate protein structure and function prediction. Prior methods rely heavily on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and homology-based profile information, which are unavailable for proteins lacking naturally occurring homologous sequences. Generating evolutionary profiles is computationally intensive, hindering large-scale prediction applications. Single-sequence-based predictors like SSCpred exist but are outperformed by MSA-based techniques when homologs are available, limiting their utility. Unsupervised deep learning methods inspired by NLP language models have recently been introduced to extract features from protein reference libraries.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether ESM-1b transformer attention maps, as an input feature to a ResNet contact-map predictor, can improve single-sequence prediction over both one-hot encoding and MSA-based methods. The study hypothesized that unsupervised attention features concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs would outperform SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for low-homology (Neff) proteins. The authors further hypothesized that an ensemble of models trained through different training approaches and feature combinations would provide additive improvement. The expected outcome was a faster, reasonably accurate alternative to evolutionary methods, particularly for genomic-scale prediction. A specific outcome was anticipated: ESM-1b's last-layer attention maps would significantly boost F1-score compared to models using only one-hot and SPOT-1D-Single features.

Methodological Details
The training dataset was derived from the ProteinNet benchmark consisting of 50,914 proteins submitted to PDB before 2016 with high resolution (< 2.5Å) and clustered at 95% sequence identity. Homology filtering was performed by comparing Hidden Markov Models generated by HHblits; proteins with hits at e-value < 0.1 were removed. This filtering reduced the training set to 39,120 proteins. Proteins with length more than 500 residues were removed, resulting in a final training set of 34,691 proteins. A validation set of 88 proteins was reserved for model selection. The SPOT-2018 test set comprised 669 proteins, constructed by removing all potential homologs in the training set using HHblits at e-value < 0.1. A stringent Neff1-2018 test set of 46 proteins with Neff=1 was separated for de-novo and isolated protein testing. Neff values were calculated with respect to the Uniclust30 dataset published in February 2020. The CASP14-FM test set included 15 free modeling targets without known structural templates at the time of release. Input features included one-hot amino acid encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (SS3, SS8, ASA, HSE, ψ, φ, θ, τ), and ESM-1b attention maps. Attention maps were extracted from all twenty attention heads of the last layer and twenty heads from every layer of the ESM-1b model. Contact is defined as Cβ atom distance ≤ 8.0Å per CASP standards, with three-type classification (long ≥24, medium 12-23, short 7-11). Performance was measured by top L/10, L/5, L/2, L/1 precision, overall F1-score, MCC, Sensitivity, AUC-PR, and AUC-ROC for short-, medium-, and long-range contacts collectively.

Procedures And Architectures
The architecture is a 12-block ResNet, chosen as the maximum depth trainable on the available GPU. The study used the improved version of ResNet published by Duta et al. (2020) rather than vanilla ResNet. Convolutional layers used a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. Six models were trained with the same architectural specifications but different input feature combinations. Models 1-3 used direct inter-residue contact prediction with Binary Cross-Entropy loss. Models 4-6 predicted inter-residue distances as distance bins using Cross-Entropy loss, then summed probabilities for distances 0-8 Å. The Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001 and batch size 1 was used for all models. Early stopping with a patience of 3 was applied to avoid overfitting. Feature combinations: Model 1 (last layer attention only); Model 2 (all layers attention only); Model 3 (all layers + one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single). Models 4-6 mirrored combinations 1-3 but for distogram prediction. One-dimensional features (one-hot and SPOT-1D-Single outputs) were converted to two-dimensional via outer concatenation. Attention maps were symmetrized and APC-corrected following Rao et al. (2020). The final ensemble SPOT-Contact-Single was formed by taking the mean of the six individual models.

Key Results
On the validation set, one-hot encoding alone yielded an F1-score of 0.15 and MCC of 0.14. Adding SPOT-1D-Single to one-hot encoding improved F1-score by 22.90%. Last-layer ESM-1b attention maps yielded F1=0.51, MCC=0.50, Precision=0.56, AUC-ROC=0.95 on the validation set. This represents a 242% improvement in F1-score over one-hot alone, and 178% improvement over one-hot+SPOT-1D-Single. Concatenating all features (one-hot + SPOT-1D + all-layer attention) added 2.92% F1-score over all-layer attention only. The ensemble SPOT-Contact-Single achieved 4% improvement over the second-best individual model for F1-score on the validation set. On the CASP14-FM test set, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.2061 and MCC=0.1925. SPOT-Contact-Single showed 15% F1-score improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. The most substantial improvement over SSCpred was in long-range contacts precision at approximately 100%. On proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.32, while TrRosetta achieved 0.22 and SPOT-Contact achieved 0.22. SPOT-Contact-Single F1 was 45% higher than ESM-1b (0.22 vs 0.32) on Neff=1 proteins. On the example protein 5YKZ_A from Neff1-2018, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.388, vs 0.215 for SPOT-Contact, 0.235 for TrRosetta, and 0.252 for ESM-1b. On CPU inference of CASP14-FM (15 proteins), SPOT-Contact-Single took 116 seconds, while TrRosetta took 1926 seconds. On GPU, TrRosetta took 1926 seconds, 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
ESM-1b's unsupervised attention maps capture structural information that complements one-hot encoding and 1D structural descriptors. The 45% gap between SPOT-Contact-Single (0.32) and ESM-1b (0.22) on Neff=1 proteins suggests that the ResNet architecture and multi-feature fusion extract more structured contact information than raw ESM-1b outputs. The method proves that unsupervised transformer features can serve as a high-quality substitute for MSA-based evolutionary profiles. The computational advantage (22-42x faster) makes the method suitable for genomic-scale screening where MSA generation is the bottleneck. The 1024-residue limitation of ESM-1b is mitigated by the domain-based modularity of proteins, retaining practical utility for large targets. Future improvements may emerge from more advanced architectures like Transformers or Performers trained without evolutionary information.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ResNet depth was capped at 12 blocks by the available GPU, which may limit model capacity. ESM-1b has a 1024 residue window limitation, making it impossible to directly predict contact maps for proteins larger than this without domain decomposition. The direct contact-map vs. distogram-based prediction strategies produced only small performance differences, limiting the impact of the choice between them. SSCpred was accessed via a web server rather than a stand-alone program for fair benchmarking, introducing potential reproducibility limitations. The comparison with SSCpred is limited to CASP14-FM (15 proteins), a small sample size for generalizability claims. The random seeds and specific hardware details for training and inference are not fully reported in the text.

Claims
SPOT-Contact-Single significantly improves single-sequence contact map prediction over SSCpred using ESM-1b attention maps. SPOT-Contact-Single achieved a 15% F1-score improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. Long-range contacts precision showed approximately 100% improvement over SSCpred. The method outperformed ESM-1b on Neff=1 proteins (F1 0.32 vs 0.22). On proteins with many homologs, SSCpred remains competitive with MSA-based techniques, suggesting the improvement is targeted at low-homology cases. The 1024 residue limit constrains the method for very large proteins. The method becomes a viable low-resource alternative for proteins without detectable homologs. It reduces the computational bottleneck of MSA generation for genomic-scale applications.
SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms both TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on proteins with no homologs (Neff=1). F1-score was 48.7% higher than TrRosetta and 48.5% higher than SPOT-Contact on Neff=1 SPOT-2018 proteins. On example protein 5YKZ_A, SPOT-Contact-Single (F1 0.388) exceeded TrRosetta (0.235) and SPOT-Contact (0.215). The improvement diminishes as Neff increases, with profile-based predictors eventually overtaking SPOT-1D-Single. MSA can still provide more co-mutation information than unsupervised learning. The method establishes a new benchmark for zero-homology contact map prediction. Evolutionary information remains superior when homologs are abundant.
The proposed method is substantially faster than MSA-based methods, making it suitable for genomic-scale applications. CPU inference on CASP14-FM: SPOT-Contact-Single 116s vs TrRosetta 1926s (22x faster). GPU inference: TrRosetta was 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single. Sequence profile generation takes significantly longer than the proposed method.  The computational efficiency enables applications on proteome-scale data where MSA generation is infeasible.

Data And Code Availability
Stand-alone programs for TrRosetta, SPOT-Contact, and ESM-1b are available at their respective GitHub and project URLs, but the paper does not explicitly state code release for SPOT-Contact-Single.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Feature importance was assessed by training a ResNet12 on one-hot alone, one-hot+SPOT-1D-Single, and adding attention maps from last-layer or all-layers. The direct contact-map vs. distogram-based training strategy was evaluated, showing small but detectable differences. Ensemble averaging of six models was shown to provide 4% F1 improvement over the second-best individual model. Attention maps from all layers provided continued precision improvement over last-layer only for short-, medium-, and long-range contacts (Supplementary Table S2).

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the ResNet12 architecture for inter-residue contact prediction. Figure 2 illustrates precision for top predictions at short-, medium-, and long-range contacts across methods. Figure 3 plots F1-score as a function of Neff values, showing the crossing point of single-sequence and profile-based methods. Figure 4 presents native and predicted contact maps for example protein 5YKZ_A from Neff1-2018. Table 1 describes feature combinations for the ensemble of six trained models. Table 2 reports F1, MCC, Precision, AUC-ROC for different input feature combinations on the validation set. Table 3 compares direct contact-map vs. distogram-based prediction strategies. Table 4 presents results of individual models and the ensemble on the validation set. Table 5 compares SPOT-Contact-Single with TrRosetta, SPOT-Contact, and ESM-1b on Neff=1 proteins. Table 6 reports CASP14-FM test set results including F1, MCC, Sensitivity, Precision, AUC, and ROC. Supplementary Table S1 provides descriptions of all test sets. Supplementary Table S2 and S3 contain extended performance metrics for contact types and strategies. Supplementary Table S4 reports long-range contacts precision for SSCpred comparison. Supplementary Table S5 reports CPU and GPU inference times.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is an ensemble of ResNet-based predictors that combine one-hot amino acid encoding, 1D structural features, and ESM-1b transformer attention maps, achieving 15% F1 improvement over SSCpred and ~49% over MSA-based methods for low-homology proteins. 2. The strongest evidence is the 15% improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, the 48%+ improvement over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on Neff=1 proteins, and the 22-42x speed advantage over evolutionary methods. 3. The future path includes extending the method to large proteins (>1024 residues) via domain decomposition and employing more advanced architectures such as Transformers or Performers trained without evolutionary information.

summary.title: EcoEvoApps: Interactive Apps for Theoretical Models in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
summary.authors: Rosa M Mcguire, Kenji T Hayashi, Xinyi Yan, Marcel Caritá Vaz, Damla Cino Glu, Madeline C Cowen, Alejandra Martínez-Blancas, Lauren L Sullivan, Sheila Vazquez-Morales, Gaurav S Kandlikar
summary.field_subfield: Ecology and Evolutionary Biology / Computational Biology Education
summary.type_of_paper: Software description and pedagogical evaluation paper
summary.executive_summary: EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package (ecoevoapps) and web platform (https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io) that provides 11 interactive Shiny apps for simulating and visualizing fundamental models in ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB). The package addresses a documented barrier to theoretical-empirical integration: the mathematical language of theoretical models often appears foreign to empirical researchers, leading to reduced citation of equation-heavy papers and poorer student evaluations in quantitative courses. To counter this, ecoevoapps offers freely available interactive simulations that allow users to independently explore model structure and outcomes, alongside R console functions (run_ and plot_ prefixes) for direct implementation. The first release includes nine apps available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese, selected from undergraduate ecology syllabi and standard textbooks (Gotelli 2008, Begon and Townsend 2020). Pedagogical value was evaluated via student surveys at UCLA (N=51, upper-division Ecology) and the University of Missouri (General Ecology), where 40/51 UCLA students (≈78%) rated the apps as moderately to very helpful (scores 6–7). Students reported better understanding of specific concepts like carrying capacity and coexistence. The package is distinguished from existing resources (Evo-Ed, HHMI BioInteractive, Populus) by being entirely open-source and written in R, facilitating community customization. The authors plan to expand to evolutionary biology and population genetics models and develop formal teaching plans for EEB educators.

claims.description: EcoEvoApps significantly improves student understanding of theoretical EEB models in classroom settings.
Interactive parameter exploration reveals the theoretical logic of model conclusions (e.g., paradox of enrichment).

judge_context:
Executive Summary
EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package (ecoevoapps) and web platform (https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io) that provides 11 interactive Shiny apps for simulating and visualizing fundamental models in ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB). The package addresses a documented barrier to theoretical-empirical integration: the mathematical language of theoretical models often appears foreign to empirical researchers, leading to reduced citation of equation-heavy papers and poorer student evaluations in quantitative courses. To counter this, ecoevoapps offers freely available interactive simulations that allow users to independently explore model structure and outcomes, alongside R console functions (run_ and plot_ prefixes) for direct implementation. The first release includes nine apps available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese, selected from undergraduate ecology syllabi and standard textbooks (Gotelli 2008, Begon and Townsend 2020). Pedagogical value was evaluated via student surveys at UCLA (N=51, upper-division Ecology) and the University of Missouri (General Ecology), where 40/51 UCLA students (≈78%) rated the apps as moderately to very helpful (scores 6–7). Students reported better understanding of specific concepts like carrying capacity and coexistence. The package is distinguished from existing resources (Evo-Ed, HHMI BioInteractive, Populus) by being entirely open-source and written in R, facilitating community customization. The authors plan to expand to evolutionary biology and population genetics models and develop formal teaching plans for EEB educators.

Research Context
Integrating theory with empirical observations is a fundamental driver of progress in the life sciences, yet substantial barriers limit this integration. Equation-heavy papers tend to be cited less often, and quantitative course instructors receive worse student evaluations. Existing quantitative training calls focus primarily on statistical models or programming skills, with few advances in the pedagogy of theoretical models. Interactive tools allowing users to explore model structure help increase student interest and understanding of quantitative concepts. There is a documented need for a platform for interactive simulations of EEB models to facilitate communication between theoretical and empirical researchers.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can interactive Shiny apps facilitate communication, learning, and classroom instruction of mathematical models in EEB? The authors hypothesized that these apps would help users become familiar with coding and implementing theoretical models. The central hypothesis is that interactive exploration of model parameters reveals the underlying logic of classic model conclusions. The authors predicted that students would find the apps helpful for learning models as a whole and specific associated topics. A predicted outcome is that interactive apps lead to substantial gains in student confidence compared to pre-activity baselines.

Methodological Details
The ecoevoapps package includes 11 interactive apps as its primary interface, with a core set of nine apps available in multiple languages. Models were selected by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and commonly-used textbooks (Gotelli 2008, Begon and Townsend 2020). A core set of nine apps are available in English, Spanish, and Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The apps are hosted on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers and can also be launched locally via the R console. The R package includes model-specific vignettes with instructions for simulating dynamics directly through R. For the classroom evaluation, 51 students were surveyed at UCLA in an upper-division Ecology course. Students used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition topics. Similar surveys were conducted in a General Ecology course at the University of Missouri. The activity included short (~15 minutes) video lectures followed by a worksheet for guided exploration. Students rated the apps on a 1–7 scale for understanding of models as a whole and specific topics. Classroom surveys were reviewed and deemed exempt by both the UCLA and MU Institutional Review Boards.

Procedures And Architectures
Under the hood, the shiny apps use R functions with the prefix run_ to simulate model dynamics given parameter vectors. A plotting suite with the prefix plot_ takes simulation outputs and returns ggplot2 objects. The predator-prey dynamics app includes a Lotka-Volterra tab and extensions with logistic growth in prey and/or a type II functional response. Each app includes a description of model structure, a parameter table, and references to relevant literature. The abiotic resource competition app models two species competing for two essential resources (Tilman 1980). The package includes 11 additional functions with the prefix shiny_ to launch apps directly from the R console. The paradox of enrichment (Rosenzweig 1971) is visualized by altering the prey carrying capacity K in the MacArthur-Rosenzweig model tab. The predictor-prey app URL is https://ecoevoapps.shinyapps.io/predator_prey_dynamics/ or launched via shiny_predprey(). The package provides instructions for customizing and deploying a private app instance on institutional servers.

Key Results
At UCLA, 40 out of 51 students (78.4%) reported that the apps were moderately to very helpful (scores 6 or 7) for learning the models as whole. Students reported better understanding of specific concepts such as carrying capacity and coexistence after using the Lotka-Volterra app. Similar results were found in the University of Missouri General Ecology course survey. Tracking individual students showed that interactive apps led to substantial gains in student confidence, especially among those with higher interest. The predator-prey app demonstrated the paradox of enrichment: K=200 shows dampened oscillations to the right of the hump, while K=500 shows unstable oscillations to the left. The package is entirely open-source and written in R, distinguishing it from closed-source or non-R resources. The apps are available as a package, a website, and directly runnable R functions for both console and GUI users.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The package serves as a bridge, enabling users to bypass years of quantitative training to gain theoretical insights through simulation. Interactive exploration reveals the logic behind classic model conclusions (e.g., the paradox of enrichment) without analytical derivation. The tool lowers the barrier for empirical researchers to engage with theoretical models, potentially increasing citation and integration. Simulation-based learning provides accessible pathways to model comprehension even if not identical to analytical solutions. The open-source R framework enables community contributions, translations, and customization, ensuring long-term sustainability.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions. The current release is the first and only covers ecological models, with evolutionary biology yet to be incorporated. The sample size for the classroom evaluation is relatively small (N=51 at UCLA; MU sample not quantified). The study evaluates the first release; future apps and translations are planned but not yet implemented. The MU results are mentioned as similar without reporting specific quantitative metrics in the main text.

Claims
EcoEvoApps significantly improves student understanding of theoretical EEB models in classroom settings. 40/51 UCLA students rated the apps moderately to very helpful (scores 6–7) for model-as-whole understanding. Students reported improved comprehension of specific concepts like carrying capacity and coexistence. MU survey showed similar positive results and substantial confidence gains. The authors note simulation-based learning may not provide all insights of analytical solutions. The MU quantitative metrics are not reported in the main text. These findings support the development of formal lesson plans for EEB educators. The package may reduce the barrier for empirical researchers to engage with theory.
Interactive parameter exploration reveals the theoretical logic of model conclusions (e.g., paradox of enrichment). Careful exploration of parameter K reveals the logic behind Rosenzweig's conclusion. Figure 2 explicitly demonstrates stable vs. unstable oscillations at K=200 and K=500. The app includes a specific tab for the MacArthur-Rosenzweig model.  The tool can be used by theoreticians and empiricists to communicate model insights.

Data And Code Availability
The ecoevoapps R package is open-source and available on GitLab. The package can be installed from GitLab for local use or deployment. The Shiny apps are freely available online on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers. A website at https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io provides documentation, vignettes, and references.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The package includes model-specific vignettes and instructions for deployment on institutional servers, supporting deployment robustness. The predictor-prey app includes three tabs (Lotka-Volterra, logistic growth in prey, type II functional response) for sensitivity analysis of model structure. The package allows for direct simulation via the R console, providing a non-GUI path for users.

Ethical Considerations
Classroom surveys were reviewed and deemed exempt by UCLA IRB #20-002179. MU IRB Project #2031063, Review #276104 also determined the studies as exempt.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 lists models and functions included in the ecoevoapps package, plus 11 shiny_ functions. Figure 1 shows the predator-prey dynamics app with Lotka-Volterra and extension tabs. Figure 2 shows screenshots of the MacArthur-Rosenzweig model with K=200 and K=500. Figure 3A presents the UCLA student ratings for model-as-whole understanding. Figure 3B shows student comprehension of specific topics (carrying capacity, coexistence).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the ecoevoapps R package, an open-source platform of 11 interactive Shiny apps plus R functions that bridge theoretical and empirical EEB research. 2. The strongest evidence is that 78.4% (40/51) of UCLA students rated the apps as helpful for model understanding, with additional gains in student confidence. 3. The future path involves incorporating evolutionary biology and population genetics models, translating existing apps, and developing formal lesson plans for EEB educators.

summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi; Tomoko Tanaka; Ryosuke Mano; Seiji Kondo; Shohta Kodama

summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the molecular mechanism by which Cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2, CTGF) regulates lymphangiogenesis in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). Intracellular signaling analysis revealed that CCN2 induces phospho-ERK (p<0.001) but does not activate VEGFR2 or VEGFR3, indicating a non-receptor-tyrosine-kinase-mediated pathway. Mechanistically, the study identifies integrin av as the critical cell surface receptor mediating CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation, as siRNA knockdown of Itgav partially decreased phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Furthermore, CCN2 was found to slightly inhibit LEC proliferation at 24h (p=0.003 at 50 ng/mL; p=0.02 at 100 ng/mL), and a time-course analysis revealed a transient ERK phosphorylation profile peaking at 4h. Immunoprecipitation demonstrated that CCN2 enhances the co-precipitation of ERK with DUSP6, the predominant DUSP isoform in LECs, and siRNA-mediated knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels (p<0.001 at 15 min and 4h; p=0.004 at 48h). judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the molecular mechanism by which Cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2, CTGF) regulates lymphangiogenesis in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). The authors demonstrate that CCN2 upregulates LEC markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4) in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, with a dramatic decrease at 200 ng/mL. Intracellular signaling analysis revealed that CCN2 induces phospho-ERK (p<0.001) but does not activate VEGFR2 or VEGFR3, indicating a non-receptor-tyrosine-kinase-mediated pathway. Mechanistically, the study identifies integrin av as the critical cell surface receptor mediating CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation, as siRNA knockdown of Itgav partially decreased phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Furthermore, CCN2 was found to slightly inhibit LEC proliferation at 24h (p=0.003 at 50 ng/mL; p=0.02 at 100 ng/mL), and a time-course analysis revealed a transient ERK phosphorylation profile peaking at 4h. Immunoprecipitation demonstrated that CCN2 enhances the co-precipitation of ERK with DUSP6, the predominant DUSP isoform in LECs, and siRNA-mediated knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels (p<0.001 at 15 min and 4h; p=0.004 at 48h). In vivo Matrigel plug assays (n=4 CCN2; n=3 control) confirmed that recombinant CCN2 promoted Podoplanin-positive vessel formation, and phosphorylated ERK and DUSP6 were detected in CCN2-supplemented plugs, whereas they were absent or minimal in controls (p<0.05). The study concludes that CCN2-mediated lymphangiogenesis is negatively regulated by DUSP6-mediated ERK dephosphorylation, and integrin av/ERK/DUSP6 signaling represents a potential therapeutic target in oral squamous cell carcinoma and related fibrotic diseases.

Research Context
CCN2 (CTGF) is a modular matricellular protein known as a key angiogenic factor in physiology and pathology. While its pro-angiogenic roles are well-documented, its specific contributions to lymphangiogenesis and intracellular signaling in LECs remained unclear. The CCN family consists of six members (CCN1-6) each containing four structural domains: IGF-binding, von Willebrand factor C repeat, TSP, and cysteine knot C-terminal domains. CCN2 interacts with several integrins; the TSP domain binds integrin a6b1, while the C-terminal motif interacts with integrins avb3, a5b1, and a6b1. Previous mouse models in renal, peritoneal dialysis-related, and liver fibrosis showed CTGF enhanced lymphangiogenesis and interacted with VEGF-C. However, the specific downstream signaling cascade of CCN2 within LECs in lymphangiogenic contexts had not been elucidated prior to this study.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether and how CCN2 signals within primary LECs to regulate lymphangiogenesis. The authors hypothesized that CCN2 would induce lymphangiogenic gene expression and activate intracellular signaling pathways in LECs. The authors further hypothesized that integrin av serves as the critical cell-surface receptor mediating CCN2-ERK signaling, given its expression in LECs. A secondary hypothesis was that the ERK signaling induced by CCN2 would be negatively regulated by a specific phosphatase, potentially DUSP6, to modulate cell growth. The in vivo hypothesis was that exogenous CCN2 would promote Podoplanin-positive vessel formation in a Matrigel plug model, reflecting the in vitro findings. The study predicted that ERK phosphorylation would be transient, suggesting a concomitant suppression mechanism.

Methodological Details
Primary cultured LECs were obtained from C57BL/6 mice (CellBiologics) and cultured in EGM2 medium at 37°C with 5% CO2 on gelatin-coated dishes. Cells up to 6 passages were used for in vitro experiments. Gene expression analysis used quantitative RT-PCR with TB Green Premix ExTaq II on a LightCycler96, with RNA prepared via Purelink RNA purification Kit. LECs were stimulated with 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100, or 200 ng/mL of recombinant rat CCN2/CTGF for 3 hours for gene expression profiling. For cell proliferation, cells were plated at 2×10⁴ cells per well in 24-well plates and treated with 0, 10, 50, or 100 ng/mL CCN2 for 24, 48, and 72 hours. siRNA-mediated gene silencing used 1.5×10⁵ cells transfected with 25 pmol target or nontarget siRNA using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX. Protein concentration was determined by BCA assay, samples (5-20 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE and analyzed by Western blot on PVDF membranes. Phospho-RTK array used 200 µg total protein incubated with a Proteome profiler mouse phospho-RTK array kit for 5 minutes treatment. Immunoprecipitation used 200 µg cell lysates incubated with anti-ERK or anti-DUSP6 antibodies overnight, followed by Protein A magnetic beads. In the Matrigel plug assay, 450 µL Matrigel was mixed with 8.33 µg CCN2 (n=4) or 50 µL PBS control (n=3) and injected subcutaneously in male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice. Plugs were analyzed at day 7 after injection and sections (4 µm thick) were stained with HE for microscopy. All experiments were performed more than three times except the RTK assay (n=2); data expressed as mean ± standard error (S.E.). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, using Student's t-test, ANOVA, Bonferroni, or Sidak for multiple comparisons.

Procedures And Architectures
Gene expression of Lyve1, Pdpn, Prox1, Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4, and Kdr was analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR following CCN2 treatment. Phosphorylation of RTKs (EGFR, EphB4, ErbB4, PDGFRα, VEGFR2, VEGFR3) was assessed using a phospho-RTK array kit. Downstream MAPK phosphorylation (p38, JNK, ERK) along with AKT, NFκB, Smad2/-3/-1/5 was examined by Western blot. Integrin mRNA expression (Itgav, Itga9, Itga2b, Itgb1, Itgb2, Itgb3) was measured by qPCR to identify LEC-relevant integrins. DUSP expression (Dusp1 through Dusp10) was profiled by qPCR to identify predominant isoforms in LECs. siRNA-mediated knockdown was performed for integrin av (Itgav), integrin a9 (Itga9), integrin b1 (Itgb1), and DUSP6 using siDirect ver.2 design. Immunoprecipitation assays tested ERK-DUSP6 interaction by incubating 200 µg lysate with anti-ERK or anti-DUSP6, capturing with Protein A beads. In vivo Matrigel plugs were processed by fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde, paraffin embedding, HE staining, and fluorescence microscopy (BZ-710X, LSM710). Immunostaining for phospho-ERK and DUSP6 in Podoplanin-positive vessels was performed using Alexa594/Alexa488 secondary antibodies. Western blot detection used ECL Prime substrate, ImageQuant TL 8.1 software for quantification, and HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies.

Key Results
CCN2 upregulated Lyve1, Pdpn, and Prox1 gene expression in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL; at 200 ng/mL, expression levels dramatically decreased. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 expression but did not affect Kdr expression. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations were unchanged by CCN2 (Fig. S1). RTK array showed EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylation increased (p<0.001), while ErbB4 and PDGFRα decreased compared to controls. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased in response to CCN2 (p<0.001), while p38 MAPK, JNK, AKT, NFκB, and Smad levels remained unchanged. Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2 treatment. Integrin Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs and their mRNA levels were increased by CCN2. Itga2b, Itgb2, and Itgb3 were not induced by CCN2 stimulation. Knockdown of integrin av (Itgav) by siRNA partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040) compared with non-target siRNA. Knockdown of integrin a9 resulted in a slight increase of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was increased by suppression of integrin b1 (p=0.05) without CCN2 stimulation, but was not altered by CCN2 in b1-suppressed LECs. CCN2 treatment (10, 50, 100 ng/mL) at 24h suppressed LEC cell growth compared to 0h (p=0.22, 0.92, and >0.99, respectively). At 24h, 50 and 100 ng/mL CCN2 suppressed cell growth compared with vehicle-treated LECs (p=0.003 and p=0.02, respectively). No changes in proliferation were observed at 48 and 72h of CCN2 treatment. Phospho-ERK increased at 15 min after CCN2, continued to increase up to 4h, decreased at 8h, and increased after 48h. DUSP6 was the predominant DUSP expressed in LECs; Dusp16 was undetected. Immunoprecipitation showed DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, and their interaction was enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 siRNA knockdown increased phospho-ERK at 15 min (p<0.001), 4h (p<0.001), 24h (p=0.04), and 48h (p=0.004) after CCN2 treatment. In Matrigel plugs, the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased by exogenous CCN2, and tubular structures were observed. Phospho-ERK was barely present in control gel but detected in the nucleus and cytosol of Podoplanin-positive cells in CCN2 gel. DUSP6 was rarely detected in control but detected in the cytosol of Podoplanin-positive cells in CCN2 gel. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression in Podoplanin-positive cells were significantly increased in CCN2 gel vs control (p<0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observation that VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 were not activated by CCN2 suggests that CCN2 and endogenous VEGF-C do not signal through VEGFRs to ERK in LECs. Integrin av, a9, and b1 are detected in LECs, and the partial reversal of phospho-ERK by Itgav knockdown implies integrin av is a necessary but not sufficient receptor for CCN2-mediated ERK activation. The increased phospho-ERK upon integrin b1 suppression without CCN2 stimulation may be due to compensatory upregulation of integrin a5, a phenotype observed in other LEC contexts. DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERK signaling in LECs, acting as a brake on CCN2-induced ERK activation to prevent excessive signaling. The transient nature of CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation, coupled with DUSP6-ERK interaction enhancement, suggests a self-regulatory feedback loop within the LEC signaling architecture. The discrepancy between in vitro weak growth inhibition and in vivo lymphangiogenic promotion is attributed to ECM and MMP-2,3 mediated proteolytic processing of CCN2 in the Matrigel environment. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis represent potential therapeutic targets for head and neck cancers (OSCC) and related fibrotic diseases.

Contradictions And Limitations
CCN2 in vitro assays showed weak growth inhibition of LECs (p=0.22-0.99 at 24h), while the in vivo Matrigel assay showed robust lymphangiogenesis, a discrepancy noted by the authors. Knockdown of integrin av only partially decreased phospho-ERK (p=0.0040), indicating other receptors or mechanisms also contribute to CCN2-ERK signaling. Integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation, but was not compensated for by increases in integrins b2 and b3, complicating the interpretation. The study did not investigate Itga5 mRNA expression because the CCN2-integrin a5 interaction has not been reported in LECs, leaving a potential compensatory mechanism unexamined. The Matrigel assay used 4 CCN2-supplemented gels and 3 control gels (n=4 vs n=3), which is a relatively small sample size for in vivo conclusions. The discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results is not claimed to be contradictory but attributed to differences in ECM and MMP-2,3 processing of CCN2. The study used primary LECs from mouse (C57BL/6), and results may not generalize directly to human LEC biology without further validation. The relationship between DUSP6 and negative ERK regulators FOXC1/FOXC2, known to cause lymphatic hyperplasia via ERK hyperactivation, was not analyzed.

Claims
CCN2 upregulates lymphangiogenic gene expression and induces ERK phosphorylation in primary LECs via integrin av. Lyve1, Pdpn, Prox1, Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 were upregulated by CCN2 up to 100 ng/mL. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased (p<0.001) by CCN2 without VEGFR2/3 activation. Itgav mRNA was increased by CCN2 and its siRNA knockdown partially reduced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Itgav knockdown only partially reduced phospho-ERK, suggesting other pathways contribute. Itga2b, Itgb2, and Itgb3 were not induced by CCN2, limiting the integrin involvement to av, a9, and b1. CCN2 provides a direct, integrin-mediated signaling route for lymphangiogenesis independent of VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase activation.
CCN2 enhances ERK-DUSP6 interaction and DUSP6 negatively regulates ERK phosphorylation in LECs. CCN2 enhanced DUSP6 co-precipitation with ERK in immunoprecipitation assays. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK at all time points post-CCN2 (p<0.001 to p=0.004). Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 were significantly detected in CCN2-supplemented Matrigel plugs (p<0.05). DUSP5 is also a known MAPK regulator in endothelium, though DUSP6 was predominant in these LECs. DUSP6 functions as a brake on CCN2-induced ERK signaling, preventing excessive ERK activity that would otherwise drive lymphatic hyperplasia.
CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo through Podoplanin-positive vessel formation and ERK phosphorylation. CCN2-supplemented Matrigel plugs showed Podoplanin-positive vessels and tubular structures. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 were detected in CCN2 gel Podoplanin-positive cells (p<0.05). CCN2 increased CD31-positive cavities and b3-Tubulin-positive nerves in plugs. In vitro cell growth was weakly inhibited by CCN2, contrasting with the pro-lymphangiogenic in vivo result. The ECM and MMP-2,3-mediated processing of CCN2 in vivo account for the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo outcomes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Integrin a9 knockdown resulted in only a slight increase of phospho-ERK, distinguishing it from the partial reduction seen with integrin av knockdown. Integrin b1 knockdown showed a p=0.05 increase in phospho-ERK without CCN2, but CCN2 had no effect in b1-depleted cells, and b2/b3 did not compensate. Time-course experiments revealed non-persistent, transient phospho-ERK kinetics, pointing to active degradation/dephosphorylation. RTK array was performed with n=2, limiting replication compared to other experiments (n>3). ERK phosphorylation was measured at multiple time points (15 min, 4h, 8h, 48h), supporting the transient kinetic model.

Ethical Considerations
Experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Fukuoka University (approval number: 2008024). All experiments were performed in compliance with relevant laws and institutional guidelines.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows dose-dependent upregulation of Lyve1, Pdpn, and Prox1 by CCN2 up to 100 ng/mL and dramatic decrease at 200 ng/mL. Figure 1B shows CCN2 increases Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 but not Kdr expression. Figure 2A-B shows phospho-ERK significantly increased (p<0.001) by CCN2; Figure 2C shows total ERK unaffected. Figure 3A shows Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 increased by CCN2; Itga2b, Itgb2, Itgb3 unaffected. Figure 3B shows Itgav siRNA partially decreased phospho-ERK (p=0.0040); Figure 3C shows Itga9 siRNA slightly increased phospho-ERK. Figure 4A shows CCN2-induced suppression of LEC growth at 24h (p=0.22-0.99); Figure 4B shows transient phospho-ERK kinetics. Figure 5A shows DUSP6 as predominant DUSP in LECs; Figure 5B shows ERK-DUSP6 interaction; Figure 5C-D show DUSP6 siRNA increases phospho-ERK. Figure 6A shows macroscopic blood vessels on CCN2 Matrigel surface; Figure 6B-C show HE-stained Podoplanin-positive vessels and tubular structures. Figure 7A-C shows immunostaining for phospho-ERK in CCN2 gel Podoplanin-positive cells; Figure 7B shows DUSP6 in CCN2 gel cytosol.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of CCN2-integrin av-ERK-DUSP6 as a novel, non-VEGF-receptor-mediated signaling axis regulating lymphangiogenesis. 2. The strongest evidence is the multi-level validation across gene expression, phospho-protein, siRNA knockdown, immunoprecipitation, and in vivo Matrigel assays, all consistently pointing to this pathway. 3. The future path includes investigating the DUSP6-FOXC1/2 axis, validating the pathway in human LECs, and targeting integrin av/ERK/DUSP6 in head and neck cancer therapies.
