summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement; Priscilla S Redd; Chunwan Lu; Alyssa D Merting; Dakota B Poschel; Dafeng Yang; Gang Zhou; David H Munn; Kebin Liu
summary.field_subfield: Immunology / Cancer Immunology and Immunotherapy
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (Mechanism-oriented study with in vivo, in vitro, and human translation)
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the mechanisms by which tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) promotes metastatic growth, particularly in the lung. The authors demonstrate that tPD-L1 does not directly suppress cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activation when only tumor cells and CTLs are present, but that knocking out PD-L1 in tumor cells significantly decreases lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner while having no effect on primary tumor growth. Through a series of in vitro (CTL:tumor co-culture, RAW264.7 macrophage co-culture) and in vivo (tail vein metastasis, orthotopic growth) experiments, the study identifies myeloid cell-expressed PD-1 (mPD-1) as the critical intermediate target of tPD-L1. 

Key findings include: (1) tPD-L1 binds mPD-1 on lung-resident myeloid cells, triggering SHP-2-mediated inhibition of type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling; (2) this inhibition represses chemokine expression (Cxcl9 and Cxcl10), thereby impairing CTL recruitment to lung metastatic sites; and (3) myeloid cell depletion via clodronate liposomes ablarges tPD-L1-driven metastasis. Validation in human metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients using single-cell RNA sequencing and PHATE analysis confirmed that PD-1 blockade releases myeloid cell differentiation restrictions, enhances interferon signaling, and restores CTL-recruiting chemokine expression. The data positions the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis as a fundamental mechanism of CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis, providing a rationale for ICB in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings and highlighting a negative feedback loop where the PD-1/L1 axis is induced by and then attenuates IFN signaling.

Research Context
PD-L1/PD-1 blockade is a well-established immunotherapy that functions primarily by blocking the engagement of PD-L1 to PD-1 on activated and exhausted cytotoxic T lymphocytes. PD-1 engagement on CTLs leads to decreased activation and effector functions through SHP-2 mediated dephosphorylation of T cell receptor and CD28 signaling cascades. It has been hypothesized that tumor-expressed PD-L1 serves as a direct molecular shield against CTL lysis of tumor cells. Emerging data suggest that the response of CTLs to PD-1/L1 blockade may depend on tumor anatomic sites and occur principally at metastatic rather than primary tumor sites. Robust tumor expression of PD-L1 promotes both micro- and macro-metastatic growth, with enhancement at metastatic sites compared to primary sites. However, how tPD-L1 differentially drives metastasis from the primary tumor remains unknown. PD-1 expression has been noted in other cell populations, including myeloid, dendritic, and tumor cells, contributing to tumor immune evasion. The connection between non-T cell-expressed PD-1 and CTL suppression via tPD-L1 is incompletely understood.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether tPD-L1 promotes metastatic growth through a direct effect on CTL activity or via an intermediate cell-mediated pathway. The authors first tested whether tPD-1:tPD-L1 interaction in a two-cell (CTL and tumor) system is sufficient to confer protection against CTL-mediated killing. A key hypothesis is that tPD-L1 targets myeloid cell-expressed PD-1 (mPD-1) to suppress type I IFN expression and function, rather than CTL PD-1. The authors predicted that attenuation of type I IFN signaling in myeloid cells would repress Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 expression, thereby impairing CTL recruitment to the lung metastatic niche. A secondary hypothesis proposed that the PD-1/L1 axis creates a negative feedback circuit, induced by and then attenuating type I interferon signaling. The study further hypothesized that myeloid cells are the obligatory bridge linking tPD-L1 expression to CTL recruitment in lung metastasis. The human translational hypothesis is that IFN-I response in myeloid cells correlates with patient response to PD-1 blockade in metastatic cancer. The ultimate model proposed is the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controlling CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis.

Methodological Details
Cell lines used include 4T1 (murine triple negative breast cancer) and CT26 (murine mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer), chosen because they show minimal response to ICB in clinical disease. PD-L1 was deleted in 4T1 and CT26 cells using CRISPR/Cas9, producing PD-L1 KO variants that cannot engage CTL PD-1 due to lack of PD-L2. The in vitro CTL-tumor interaction system used 2/20 tumor-specific CTLs sensitive to PD-1-mediated inhibition, recognizing the H2-Ld-restricted AH1 epitope (residues 6-14) of gp70. 2/20 CTLs were chosen because they exert antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes without prior differentiation, recapitulating the effector CTL:tumor interaction in the TME. For in vivo orthotopic tumors, 4T1 cells were injected into the right second mammary gland of syngeneic mice. For subcutaneous tumors, CT26 cells were injected into the right flank. For experimental metastasis, tumor cells were injected into the lateral tail vein of Balb/c mice. Lung metastasis was quantified by India ink solution inflation after tail vein injection. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on lungs 7 days after tail vein injection, with RNA extracted via Direct-zol RNA microprep and sequenced by Novogene. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on lungs 14 days after tail vein injection, capturing ~2-3 x 10^3 cells per sample on Chromium Chip B (10x Genomics). scRNA-seq reads aligned to mm10 generated 30-39K reads/cell, 75-102 million reads per sample, and ~1600 median genes per cell at 88% Q30 in RNA read. Flow cytometry was conducted on a FACSCalibur with CellQuestPro or LSRFortessa with BD Diva 8.01; analysis was performed in FlowJo v10.6.0. Statistical analysis used Prism8 with two-tailed Student's t-test and log-rank test for survival groups. Myeloid cell depletion was performed using clodronate liposomes in tumor-bearing mice. Human patient data included metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients with single-cell sequencing before and after PD-1 blockade, accessed via TCGA and BMS038 datasets. Cell lines (4T1, CT26, RAW264.7, J774M, 293FT, CMS4-met) were obtained from ATCC or as previously described; all tested bi-monthly for mycoplasma. Antibodies for neutralization experiments included 200 µg of anti-CD8α (53-6.7, BioXcell) or isotype control (2A3, BioXcell) injected i.v. every other day. The colonization assay involved tail vein injection, sacrificing at 24 hours, and homogenization in Trizol for PCR analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
CRISPR lentivirus was produced by co-transfecting HEK293FT cells with pCMV-VSV-G, psPAX2, and lentiCRISPRv2 plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000. Tumor cells were transduced with CRISPR lentivirus, selected with puromycin, and sorted for marker --cells using BD FACSARIA. For bulk RNA-seq, reads were aligned to mm10 reference using STARv2.5; quantification with HTSeqv0.6.1; rank-log transformed counts from DESeq2 for GSEA, GO, and PCA. GSEA was performed with GSEA4.0 (Broad) using gene-set permutation; GO pathway enrichment with clusterprofiler. For scRNA-seq, libraries generated with Chromium Single Cell 3' Reagent Kit v3; sequenced on Illumina NextSeq 500 (28bp R1, 8bp indexing, 91bp RNA R2). Reads mapped to mm10 via STAR in Cell Ranger 3.1.0 pipeline; high-quality cells extracted (200 < feature count < 4000, percent mitochondrial reads < 10). Cells clustered using first fifty principal components; Myeloid and T cell subsets reclustered on top twenty principal components; annotation via comparison to pre-existing datasets using SingleR. MSigDB and signature sets generated during the study loaded into VISION for single-cell scoring. tPD-L1 loss gene signature: genes increased ≥2-fold with padj < 0.05 by DESeq2 from bulk RNA-seq. SHP-2 activation signature: genes increased 2-fold (padj < 0.05) in myeloid cells following SHP099 treatment, with score inverted. MA, MB, and MC gene signatures: Seurat TransferData function transferred labels from macrophage PHATE clusters to human lung tumor-resident macrophage dataset. For patient analysis, mRNA and survival datasets from TCGA; BMS038 data accessed from authors' processed files; PRJEB23709 dataset pseudo-aligned with kallisto. Batch effects in melanoma cohort corrected by Harmony; tumor-infiltrating macrophages subsetted and analyzed with Seurat pipeline. Immunohistochemistry: tissue fixed in 10% formalin, paraffin-blocked, cut into sections; stained and analyzed with LAS4.1 software; CD3+ cells quantified by quPATH. Western blotting: lysates subjected to electrophoresis and transfer; antibodies listed in Table S1. For co-culture cytotoxicity, supernatant and cells stained with APC-AnnexinV and propidium iodide.

Key Results
In vitro: when only 4T1 or CT26 cells and 2/20 CTLs were present, tPD-L1 conferred no survival advantage or reduced CTL killing, supporting the null hypothesis of direct protection. In vivo: no difference in primary tumor growth was observed between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 orthotopic tumors, or between WT and KO CT26 subcutaneous tumors. Increased infiltration of CD3+ cells after loss of tPD-L1 in lung (but not in primary tumor) indicated tPD-L1 blocked T cell infiltration at the metastatic site. No difference in initial tumor cell colonization (gp70 level in lungs one day after injection) demonstrated PD-L1 does not enhance DTC colonization efficiency. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in adaptive-immune deficient RAGII-KO mice, indicating tPD-L1 requires a functioning adaptive immune system. Genetic ablation of MHC class I antigen presentation or antibody-mediated CD8+ T cell depletion revealed tPD-L1 drove metastasis by suppressing CTL killing. scRNA-seq of CD45+ leukocytes from WT and PDL1-KO lungs (~7500 cells) revealed differentially expressed transcripts involved in antigen presentation; no change in bulk myeloid cell composition observed but enhanced antigen presentation machinery detected in macrophages. Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) identified as marker for IFN-stimulated myeloid cells; its differential expression in 4T1-colonized lungs occurred as early as one day after injection, before robust CTL infiltration. Myeloid cell surface PD-1 expression was enhanced following tPD-L1 loss in lungs. In vitro co-culture: 4T1-tPD-L1 bound to RAW264.7 macrophages upregulated surface PD-1 in cell-contact and IFNAR-dependent manner; engagement enhanced SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1 levels. RAW PD-1 loss led to increased sensitivity to TLR3 ligand poly(I:C) as measured by surface marker BST2 on both RAW and 4T1 cells. Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFN-beta production, confirming a negative feedback circuit where PD-1/L1 is induced by and attenuates IFN signaling. Myeloid cell depletion with clodronate liposomes diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting tumor growth in lungs. Human patient PHATE analysis: PD-1 blockade released myeloid cell differentiation restriction, leading to enhanced interferon signaling, antigen presentation, and CTL-recruiting chemokine expression. TCGA analysis and BMS038 data supported that IFN-I response in myeloid cells correlates with PD-1 blockade efficacy.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary mechanistic conclusion is that tPD-L1 does not inhibit CTL killing directly but operates via a myeloid cell-dependent pathway to create an immunologically cold metastatic niche. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis represents a novel pathway by which tumors previously considered ICB-resistant nevertheless depend on PD-L1 to evade immune clearance of metastases. The PD-1/L1 axis functions as a negative feedback circuit induced by IFN signaling, explaining why low response rates in interferon alpha therapies may result from compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. The findings provide a rationale for neoadjuvant and adjuvant ICB, where sustained remission relies on coordinated suppression of metastases. Type I IFN signaling is established as essential for myeloid cell function in CTL recruitment to the lung metastasis niche. The work aligns with recent observations of CTL infiltration into metastases post-PD-1 blockade and supports the hypothesis that PD-L1 at dendritic cells controls CTL function.

Contradictions And Limitations
A limitation is that the study exclusively analyzed lung metastases, which due to their location in barrier tissue may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment. Conflicting findings regarding the role of tPD-L1 in PD-1 blockade efficacy have been reported, though consensus exists that tPD-L1 may be sufficient but not necessary for response. The study was limited to two tumor cell lines (4T1, CT26) and one myeloid cell line (RAW264.7) for in vitro validation. The human dataset was restricted to a specific cohort of metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients with single-cell sequencing, limiting generalizability across cancer types. The single-cell RNA-seq analysis of mouse lungs used only the first fifty principal components for clustering, which may not capture all dimensions of heterogeneity.

Claims
Tumor PD-L1 has no direct effect on CTL cytotoxic activity in the absence of other tumor microenvironmental factors. In vitro 2/20 CTL co-culture with 4T1 and CT26 cells showed no reduced cytotoxicity when PD-L1 was present. PD-L1 KO tumor cells showed no PD-L2 expression, eliminating the only alternative PD-1 ligand. Some prior studies have suggested direct effects, but the authors' controlled in vitro system explicitly ruled this out for the specific models tested. This necessitates looking for a third-party cell type, which the authors identified as myeloid cells via scRNA-seq.
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis through a myeloid-cell-dependent pathway involving PD-1 engagement, IFN-I suppression, and chemokine downregulation. Myeloid cell depletion by clodronate liposomes diminished PD-L1-driven lung tumor growth. scRNA-seq revealed PD-L2 (Pdcd1lg2) upregulation in myeloid cells as early as one day after injection, prior to CTL infiltration. Co-culture demonstrated PD-L1:mPD-1 engagement via SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1 and MHCII expression. RAW PD-1 loss increased BST2 expression in response to poly(I:C), confirming a type I IFN response pathway. Human PHATE showed PD-1 blockade released myeloid differentiation restriction and enhanced interferon signaling. No change in bulk myeloid cell composition was observed, though enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages. The tPD-L1/mPD-1 axis defines a therapeutic vulnerability in the metastatic niche, supporting ICB in adjuvant settings.
The PD-1/L1 axis forms a negative feedback circuit that is induced by type I interferon but attenuates subsequent IFN signaling. Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 enhanced IFN-beta production in co-culture. Type I IFN is known to induce PD-L1 more rapidly than PD-1 in myeloid cells.  This may explain why interferon alpha therapies had low response rates and supports combination therapy with TLR/STING agonists.

Data And Code Availability
The patient dataset from TCGA was accessed via standard repositories; the BMS038 dataset was accessed from authors' processed files at https://github.com/riazn/bms038_analysis. A previously published dataset of response following PD-1 treatment (PRJEB23709) was accessed from EMBL.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Genetic ablation of MHC class I antigen presentation and antibody-mediated CD8+ T cell depletion confirmed the phenotype is CTL-mediated. RAGII-KO mice demonstrated that PD-L1 function in metastasis requires a functioning adaptive immune system. SHP-2 inhibitor SHP099 was used to generate the SHP-2 activation signature, validating the pathway's causal link to PD-1 signaling. The PD-L1 KO and WT variants were tested in both the orthotopic (4T1) and subcutaneous (CT26) models. Cell lines were tested bi-monthly for mycoplasma and confirmed mycoplasma-free at the time of experiments. Doublet removal in scRNA-seq was performed twice (manual identification and then DoubletFinder) to ensure data quality.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows in vitro cytotoxicity of 4T1 and CT26 cells with 2/20 CTLs, demonstrating tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage. Figure 2 presents primary tumor growth comparisons between WT and PD-L1 KO 4T1 and CT26, showing no significant differences. Figure 3 displays increased CD3+ cell infiltration in lungs after PD-L1 loss, absence of differences in initial colonization, and RAGII-KO metastasis results. Figure 4 shows single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ leukocytes from WT and PDL1-KO lungs, with UMAP clustering. Figure 5 displays Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) expression changes in myeloid cells, antigen presentation machinery in macrophages, and flow cytometry validation. Figure 6 shows myeloid cell surface PD-1 enhancement, RAW co-culture with SHP-2 and pSTAT1, BST2 response to poly(I:C), and IFN-beta production results. Figure 7 presents human patient PHATE analysis before and after PD-1 blockade, showing differentiation restriction release and enhanced interferon signaling.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis not by direct inhibition of CTL cytotoxicity, but by engaging myeloid-cell PD-1 to repress type I IFN, thereby blocking CTL recruitment via downregulated Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of in vitro co-culture validation (SHP-2, pSTAT1, BST2, IFN-beta), myeloid cell depletion in vivo, and human single-cell sequencing showing IFN-I restoration post PD-1 blockade. 3. The future path lies in developing combination therapies targeting the IFN-I/STAT1 axis (e.g., TLR/STING agonists) in conjunction with ICB for metastatic cancer, and extending findings to other organ-specific metastatic niches.

summary.title: Stem Cell Microarrays for Assessing Growth Factor Signaling in Engineered
summary.authors: Glycan Microenvironments (University of California San Diego); Austen L Michalak (University of California San Diego); Greg W Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kelsey A Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kamil Godula (University of California San Diego)
summary.field_subfield: Biomaterials / Glycobiology - Stem cell engineering and glycan signaling
summary.executive_summary: This study describes the development of a stem cell microarray platform that integrates glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates into a polyacrylamide hydrogel to directly measure the contribution of extracellular glycans to growth factor signaling in murine embryonic stem cells. The authors addressed the challenge of structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity in glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) by using chemically well-defined HS structures—produced via synthetic, chemoenzymatic, and genetic engineering routes—immobilized on a non-biofouling acrylamide scaffold. Heparin was covalently crosslinked to gelatin via NHS-ester chemistry to prevent leaching during cell culture, with ∼15% crosslinking per chain targeted to preserve GF binding activity. Murine Ext1−/− embryonic stem cells, lacking endogenous cell surface HS, served as the cell model. Key validation showed: (1) NHS-crosslinked heparin provided 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal compared to physisorbed heparin; (2) ~40% FGF2 binding was retained after 48 hours of serum-free culture; (3) FGF2 binding selectivity to fully sulfated heparin vs. 2O- and 6O-desulfated forms matched known requirements; and (4) the optimal seeding density of 40,000 cells/cm² supported confluent ESC monolayers with Oct4 expression. The functional assay demonstrated that immobilized heparin at 500 µg/mL stimulated ERK1/2 phosphorylation in response to 0.5 ng/mL FGF2, though with somewhat lower MAPK activity compared to soluble heparin (5 µg/mL), likely due to limited FGFR accessibility. The platform offers a rapid, multiplexed tool for optimizing functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study describes the development of a stem cell microarray platform that integrates glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates into a polyacrylamide hydrogel to directly measure the contribution of extracellular glycans to growth factor signaling in murine embryonic stem cells. The authors addressed the challenge of structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity in glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) by using chemically well-defined HS structures—produced via synthetic, chemoenzymatic, and genetic engineering routes—immobilized on a non-biofouling acrylamide scaffold. Heparin was covalently crosslinked to gelatin via NHS-ester chemistry to prevent leaching during cell culture, with ∼15% crosslinking per chain targeted to preserve GF binding activity. Murine Ext1−/− embryonic stem cells, lacking endogenous cell surface HS, served as the cell model. Key validation showed: (1) NHS-crosslinked heparin provided 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal compared to physisorbed heparin; (2) ~40% FGF2 binding was retained after 48 hours of serum-free culture; (3) FGF2 binding selectivity to fully sulfated heparin vs. 2O- and 6O-desulfated forms matched known requirements; and (4) the optimal seeding density of 40,000 cells/cm² supported confluent ESC monolayers with Oct4 expression. The functional assay demonstrated that immobilized heparin at 500 µg/mL stimulated ERK1/2 phosphorylation in response to 0.5 ng/mL FGF2, though with somewhat lower MAPK activity compared to soluble heparin (5 µg/mL), likely due to limited FGFR accessibility. The platform offers a rapid, multiplexed tool for optimizing functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies.

Research Context
Extracellular glycans such as glycosaminoglycans provide essential regulatory components during tissue development and maintenance. GAGs harbor binding sites for growth factors and establish gradients in the extracellular matrix. However their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make establishing structure-function relationships difficult. Recent advances in synthetic and chemoenzymatic HS oligosaccharide synthesis have produced well-defined structures. Arrays of isolated HS on glass surfaces are routinely used to profile HS-binding protein specificity. A gap exists for multiplexed on-array analysis of HS-dependent cellular signaling to streamline biomaterial discovery.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a hydrogel-based microarray can present GAG-protein conjugates to progenitor cells in a spatially isolated format to measure growth factor signaling contributions. The authors hypothesized that covalent crosslinking of GAGs to a protein matrix within the hydrogel would retain the polysaccharide without compromising GF-binding ability. It was predicted that specific sulfation patterns of HS would determine FGF2 binding selectivity on the array, matching known structural requirements. The platform was expected to support ERK1/2 phosphorylation in response to FGF2 in Ext1−/− ESCs, mimicking the endogenous HS-GF-FGFR signaling complex.

Methodological Details
The substrates were thin poly(acrylamide) hydrogels deposited on glass according to a method by Brafman et al. Gelatin was used at a concentration of 500 µg/mL in PBS to support ESC growth. Heparin was used as a model HS glycan at molecular weight 12 kDa. Heparin concentrations ranged from 50 to 750 µg/mL for array optimization. The cell model was murine Ext1−/− ESCs, which lack cell surface HS and are unable to engage HS-dependent GFs. Seeding densities tested included 20,000, 40,000, and 100,000 cells/cm². FGF2 stimulation was performed at 0.5 ng/mL for 15 minutes at 37 °C. MAPK activity was quantified by immunofluorescence for pErk1/2 and total Erk1/2. Soluble heparin at 5 µg/mL served as a positive control for ERK phosphorylation. The array was washed for 3 hours prior to fluorescent staining.

Procedures And Architectures
Dry acrylamide substrates were spotted with gelatin solutions containing heparin or crosslinked heparin. Heparin was activated via NHS treatment in HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH = 7.4) with EDC at 4 °C for 18 hours. Purification was performed by size exclusion on a PD10 column to remove small molecule reagents. The target crosslinking level was approximately 15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain to promote retention while preserving GF binding. ESCs were seeded for 24 hours in embryonic culture media with LIF and FBS, then cultured for an additional 24 hours serum-free. Cells were fixed, permeabilized, and immunoassayed after FGF2 stimulation. Fluorescence was detected using a microarray scanner and validated via fluorescence microscopy. The pERK/ERK ratio was used to quantify signaling, with signal detection via microarray scanner validated by ImageJ analysis.

Key Results
NHS-crosslinked heparin provided 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin on the array. After 48 hours of ESC culture, the heparin arrays retained approximately 40% of FGF2 binding activity. FGF2 bound most strongly to fully sulfated heparin, with progressive loss of activity upon removal of 6O-, 2O-, and N-sulfates. CS56 and HABP proteins exhibited high specificity for CS and HA, respectively, confirming preservation of binding specificity post-crosslinking. The optimal seeding density of 40,000 cells/cm² produced consistent ESC monolayers with Oct4 expression and no Nestin differentiation. Only Ext1−/− ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin showed significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation. MAPK activity on the arrayed heparin was somewhat lower than with its soluble form, likely due to limited FGFR accessibility. FGF2 stimulation showed a heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation across 0-500 µg/mL immobilized heparin.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The crosslinking strategy confirms that covalent tethering of GAGs to a protein matrix does not alter their intrinsic protein-binding specificity. The requirement for HS in FGF2-FGFR signaling complex formation is validated in the context of immobilized glycan arrays. The platform enables rapid, multiplexed screening of the expanding repertoire of synthetic and chemoenzymatic GAG structures for biomaterial design. The results support the hypothesis that GAG sulfation patterns directly dictate growth factor binding and subsequent cellular signaling.

Contradictions And Limitations
MAPK activity was somewhat lower on the array compared to the soluble heparin benchmark, suggesting incomplete FGFR accessibility at the cell-array interface. The crosslinking strategy targeted ∼15% per chain, but the exact quantitative distribution per spot was not explicitly measured. Only 40% FGF2 binding activity remained after 48 hours, indicating substantial loss of immobilized heparin over two days of culture. The paper does not report the exact statistical p-values or confidence intervals for the 5-to-10-fold signal difference.

Claims
NHS-crosslinking of heparin to gelatin preserves GAG protein-binding specificity while improving array stability. Crosslinked heparin provided 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal than physisorbed heparin. Binding selectivity to 6O-, 2O-, and N-desulfated forms matched known structural requirements. CS56 and HABP maintained specificity for CS and HA respectively. Only 40% of binding activity was retained after 48 hours, suggesting significant hydrolysis or leaching. This enables the confident use of crosslinked GAGs in biomaterials without fear of altered function.
The hydrogel-based microarray platform directly detects FGF2-mediated ERK1/2 activation in live stem cells. Only Ext1−/− ESCs with immobilized or soluble heparin showed significant pErk1/2. Doseresponsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation was observed from 0 to 500 µg/mL heparin. FGF2 stimulation with 0.5 ng/mL heparin at 37 °C produced measurable pErk1/2. Immobilized heparin produced somewhat lower MAPK activity than soluble heparin. The platform can be used to rapidly optimize glycomaterial compositions for regenerative therapies.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The array was tested at heparin concentrations ranging from 50 to 750 µg/mL to establish dose-dependence. Three ESC seeding densities (20,000, 40,000, 100,000 cells/cm²) were tested to optimize colony growth without detachment. The array was subjected to 48 hours of ESC culture conditions at 37 °C, 5% CO₂ to assess heparin retention. FGF2 binding selectivity was assessed using HABP and CS56 in addition to FGF2 to confirm specificity for multiple GAG classes. N-desulfated heparin with acetamide-capped amino groups (NAc-Hep) was included to better represent native HS structures.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows a schematic of the hydrogel microarray approach with GAGs conjugated to gelatin on an acrylamide scaffold. Figure 2A demonstrates that covalently linked heparin shows superior FGF2 binding capacity compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin. Figure 2B shows FGF2 retention on the array surface for 48 hours under cellular culture conditions. Figure 2C displays GAG molecular recognition selectivity using FGF2, HABP, and CS56 across a panel of HS, CS, DS, and HA variants. Figure 3A shows ESC monolayer formation on gelatin/heparin spots at optimal seeding density. Figure 3B confirms Oct4 expression and absence of Nestin differentiation in array-grown ESCs. Figure 4A shows ESC culture conditions for the FGF2 signaling assay on gelatin spots with or without NHS-crosslinked heparin. Figure 4B presents the microarray scanner quantification of pErk1/2 vs total Erk1/2 across all conditions including soluble heparin control. Figure 4C provides fluorescence microscopy validation of the microarray scanner results showing co-localization of pErk and Erk signals. Figure 4D shows the heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation from 0 to 500 µg/mL immobilized heparin.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a hydrogel-based GAG microarray platform that enables multiplexed, direct measurement of growth factor signaling in stem cells, integrating covalently crosslinked GAG-protein conjugates. 2. The strongest evidence is the 5-to-10-fold higher FGF2 binding of NHS-crosslinked heparin, the preservation of 40% binding after 48 hours of culture, and the dose-responsive ERK1/2 activation confirming functional signaling. 3. The future path involves capitalizing on the rapidly expanding repertoire of synthetic and chemoenzymatic GAG structures to systematically optimize bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal (University of Maryland); Priya Aggarwal (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology); Luiz Pessoa (University of Maryland); Anubha Gupta (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Neuroscience / Deep Learning (Brain-computer interface, fMRI state decoding)
summary.type_of_paper: Research article / Methods and validation study
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes and validates a bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network architecture for decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data. The central innovation is the use of both forward and backward temporal context to account for the inherent latency and dynamics of the BOLD signal, removing the need for the conventional hard-coded delay adjustments typically required when synchronizing stimuli with fMRI responses. The authors argue that future temporal context carries useful information for capturing BOLD dynamics and that a unidirectional LSTM, which only processes past information, is insufficient. The model is implemented with two hidden LSTM layers, each having 256 hidden activations, followed by a fully-connected layer with 9 neurons and softmax activation. The merging of forward and backward activations is implemented as vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). The model was trained on a 10-fold inter-subject cross-validation of 400 participants from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) working memory task data. Quantitative results show that the bi-LSTM (concatenation variant) achieved a classification accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02, an 18% absolute improvement over the unidirectional LSTM baseline of 0.66 ± 0.18. The model required no delay adjustment, and class imbalance was addressed using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine. Key findings highlight that while both models struggle most with the "Others" (fixation) class, the bi-LSTM significantly reduces misclassifications across all brain states. The confusion matrix analysis reveals specific stimulus-state mixing, such as between body and tools stimuli. The study concludes that bidirectional modeling of temporal context improves fMRI state decoding robustness and suggests future work in window-size optimization and class imbalance refinement.

claims.description: A bidirectional LSTM that encodes both past and future temporal context significantly outperforms a unidirectional LSTM for fMRI brain-state decoding, eliminating the need for BOLD signal delay adjustment.

Executive Summary
This paper proposes and validates a bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network architecture for decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data. The central innovation is the use of both forward and backward temporal context to account for the inherent latency and dynamics of the BOLD signal, removing the need for the conventional hard-coded delay adjustments typically required when synchronizing stimuli with fMRI responses. The authors argue that future temporal context carries useful information for capturing BOLD dynamics and that a unidirectional LSTM, which only processes past information, is insufficient. The model is implemented with two hidden LSTM layers, each having 256 hidden activations, followed by a fully-connected layer with 9 neurons and softmax activation. The merging of forward and backward activations is implemented as vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). The model was trained on a 10-fold inter-subject cross-validation of 400 participants from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) working memory task data. Quantitative results show that the bi-LSTM (concatenation variant) achieved a classification accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02, an 18% absolute improvement over the unidirectional LSTM baseline of 0.66 ± 0.18. The model required no delay adjustment, and class imbalance was addressed using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine. Key findings highlight that while both models struggle most with the "Others" (fixation) class, the bi-LSTM significantly reduces misclassifications across all brain states. The confusion matrix analysis reveals specific stimulus-state mixing, such as between body and tools stimuli. The study concludes that bidirectional modeling of temporal context improves fMRI state decoding robustness and suggests future work in window-size optimization and class imbalance refinement.

Research Context
Conventional brain-state decoding methods from fMRI rely on univariate analysis of thousands of brain locations, treating each separately. Multivariate analysis was developed to integrate distributed but overlapping information across the spatial domain. Time-sensitive machine learning frameworks, particularly RNNs including Echo-state Networks and LSTM models, have shown better performance in characterizing dynamic fMRI information. LSTM models store information from the past as contextual information for learning robust features, but they do not naturally capture future temporal context. The BOLD response contains inherent latency and time-lag relative to stimulus presentation, necessitating conventional delay adjustments in univariate approaches. Existing unidirectional LSTM approaches for fMRI integrate only temporal information from past time points, leaving the future temporal context unused. Variations in latency across BOLD responses suggest that temporal context from future instances is also important for capturing BOLD dynamics.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether encoding both past and future temporal context through a bidirectional LSTM architecture improves brain state decoding compared to unidirectional LSTM. The authors hypothesize that the forward and reverse hidden activations of bi-LSTM can be collated to build the model's memory and robustly predict brain states at every time instance. A secondary hypothesis is that this bidirectional framework can eliminate the need for any hard-coded time-delay adjustment for stimulus and BOLD response synchronization. The authors assert that future temporal context contains useful information for capturing BOLD response dynamics due to variations in latency across time. The predicted outcome is superior classification accuracy for bi-LSTM over unidirectional LSTM across all brain states when trained on working memory fMRI data.

Methodological Details
The study used task fMRI data of the working memory task from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) data release. A random sample of N = 400 participants was selected from the total N = 1200 data release. The working memory task consisted of a 2-back task (matching current stimulus with the one two stimuli before) and a 0-back control condition. The task also combined category representation with four stimulus types: tools, places, faces, and body parts. Each participant provided data for two runs, each with 8 task blocks per stimuli-task combination. Each block lasted 27.5 seconds, with four fixation blocks of 15 seconds each after every two task blocks. Each fMRI scan yielded a sequence of 405 time-points long. The available preprocessed data included field-map distortion correction, functional to structural alignment, and intensity normalization. Motion-related variables (6 translation parameters and their derivatives) were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve with the ortvec option in AFNI. Low-frequency signals were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve with the polort option. Only cortical data from surface representation was used, with brain regions separated into 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs) via parcellation. The region-averaged timeseries served as the input feature vector, structured as a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. Each time-point in task blocks was assigned one of the brain states, and fixation blocks were labeled as "others", yielding S = 9 brain states in total. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed to adjust for delay in the BOLD response.

Procedures And Architectures
Brain-state decoding is modeled as a classification task where the RNN predicts the brain state of each time point based on input activation and temporal dependency. The LSTM uses gated cells with forget gate, input gate, cell activation, and hidden activation defined by transition equations. Bidirectional LSTM processes time-series data in both directions using separate hidden layers. The forward hidden activation is computed via standard LSTM equations, and the backward hidden activation uses future temporal dependency h_{t+1}. Three merging schemes are tested: vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). The bi-LSTM architecture has two hidden layers, each with 256 hidden activations per LSTM cell. A fully-connected layer with S = 9 neurons and softmax activation follows the last LSTM layer to map features to brain states. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed: N = 360 subjects for model development and N = 40 subjects as a held-out test set. The development set (9 folds) was further split 80-20 into training and validation sets. The full-length training data was windowed into small overlapping sequences of window size w = 40 with an overlap of 10 points. The model was implemented in Keras, trained on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with batch size of 32 and ADAM optimizer learning rate of 0.001. Training was performed for 100 epochs with no early stopping. A dropout of 0.3 was applied to LSTM layers to prevent overfitting. Class imbalance was handled using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine, weighting instances inversely proportional to their frequency. The number of layers and neural units for baseline LSTM and feed-forward NN models were kept identical to the bi-LSTM for controlled comparison.

Key Results
The overall classification accuracy of the unidirectional LSTM model was 0.66 ± 0.18. The classification accuracy of the bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM-c concatenation variant) was 0.84 ± 0.02. The bi-LSTM performed 18% better in terms of accuracy compared to its unidirectional counterpart. The highest misclassification rate for both models occurred for the "Others" (fixation) class due to its overrepresentation in the data. For every brain state, the LSTM model misclassified to a larger extent than the bi-LSTM-c model. When participants were stimulated with "faces" and "places", the second-highest confusion was with the task (0-back or 2-back), though the stimuli were correctly detected. The model also showed confusion between the stimuli "body" and "tools", indicated as the next highest confusion. Mean normalised confusion matrices illustrated in Figure 2 compare miss-classifications of both LSTM and bi-LSTM-c. The bidirectional LSTM achieved superior performance across all task states without hard-coded delay adjustment.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The superior performance of bi-LSTM demonstrates that future temporal context contains useful information for capturing BOLD response dynamics that unidirectional models cannot access. The bidirectional framework eliminates the need for conventional, hard-coded time-delay adjustments, suggesting that temporal dynamics alone can align stimuli and BOLD responses. The results support the assertion that temporal context from the future is important for generating accurate BOLD response representations. The confusion between "body" and "tools" stimuli suggests that certain cortical regions or feature representations may overlap for these categories, warranting further anatomical analysis. The model's reliance on both past and future information implies that BOLD dynamics are not purely causal in a single-directional sense when viewed through a classifier.

Contradictions And Limitations
The problem of class imbalance, though handled via compute_class_weight, still requires more sophisticated handling as the "Others" class misclassification remains highest for both models. The study used a fixed window length of w = 40 and overlap of 10, which may not be optimal; future work is needed to tune these parameters. The model was trained for 100 epochs without early stopping, and it is not reported whether the training loss converged or reached a plateau. It is not specified whether the 18% improvement is absolute or relative, though the numerical difference between 0.66 and 0.84 suggests an absolute improvement of 0.18. The paper does not report the specific number of epochs or the exact loss values at convergence for either the LSTM or bi-LSTM models. The confusion between stimuli and task states (e.g., faces/places vs. 0-back/2-back) suggests a residual failure in separating stimulus identity from task instruction.

Claims
A bidirectional LSTM that encodes both past and future temporal context significantly outperforms a unidirectional LSTM for fMRI brain-state decoding, eliminating the need for BOLD signal delay adjustment. The bi-LSTM accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02 versus unidirectional LSTM's 0.66 ± 0.18 demonstrates a substantial gain in predictive performance. The 18% absolute accuracy improvement confirms the effectiveness of bidirectional modeling. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed for delay adjustment in the bi-LSTM framework. The LSTM model misclassified to a larger extent compared to bi-LSTM-c for every brain state. Misclassification is still highest for the "Others" (fixation) class in both models, indicating a ceiling effect on the baseline. The model still confuses task states (0-back/2-back) with stimuli identity for face and place stimuli. Confusion between body and tools stimuli indicates the model is not perfect at resolving stimulus-level discriminability. The elimination of delay adjustment simplifies fMRI decoding pipelines by removing the need for estimated BOLD lag parameters. Bidirectional architectures may generalize to other temporal fMRI tasks beyond working memory. Future decoding methods should consider both temporal directions rather than purely causal past-to-present modeling.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The three merging schemes (concatenation, addition, averaging) were all implemented as bi-LSTM variants, with bi-LSTM-c (concatenation) serving as the primary comparison. A three-layer feed-forward NN was included as a non-temporal baseline with identical number of layers and neural units to ensure controlled comparison. The dropout of 0.3 in LSTM layers served as a regularization measure to prevent overfitting. The development set was randomly shuffled before the 80-20 training-validation split, reducing order-based bias. The model was evaluated on a held-out test fold of N = 40 subjects that was not seen during training or hyperparameter tuning.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 provides a schematic illustration of the Bidirectional LSTM architecture, showing the forward and backward hidden activation paths. Figure 2 shows mean normalised confusion matrices on classification accuracy for comparing miss-classifications of both LSTM and bi-LSTM-c.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that bidirectional LSTM architectures encoding both past and future BOLD dynamics outperform unidirectional LSTMs for fMRI brain-state decoding, achieving 0.84 ± 0.02 accuracy without any hard-coded delay adjustment. 2. The strongest evidence is the 18% absolute accuracy improvement (0.84 ± 0.02 bi-LSTM vs 0.66 ± 0.18 LSTM) achieved on N=400 HCP working memory participants, with the bi-LSTM reducing misclassifications for every brain state. 3. Future paths include tuning window size and overlap for time-series chunking, refining class imbalance handling, and investigating cortical regions specifically engaged in stimuli that the model confuses (body vs. tools).

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This phylogenetic and comparative genomic study investigated three closely related thermophilic genera within the family Bacillaceae: Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus, using 113 publicly available whole-genome sequences. The primary objective was to resolve the taxonomic placement of these genera which are moderate thermophiles capable of spore formation, often co-isolated from geothermal environments. The authors constructed a maximum-likelihood tree from 662 orthologous core genes and calculated two-way Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) for all genome pairs. The key finding is that the genomes split into two main clades: Clade I containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, while Clade II contains the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I was further partitioned into three distinct clades corresponding to Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade (I-c) containing Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies. The authors argue that this third clade is phylogenetically distinct enough from the other three genera to warrant elevation to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Additionally, two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning across different tree-building methods and could not be confidently assigned. The study underscores the necessity of considering closely related genera simultaneously during taxonomic assignment, as single-genus analyses can mask broader evolutionary relationships and lead to incongruent genus designations for new strains.

Research Context
Recent decades have seen a shift from DNA-DNA hybridization as the gold standard for bacterial taxonomy toward whole-genome approaches. While 16S rRNA gene sequencing is widely used, its low resolution at the genus and species levels limits its usefulness for precise classification. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) provides higher resolution for detecting relatedness among bacterial genomes than 16S rRNA sequencing. ANI is calculated by comparing two genome sequences and estimating the percentage identity of aligned nucleotides using BLAST. For comparisons between distant genomes, average amino acid identity (AAI) is recommended as amino acid similarity is better conserved than DNA sequence similarity. The three genera under study—Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus—belong to the family Bacillaceae and are moderate thermophiles capable of spore formation. Anoxybacillus was proposed in 2000 as a new genus within Bacillaceae based on a strain isolated from animal manure with anaerobic growth characteristics. Geobacillus was originally classified within the genus Bacillus, but a 2001 taxonomic study split eight species out to form Geobacillus. In 2016, Parageobacillus was defined by reassigning a clade from Geobacillus containing five species, based on core gene phylogeny, GC content, and ANI. Prior to this study, each genus had been studied largely in isolation or within limited subsets, creating uncertainty about intergeneric boundaries.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the taxonomic boundaries between Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus are accurately resolved when each genus is considered independently versus when they are analyzed as a unified phylogenomic group. A secondary question concerns the preliminary placement of 7 newly isolated strains of these genera in their respective phylogenetic groups. The implicit hypothesis is that considering closely related genera together will reveal incongruent placements and support the need for a new genus designation that a single-genus approach would miss. The study predicts that clade I-c, which had been assigned to Anoxybacillus and Geobacillus in different instances, would show enough distinctiveness to warrant its own genus designation. The authors hypothesize that ANI and AAI values, combined with core-gene tree topology, will provide sufficient evidence for a new genus proposal. A specific prediction is made that two species of Anoxybacillus would show inconsistent positioning across different methods and cannot be clearly resolved. The study also aims to confirm prior suggestions that G. galactosidasius and G. yumthangensis belong to Parageobacillus, a conclusion previously proposed by Najar and Thakur. The overarching outcome expected is a revised taxonomic framework for these thermophilic bacilli that integrates intergeneric phylogenomic evidence.

Methodological Details
A total of 113 genome assemblies were selected from the RefSeq database for phylogenomic analysis. The 113 genomes comprised thirty-two Anoxybacillus strains, seventy-three Geobacillus strains, and seven Parageobacillus species (one representative per species). Two Anoxybacillus, four Geobacillus, and one Parageobacillus strains obtained from a study of thermophiles in Australia were included as additional genomes. Of these additional 7 genomes, 31 were chromosome-level assemblies, 33 were scaffold genomes, and 49 were up to the contig level. Anomalous genome assemblies with suppressed RefSeq status, identified as chimeric, contaminated, or frameshifted, were excluded. The core genome was identified using EDGAR 2.0 with the genome of Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 as the starting reference. The genome of Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T was included as an outgroup in the core gene analysis. During core gene discovery, five assemblies with relatively low numbers of CDS were excluded because they significantly reduced the number of recognized core genes. One assembly was removed as it was an exact duplicate of another Anoxybacillus Suryakundensis strain. The final analysis used 114 genomes: 32 Anoxybacillus, 73 Geobacillus, 8 Parageobacillus, and one Bacillus (the outgroup). The obtained CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE, and the alignments were used to build a maximum-likelihood tree with FastTree. Two-way ANI values were calculated between all genome pairs using the ani.rb script with default parameters. Two-way AAI values were calculated between all genome pairs using the aai.rb script. Draft genomes were concatenated with 100 N bases introduced between contigs before AAI calculation. ANI and AAI similarity matrices were used as input to the DendroUPGMA web server with UPGMA clustering to obtain dendrograms. Genes unique to clade I-c were identified using BLASTn alignment against all assemblies in the NCBI RefSeq and nt databases. The relaxed BLASTn filtering criteria were percentage identity 30%, bitscore 10, and percentage overlap of 1%. The CDS used for alignment were from the assembly Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2, a member of clade I-c. CDS were considered unique to clade I-c if present in all clade I-c members and no members of clade I-a, I-b, or clade II. GC content and genome size were calculated for all genomes for taxonomic delimitation. The methodological approach followed methods used for reassessment of the genus Geobacillus by Aliyu et al. [36].

Procedures And Architectures
The core genome was identified by comparing all CDS from the Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 starting reference against all selected genome assemblies via BLAST. The identification of a core genome required that CDS from the reference assembly have orthologs in all other selected assemblies. The core gene tree was built as a maximum-likelihood tree from the alignment of 662 orthologous core genes. FastTree software was used for maximum-likelihood tree construction from concatenated CDS alignments. MUSCLE was used to align the concatenated CDS sequences. The EDGAR 2.0 platform was used for the core genome identification process. ANI calculations utilized the ani.rb script with default parameters for two-way comparisons between all 114 genomes. AAI calculations utilized the aai.rb script, with draft genomes having 100 N bases inserted between contigs prior to concatenation. Both Ruby scripts for ANI and AAI are part of the enveomics package. UPGMA clustering was used for the similarity matrices on the DendroUPGMA web server to produce dendrograms. The Interactive Tree Of Life web-based tool was used to plot the final trees. BLASTn searches were performed against both NCBI RefSeq and NCBI nt databases to identify genes unique to clade I-c. GC content was calculated for all 114 genomes as a supplementary taxonomic metric. Genome size was also calculated for all 114 genomes. The study followed the taxonomy where G. galactosidasius and G. yumthangensis were reclassified as P. galactosidasius and P. yumthangensis, consistent with Najar and Thakur.

Key Results
A total of 662 orthologous genes were identified as the core gene set from 114 genomes, used to produce a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree. The core gene maximum likelihood tree splits into three major groups: the outgroup (Bacillus subtilis spizizenii), clade I (87 genomes), and clade II (24 Anoxybacillus genomes). Clade I consists of 87 genomes, while Clade II consists of 24 Anoxybacillus genomes. Clade II includes species: A. flavithermus, A. pushchinoensis, A. gonensis, A. kamchatkensis, A. thermarum, A. ayderensis, A. mongoliensis, A. suryakundensis, and three unnamed Anoxybacillus species. Clade I was further partitioned into three sub-clades: Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade (I-c) containing A. tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies. Two-way ANI values were calculated between all 114 genome pairs and used to build a UPGMA dendrogram. The genome of Anoxybacillus sp. CHMUD had the most distant ANI value at 95.03 and an AAI of 95.81. Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL, Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3, and Geobacillus sp. DSP4a had ANI values of 97.99, 97.14, and 97.64, respectively. Two-way average AAI values were calculated between all 114 genome pairs and used to build a second UPGMA dendrogram. A total of 6 CDS were found to be unique to clade I-c, present in all members of the clade and absent in all other clades. The average ANI and AAI values for the candidate new genus (clade I-c) suggest it is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus than to Geobacillus or the other Anoxybacillus clade. The GC content of the three genomes in clade I-c was reported as lower than the GC content of the two species in clade I-a (the two species consistently in clade I-c). The two species of Anoxybacillus, A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning among the trees produced by differing methods and could not be clearly resolved. The data from the present study agreed with the conclusion that G. galactosidasius and G. yumthangensis belong to Parageobacillus. The three phylogenetic trees (core gene ML, ANI UPGMA, AAI UPGMA) reaffirmed the distinctiveness of the two species consistently present in clade I-c with respect to the three existing genera.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The core finding is that genomes belonging to the same genus can be split into distinct clades when viewed within the context of closely related genera, and conversely, the same species can be assigned to different genera depending on the scope of the phylogenetic analysis. The genome from clade I-c had previously been assigned to the genus Anoxybacillus in one instance and to the genus Geobacillus in another, illustrating how single-genus approaches can produce incongruent taxonomic results. The authors argue that the breadth of species assessed together is essential for delimiting genera; a narrow scope fails to reveal the intergeneric relationships that place clade I-c outside both Anoxybacillus and Geobacillus clades. The proposal of Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. is grounded in the simultaneous convergence of core-gene tree topology, ANI and AAI dendrogram structure, and GC content differences. The study demonstrates that taxonomic affiliation of new genomes should be verified using both average nucleotide identity and multilocus (core-gene) phylogenetic analysis together, rather than either in isolation. The incongruent positioning of A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus underscores that even within well-defined genera, certain species may have evolutionary histories that cannot be simplified into a single-genus assignment using current methods. The findings imply that the bacterial taxonomy of Bacillaceae, and thermophilic Bacilli more generally, requires a multi-genus phylogenomic approach to avoid taxonomic inconsistencies and incorrect genus designations for new isolates.

Contradictions And Limitations
Two species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning among trees produced by different methods and could not be clearly resolved into any of the existing or new genera. The study was a preprint (bioRxiv) and had not been certified by peer review at the time of publication. The core gene tree was built from 662 orthologs, which represents only a fraction of the total proteome; the authors did not specify if this set was sufficient to capture all gene family signals. The study used publicly available genome sequences, which may vary in quality, assembly completeness, and annotation consistency. The relaxed BLASTn filtering criteria (30% identity, 10 bitscore, 1% overlap) for identifying clade-unique genes may introduce false positives or negatives; the authors did not perform a sensitivity analysis of these parameters. The proposal for Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. is preliminary; the authors note the two species in clade I-c were the only ones consistently placed, and the unnamed genomospecies had limited data. The authors note an alternative approach may be to merge the two clade I-c species with Parageobacillus, but this would create cascading taxonomic problems involving merging Parageobacillus with Geobacillus. The study did not include genomes from all 24 validly described Anoxybacillus species, as 11 lacked genome assemblies; the missing genomes might contain information that alters the clade topology. The study did not include any Geobacillus species that lacked genome assemblies, though the authors noted all 16 valid species had genome assemblies available.

Claims
The clade I-c, containing Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies, is sufficiently distinct from Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus to justify elevation to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus. The three phylogenetic trees (core gene ML, ANI UPGMA, AAI UPGMA) independently reaffirmed the distinctiveness of clade I-c. Six CDS were found to be unique to clade I-c, present in all clade members and absent in all other clades. Average ANI and AAI values indicate clade I-c is more closely related to Parageobacillus than to the other genera. GC content also supports a closer affinity to Parageobacillus over the other genera. The core gene tree shows clade I-c as a separate partition within clade I, distinct from the Geobacillus and Parageobacillus sub-clades. An alternative interpretation could be to merge the two clade I-c species with Parageobacillus, though this would cascade into merging Parageobacillus with Geobacillus. The unnamed genomospecies in clade I-c has limited data compared to the type species A. tepidamans. The proposal is framed as a preliminary placement based on the available 113 genomes. The creation of Quasigeobacillus would reorganize the taxonomy of thermophilic Bacillaceae, removing the two species from Anoxybacillus and placing them in a new genus. The proposal underscores that intergeneric phylogenomic analysis is required for accurate taxonomic delimitation. If the alternative merger were adopted, it would collapse Parageobacillus into Geobacillus, significantly simplifying the Bacillaceae taxonomy but potentially obscuring evolutionary signal.
The taxa G. galactosidasius and G. yumthangensis belong to Parageobacillus, confirming a prior hypothesis by Najar and Thakur. The ANI, AAI, and core-gene tree data from this study align with the earlier conclusion that these species belong to Parageobacillus. The two species cluster with the Parageobacillus clade in all three phylogenetic metrics. The reclassification has been adopted in the taxonomy used for this study.  The reclassification reduces the number of described species in Geobacillus and increases them in Parageobacillus. The stability of this classification is now reinforced by whole-genome evidence rather than just gene-level phylogeny.
A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus exhibit inconsistent phylogenetic placement and their genus-level affinity remains unresolved. The two species showed incongruous positioning across the different tree-building methods. The authors explicitly state their affinities remain unresolved at this point. No definitive counter-evidence is provided, as the ambiguity is a direct finding of the study. These species may need further sequencing, additional genome comparisons, or different phylogenetic methods to resolve their placement. The uncertainty highlights the limitations of even multi-method phylogenomic approaches for certain divergent taxa.

Data And Code Availability
The study used 113 publicly available whole-genome sequences from the NCBI RefSeq database. The two Ruby scripts used for ANI and AAI calculation (ani.rb and aai.rb) are publicly available in the enveomics package. The core gene set, tree topologies, ANI and AAI similarity matrices, GC content, and genome size data are summarized in Supplementary Tables S1-S5 and Figures 1-3. The authors did not explicitly mention a GitHub repository or code deposition for the tree-building or unique-gene identification scripts.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used three independent phylogenetic metrics (core-gene ML tree, ANI UPGMA dendrogram, AAI UPGMA dendrogram) and compared their topologies. Convergence across all three metrics was used to support the distinctiveness of clade I-c. Five assemblies with low CDS counts and one duplicate were excluded during core gene identification as sensitivity checks. The Relaxed BLASTn filtering criteria (30% identity, 10 bitscore, 1% overlap) were used for identifying unique genes, but no sensitivity analysis of these parameters was reported. The authors noted that the two species in clade I-c were the only ones consistently present across all three tree types, indicating method-dependent instability for other genomes.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the core gene maximum likelihood tree with 114 genomes, splitting into outgroup, clade I (87 genomes), and clade II (24 genomes). Figure 2 shows the two-way ANI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Figure 3 shows the two-way AAI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Table 1 reports the ANI and AAI values separating the candidate new genus (clade I-c) from members of the three existing genera. Table 2 reports the GC content differences supporting the closer affinity of clade I-c to Parageobacillus. Table 3 shows the pairwise ANI values for all 114 genomes, with the most distant pair being 95.03. Table 4 lists the 6 CDS unique to clade I-c with names, descriptions, and products. Table 5 provides the DNA sequences for each of the 6 clade I-c unique CDS. Table 6 shows BLASTn alignment results of the 6 clade I-c unique CDS against all members of the clade. Table 7 shows the best hit analysis for clade I-c unique genes. Supplementary Table S1 lists all 114 genomes included in the analysis. Supplementary Table S2 lists the assemblies removed during core gene identification.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that a combined multi-genus phylogenomic analysis reveals intergeneric boundaries—specifically identifying that clade I-c, previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus, is distinct enough to warrant a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. 2. The strongest evidence is the convergence of three independent metrics—the 662-gene maximum-likelihood core tree topology, ANI UPGMA dendrogram, AAI UPGMA dendrogram, and GC content profiles—all placing clade I-c outside of Geobacillus and Anoxybacillus while showing affinity to Parageobacillus. 3. The future path involves applying this multi-genus phylogenomic approach to other groups of closely related genera within Bacillaceae to identify hidden generic boundaries, and resolving the placement of outlier species such as A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus.
