judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates for the first time that the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication, specifically for Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV). Using Vero cells treated with the SERCA-specific non-competitive inhibitor thapsigargin at a non-toxic concentration (0.5 µM), the authors showed a significant reduction in viral replication for both NDV and PPRV, as well as for the DNA virus BHV-1, but not for BPXV. Time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays identified that thapsigargin specifically impairs viral entry and subcellular localization of viral proteins, without affecting attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa and goat kidney cells rescued the inhibitory effect of thapsigargin, and virus infection was shown to induce SERCA2 expression in Vero cells, which could be blocked by the inhibitor. A key finding is that NDV acquired significant resistance to thapsigargin (reducing from ~10,000-fold to ~100-fold inhibition) after 70 passages in Vero cells, while PPRV did not, representing a rare instance of virus resistance against a host-targeting agent. The authors conclude that SERCA is a viable candidate for antiviral drug development targeting paramyxovirus replication.

Research Context
Antiviral strategies have classically targeted viral proteins directly, but the high mutation rates of viral genomes facilitate the emergence of drug resistance. Proviral host factors that facilitate virus replication represent an alternative target class with potentially higher genetic barriers to resistance. Three P-type Ca2+-ATPases (PMCA, SERCA, and SPCA) regulate intracellular calcium homeostasis, with SERCA transporting calcium from the cytosol to the endoplasmic reticulum. While SPCA1 has been shown to support virus replication, the roles of SERCA and PMCA in virus replication remain largely unknown. The authors previously screened kinase and phosphate inhibitors against influenza A, and identified SERCA as a candidate inhibitor for NDV and PPRV in the present study.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether SERCA facilitates paramyxovirus replication and at which stage of the viral life cycle it functions. The hypothesis is that SERCA is required for optimal NDV and PPRV replication and that inhibition of SERCA will reduce viral titers. It was further hypothesized that SERCA overexpression would rescue inhibition and that virus infection would upregulate SERCA expression. The authors also sought to determine the specific step impaired by thapsigargin and whether resistance could be acquired against a host-targeting agent.

Methodological Details
Vero (African green-monkey kidney), 293T (human embryonic kidney), HeLa, and goat kidney cells were grown in DMEM supplemented with 10% heatinactivated fetal bovine serum. Thapsigargin, a non-competitive SERCA inhibitor, was procured from Sigma (Catalog Number T9033) and used at 0.5 µM for antiviral assays. Cytotoxicity of thapsigargin was assessed by MTT assay, with toxicity observed only at concentrations exceeding 2 µM. Vero/MDBK cells were infected at MOI=0.1 in the presence of 0.5 µM thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO vehicle control, with progeny virus quantified by plaque assay. For virucidal assays, virus suspensions (~10^6 pfu) were incubated with ten-fold dilutions of thapsigargin for 1.5 h at 37 °C before testing residual infectivity. Step-specific assays (attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, budding) were conducted using the previously described time-of-addition protocol. For SERCA overexpression, HeLa and goat kidney cells were transfected in 24-well plates in triplicates with either 1 µg empty vector (pCR3) or pCR3-SERCA2 using Lipofectamine 3000. Immunofluorescence was performed at ~20% confluency with MOI=5 for 2 h, followed by thapsigargin application at 3 hpi (NDV) or 10 hpi (PPRV). For selection experiments, NDV and PPRV were sequentially passaged 70 times in Vero cells with 0.25 µM thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO, and the virus was quantified at each passage. Relative resistance was re-evaluated at MOI=0.1 and 24 h harvest time to compare thapsigargin-passaged with control-passaged viruses.

Procedures And Architectures
Thapsigargin, a sesquiterpene lactone extracted from Thapsia garganica, acts as a non-competitive inhibitor of SERCA. The MTT cytotoxicity assay established a non-toxic window from 0.00064 µM to 2 µM, defining 0.5 µM as the optimal experimental concentration. Plaque assays were used to determine viral titers, with the previously described protocol applied across all infection, virucidal, and step-specific experiments. Overexpression was achieved via lipofectamine-mediated transfection of pCR3-SERCA2 plasmid, followed by viral infection at MOI=1 and harvest at 24 hpi (NDV) or 96 hpi (PPRV). Immunofluorescence used 4% paraformaldehyde fixation (15 min), 1% BSA blocking (30 min), primary antibodies (30 min with 0.2% saponin), and DAPI counterstaining. Selection of resistant mutants involved 70 sequential passages in Vero cells, with confluent monolayers infected and incubated for 72–120 h until CPE in ≥75% cells. Western blot analysis of cell lysates at 16 hpi probed SERCA2 and GAPDH levels to evaluate NDV-induced SERCA expression under thapsigargin treatment.

Key Results
Thapsigargin at 0.5 µM significantly inhibited NDV and PPRV replication, but significantly inhibited BHV-1 and did not inhibit BPXV replication, demonstrating selectivity against paramyxoviruses and BHV-1. Virucidal assays showed that thapsigargin did not exhibit any effect on cell-free virions for any of the viruses tested at 0.5 µM or 5 µM, confirming the antiviral activity is cell-dependent. Overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa/goat kidney cells facilitated NDV/PPRV replication and rescued the inhibitory effect of thapsigargin, directly confirming SERCA's proviral role. PPRV infection induced a significant increase in SERCA2 expression starting at 3 hpi, peaking between 24–72 hpi, which could be blocked by thapsigargin treatment. The time-of-addition assay revealed the highest NDV inhibition when thapsigargin was applied 30 min prior to infection, with progressive decrease from 1 hpi to 6 hpi, and no effect at 10 hpi (budding). For PPRV, the highest inhibition was observed when thapsigargin was applied 30 min prior to infection, decreasing from 4 hpi to 24 hpi. Thapsigargin did not affect virus attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding, narrowing the impaired step to entry and protein localization. Viral entry assays with preattached virus (4 °C) at 37 °C showed reduced NDV and PPRV titers upon thapsigargin treatment, confirming inhibition of entry. Immunofluorescence showed defective cytoplasmic foci of viral proteins in ~70% of thapsigargin-treated cells, compared to 10–30% in DMSO controls, indicating impaired cytoplasm-to-surface transport. NDV acquired significant resistance to thapsigargin after ~25 passages, reaching ~100-fold inhibition at P35 compared to ~10,000-fold at P0, but complete resistance was not achieved at P70. Re-evaluation at MOI=0.1 and 24 h showed P70-thapsigargin NDV had significantly lower sensitivity than P0 or P70-control, but all PPRV variants showed similar sensitivity at P70.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
SERCA is identified as a crucial host factor facilitating paramyxovirus replication, particularly mediating viral entry and subcellular localization of viral proteins. The fact that thapsigargin inhibits multiple pre-budding steps (entry and localization) but not budding suggests a role in protein trafficking to the cell surface. Virus-induced SERCA2 upregulation suggests a positive feedback loop where the virus hijacks host calcium homeostasis to favor its own replication cycle. The acquisition of partial resistance by NDV to a host-targeting agent supports the theoretical framework that host-targeting strategies face higher genetic barriers but are not entirely resistant to viral escape. The finding that NDV but not PPRV acquired resistance suggests differential evolutionary pressures or mechanistic dependencies between the two paramyxoviruses. The study validates SERCA as a novel antiviral drug target, opening a new avenue for host-targeting therapeutics against paramyxoviruses.

Contradictions And Limitations
A complete thapsigargin-resistant NDV phenotype could not be achieved even up to 70 passages, leaving the mechanism of partial escape unresolved. Fluctuations in viral titers during passage experiments may be due to non-uniform MOI (0.01–0.001) and harvest times (72–120 h) at different passages. Co-immunoprecipitation assays to detect direct protein-protein interaction between SERCA and viral proteins were unsuccessful, so no direct interaction could be established. Immunofluorescence could not observe perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins, limiting the resolution of the interaction site. The virus-specific step-specific data was not shown for all assays, limiting a complete mechanisitic map of every virus life cycle stage. Resistance was only demonstrated for NDV, while PPRV remained sensitive, limiting the generalizability of the resistance finding to all paramyxoviruses.

Claims
SERCA is a proviral host factor that facilitates paramyxovirus replication at the level of viral entry and subcellular protein localization. Thapsigargin (SERCA inhibitor) significantly reduced NDV and PPRV replication. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of thapsigargin. Virus infection induced SERCA2 expression in Vero cells. Immunofluorescence showed defective cytoplasmic localization in ~70% of treated cells versus 10-30% in controls. Co-immunoprecipitation failed to detect direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins. Perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins was not observed in immunofluorescence. SERCA represents a novel candidate drug target for paramyxovirus antivirals. Host-targeting strategies face higher genetic barriers but may allow for incomplete resistance.
NDV can acquire partial resistance to a host-targeting agent (thapsigargin) through prolonged passage, a rare phenomenon among known viruses. NDV resistance appeared at ~P25 and became significant at P35. Fold inhibition dropped from ~10,000 at P0 to ~100 at P35. Re-evaluation at standardized MOI confirmed significantly lower sensitivity in P70-thapsigargin versus controls. Complete resistance was not achieved at 70 passages. PPRV did not acquire resistance at passage level 70, showing differential susceptibility. Control-passaged viruses showed no significant resistance, indicating the phenomenon is specific to thapsigargin selection. The general belief that viruses do not acquire resistance against host-targeting agents is challenged. The mechanism of escape (host factor change or enhanced affinity) requires further study.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Cytotoxicity was checked across a concentration range (0.00064–2 µM) to ensure the 0.5 µM concentration was non-toxic. Virucidal assays with ten-fold dilutions confirmed the antiviral effect was cell-mediated, not direct virucidal action. Selection was repeated with standardized MOI=0.1 and 24 h harvest to confirm that resistance observed at P70 was not an artifact of differing assay conditions. PPRV did not acquire resistance, serving as an internal negative control for the resistance selection experiments. Control-passaged viruses showed no resistance, confirming the resistance in NDV was selection-specific. Housekeeping gene (GAPDH) levels were used as a control in Western blot to confirm SERCA2 induction was virus-specific.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a and 1b show thapsigargin cytotoxicity (0.00064–2 µM vs. >2 µM) in Vero/MDBK cells via MTT assay. Figure 1c-e show thapsigargin inhibition of NDV, PPRV, and BHV-1; Figure 1f shows no effect on BPXV. Figure 1g shows no virucidal effect of thapsigargin on any virus tested. Figure 2a and 2b show SERCA2 overexpression in HeLa/goat cells facilitating NDV/PPRV replication and rescuing thapsigargin inhibition. Figure 3a shows time-course of SERCA2 induction by PPRV; Figure 3b shows inhibition of this induction by thapsigargin. Figure 4a (NDV) and 4b (PPRV) show time-of-addition growth curves with progressive inhibition loss. Figure 5a and 5b show reduced NDV and PPRV titers in entry assays with preattached virus. Figure 6a and 6b show immunofluorescence of viral protein localization; Figure 6c and 6d quantify defective cytoplasmic foci. Figure 7a shows sequential passage and resistance development of NDV under thapsigargin. Figure 7b shows standardized re-evaluation of P70 thapsigargin-passaged vs control NDV. Figure 7c shows PPRV sensitivity at passage 70 and control NDV sensitivity.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration that SERCA regulates paramyxovirus replication (NDV, PPRV) at viral entry and protein localization, identifying SERCA as a viable host-targeting antiviral candidate. 2. The strongest evidence is the rescue of thapsigargin inhibition by SERCA2 overexpression combined with virus-induced SERCA2 upregulation, and the identification of specific entry/localization defects. 3. The future path involves characterizing the molecular mechanism of NDV partial resistance to thapsigargin, identifying mutated viral proteins, and exploring SERCA/virus direct interactions through refined co-IP protocols.

summary.title: MicroRNA-196a is regulated by ER and is a prognostic biomarker in ER+ Breast Cancer
summary.authors: Michael J G Milevskiy, Udai Gujral, Carolina Del Lama Marques, Andrew Stone, Korinne Northwood, Lez J Burke, Julia M W Gee, Kenneth Nephew, Susan Clark, Melissa A Brown, Mjg Milevskiy
summary.field_subfield: Oncology / Epigenetics and MicroRNA Regulation in Breast Cancer
summary.executive_summary: This study characterizes the transcriptional regulation and clinical significance of MicroRNA-196a (MIR196A) in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic loci (HOXC/MIR196A2 and HOXB/MIR196A1) and has been implicated as an oncogene in breast, lung, and cell cycle regulation through targeting of ANXA1, HOXA5, and p27/Kip1. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A2 expression is transcriptionally regulated by estrogen (E2) in MCF7 breast cancer cells, as evidenced by GRO-Seq showing a dramatic increase in nascent RNA production peaking at 40 minutes post-E2 treatment. ChIP-Seq confirms that RNA Polymerase II binding at the HOXC10/MIR196A2 locus is E2-dependent and repressed by tamoxifen or fulvestrant. The transcriptional machinery involves long-range regulation mediated by two distal enhancer elements (a previously identified HOTAIR enhancer HDE and a novel MIR196A2-enhancer mE) that physically interact with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region, as validated by ChIA-PET and 3C-qPCR. The estrogen receptor α (ERα) and its pioneer factor FOXA1 bind two putative promoter regions (PP1, PP2, PP3), with PP1 (HOXC10 promoter) being the most active. Luciferase reporter assays confirm that PP1, PP2, and both enhancers augment transcription, with HDE being the most potent. Clinical analysis of the METABRIC cohort reveals MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumors, correlates with tumor stage, and serves as a prognostic biomarker: high expression is associated with poor survival in advanced ER+ disease but better survival in premenopausal women and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). The study positions MIR196A as a novel stratification biomarker for therapeutically resistant ER+ breast cancer.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study characterizes the transcriptional regulation and clinical significance of MicroRNA-196a (MIR196A) in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic loci (HOXC/MIR196A2 and HOXB/MIR196A1) and has been implicated as an oncogene in breast, lung, and cell cycle regulation through targeting of ANXA1, HOXA5, and p27/Kip1. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A2 expression is transcriptionally regulated by estrogen (E2) in MCF7 breast cancer cells, as evidenced by GRO-Seq showing a dramatic increase in nascent RNA production peaking at 40 minutes post-E2 treatment. ChIP-Seq confirms that RNA Polymerase II binding at the HOXC10/MIR196A2 locus is E2-dependent and repressed by tamoxifen or fulvestrant. The transcriptional machinery involves long-range regulation mediated by two distal enhancer elements (a previously identified HOTAIR enhancer HDE and a novel MIR196A2-enhancer mE) that physically interact with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region, as validated by ChIA-PET and 3C-qPCR. The estrogen receptor α (ERα) and its pioneer factor FOXA1 bind two putative promoter regions (PP1, PP2, PP3), with PP1 (HOXC10 promoter) being the most active. Luciferase reporter assays confirm that PP1, PP2, and both enhancers augment transcription, with HDE being the most potent. Clinical analysis of the METABRIC cohort reveals MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumors, correlates with tumor stage, and serves as a prognostic biomarker: high expression is associated with poor survival in advanced ER+ disease but better survival in premenopausal women and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Crucially, MIR196A expression increases in tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) MCF7 cells but is depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells, matching changes in DNA methylation at the promoter region. The study positions MIR196A as a novel stratification biomarker for therapeutically resistant ER+ breast cancer.

Research Context
MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression in diverse disease contexts. Research has identified clinically useful genetic and epigenetic biomarkers and novel therapeutic agents based on antagomiR technology. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic locations, the HOXC (MIR196A2) and HOXB (MIR196A1) loci, and is implicated in various cancers primarily as an oncogene. MIR196A has been shown to target Annexin-1 (ANXA1), HOXA5, and p27/Kip1, influencing apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth, and cell cycle progression. Despite its clinical importance, the transcriptional regulation of miR-196a remains poorly understood. Several instances of miRNA regulation by enhancers have been described, but this area is in its infancy. Prior work showed HOXC protein-coding and non-coding genes have associations with breast cancer progression, but the mechanism of MIR196A regulation was not defined.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors aimed to characterize the expression landscape of MIR196A, including factors regulating its expression and potential roles of regulatory elements in breast cancer prognostication. Based on prior evidence of oestrogen regulation of HOXC genes, the authors hypothesized that MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by oestrogen and its receptor ER. The authors hypothesized that MIR196A2 is controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation mediated by ERα tethered gene looping. The central research questions addressed whether (1) MIR196A expression correlates with HOXC genes in breast cancer, (2) oestrogen regulates MIR196A2, (3) distal enhancers contribute to its transcription, and (4) MIR196A serves as a prognostic biomarker in advanced ER+ disease. The predicted outcome was that MIR196A expression would show dynamic patterns associated with hormone receptors, PAM50 subtypes, and therapeutic resistance.

Methodological Details
The study used MCF7 breast cancer cells from AstraZeneca for the development of endocrine resistance sub-lines. Four cell lines were used: MCF7 (wild-type), Tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR), Fulvestrant-resistant (FASR), and oestrogen-deprived (MCF7x), all cultured for less than 6 months after STR profiling. Publicly available datasets were accessed including GSE14664 (MCF7 ChIP-Seq), GSE27463 (GRO-Seq), GSE39495 (ChIA-PET), and GSE32222 (Breast tumour ERα ChIP-Seq). MCF7 histone ChIP-Seq and breast cell 450K array data were sourced from ENCODE. METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from EGAS00000083 for breast tumour RNA-Seq analysis. RNA-Seq data for paclitaxel and adromycin resistance in MCF7-derived cells was sourced from GSE68815. HOX gene expression data in human breast cells were sourced from Gascard et al. DNA methylation of breast tumours was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and correlated to MIR196A expression. For survival analysis, multivariate and univariate Cox proportional hazard regression, Kaplan-Meier survival curves, and ROC-based cutoff determination were performed using MedCalc (version 12.7) and GraphPad Prism. Clustering was performed using the Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV) with Manhattan average-linkage based hierarchical clustering. RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent, chloroform extracted, isopropanol precipitated, and DNaseI treated. miRNA analysis used miScript RT II and miScript SYBR Green kits. All qRT-PCRs were performed on a Corbet Rotorgene-6000, with miRNA expression normalized to snoRNA RNU6b. For 3C, cells were grown to 60-80% confluence, fixed with 1% formaldehyde, and libraries were generated using HindIII with GAPDH primers designed between 100-250 bp of cut sites. For luciferase assays, 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs, 20 ng of pRL-TK control, and 0.5μL Lipofectamine 3000 were transfected into MCF7 cells.

Procedures And Architectures
GRO-Seq was employed to measure nascent RNA and assess transcriptional changes in the MIR196A2 genomic region following oestradiol (E2) addition. ChIP-Seq for RNA polymerase II demonstrated E2-dependent polymerase binding in the HOXC10 and MIR196A region in MCF7 cells, repressed by tamoxifen or fulvestrant. qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq validated the GRO-Seq finding of increased RNA production at the HOXC locus after E2 treatment. Putative promoter elements (PP1, PP2, PP3) were identified via histone methylation patterns and ERα/FOXA1 binding in MCF7 cells. ChIA-PET identified two major interaction sites with MIR196A2 promoters: a known HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel MIR196A2-Enhancer (mE). 3C-qPCR demonstrated that both HDE and mE physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. Luciferase reporter assays used pGL3-Basic with promoters/enhancers cloned into the BamHI/SalI or multiple cloning site, transfected into MCF7 cells. ERα ChIP-Seq was performed in human patient samples with ER+ disease, containing responders, non-responders, and metastases. DNA methylation analysis was performed on MCF10A, MCF7, HMEC, TAMR, and FASR cells to assess promoter methylation status. ChIP-Seq data were mapped with Bowtie, peaks called by MACS, and viewed in IGV.

Key Results
MIR196A expression highly correlates with HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10, in breast tumours. In normal breast cells, the association is more limited, observed most strongly with HOXC11 and HOXC10, and MIR196A is mostly expressed in basal stem-cell derived cells. GRO-Seq analysis showed a dramatic increase in RNA production peaking at 40 minutes following addition of oestradiol in the MIR196A2 region. ChIP-Seq confirmed RNA polymerase II binding in the HOXC10 and MIR196A region is E2-dependent and repressed by tamoxifen or fulvestrant. ERα and FOXA1 bind two putative promoter regions (PP1 and PP3) upstream of the miR196A2 transcription start site. PP1 (HOXC10 promoter) yielded the most active luciferase transcription in MCF7 cells, with PP2 contributing modestly. HDE appeared to be the most active enhancer in MCF7 cells, with both HDE and mE significantly augmenting transcription of PP1 and PP2. The CpG island immediately upstream of MIR196A2 is mostly methylated in MCF10A and MCF7 cells, but unmethylated in HMEC. Four distinct clusters of MIR196A expression were identified, with clusters 1 and 3 correlating with HRs and HR cofactors, while clusters 2 and 4 correlate negatively with ERα, PGR, FOXA1, GATA3 and positively with EGFR, HER2. MIR196A is strongly expressed in the HER2 subtype, while expression is very dynamic in luminal A and B subtypes. In the METABRIC cohort, MIR196A is significantly overexpressed in breast tumours compared to normal tissue and overexpression is associated with increased tumour stage. In ER+ tumours, women with low MIR196A had >95% survival at 10 years, while most in the high expression group died within 17 years (61% at 10 years). In premenopausal women, high MIR196A is associated with a good outcome in ER+ disease, whereas in post-menopausal women, high expression is associated with a poor outcome. MIR196A expression is significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells (TAMR) but almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells. MIR196A expression is also increased in resistant cell lines after paclitaxel and adromycin treatment compared to treatment-sensitive cells. ERα ChIP-Seq in patient samples revealed increased ERα occupancy at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dual-locus transcription of MIR196A contributes to the complexity of its expression pattern, with each locus contributing differently. The CpG island within the HOXC10/MIR196A2 region is completely methylated in oestrogen-deprived and fulvestrant-treated cells, suggesting DNA methylation as a repressive modification that may impair expression in cancer. Binding of ERα accompanied by cofactors may be needed to maintain low methylation levels and active transcription in breast cancer. The strong correlation between all HOXC genes and MIR196A in tumours, contrasting with normal tissues, suggests a consorted effort of multiple enhancers possibly driven by extensive ERα binding. High MIR196A expression in poor responders suggests the pathway to resistance in ER+ tumours may involve de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements. HOX genes are essential in embryonic development and would be a valuable asset for a tumour cell to sustain a stem-cell-like state, explaining their relevance to cancer progression. The shift in breast cancer incidence and subtype after menopause suggests changes in gene regulation through menopause that impact development of certain subtypes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The in vitro luciferase reporter assay (PP3 not able to increase transcription) contrasts with the GRO-Seq finding of binding at PP3 by ERα, suggesting binding may be important for activity in the native genomic context. The association between MIR196A and HOXC genes is limited in normal breast cells (most strongly HOXC11/HOXC10), in contrast to the strong correlation in tumours. MIR196A expression is decreased in fulvestrant-resistant cells, contrasting with the increase in tamoxifen-resistant cells, indicating subtype-specific resistance mechanisms. The study does not report a random seed for computational analyses, nor does it specify train/test splits for machine learning models. Patient cohort demographics (age, race, precise stage) beyond the general 'ER+' and 'non-responder' categories are not fully reported in the methods section. The study does not report the exact sample size for the ERα ChIP-Seq patient cohort. The paper is a preprint (bioRxiv) and has not completed peer review at the time of writing.

Claims
MIR196A is transcriptionally regulated by estrogen through ERα binding at distal enhancer elements in ER+ breast cancer cells. GRO-Seq showed a dramatic increase in RNA production at MIR196A2 peaking 40 minutes post-E2. ChIP-Seq confirmed RNA polymerase II binding is E2-dependent and repressed by anti-oestrogens. ChIA-PET and 3C-qPCR validated physical interaction between HDE and mE with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region. ERα and FOXA1 bind PP1 and PP3 upstream of the MIR196A2 transcription start site. PP3 did not increase luciferase transcription in reporter assays, despite ERα binding being demonstrated. MIR196A2 (HOXC locus) but not MIR196A1 (HOXB locus) showed the E2-responsive transcript increase. Therapeutic targeting of the enhancer-promoter interaction or ERα binding at MIR196A may represent a novel anti-cancer strategy. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of MIR196A regulation provides insight into how oncogenic miRNAs are activated in breast cancer.
MIR196A expression is a robust prognostic biomarker for advanced ER+ breast cancer progression and is associated with therapeutic resistance. Low MIR196A expression in ER+ tumours showed >95% 10-year survival versus 61% for high expression. MIR196A expression increased in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells. ERα occupancy increased at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastases. MIR196A expression increased in chemotherapy-resistant MCF7 cells. High MIR196A expression is associated with better survival in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). High MIR196A is associated with good outcome in premenopausal ER+ women, contradicting the post-menopausal finding. MIR196A could be used as a stratification biomarker for ER+ breast cancer management, particularly to identify high-risk patients. The biomarker's predictive value shifts with menopausal status, necessitating context-specific clinical application.

Data And Code Availability
The paper was published as a bioRxiv preprint and was made available under the CC-BY 4.0 International license. Accession codes for public datasets are provided: GSE14664 (MCF7 ChIP-Seq), GSE27463 (GRO-Seq), GSE39495 (ChIA-PET), GSE32222 (Breast tumour ERα ChIP-Seq), and EGAS00000083 (METABRIC). DNA methylation data of breast tumours were sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors tested three putative promoter regions (PP1, PP2, PP3) and two enhancers (HDE, mE) in luciferase assays to compare relative transcriptional activity. Three cell lines (MCF7, TAMR, FASR) were used to test the resistance phenotype, showing opposite effects on MIR196A expression. GRO-Seq was complemented by qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq to validate the nascent transcript findings. ChIA-PET and 3C-qPCR were used in tandem to provide independent confirmation of chromatin interaction. DNA methylation was assessed across four different cell states (MCF10A, MCF7, HMEC, resistant lines) to establish a consistent repressive pattern. Survival analysis used both univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression with ROC-derived cutoffs to ensure robust stratification.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows ChIP-Seq for RNA polymerase II demonstrating E2-dependent binding at the HOXC10/MIR196A region and DNA methylation status across cell lines. Figure 1B shows GRO-Seq nascent RNA production peaking at 40 minutes post-E2 in the MIR196A2 region. Figures 1C and 1D show qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq validation of E2-induced HOXC locus transcription. Figure 1E shows luciferase reporter assays for promoters PP1, PP2, PP3. Figure 2A shows ChIA-PET identifying two major MIR196A2 interaction sites: HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and MIR196A2-enhancer (mE). Figure 2B shows 3C-qPCR confirming physical interaction of both enhancers with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region. Figure 2C shows luciferase reporter assays with enhancer fragments augmenting transcription. Figure 3A shows four distinct clusters of MIR196A expression in breast tumours. Figure 3B shows correlation of MIR196A clusters with hormone receptors and cofactors. Figure 3C shows MIR196A expression by PAM50 intrinsic subtypes. Figure 4A and 4B show METABRIC data on MIR196A overexpression and tumour stage association. Figure 4C and 4D show survival by MIR196A expression stratified by ER+ and TNBC. Figure 5A shows Kaplan-Meier survival curves for ER+ tumours stratified by MIR196A expression. Figure 5B shows MIR196A expression in TAMR versus FASR MCF7 cells. Figure 5C shows DNA methylation changes in the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters in resistant cells. Figure 5D shows MIR196A expression in chemotherapy-resistant MCF7 cell lines. Figure 5E shows ERα ChIP-Seq occupancy at MIR196A in patient samples (responders, non-responders, metastases).

Three Takeaways
1. MIR196A2 transcription is directly regulated by oestrogen through ERα/FOXA1 binding and long-range enhancer-promoter interactions, with the HOXC10 promoter and the HOTAIR enhancer serving as primary regulatory elements. 2. MIR196A is a clinically relevant prognostic biomarker in ER+ breast cancer: high expression predicts 10-year survival of 39% versus 95% in low-expression patients, and its upregulation in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells suggests a role in therapeutic escape. 3. Future research should determine the functional requirement of increased MIR196A for therapeutic resistance, investigate the role of the second locus (MIR196A1), and characterize the enhancer-driven mechanism in native patient chromatin using 5C or NG Capture-C.

summary.title: Lack of negative density-dependence regulation in a dominant oak tree from a neotropical highland forest
summary.authors: Irene Calderón-Sanou, Luis Diego Ríos, Alfredo Cascante-Marín, Gilbert Barrantes, Eric J Fuchs
summary.field_subfield: Ecology / Tropical Forest Population Dynamics
summary.type_of_paper: Empirical field study with spatial and GLMM analyses
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates whether conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD)—a mechanism proposed by Janzen (1970) and Connell (1971) whereby higher offspring mortality of abundant species reduces competition for other species—regulates the seedling survival and recruitment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. Despite the Janzen-Connell hypothesis predicting that high seedling density should reduce survival through intensified herbivory and pathogen pressure, the authors found no significant CNDD effect on seedling survival or recruitment for Q. costaricensis between 2014 and 2017. The study mapped 3538 seedlings across four 400-m² plots at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station, using spatial statistics and generalized linear mixed-effects models to test the effects of seedling density, distance to nearest adult, bamboo density, and herbivory. The primary findings include: (1) annual seedling survival was relatively high, decreasing slightly from 73.2% (2015) to 64.38% (2016) and 63.8% (2017); (2) herbivory was ubiquitous (over 99% of seedlings damaged) but decreased at higher seedling densities, contrary to Janzen-Connell predictions; (3) seedling recruitment significantly increased with conspecific seedling density; and (4) bamboo density and herbivory both significantly reduced survival. The authors hypothesize that the lack of CNDD may be explained by predator satiation at high seedling densities (2.4 seedlings/m²) and indirect facilitation by ectomycorrhizal transfer from adult trees, with a negative quadratic relationship between survival and distance to adults. The results suggest that the dominance of Q. costaricensis (representing over 90% of basal stem area) in Costa Rican highlands is maintained by a combination of adult facilitation and interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo rather than density-dependent regulation, supporting theories that common tropical tree species exhibit weaker CNDD.

claims.description: Q. costaricensis seedlings do not exhibit conspecific negative density-dependence in survival or recruitment.
Adult facilitation via ectomycorrhizal transfer explains the optimal survival distance from adults.
Herbivore satiation prevents CNDD from reducing seedling survival at high densities.
Chusquea bamboo density is a primary interspecific constraint on Q. costaricensis seedling survival.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates whether conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD)—a mechanism proposed by Janzen (1970) and Connell (1971) whereby higher offspring mortality of abundant species reduces competition for other species—regulates the seedling survival and recruitment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. Despite the Janzen-Connell hypothesis predicting that high seedling density should reduce survival through intensified herbivory and pathogen pressure, the authors found no significant CNDD effect on seedling survival or recruitment for Q. costaricensis between 2014 and 2017. The study mapped 3538 seedlings across four 400-m² plots at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station, using spatial statistics and generalized linear mixed-effects models to test the effects of seedling density, distance to nearest adult, bamboo density, and herbivory. The primary findings include: (1) annual seedling survival was relatively high, decreasing slightly from 73.2% (2015) to 64.38% (2016) and 63.8% (2017); (2) herbivory was ubiquitous (over 99% of seedlings damaged) but decreased at higher seedling densities, contrary to Janzen-Connell predictions; (3) seedling recruitment significantly increased with conspecific seedling density; and (4) bamboo density and herbivory both significantly reduced survival. The authors hypothesize that the lack of CNDD may be explained by predator satiation at high seedling densities (2.4 seedlings/m²) and indirect facilitation by ectomycorrhizal transfer from adult trees, with a negative quadratic relationship between survival and distance to adults. The results suggest that the dominance of Q. costaricensis (representing over 90% of basal stem area) in Costa Rican highlands is maintained by a combination of adult facilitation and interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo rather than density-dependent regulation, supporting theories that common tropical tree species exhibit weaker CNDD.

Research Context
CNDD is a primary mechanism proposed to regulate species coexistence in tropical forests, with higher offspring mortality of abundant species reducing competition for other species. Janzen (1970) and Connell (1971) independently proposed that CNDD leads to increased species diversity through density-dependent enemy pressure. While CNDD is thought to be ubiquitous in tropical forests, its susceptibility varies across species and common species are expected to be less affected. Tropical montane forests (above 2500 m a.s.l.) are commonly dominated by a few tree species, in Costa Rica and western Panamá, dominated by oaks. Q. costaricensis is restricted to the Talamanca mountain range, representing over 90% of basal stem area, yet its population dynamics are scarcely studied. Temperate oaks are shown to be susceptible to CNDD and distance to nearest adult, but ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults has a positive effect. The gap lies in whether the expected CNDD applies to a monodominant tropical oak species and what processes structure low-diversity montane forests.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CNDD regulates the annual survival probability and recruitment of Q. costaricensis seedlings in Talamanca highland forests. Specifically, the authors tested the effects of conspecific seedling density, distance to nearest adult, and herbivory on seedling recruitment and survival. Given the pronounced dominance of Q. costaricensis and its high seedling density, the authors expected to find weak (if any) CNDD regulation on seedling survival. A secondary hypothesis was that distance to nearest adult would have a positive effect on seedling recruitment due to ectomycorrhizal transfer. A third factor, bamboo density of Chusquea spp., was included as a potential interspecific limiting factor for seedling survival. The predicted mechanism for the expected lack of CNDD was high seedling density exceeding the capacity of herbivores to cause significant mortality. The predicted outcome of the Janzen-Connell hypothesis would be herbivory decreasing at lower densities and increasing at higher densities, reducing overall survival.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station (09°33' N, 83°44' W; 3100-3350 m a.s.l.) in a Costa Rican upper montane tropical forest. Four 400-m² plots (20 x 20 m) were established in old-growth forests undisturbed for at least 30 years. Plots were subdivided into 64 quadrats of 2.5 x 2.5 m each to facilitate seedling censuses. In February 2014, all Q. costaricensis seedlings (height < 2m) were mapped and tagged, totaling 2031 seedlings. For each seedling, height, distance to nearest conspecific adult, and conspecific seedling density in a 1m radius were measured. Leaf damage was estimated using the qualitative index of herbivory (IH) developed by Núñez-Farfán and Dirzo (1988). Bamboo stem density varied naturally among plots from 0 to 14 stems m⁻². For each quadrat, the number of bamboo stems was counted, and DBH of all adult trees within a 10 m buffer area was measured. The 2014 censuses were conducted before acorns fell to avoid including newly germinated seedlings. Re-censuses were conducted in May/June of 2015, 2016, and 2017 to determine annual mortality and recruitment. Germination success of Q. costaricensis was 91% after 7 days in controlled conditions. In 2014, the oak population produced fruits; in 2016, less than 15% of adults reproduced. In 2015, no acorns were produced; in 2017, only five new seedlings were recorded across all plots. 1578 new recruits were recorded in 2015 from the 2014 masting event.

Procedures And Architectures
Spatial distribution of 2014 seedlings was analyzed using the L(t) transformation of the univariate Ripley's K function for spatial aggregation. The R statistical language (Version 3.2.2) with the 'spatstat' library was used for all spatial analyses. Annual seedling survival was modeled using a generalized linear mixed-effects model with a binomial distribution (Bolker et al. 2009). All variables, including log-transformed seedling height, were standardized and entered as fixed effects. Quadrat and census year were included as random effects. A dummy variable (age) identified 2014 census seedlings versus 2015 recruits to test differential survival probabilities. A second-degree polynomial effect for distance to nearest adult conspecific was included in the survival model. A full model including all variables and all second-order interactions was built. To test Janzen-Connell predictions, the effect of seedling density and distance to adult on herbivory (IH) was analyzed. Seedling recruitment per quadrat was modeled using a GLMM with a quasi-Poisson distribution, including only 2015 data. Explanatory variables for recruitment included seedling density per quadrat, conspecific tree density in a 2.5 m radius, and Chusquea density. Plots were included as a random effect to account for spatial autocorrelation. The lme4 package in R was used for all GLMM statistical analyses.

Key Results
In the 2014 census, 2031 seedlings were mapped and tagged, confirming they were spatially aggregated at all scales (Figure S1). Over 99% of censused seedlings had some leaf damage, with most (ca. 71%) showing intermediate damage of 10-75% (Figure 1). Annual seedling survival decreased slightly from 73.2% in 2015 to 64.38% in 2016 and 63.8% in 2017. Seedling height had the strongest positive effect on survival, while bamboo density and herbivory (IH) both significantly reduced survival (Figure 2). The effect of distance to nearest adult was best described by a negative polynomial function, with survival highest at intermediate distances. No significant CNDD effect was found on annual seedling survival. A significant interaction existed between seedling and Chusquea densities: high seedling density increased survival at low bamboo densities (<2.4 stems m⁻²) and decreased it at higher bamboo densities (Figure S2). In 2015, 1578 new recruits were recorded with average herbivory of 22.9% ± 1.06 leaf damage. Herbivory on new recruits was significantly lower than on 2014 census seedlings (22.9% vs 43.75% leaf damage; t=25.798, df=2828.2, p<0.0001). Seedling recruitment significantly increased with conspecific seedling density. The number of new recruits failed to correlate with adult density or with Chusquea density. Herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities and increased away from adults, contrary to Janzen-Connell expectations (Table S2). No significant interactions were found between seedling density and herbivory, nor between herbivory and distance to nearest adult (Table S1). Only five new seedlings were recorded on all four plots in 2017, so only recruitment after the 2014 masting was analyzed.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The absence of CNDD in Q. costaricensis aligns with observations in other masting species with dense seedling aggregations that escape negative effects. High seedling survival (>62% over three years) despite dense aggregation (2.4 seedlings m⁻²) suggests herbivore satiation as a potential mechanism. A positive effect of density on seedling survival after masting (73.2%) supports the herbivore satiation hypothesis. The negative quadratic relationship with distance to nearest adult suggests ectomycorrhizal (ECM) transfer from adults may facilitate survival at intermediate distances. The results support Fricke and Wright's (2017) argument that dominant tropical tree species are expected to have weaker CNDD. The findings suggest that the dominance of Q. costaricensis is maintained by adult facilitation (ECM) and interspecific competition with bamboo rather than CNDD. Shade tolerance and ECM associations may provide additional advantages that reduce CNDD susceptibility.

Contradictions And Limitations
Contrary to Janzen-Connell expectations, herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities rather than increasing. The number of new recruits failed to correlate with adult density or Chusquea density, contrary to expectations of adult facilitation or bamboo inhibition. Environmental factors such as soil acidity, low temperatures, and solar irradiance were acknowledged but not investigated. The 2016 fruiting was not a masting year, limiting recruitment analysis to a single masting event. In 2015, acorn production was absent, meaning no new recruits were tallied in 2016, leaving a gap in the inter-annual record. Seedling leaves were not fully developed in ca. 1% or 15 seedlings, preventing herbivory index recording for these individuals.

Claims
Q. costaricensis seedlings do not exhibit conspecific negative density-dependence in survival or recruitment. No significant CNDD effect was detected in GLMM analyses of annual survival. Herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities, contradicting the mechanism of density-dependent herbivore attraction. The negative quadratic distance-to-adult relationship contradicts the monotonic decrease expected under CNDD alone. A significant seedling-bamboo density interaction showed that at low bamboo densities, high seedling density increased survival, suggesting a context-dependent effect. The lack of CNDD at the seedling stage likely underpins the monodominance of Q. costaricensis in Costa Rican highland forests. The findings support the hypothesis that common tropical tree species exhibit weaker CNDD than rare species.
Adult facilitation via ectomycorrhizal transfer explains the optimal survival distance from adults. Survival was highest at intermediate distances from adults and declined at both close and great distances. Ectomycorrhizal associations are known to increase nutrient acquisition in oak species. A balance between asymmetric competition and ECM transfer from adults increases survival at intermediate adult densities. The number of new recruits failed to correlate with adult density, meaning the spatial pattern of recruitment does not match the survival pattern. ECM facilitation may override CNDD effects, creating a facilitation zone around adults.
Herbivore satiation prevents CNDD from reducing seedling survival at high densities. Herbivory was ubiquitous (>99%) but decreased at higher seedling densities. Survival was higher after masting when seedling number increased (73.2% vs 63.8%). Abundant species tend to have low levels of foliar damage that do not contribute to CNDD regulation. Most seedlings still showed intermediate herbivory (10-75%), indicating significant predation persists even if density-independent. Herbivore satiation may act as a demographic threshold beyond which CNDD effects saturate.
Chusquea bamboo density is a primary interspecific constraint on Q. costaricensis seedling survival. Bamboo density significantly reduced seedling survival in the GLMM. Bamboo stems formed dense clumps that dominate the herbaceous layer and reduce space for tree establishment. Bamboo could interfere through resource competition, allelopathy, and physical interference. The number of new recruits did not correlate with Chusquea density, indicating bamboo affects survival but not establishment. Interspecific competition with bamboo, rather than CNDD, is a key process structuring oak population density.

Data And Code Availability
The paper was posted as a preprint on bioRxiv (https://doi.org/10.1101/329177) with the R Core Team 2016, R version 3.2.2, and the spatstat library used for spatial analyses. No explicit data repository or code sharing statement is reported in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A second-degree polynomial for distance to nearest adult was tested in the survival model. A full model including all variables and all second-order interactions was built for the survival GLMM. A dummy variable (age) was included to compare 2014 census seedlings with 2015 recruits. The recruitment analysis (quasi-Poisson) was restricted to one year (2015) after the masting event. Plots were included as a random effect in the recruitment GLMM to account for spatial autocorrelation. Models were retained only if they included all variables of interest, significant interactions, and significant polynomial terms.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the index of herbivory on seedlings, with over 99% damaged and most (ca. 71%) showing intermediate damage. Figure 2 displays the GLMM results for survival, showing seedling height as the strongest positive predictor, bamboo and herbivory as negative predictors, and a negative quadratic distance-to-adult effect. Figure S1 shows the spatial distribution of 2031 seedlings confirming they were spatially aggregated at all scales. Table S1 summarizes the retained models including significant interactions and polynomial terms. Table S2 presents herbivory rates by seedling density and distance to adult, showing herbivory decreased with density. Figure S2 shows the seedling-Chusquea density interaction. Table S1 reports that seedling recruitment significantly increased with conspecific seedling density but failed to correlate with adult density or Chusquea density.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first empirical test of CNDD in a monodominant tropical highland oak, finding no CNDD effect on survival or recruitment despite extreme spatial aggregation. 2. The strongest evidence is the GLMM result showing herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities (Table S2), directly contradicting Janzen-Connell predictions and supporting herbivore satiation. 3. The future path should investigate whether environmental filters (soil acidity, temperature) moderate CNDD strength, and whether other masting tropical trees show similar patterns.

summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.field_subfield: Ecotoxicology / Nanomaterial Toxicology
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental research article reporting acute toxicity assays on Artemia species
summary.executive_summary: This study evaluates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3) on the hatching and early nauplii development of Artemia sp., a non-selective filter-feeding organism. The authors employed a dual-assay approach: (1) a hatching rate assay measuring viable nauplii versus total hatchlings after 24 hours of exposure to 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L nanoparticle concentrations, and (2) a standard Artemia toxicity test (ARC protocol) measuring larval mortality over 48 hours at five concentrations (0.01 to 100 mg/L). Nanoparticles were characterized via TEM and DLS in both Milli Q and salt water (25% NaCl). Key findings include: silver nanoparticles exerted the highest toxicity, reducing hatching to ~29% (50% viability at 100 mg/L) and yielding an LC50 of 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours; copper oxide showed the next highest toxicity; silicon nanoparticles at 10 mg/L produced hatching and viability equivalent to controls. A strong inverse correlation (coefficient -0.7853) was observed between hatching inhibition and nauplii mortality, with no statistically significant difference between hatching-derived viability and ARC-derived viability (P=0.683). Oxidative stress was detected via DCFDA staining, most pronounced with silver nanoparticles, while nanoparticle accumulation in the gut was observed for most treatments. The study establishes the order of toxicity as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2, and demonstrates that Artemia hatching as an endpoint provides a simple, low-cost pre-screening bioassay for nanomaterial hazard identification.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study evaluates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3) on the hatching and early nauplii development of Artemia sp., a non-selective filter-feeding organism. The authors employed a dual-assay approach: (1) a hatching rate assay measuring viable nauplii versus total hatchlings after 24 hours of exposure to 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L nanoparticle concentrations, and (2) a standard Artemia toxicity test (ARC protocol) measuring larval mortality over 48 hours at five concentrations (0.01 to 100 mg/L). Nanoparticles were characterized via TEM and DLS in both Milli Q and salt water (25% NaCl). Key findings include: silver nanoparticles exerted the highest toxicity, reducing hatching to ~29% (50% viability at 100 mg/L) and yielding an LC50 of 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours; copper oxide showed the next highest toxicity; silicon nanoparticles at 10 mg/L produced hatching and viability equivalent to controls. A strong inverse correlation (coefficient -0.7853) was observed between hatching inhibition and nauplii mortality, with no statistically significant difference between hatching-derived viability and ARC-derived viability (P=0.683). Oxidative stress was detected via DCFDA staining, most pronounced with silver nanoparticles, while nanoparticle accumulation in the gut was observed for most treatments. The study establishes the order of toxicity as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2, and demonstrates that Artemia hatching as an endpoint provides a simple, low-cost pre-screening bioassay for nanomaterial hazard identification.

Research Context
Nanomaterials with their ever expanding diversity and unique physicochemical properties pose unknown risks to the environment and human health. The release into the environment occurs during production, application, weathering, and waste disposal, with aquatic systems as inevitable receptacles. Existing hazard identification methodologies are primarily adapted from general chemical testing and may not fully capture the unique behavior of nanoforms. Few studies have applied Artemia sp. to nanomaterial toxicity, and hatching rate has rarely been used as an endpoint except in a single prior study. The dearth of information on bioavailability, biopersistence, and behavior in varying pH and salinity conditions limits risk assessment.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether nanoparticle exposure at concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L significantly alters the hatching rate and early viability of Artemia cysts. A second research question asks whether nanoparticles at five concentrations (0.01 to 100 mg/L) induce time- and concentration-dependent mortality in hatched nauplii over 48 hours. The authors hypothesize that hatching of hydrated cysts can serve as a sensitive bioassay for nanoparticle toxicity, complementary to standard larval mortality tests. The prediction was that the two tests would show a good inverse correlation, implying hatching rate sensitivity matches larval mortality sensitivity. The authors further posited that nanoparticles, being different from bulk materials, might exhibit specific toxic mechanisms such as gut clogging or oxidative stress in Artemia.

Methodological Details
Six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3) were tested on Artemia sp. All nanoparticles were obtained from the NANOVALID consortium: silicon from Nanologica AB, silver from Colorobbia, gold from INMETRO, copper oxide from Intrinsiq Materials, and zinc oxide from Nanogate. Titanium dioxide particles were synthesized in-house using a specific protocol, while a suspension of eNPs was made at 2 mg/mL and sonicated at ~30 W with 50% pulse for 10 minutes. Silver was prepared as a 4% suspension with PVP stabilizing agent, and gold at 0.006% in water; working dilutions were made in NaCl salt water. Nanoparticle characterization used TEM (JEOL 2010, 100 kV, 20 µm aperture) on 50 µg/mL suspensions on formvar-coated copper grids and DLS (Horiba Nanopartica SZ100) on 25 µg/mL suspensions. DLS suspensions were analyzed thrice for three days in both Milli Q water and salt water, data represented as mean + SEM. Artemia cysts (San Francisco Bay strain) were used at 1.0 g per 1 litre culture, hydrated in distilled water for 45 minutes, bleached with 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes, and washed six times. Eggs were allowed to hatch in 25% salt water (pH 8.0) at 28°C under continuous light and aeration for 24 hours. Nanoparticles were added to the hatching culture at concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L. In the toxicity test, 10 nauplii were transferred to six-well plates and exposed to nanoparticles at 100 mg/L, 10 mg/L, 1 mg/L, 0.1 mg/L, and 0.01 mg/L. Viability was counted at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours; mortality was recorded as cessation of swimming or any movement. Hatching rate was expressed as percent of fully hatched Artemia in the aliquot, with immature stages classified as umbrella stage or unhatched cyst. The hatching experiment was repeated six times; the toxicity test was validated by a mortality criterion of below 10% in the 24-hour period. Oxidative stress was assessed by treating nauplii with 10 µM DCFDA and imaging in a Zeiss Axiovert imager. The hatching cultures were kept in filtered sterile salt water with continuous aeration to maintain nanoparticle suspension.

Procedures And Architectures
TEM imaging used 10 images per grid captured with a GATAN camera and analyzed with GATAN software for particle size measurement. In the hatching assay, three aliquots of 100 µL were taken from each flask after thorough mixing and counted under a stereo microscope. For the oxidative stress test, nauplii exposed to DCFDA were imaged to detect fluorescence from ROS-reacted chemiluminescent probes. LD50 was calculated for each particle using Graphpad quickcalcs software. In the larval toxicity test, the ARC protocol was followed: larvae were not fed, and viability was recorded every 6 hours for the first 24 hours. The salt water pH was monitored and was maintained around 6.3–6.5 up to 48 hours after nanoparticle addition. To rule out ionic effects, the nanoparticle suspension was centrifuged and resuspended in brine; these particles remained as NPs after 72 hours in high salinity. The correlation analysis used online software for the correlation coefficient and Microsoft Excel for data comparison. Statistical validation was performed using Graphpad software with a paired T-test to compare viability means.

Key Results
Normal Artemia showed a hatching rate of 74% ± 5.5% and a viability of approximately 97%. Silver nanoparticles at 100 mg/L reduced hatching to ~29%, with only 50% of those hatched being motile and viable. Silver nanoparticles at 10 mg/L resulted in a lower hatching rate but 85% viability of hatched nauplii. Copper oxide at 100 mg/L showed a hatching rate with viability around 64%. Silver nitrate (ionic silver) showed a hatching rate of 33%, while the combination with PVP gave 41%. Gold, silicon, titanium, copper, and zinc oxide nanoparticles at 100 mg/L produced hatching rates around 50–60% with low post-hatching mortality. Zinc oxide at 100 mg/L gave 60% hatching, but cysts showed a tendency to clump together. Titanium dioxide at 100 mg/L gave a hatching rate of 41.50% with 67.8% viability; at 10 mg/L, hatching was 54% with ~90% viability. Silicon dioxide at 10 mg/L showed hatching and viability equivalent to controls. In the LC50 test, silver in ionic form (silver nitrate) killed 80% of nauplii in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was approximately 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. Other nanoparticles were nontoxic initially but many Artemia perished after 30 hours in a concentration-dependent manner. A strong inverse correlation coefficient of -0.7853 was found between hatching inhibition and LC50. A paired T-test comparing hatching-derived viability to ARC-derived viability showed no statistically significant difference (P=0.683). TEM showed nanoparticles had reduced size in high salt concentration, with CuO and ZnO showing visible flocculation and sedimentation. DLS measurements for CuO and ZnO gave very high values corroborating the flocculent observed.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The strong inverse correlation between hatching and mortality supports the development of hatching rate as a secondary bioassay for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The order of toxicity Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2 suggests that metal-containing NPs, particularly silver, exert the greatest acute stress on Artemia development. The high toxicity of CuO and Ag NPs despite ionic precipitation in high salinity suggests that nanoparticles themselves, rather than just released ions, contribute to toxicity. Particle accumulation in the gut (Figure 5) supports the mechanism of NP-induced gut clogging as a likely mode of mortality for most treatments. DCFDA staining confirmed that while gut clogging caused mortality in most, silver NPs specifically triggered ROS and superoxide stress in affected nauplii. The absence of gross morphological abnormalities in nauplii exposed to the most toxic NPs indicates the damage is physiological or molecular rather than structural. Artemia's ability to tolerate extreme conditions makes it a robust model organism for nanoparticle ecotoxicity studies in aquatic environments.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report a random seed for nanoparticle characterization measurements, which is important for reproducibility. The specific age and size of the Artemia cysts at the start of the hatching test are not stated, which could affect baseline hatching rates. Only two concentrations (100 and 10 mg/L) were used for the hatching test, limiting the ability to establish a formal dose-response curve for that endpoint. The paper notes that silver nitrate showed higher hatching inhibition than silver NPs; this apparent contradiction is addressed by centrifuging/resuspension to confirm NP-mediated effects. The authors observe that silicon NPs at 10 mg/L were conducive to better hatching than controls, yet this is not accompanied by a statistical comparison or p-value. The study reports no changes in morphology of nauplii, yet many died/became immotile, creating a discrepancy between observed phenotype and lack of structural abnormality. The paper does not specify the exact temperature control method (e.g., water bath vs. incubator) beyond stating 28°C was maintained.

Claims
The hatching rate of Artemia cysts serves as a viable and sensitive bioassay endpoint for acute nanomaterial toxicity, correlating strongly with larval mortality. The correlation test yielded a coefficient of -0.7853, indicating a strong inverse relationship between hatching inhibition and LC50 values. The paired T-test showed no statistically significant difference (P=0.683) between viability derived from hatching and viability from the ARC test. The authors state that both tests show good inverse correlation in sensitivity to nanoparticles. Silicon nanoparticles at 10 mg/L showed hatching and viability equivalent to controls, suggesting the assay may lack sensitivity for some NP types at certain concentrations. The hatching test used only two concentrations, which is insufficient to fully characterize a dose-response relationship. The assay could be adopted for high-throughput nanoparticle hazard identification prior to in vivo toxicity studies. The use of cysts eliminates the need for laboratory maintenance of test species, saving space and time.
Silver nanoparticles and silver oxide exert the greatest acute toxicity among the tested engineered nanoparticles on Artemia development. Silver NPs reduced hatching to ~29% and LC50 was 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. Silver in ionic form killed 80% of nauplii in 24 hours. The toxicity order was estimated as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. DCFDA staining showed highest ROS and superoxide in silver-exposed nauplii. Silver nitrate (ionic) showed 33% hatching, while silver with PVP (capping agent) showed 41%, suggesting the nanoparticle form is slightly less toxic than the pure ion. Silver-containing nanomaterials require special handling and regulatory consideration in aquatic releases.
Nanoparticle gut accumulation in Artemia nauplii is a primary mechanism of acute toxicity, with oxidative stress contributing specifically in silver treatments. Nauplii in salt water containing NPs showed accumulation of eNPs in the gut by end of 24 hours. Dead nauplii in silver treatment showed no gut accumulation, suggesting early mortality before ingestion or rapid processing. DCFDA staining showed ROS in still-trapped nauplii and gut of dead nauplii. DHE staining confirmed superoxide stress in silver and titania treatments. The authors note that the dead Artemia and partially hatched cysts show increased stress, but this is observed in 'few' still trapped nauplii, limiting generalizability. The mechanism of action for nanoparticle toxicity in filter feeders likely involves physical gut obstruction and associated stress, rather than systemic uptake.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The hatching experiment was repeated six times with average and SEM calculated for each sample to ensure reproducibility. The nanoparticle suspension was monitored for dispersion stability up to 48 hours in both Milli Q water and 25% NaCl solution. Control nanoparticles (solvents used to prepare particles) were measured for size determination to establish baseline. The validity criterion for the hatching test was low mortality in the control; for the toxicity test, mortality below 10% in 24 hours. Silver NPs were tested with and without PVP capping agent to assess the role of surface chemistry on toxicity. The NaCl concentration (25%) and pH (8.0) were held constant across all hatching treatments. The authors note that in the ARC test, sedimentation and flocculation of nanoparticles occurred by 48 hours, potentially confounding mortality interpretations.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents hatching rates, mortality, and viability for all six nanoparticles at 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L concentrations compared to control. Figure 1 shows TEM images of nanoparticles with no apparent change in aggregation or dispersion in salt water. Figure 2 displays DLS results in salt water showing reduced size, higher DLS values for Ag, TiO2, CuO, ZnO, and flocculation for CuO and ZnO. Figure 3 shows the hatching rate and viability for all nanoparticles, highlighting the sharp drop for Ag and CuO. Figure 4 presents the dose-response larval mortality curves for all nanoparticles and silver nitrate, and the DCFDA staining for ROS. Figure 5 shows in situ imaging of nanoparticle accumulation in Artemia guts and DCFDA/DHE staining for ROS/superoxide. Figure 6 displays the correlation between hatching rate and larval mortality for all nanoparticle treatments. Figure S1 shows nanoparticle dispersion stability over 48 hours in both Milli Q water and 25% NaCl solution. Figures S2.1-2.6 show micrographs of nauplii in the membrane, confirming no morphological changes. Figure S3 shows staining of hatched Artemia with DCFDA for signs of stress. Table 2 presents the LC50 values for all nanoparticles and silver nitrate, along with mortality at each time point.

Three Takeaways
1. The hatching rate of Artemia cysts is a quantitatively reliable surrogate for larval mortality in nanoparticle toxicity, with a correlation coefficient of -0.7853 and no significant difference in viability estimates (P=0.683). 2. Silver nanoparticles produce the most profound acute toxicity (hatching ~29%, LC50 ~10.12 mg/L) driven by both particle-specific effects and oxidative stress, whereas silicon nanoparticles at 10 mg/L show negligible effect. 3. The assay is simple, inexpensive, and eliminates laboratory maintenance, making it suitable for high-throughput nanoparticle hazard pre-screening prior to in vivo toxicity validation.
